en: Separate Translation of the Saṃyukta Āgama, Scroll One.
Translator’s name lost; now appended to the Qin Records.
1. First Recitation. First Recitation, Part One.
1. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Āmra Park in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the Venerable Sujāta, having recently gone forth and shaved off his hair and beard, approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This son of good family, Sujāta, possesses two kinds of excellence:
first, his countenance is magnificent and his natural appearance is exceptionally distinguished."

Second, they are able to shave off their hair and beard, don the Dharma robes upon their bodies, and with deep faith that the worldly way leads inevitably to impermanence, they leave the home life to study the Path. They exhaust all afflictions, become fully endowed with the untainted mind and attain liberation of mind and liberation through wisdom. They personally realize the unconditioned, bring an end forever to birth and death, establish the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and no longer undergo future existence.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, he uttered these verses:
“The bhikṣu who is constantly in tranquil concentration, Who has eliminated desire and departed from birth and death,
Dwelling in his final body, Is able to shatter the army of Māra.”
"Cultivating the mind to sever all fetters, one becomes upright and peerless.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. (II) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose complexion was haggard and who lacked majestic virtue; he approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence toward the bhikṣus, and sat to one side.
At that time, all the bhikṣus had this thought:
"For what reason does this bhikṣu now have such a haggard and withered countenance, devoid of majestic virtue?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bhikṣus, addressed them, saying:
"Bhikṣus, did you see that bhikṣu prostrate before me?"
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Indeed, we have seen it.”
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"You should not now conceive a lowly notion regarding him. Why is this?"
That bhikṣu has accomplished what was to be done, attained arhatship, laid down the heavy burden, exhausted all fetters of existence, and realized perfect liberation.
Now, you all should not give rise to thoughts of contempt toward him.
Only when you perceive and understand him as I do may you then proceed to evaluate him.
"If one falsely evaluates [others], one will only bring harm upon oneself.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Though the peacock adorns its body with color, It cannot soar as high as the wild goose."
Though one may possess a beautiful and dignified appearance, it does not equal the merit of one who has severed the outflows.
This bhikṣu is like a fine horse, able to skillfully subdue his own mind and conduct;
having severed desire and extinguished the fetters, he is liberated from birth and death, having received his final body and destroyed the army of Māra.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
3 (3) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, Devadatta attained the four dhyānas and thought to himself:
"Who is the most eminent in this kingdom of Magadha?
He then reflected further:
"Today Prince Ajātaśatru shall succeed to the royal throne; if I can now subdue him, I will be able to control the people of the entire kingdom."
At that time, having formed this thought, Devadatta went to where Ajātaśatru was; he manifested as a precious elephant, entering through the gate and exiting not through the gate.
He further manifested as a horse-treasure, also in this same manner.
He again manifested as a śramaṇa, entering through the gate and flying out through the air.
He further manifested as a young child, his body adorned with various precious necklaces, sitting upon the lap of Ajātaśatru.
At that time, Ajātaśatru took him up in his arms, kissed him, and spat into his mouth.
Because Devadatta was greedy for gain and offerings, he immediately swallowed the saliva.
Devadatta transformed from the form of a small child and returned to his original body.
At that time, having witnessed these events, Ajātaśatru conceived a wrong view, thinking that Devadatta’s supernormal powers and transformations surpassed those of the World-Honored One.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru conceived a deep sense of reverence and faith toward Devadatta, and he sent five hundred cartloads of food every day to provide for him.
Devadatta, together with his retinue of five hundred people, received these offerings as a group.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having put on their robes and taken up their alms bowls, entered the city to beg for food.
Having finished eating and drinking, they went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
Having arrived at the proper time, he entered the city to beg for alms and saw Devadatta gathering people from near and far, receiving great offerings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should not give rise to a heart of longing or envy toward Devadatta."
Why is this so? This Devadatta will surely be harmed by his pursuit of gain and offerings.
It is just as when a plantain tree dies upon bearing fruit, or as with reeds, bamboos, and rattan, or as when a mule dies upon becoming pregnant; it is exactly like this.
Devadatta obtained gain and offerings no differently than he did before;
Devadatta was foolish and lacked wisdom, failing to understand the principles of the Dharma, and thus suffered for a long night.

Therefore, you all, upon seeing how Devadatta was brought to ruin by his pursuit of gain and offerings, should abandon all greedy seeking; you must examine this with careful scrutiny and understand it thus: do not crave gain and offerings.
He then spoke in verse:
“The plantain tree dies when it bears fruit; The reed, the bamboo, and the cane are likewise.
So it is with those who crave profit: They will surely bring harm upon themselves.”
Yet this gain and honor will surely lead to decline and diminution;
for the foolish, through their pursuit of gain, can destroy their pure virtue.
It is like the tāla tree: once cut down, it does not grow again.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4 (IV) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, when the hour for the meal had arrived, a great number of bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city to beg for food.

Then, having heard that the Śākya son, the bhikṣu Hastikaśīrṣa, had fallen ill within the city and passed away, the bhikṣus finished their meal and returned. They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

This morning, we bhikṣus donned our robes and took up our bowls to enter the city for alms. We heard that the bhikṣu Hastiśīrṣa has passed away. We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us where the bhikṣu Hastiśīrṣa has been reborn."
"What karmic retribution will they receive?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Those who increase these three unrighteous dharmas will, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, inevitably fall into hell."
What are called the three kinds of unrighteousness?
They are the increase of stinginess and greed, ignorance, and anger.
Now this bhikṣu has committed these three unrighteous acts; let the bhikṣus know that he shall fall into hell.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts, Accomplishing greed, hatred, and delusion,
One commits evil with this very body, Which in turn brings harm back upon oneself."
Just as the plantain tree destroys itself by bearing fruit, so too,
if one is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, this is called wisdom;
not harming one's own person is what is meant by a superior man.
"Therefore, one should eliminate and sever greed, hatred, and delusion—the great afflictions.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
5. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Elder Nanda, wearing fresh and clean robes and holding a fine alms-bowl, was arrogant and haughty in his demeanor; he looked down upon others and spoke with self-conceit, saying:
"I am the younger brother of the Buddha and the son of my maternal aunt.
At that time, a great multitude of bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The bhikṣu Nanda wears fresh, clean robes and holds a pure alms-bowl; claiming to be the Buddha’s younger brother and the son of his maternal aunt, he is inwardly arrogant and treats others with contempt.”
When the Buddha had heard these words, he dispatched a bhikṣu to go and summon Nanda.
At that time, the bhikṣu, having received the Buddha’s command, went to where Nanda was and said to him:
“The World-Honored One calls for you.”
Having heard this, Nanda immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
The Buddha said to Nanda:

“Is it true that you, wearing fresh and clean robes and holding a fine alms-bowl, claim to be the Buddha’s younger brother and the son of his maternal aunt, yet act with arrogance toward others? Is such a thing so?”
Nanda replied,
“It is indeed so, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Nanda:
"You should not act in this way now; you should instead delight in the forest, dwell among cemeteries and at the foot of trees, wear rag-robes, and beg for alms."
"If he is my younger brother born of my maternal aunt, I ought to practice such deeds as these.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"How shall I see him?"
"Just as those forest-dwellers, sitting among burial mounds,
begging for food in the secluded places of mountains and forests, abandon desire and enter meditative concentration.
When the Buddha had spoken these verses, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
6. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among those who eloquently expound the Dharma, the bhikṣu Nanda is foremost.
Among those of handsome appearance and noble lineage, the bhikṣu Nanda is foremost."
In being able to renounce intense desire, the bhikṣu Nanda is foremost.

In restraining the sense faculties, knowing moderation in food and drink, and practicing the path with diligence during the first and last watches of the night while cultivating the factors of awakening so that mindfulness is always present before him, the bhikṣu Nanda is foremost.
What is meant by saying that the bhikṣu Nanda is able to restrain his sense faculties?
He does not become attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; this is called Nanda being able to restrain his sense faculties.
What is meant by the bhikṣu Nanda knowing the proper measure in eating?

He eats to stave off hunger, not for the sake of physical beauty or strength, but for the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya), taking only what is sufficient for himself, just as one uses grease to lubricate a cart.
Furthermore, it is like treating an abscess: one does not do so for the sake of physical strength, plumpness, freshness, or comeliness. This is called Nanda’s moderation in eating.
What is meant by the bhikṣu Nanda diligently practicing the Way during the first and last watches of the night?
By day he practiced walking meditation, and by night he sat in dhyāna to remove the hindrances of the mind.

During the first watch of the night, having finished washing his feet, he sat upright with his body straight, binding his mindfulness before him, and entered meditative concentration, remaining thus until the end of the first watch.
Furthermore, during the middle watch of the night, he lay on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, fixing his mind on light and cultivating the awakening factor of mindfulness.
At the beginning of the final watch of the night, he sat upright with his body straight, binding his attention before him.
And this Nanda, throughout the first and last watches of the night, applied himself single-mindedly to the practice of the Way without distinction.

Son of good family, Nanda attained the supreme awakening of mindfulness; the bhikṣu Nanda restrained his mind so that it was not distracted, and as he correctly contemplated the eastern direction, he did likewise for the southern, western, and northern directions.
Examining the mind with discernment, do not allow it to become confused or distracted.

Regarding painful sensations, pleasant sensations, and sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant, know them all as arising from conditions; know the duration and proximity of the arising and ceasing of these various sensations.
He also knows the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of all thoughts, and he also knows the causes and conditions for the abiding, arising, and ceasing of all perceptions.

He instructs the bhikṣus to train in this way: to guard and restrain the sense faculties, to know moderation in eating and drinking, and to practice with diligence during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, cultivating the supreme mindfulness and awakening just as Nanda does.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now instruct you to train in the practice cultivated by the bhikṣu Nanda. Should there be any bhikṣu whose practice is like that of Nanda, I shall likewise instruct you all to train in it."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One who is able to skillfully restrain the sense faculties, And is likewise able to maintain mindfulness and moderate their diet—
Such a person is called wise."
"Nanda, I praise those who well understand the essential nature and characteristics of the arising of the mind; you all should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7. (Seven) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Tiṣya, who was the son of the Buddha’s paternal aunt.
Relying upon the Buddha, they constantly harbor arrogance and do not respect elder bhikṣus of virtuous character; lacking a sense of shame or remorse, they are always given to much talk.
If other bhikṣus say even a little, they immediately give rise to anger.
At that time, seeing this, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, joined their palms, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The bhikṣu Tiṣya was constantly prone to arrogance; he claimed, "I am the son of the Buddha’s paternal aunt," and he treated all other elder bhikṣus with contempt, always engaging in excessive speech.
"If the bhikṣus say even a little, they immediately give rise to anger and resentment.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should now go and summon that bhikṣu, Tiṣya."
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus went to summon the potter.
Having received the command, the potter immediately proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling; after prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he stood to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed Tiṣya, saying:
"You see that the elder bhikṣus lack a mind of reverence; they are without shame and without remorse, and speak excessively of themselves."
"If the bhikṣus were to say even a little, they would immediately give rise to anger and resentment.
Is this truly so? Śreṇika replied:
“It is indeed so, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Tiṣya:

“If you are now the son of my paternal aunt, you should give rise to deep reverence for the elder bhikṣus of long-standing virtue; possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, you should speak little yourself.”
"When hearing what others say, one should endure it with patience.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One should constantly cultivate goodness and never give rise to anger; if anger arises, it is called unwholesome."
“Tiṣya, you should now before me sever your anger and pride;
practice all that is wholesome and cultivate the holy life. If you do so, I shall rejoice.”
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
8 (8) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the śramaṇa Vaiśākha Pāṭhikaputra was in the lecture hall, assembling the bhikṣus and preaching the Dharma to them. His speech was perfect and his exposition was unhindered; he was able to bring joy to the great assembly who heard him, such that they never grew weary of listening and immediately attained realization and understanding.

At that time, having heard what was said, the bhikṣus leaped for joy and, with sincere hearts, listened and received it; they made offerings and showed reverence, restraining their minds and concentrating their attention as they listened to his preaching of the Dharma. They did so not for the sake of gain or fame, but because his eloquence accorded with the truth and was inexhaustible, enabling those who heard it to remember and never forget. At that time, the entire great assembly listened in this manner.
There were certain bhikṣus who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The bhikṣu Viśākha Pañcālaputra was preaching the Dharma to the assembly in the lecture hall; he did so not for the sake of gain, fame, or praise, but with a power of eloquence consistent with the truth that was inexhaustible, enabling those who heard it to remember and never forget it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“You may go and summon that Vaiśākha Pāṭaliputra.
Then, having received these instructions, the bhikṣus went to summon Vaiśākha.
Having received the command, she went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side.
The Buddha asked Viśākhā:
"Is it true that you assembled the bhikṣus and preached the Dharma for them, even causing the bhikṣus to listen with a sincere mind?"
"Is this the case? He replied,
"It is indeed so."
The Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"Viśākhā! You have gathered the bhikṣus in the lecture hall and preached the Dharma for them; furthermore, you did so not for the sake of gain or fame, with perfect speech that brought joy to those who heard it, and they received it with sincere faith."
From this day forward, you should always benefit others by preaching the Dharma in this manner.
You bhikṣus, whether many or few, should practice two things:
first, you should preach the essentials of the Dharma.
Second, if there is nothing to be said, one should remain silent and must not discuss various other mundane matters.
You all should not now disparage silence.
"To remain silent, however, brings great benefit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If within a great assembly, The foolish and the wise gather together,"
If nothing is spoken, people will not distinguish and know;
only when something is clearly explained can they then distinguish and know.
Therefore, you should now always preach the essentials of the Dharma.
They blaze the torch of the Dharma and raise the banner of the sages and saints.
All the Arhats take the sublime Dharma as their banner;
all the sages and superior persons take virtuous speech as their banner.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9 (9) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus had gathered in the lecture hall, each making robes for themselves.
At that moment, there was a young bhikṣu who had not long since gone forth and had newly received full ordination; he sat among the saṃgha, yet did not make a robe for the community.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having finished making their robes, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"O monks, while we were cutting and sewing robes in the lecture hall, this young monk sat among the assembly without preparing robes for the community."
The Buddha asked the young bhikṣu,
“Is it true that you did not assist the Saṃgha in making robes?
The bhikṣu replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
According to my ability and strength, I too shall serve the Saṃgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in that bhikṣu’s mind, addressed the bhikṣus:

"Do not despise these young bhikṣus for having nothing to do; for those bhikṣus have accomplished what was to be done, they have attained arhatship, their taints are exhausted, they have laid down the heavy burden, they have realized true knowledge, and their minds are liberated."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The Dharma of my nirvāṇa shall never be obtained by those who are indolent and lacking in wisdom.”
Like a noble steed, the great man has severed the fetters of craving and exhausted all afflictions.
Having cast off the four kinds of clinging and attained nirvana, he is able to destroy the armies of Māra and dwells in his final body.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10 (10) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu named Jīrṇaka who dwelt alone in a single room, praising the life of solitary residence.
Then, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This elder bhikṣu praises dwelling alone, traveling alone, and sitting alone.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"You may call that elder bhikṣu.
Then, a certain bhikṣu went to where he was and said to the elder:
“The World-Honored One summons you.
Having received this instruction, the elder bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
The Buddha asked the Elder,
"Is it true that you dwell alone and praise the practice of solitary sitting?
The Elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is indeed so, World-Honored One.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Why is it that you now delight in dwelling alone and praise dwelling alone?"
The Elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is indeed true that I enter the village alone, leave it alone, and sit alone.”
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"There is another form of solitary dwelling that is superior to your solitary dwelling. What is it?"
When the root of desire is dried up, future desires do not arise, and present desires do not manifest; such a person is called a *brāhmaṇa*.
Being free from "self" and "what belongs to self," having severed the fetter of doubt, having distanced themselves from the sense bases (*āyatana*), they have extinguished all afflictions (*kleśa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“I fully know all the worlds; I have relinquished everything and exhausted all fetters of craving.”
"This sublime Dharma is called 'dwelling alone.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
11 (Eleven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Elder Saṅgāmaji, having traveled from the country of Kośala, arrived at Śrāvastī and reached the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the former wife, knowing that Saṃgharakṣita had arrived in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, dressed herself in robes and necklaces, adorned with various ornaments, and taking her son with her, went to Saṃgharakṣita’s dwelling.
At that time, the Venerable Saṅkha was walking in meditation in the open air.
He approached the Venerable [Mahākāśyapa] and said to him, "My son is young and unable to support himself; therefore, I have come to see you, Venerable Sir."
Although they met face-to-face, they did not speak with him.
A second and a third time, they spoke in this same manner.
Although the Venerable Saṅgharakkhita stood opposite him, he did not look at him at all, nor did he speak with him.
The two mothers then said, "We came to see you, yet you do not speak with us. This is your son; you yourself must nourish and raise him.
Having placed him at the head of the path where the monks walk, they abandoned him and departed, staying at a distance to watch from afar.
At that time, the Venerable One likewise did not speak with his son.
His former wife then thought to herself:
"Now this śramaṇa has attained liberation well; he is able to sever the fetters of craving."
"Whatever that seer had cut off, he has now fully obtained.
Not having fulfilled his wish, he returned to take his child, carrying him back toward his home.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with the pure divine ear surpassing that of humans, heard in its entirety what Saṃkicca and the former wife were saying.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To see one coming brings no joy; To see one departing brings no sorrow.
One who has abandoned and eliminated craving and desire Is the supreme Brahmin."
"Neither rejoicing when coming, nor grieving when departing,
one whose conduct is stainless and pure is called a wise brāhmaṇa.
Having spoken this verse, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(12) Sujaṭa and Duvanna, Devadatta and Hatthika;
the two Nandas, Tiṣya, Pañcāla, Kumāra, Thera, and Saṅkicca. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Ṛṣigiri near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, dwelling in seclusion, reflected silently to himself:
"In the past, the World-Honored One spoke of three kinds of fragrance—namely, the fragrance of roots, stems, and flowers—and among all fragrances, none exist outside these three."
"However, as for these three kinds of incense, they are smelled when with the wind, but not when against the wind.
Having reflected thus, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Just now, while dwelling alone in a quiet and secluded place, I was reflecting silently to myself:"
“The fragrances of the roots, stalks, and flowers spoken of by the World-Honored One are the most excellent among all fragrances;
yet their scent is perceived when with the wind, but not when against it.”
“World-Honored One!
Is there perhaps any fragrance that can be smelled both with the wind and against the wind?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is so, it is so. In this world there are excellent fragrances that are perceived both with and against the wind. What are they? "

Whether in villages or cities, if men or women practice non-killing, non-stealing, non-sexual misconduct, non-lying, and non-drinking of intoxicants, all the devas and those who possess the divine eye will praise them without exception.
"In those cities and villages, whether it be men or women who uphold the five precepts, the fragrance of such precepts shall be smelled by all, both with and against the wind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If it be sandalwood or aloeswood, Whether from roots, stems, flowers, or leaves,"
This incense is smelled with the wind, but against the wind it cannot be smelled.
The man who maintains the fragrance of precepts has an aroma that pervades the world;
his fame fills the ten directions, and it is smelled by all, whether with or against the wind.
Sandalwood and aloeswood, blue lotus and bālāśa—
such fragrances as these are faint and inferior, not equaling the fragrance of moral discipline.
While such various scents do not reach far from where they are heard, [the fragrance of virtue spreads everywhere].
The fragrance of the precepts pervades the ten directions, surpassing all the fragrances of the devas.
Such pure precepts have heedfulness as their root;
abiding in the outflow-free Dharma, one attains liberation through right wisdom.
Though the hosts of Māras seek him, they cannot know his location;
this is called the path of peace.
This path is most pure, forever departing from all directions and relinquishing all realms of existence.
When the Buddha had spoken these verses, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 13 (13) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha together with a thousand bhikṣus.

Previously, there was an elder Brahmin of great virtue who had attained arhatship; his taints were exhausted, all fetters of existence were severed, he had accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, and realized his own benefit.

The Tathāgata went to the Devakula shrine forest of the Sthāvaras. When King Bimbisāra heard that the Buddha had arrived at that shrine forest, he immediately set out with his cavalry, accompanied by eighteen thousand palanquins and twelve thousand chariots, surrounded by several billion Brahmins and householders, and proceeded to where the Buddha was.

Having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, he left behind his elephants, horses, and chariots, removed his finery and ornaments, and approached the Buddha. Kneeling with palms joined, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I am King Bimbisāra of Magadha," he declared three times.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, King Bimbisāra of Magadha.
Then, having prostrated at the Buddha's feet, Bimbisāra sat down to one side.
The brahmins and householders of the kingdom of Magadha, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, each took a seat before him.
At that time, among those seated, some raised their hands while others sat in silence.
At that time, as Uruvilvā Kāśyapa sat in the presence of the Buddha, the people of Magadha were all filled with doubt and thought to themselves:
"Is the Buddha his teacher, or is Uruvilvā Kāśyapa his teacher?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the deep thoughts in the minds of the people of Magadha, addressed Kāśyapa with a verse:
"You have long practiced the rite of serving the fire at Uruvilvā;
by what cause and condition have you now suddenly come to abandon this practice?"
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa replied with a verse:
"When I formerly served the fire, I craved delicious flavors as well as the forms of the five desires; all of these are defilements."
"For this reason, I have abandoned the practice of serving and worshipping the fire.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I know that you do not delight in the five desires or the flavors of form; [therefore, I have abandoned them]."
"What you now believe and delight in, you should proclaim to humans and devas.
The Venerable Uruvelā Kassapa spoke again in verse:
"Formerly I was extremely deluded, not recognizing the Dharma of the Truly Perfected One."
Sacrificing to fire and practicing austerities— these they call the causes of liberation.
Like one born blind who cannot see the path to liberation,
I have now encountered the Great Man, the Dragon, who shows me the Dharma of Right View.
Today, for the first time, I behold the trace of the unconditioned, true, and real;
it benefits all beings and brings them to liberation through its mastery.
The Buddha has appeared in the world to reveal the ultimate truth.
"May all classes of sentient beings All behold the light of wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"You have now come as one welcome; That which you sought has already been attained."
You possess the power of skillful reflection and are able to distinguish the most excellent Dharma.
You should now observe the profound intentions of this great assembly;
manifest spiritual transformations for their sake, so that they may give rise to reverence and faith.

The Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa immediately entered meditative absorption and manifested various supernormal powers; his body ascended into the air, where he sat, lay down, and walked, displaying the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—in the eastern direction.
Water issued from the upper part of his body and fire from the lower part;
water issued from the lower part of his body and fire from the upper part.

He entered the Fire-Light Samādhi and emitted various colored rays of light, manifesting supernatural transformations in the eastern direction, and likewise in the southern, western, and northern directions.
Having manifested his supernormal powers, he stood before the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, and said:
“The Great Sage, the World-Honored One, is my teacher; I am now a son of the Buddha.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is.
You have studied under me; you are my disciple."
The Buddha again commanded him,
saying, "Return to your seat.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
14 (14) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa of the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Dabba Mallaputta.
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded the bhikṣu Dabba to attend to the affairs of the Saṃgha; the bhikṣu Dabba accepted the command and took charge of them.
Later, on one occasion, there was a bhikṣu named Mithila who, according to the seniority of the assembly, was due to receive an invitation.
At that time, Dabba followed the order of seniority among the Sangha and dispatched the bhikṣu Mithila to accept the invitation and visit them.
Upon arriving, he found that the food and drink provided for the offering were coarse and unpalatable.
Having said this two or three times, she was privately despondent and gave rise to great distress, saying to her sister, the bhikṣuṇī Mitrā:
"The assignments given by Dharmapāla have always been coarse and harsh, causing me great suffering."
She then said to the bhikṣuṇī Mitrā: "Sister!
The bhikṣu Dharmadinnā has three times distressed me with foul food."
"And yet, why do you not now employ some skillful means for my sake to repay that enmity?
The bhikṣuṇī Maitrā replied,
"How could I possibly be able to assist you?"
The bhikṣu Maitreya said:
"According to my calculation for you, you should go to the Buddha and say:
'The bhikṣu Dharmapāla previously committed unchaste conduct with me.'"
I shall testify, saying:
"It is so, it is so. Thus spoke the bhikṣuṇī Mithilā.
"How could I ever slander one who maintains pure precepts?
Maitreya said, "Sister,
if you cannot do this for me, from this day forward, I shall no longer speak with you."
The bhikṣuṇī said,
"If that is indeed your intention, I shall comply with you.
The bhikṣu Maitreya said:
"Sister, I shall go on ahead; you may follow later.
The bhikṣu Maitra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
The bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyāṇī again went to the place where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, she stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How could Dravya Māṭhara have committed unchaste conduct in my presence?
The bhikṣu Maitreya replied,
"It is true, World-Honored One."
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmapāla was in the great assembly.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣu Dharmapāla, saying:
"Did you hear these words?"
At that time, the bhikṣu Dabba addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha himself knows me.”
The Buddha told Dabba:
"You should not speak in such a manner now; if you have performed such an act, you should say that you remember it;
if you have not performed it, you should say that you do not remember it."
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I truly do not recall such a thing having occurred."
Then Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Bhikṣu Dharmapāla has engaged in unchaste conduct with the Bhikṣuṇī Mettā.”
The bhikṣu Maitreya testified, saying:
"I saw the bhikṣu Dabba committing unchaste conduct with the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā; what does the bhikṣu Dabba intend to say?"
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"If that bhikṣuṇī Mitrā should falsely slander you, saying:
'Rāhula has now committed unchaste conduct with me.'"
The bhikṣu Mettiya also testified, saying:
"I truly saw Rāhula committing unchaste conduct with that bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā."
"What did you say? Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If I am falsely accused, I shall say only this: 'The Blessed One himself knows me.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"If even you know this, how much more so for one who is pure and has committed no offense; yet he would speak such words as if he did not know."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You may perform a *smṛti-karman* (act of remembrance) against the bhikṣu Dabba;
as for the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā, since she has made her own confession, you shall carry out her formal expulsion."
At that time, having received the Buddha’s command, the bhikṣus strictly interrogated the bhikṣu Mettiya, saying to him:
“Where did you see the bhikṣu Dabba engaging in unchaste conduct with the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā?”
"Was this seen by you alone, or was it seen by others?

When questioned in this manner, the bhikṣu Mithyādarśana (Mīduqiu) was unable to provide an answer; he then began to falsely slander the bhikṣu Dabba Mallaputta, saying, "Previously, when the turn came for me to receive invitations according to the seniority of the Saṅgha, I received coarse food on three occasions."
"I have indeed now given rise to this slander because of greed, hatred, and delusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from his quiet chamber and sat upon a seat spread before the assembly of monks.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

You have already performed the *smṛti-karman* (act of recollection) for the bhikṣu Dabba; you have further completed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against the bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā; and you have already questioned Mettiyāputta, learning that his slander was false."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“If one accomplishes everything— namely, the utterance of falsehoods—
then one abandons the future life and there is no evil that one will not commit.”
"It would be better to swallow glowing iron balls with this very body than,
with a body that has broken the precepts, to accept the offerings of those with pure faith.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
15 (Fifteen). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa of the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmapada went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet amidst the great assembly, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to enter nirvana; I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to pass into extinction.
Thus he requested three times.
The Buddha told Dhāva:
"As for your entry into nirvana, I do not obstruct you.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dhāva performed eighteen kinds of miraculous transformations before the Tathāgata, leaping into the air.
Thereupon, in the eastern direction, he manifested the four modes of deportment and various forms and colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—or appeared as water, or appeared as a mass of fire.
Water issued from the upper part of his body and fire from the lower part;
fire issued from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part.
He sometimes manifested a massive body that filled the entirety of space, and at other times he manifested a minute form.
He walked upon water as if on land, and walked upon land as if on water;
it was likewise so in the south, west, and north.

Having performed these deeds, he immediately entered the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) in mid-air; flames blazed forth like a great mass of fire, and he entered *nirvāṇa* without leaving behind any embers, just as clarified butter is entirely consumed at once.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as when red-hot iron is struck with a hammer, sparks fly forth;
once scattered, they vanish instantly, and one knows not where they have gone."
Attaining right liberation is likewise so.
Having emerged from the mud of afflictions and all desires,
no one can know the direction or destination toward which they have gone.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
16 (16) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was wandering and teaching in the country of Magadha, staying in the Mango Grove by the River.
Seeing a cowherd, [the Buddha] heard him say, "In this forest there is a bandit named Aṅgulimāla, who may harm people.
The Buddha said to the cowherd,
"That bandit may not actually cause you harm."
He then proceeded forward.
He again encountered a cowherd who spoke these same words, and the Buddha answered as before; this occurred up to three times.
The Buddha nevertheless replied:
“That wicked man may not even see me harmed.

When the Buddha arrived at the grove, Aṅgulimāla saw the Buddha coming from afar; holding his scabbard in his left hand and drawing his sword with his right, he sprang forward. Although he ran with all his might, the Tathāgata walked slowly and could not be overtaken.
Aṅgulimāla ran with all his might until his strength was exhausted, and he said to the Buddha:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Śramaṇa," the Buddha said to him,
"I now abide eternally; it is you who do not abide."
Aṅgulimāla then spoke this verse:
“The śramaṇa’s practice does not cease, Yet he says, ‘I am eternally abiding.
Now that I truly abide myself, He now says, ‘I do not abide.’”
"Why do you say that you abide, while I practice the Way without abiding?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Regarding all sentient beings, I have long since laid aside the sword and staff of harm."
"You harass and disturb sentient beings, and do not abandon these evil karmas;
for this reason I say you 'abide,' yet your name is 'Non-abiding.
As for me, among all forms of existence, I have abandoned all poisonous evils and harms."
"You do not cease from evil deeds, but constantly perform unwholesome actions;
therefore I say you 'dwell,' yet you are called 'non-dwelling.
I have abandoned all afflictions and harms toward all living beings."
"You have harmed living beings and have not yet eliminated dark karma;
for this reason, though I say you 'abide,' you are called 'non-abiding.
I delight in my own Dharma, having gathered my mind in heedfulness."
"Do you not see that the fourfold assembly abides nowhere at all?
This is called my true abiding; as for you, you are called 'non-abiding.
Aṅgulimāla spoke again in verse:
“I have long dwelt in the wilderness, yet never before have I seen such a person as the Bhagavān;
coming here, you have shown me the wholesome Dharma.
Having long cultivated evil karma, today I renounce it all.”
I now listen to your words, which accord with the Dharma and sever all evils.
Like drawing a sword from its scabbard and casting it away into a deep pit,
you have immediately prostrated in worship and taken refuge in the World-Honored One.
With faith most fierce and sharp, he resolved to seek renunciation.
The Buddha, giving rise to great compassion to benefit all the world, immediately said to him, "Welcome, well-come! and he instantly became a śramaṇa.

At that time, the son of noble family Aṅgulimāla’s hair and beard fell away naturally, and having donned the dharma robes, he was ordained. Dwelling in a secluded and quiet place, his mind was free from negligence; he focused single-mindedly on practicing the Way and diligently cultivated vigor.

Being able to apply oneself with single-minded diligence, to collect the mind in right mindfulness, and to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life, one reaches the end of all suffering; within this very life, one personally attains realization and knowledge, knowing for oneself: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
At that time, the Venerable Ahiṃsaka had become an arhat and attained the bliss of liberation.
He then spoke this verse:
"I am now named Ahiṃsaka, Yet later I became a great destroyer."
I am now called "Possessing Reality," for truth is indeed non-harming.
My body is now free from harm, and my speech and mind are likewise;
never shall I harm another—this is truly what is meant by "non-harming."
My body was once smeared with blood, and thus I was named Aṅgulimāla;
having been swept away by a great torrent, I therefore take refuge in the Buddha.
Having taken refuge, I attained full ordination and immediately acquired the three types of supernormal knowledge.
Fully understanding the teachings of the Buddha, they follow them with reverence and practice accordingly.
The World-Honored Tamer disciplines [beings] with swords,
staves, and whips, with iron hooks, lashes, and bridles, and with all manner of various punishments.
The World-Honored One, the Great Tamer, has abandoned all unwholesome dharmas;
having cast away the sword, staff, and cudgel, he is truly the Right Tamer.
To cross water one requires a bridge or a boat; to straighten an arrow one must use fire.
As a craftsman straightens wood with his axe and adze, so does wisdom discipline itself through insight.
If a person first commits evil but later ceases and never does it again,
they illuminate the world like the moon when the clouds have vanished.
If a person was formerly heedless, but later ceases to be heedless,
with right mindfulness they leave behind the thorns of affliction and, with single-minded focus, cross to the further shore.
Having completed evil deeds, one will inevitably fall into the miserable realms.
Having received the Buddha’s removal of my transgressions, I have been freed from evil karma.
May all people who hear my words cast away the knots of resentment in their hearts;
with the pure eye of patience, they shall realize that the Buddha taught non-contention to be supreme.
17 (17) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu, before the break of dawn, went to the riverbank, folded his robes and placed them in one spot, entered the river to bathe, emerged from the water naked, and stood on the riverbank to dry his body.
A deva emitted light that illuminated the riverbank and said to the bhikṣu:
"You have not long since left the household life; you are in the prime of youth with fine hair. Why do you not enjoy the pleasures of the five desires, instead leaving home at an improper time?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"I have now gone forth; this is precisely the right time, yet I have obtained it at an improper time.
The deva said to the śramaṇa:
“How is it that when one has left the household life, one encounters what is ‘untimely’?
The śramaṇa replied:
“The Blessed One, the World-Honored One, has taught that the five desires are ‘timely,’ while the Buddha-dharma is ‘untimely.’”
The pleasures of the five desires yield very little flavor, yet their afflictions are manifold, being the gathering place of sorrow and distress.
Within my Buddha-dharma, one realizes and attains realization in the present body, free from all burning torments.
"In all that one undertakes, one does not observe the timing or the day.
By planting even a small, subtle cause, one obtains a great fruit.
The deva asked again:
“How does the Buddha describe the five desires as being ‘timely,’ and why are the Buddha’s teachings called ‘untimely’?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I am still young and have not long been ordained; my days of study are also few. How could I possibly proclaim the vast and profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth?
The Bhagavān is currently nearby at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove; you should go there yourself and ask him about your doubts."
The deva replied to him, saying:
"At present, the Buddha’s attendants—devas of great majestic virtue—are gathered in abundance at his side; being weak and inferior as I am, I am unable to see him."
"Now, for my sake, go and inform the World-Honored One: 'If the Tathāgata, out of compassion and pity, would deign to grant me his permission, I shall go to him to inquire about my doubts.
The bhikṣu replied, "If you are able to go, I shall inform the World-Honored One on your behalf."
The deva replied again,
"I shall follow you to the presence of the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and reported the celestial questions in full to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Within name-and-form, the characteristic of arising is conceived as truly existent.”
One should know that such a person is said to belong to the path of death.
If one realizes that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is fundamentally empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, this is called honoring the Buddha;
one will forever be free from the various realms of existence.
The Buddha asked the deva,
"Have you understood it yet?
The deva immediately replied:
“I do not understand,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha spoke again in verse:
"Superiority pride, equality pride, and likewise inferiority pride—
those who possess these three types of pride are subject to dispute.
To extinguish and eliminate these three prides is called the perception of immovability."
The Buddha asked the deva,
"Have you understood it yet?
The deva replied to the Buddha:
“I do not understand,
World-Honored One.
The Buddha spoke again in verse:
“Having severed craving and name-and-form, And having eliminated the three kinds of conceit;
Not touching upon any sensual desires, And having eliminated ill-will;
Having uprooted all poisonous roots, All perceptions, wishes, and desires are exhausted.”
"If one can act in this way, one shall cross over the ocean of birth and death.
The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have now understood."
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
18 (18) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who, at the break of dawn, went to the riverbank, removed his robes to bathe, and then emerged onto the shore to dry his body.
A deity emitted light, illuminating the riverbank, and asked the bhikṣu:
"Bhikṣu! This is a nest;
at night smoke issues from it, and during the day it burns with fire."
A certain brāhmaṇa, having seen this, destroyed that nest and dug up the ground.
At that time, a wise man said to the brāhmaṇa:
"Dig the ground with a knife."
Seeing a tortoise, the brahmin said, "Bring that tortoise here.
He then told him to dig into the ground; seeing a viper there, he told him to seize it.
He spoke again, telling him to dig the ground; they saw a piece of flesh and told him to pull it out.
He spoke again, telling him to dig the ground; they saw a sword-hilt, and the brāhmaṇa said, "This is a sword-hilt."
He told him to dig it up.
Again he told him to dig the ground; seeing a *laṅgika* venomous insect, he told him to dig it up.
Again he told him to dig the ground; seeing two paths, he again told him to dig them out.
He told him to dig further into the ground, where they saw a heap of stones; he told him to remove the stones.
He told him to dig again, where they saw a dragon. The Brahmin said:
"Do not disturb the dragon."
He then knelt before that nāga.
The deva said to the bhikṣu:
"Do not forget my words; you may ask the Buddha about this."
Whatever the Buddha has taught, you should remember and uphold it with a sincere heart. Why is this?

Because, apart from the Buddha and his śrāvaka disciples—the bhikṣus—I see no one among the devas, Māras, or Brahmās who could analyze [these matters], nor anyone capable of understanding such questions.
At that time, the bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
He related in full to the Buddha what he had heard from the deva, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
What is this nest from which smoke issues at night and fire blazes by day?
Who is a brāhmaṇa?
Who is a wise man?
What is the sword?
What is the digging tool?
And what is the tortoise?
What is the viper?
What is the piece of flesh?
What is the knife-house?
What is the *laṅgīmā* venomous insect?
What are the two paths?
What is the heap of stones?
"What is meant by 'dragon'?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Listen attentively!"
Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you.
That which is called a "nest" or "cave" is this very body.
Having received the vital essence from one's parents, the four great elements combine; nourished by food and clothing, the body is thus formed.
Yet this body will inevitably reach a state of decay and ruin, becoming bloated, infested with worms, putrefied, and finally shattered to pieces.
The smoke issuing at night represents various discursive thoughts (*vitarka* and *vicāra*).
The fire burning during the day represents the extensive activities performed through bodily and verbal karma.
The Brahmin is none other than the Tathāgata.
Those who possess wisdom are the śrāvakas.
The sword is a metaphor for wisdom.
Digging the earth is a metaphor for diligence.
The tortoise is a metaphor for the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
The viper is a metaphor for anger, vexation, and malice.
The piece of meat is a metaphor for stinginess, greed, and envy.
The "knife-house" is a metaphor for the five desires.
The venomous insect *laṅgīmā* is a metaphor for ignorance.
The "two paths" are a metaphor for doubt.
"The various heaps of stones are a metaphor for the conceit of self (asmimāna).
The dragon is a metaphor for the Arhat, who has exhausted all fetters of existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“The nest is called the body; applied and sustained thought are like its smoke;
volitional formations blaze like fire.
The wise one is a śrāvaka; the sword is wisdom itself.”
Diligence is like digging the earth;
anger is like a venomous serpent; greed and envy are like pieces of meat;
and the five desires are like a house of knives.
Ignorance is like a *laṅgaka* tree; doubt is like a forked path; the view of self is like a heap of stones.
Do not trouble the dragon now!
This dragon is a true arhat.
"Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to skillfully answer difficult questions.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
19. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park of the Ṛṣis.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed and taken his bowl, entered the city of Vārāṇasī. There he saw a bhikṣu whose body and mind were unsettled and whose faculties were distracted.
At that time, having seen the Buddha from afar, that bhikṣu bowed his head in shame.
After the Buddha had finished his almsround, he washed his feet, entered the monastery, emerged from his quiet chamber, and sat among the assembly of monks. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This morning, I saw a bhikṣu who did not restrain his sense faculties. When that bhikṣu saw me from afar, he showed a look of shame, bowing his head to check his emotions. Who might this be?"
Then, that bhikṣu rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over his right shoulder, joined his palms in añjali, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"One whose mind is unsettled and whose faculties are scattered is none other than myself.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent!"

"Monks! Since you were able to restrain your emotions and control your minds upon seeing me, you should likewise do so when seeing the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; you should restrain your emotions and control your minds as if you were seeing me."
"If you are able to do so, you will bring peace, happiness, and benefit for a long night.
Then, a certain bhikṣu spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"A bhikṣu enters a village seeking alms, His mind and thoughts are loose and distracted, not settled for even a moment."
"Seeing that the Buddha’s diligence restrains all the sense faculties, for this reason the Buddha has praised him, saying, ‘Excellent! (20) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, the dwelling place of the ancient seers.

2. First Recitation, Second [Section], 23 (2-3). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, dwelling in the Śītaśāyana Forest.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Human life is brief, and its end is inevitable; you should diligently practice the Way and purely cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya). Therefore, you should not be indolent, but should cultivate wholesome conduct, the meaning of the Dharma, and true practice."
At that time, having heard these words, the Māra King immediately thought to himself:

At that time, after the Māra King had formed this thought, he transformed himself into a young brahmin (maṇava), went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and spoke in verse:
“May human life be long, free from all afflictions and distress; may there always be peace and security, with no path to death.”
The Buddha thought to himself:
"Māra, the Evil One, has come to cause disturbance.
He then spoke this verse:
“Human life is short and beset by many afflictions; one should swiftly cultivate goodness as if extinguishing a fire on one’s head.

"The śramaṇa Gautama knows my thoughts.

24 (Twenty-four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Śītavana forest near Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, swift and unceasing, and not to be relied upon; they are subject to decay and disintegration. One should quickly leave them behind and proceed upon the path to liberation."

"The śramaṇa Gautama is staying in the Śītavana forest near Rājagṛha, teaching such a Dharma to his śrāvakas; I shall go there to disturb and confuse him."
At that time, having formed this thought, the Māra King transformed himself into a young brahmin (*maṇava*), went to where the Buddha was, stood to one side, and spoke these verses:
"Day and night it ever abides; Life constantly revolves and returns, Like the turning of a wheel’s axle, Circling on without end."
The Buddha, knowing that the Māra King had come to cause disturbance, spoke this verse:

"Therefore, you, Pāpīyan, should not cause such disruption.
Māra thought to himself:

The Buddha thought to himself:

Why do you sleep?

"I shall go there and cause disruption.

The great ocean and the vast earth may all be shattered into pieces;

"The śramaṇa Gautama knows my thoughts.

28 (Twenty-eight). Thus have I heard:

Then, during the middle watch of the night, the World-Honored One walked up and down on the open ground. Having washed his feet, he entered the quiet chamber, adjusted his body to sit upright, and fixed his mindfulness before him.

its form was immense, like a great ship, and its two eyes were brilliant and clear, like *kosa-ala* bowls.

Though venomous snakes are extremely fierce and their forms are most terrifying,
and though mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice cause all manner of irritating contacts,
they cannot move even a single hair of mine; how much less could they ever cause me fear?
Even if the void were to split asunder, and the great earth were to tremble in its entirety,
causing all sentient beings to give rise to great alarm and fear—
there is no possibility that such things could ever cause me to be terrified.

at the very moment it pierced me, I would never seek protection;
yet even this poisoned arrow shall not strike me.
At that time, having heard the verses spoken by the Buddha, the Māra king thought to himself:

"Sitting upright beneath the tree, Tranquil and alone in contemplation,"
Is it because you have lost your wealth and treasures, or because you seek great riches?
Since you harbor no heart of attachment toward cities or villages,
why not become a close friend to all people?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with these verses:
“I have obtained great wealth; within my heart I have attained tranquility.
I have shattered the army of craving and desire; I am entirely unattached to exquisite forms.”
Sitting in meditation while dwelling alone, one experiences the foremost bliss;
for this reason, one seeks no friends or kin at all.
The demoness, her desires satisfied, spoke again in verse:
“In what state does a bhikṣu abide, able to cross the five swift currents and transcend the six as well?
Into what meditative absorption does he enter to reach the far shore of great desire and forever leave behind the bonds of existence?”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The body attains the bliss of suppleness, The mind achieves excellent liberation;
The mind is detached from all karmic actions, And the intellect no longer regresses."
Having attained the cessation of applied and sustained thought, having become free from aversion, attachment, and agitation,
and dwelling securely in this state, one is able to cross the five swift currents and cross the sixth as well;
practicing such meditative sitting, one attains liberation.
"Able to cross over the fetters of great desire, And likewise leave behind the currents of worldly existence.
The demoness, pleased by him, spoke again in verse:
"Having severed the fetters of craving, You have left behind all places of attachment."
"Those with many desires cannot cross the swift current; those with many desires cannot cross the shore of death.
Only the wise one is able to cross such a peril.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Great diligence delivers and rescues; the Tathāgata’s True Dharma provides the crossing.
Those who attain liberation according to the Dharma—there is no wise person who does not rejoice.
The three daughters, their wishes unfulfilled, returned to their father's place.
At that time, the Māra King rebuked his three daughters and spoke this verse:
"O three daughters, you sought to ruin him, whose form is like a flash of lightning;
yet toward that Great Striver, you were like the wind blowing upon cotton wool."
With their fingernails they seek to shatter mountains; with their teeth they bite iron balls;
with lotus fibers, the ignorant and foolish seek to suspend Mount Tai.
The Buddha has already transcended all attachments; yet they wish to debate with him.
To cast a net to catch the wind, To bring down the moon from the void;
To cup the great ocean in one's hands, Hoping to drain it dry— The Buddha has already transcended all attachments; Yet you wish to go and debate with him.
"Raising his foot to cross over Mount Sumeru, seeking dry land within the great ocean—
the Buddha has already emerged from all attachments— yet he goes to engage in debate.
The Māra King, filled with sorrow and regret, immediately vanished and returned to his celestial palace.
32 (Thirty-two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Buddha, together with the bhikṣus, praised the Dharma of Nirvāṇa.
The Māra King thought to himself:
"The Buddha is in Rājagṛha, praising the Dharma of Nirvāṇa to the bhikṣus.
I shall now go there to cause confusion and disruption."

Having formed this thought, he immediately manifested his form, transforming himself into a hundred people—fifty of whom were exceedingly handsome and fifty of whom were exceedingly ugly. At that time, all the bhikṣus were struck with wonder and asked, "For what reason are some so exceedingly handsome, while others are so exceedingly ugly?"
The Buddha knew that Māra had come with the intent to cause disruption and confusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pāpīyan, saying:
"Throughout the long night of saṃsāra, you have fully experienced such forms, both auspicious and inauspicious; how then shall you attain crossing to the far shore of suffering?"
"What is the use of such transformations?
If there were those who were attached to men or women, you should manifest various forms for them.
Now, I am entirely devoid of the characteristics of male or female; what need have I for transformations into various forms?"
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Longevity, Khanti, and the snare; sleep, walking meditation, and the great venomous snake;
doing nothing, seeking virtue, and the māra-maiden; destroying and disturbing, changing form, and the beautiful and the foul.
33 (Thirty-three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Being filial and obedient to one's parents;
showing reverence to elders and superiors;
speaking with gentle words and abandoning divisive speech;
He delights in giving;
he is free from stinginess;
he constantly cultivates truthful speech and never deceives or cheats.

"Extremely filial and obedient toward one's parents, And likewise toward all elders and superiors..."
With a profound mind of reverence, they constantly act with gentleness and kindness; they speak words of grace and softness, severing double-tongued speech, as well as stinginess, greed, and anger.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven each spoke these words:
"A practitioner such as this surpasses those like us; he ought to dwell apart and serve as the Heavenly King."

35 (35) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

the gods of that time were called Śakra.

The Buddha said:

He asked again:
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions is he named Kauśika?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When Śakra was originally a human being, his clan name was Kauśika; therefore, he is named Kauśika.
For what further reason is he named 'Lord of Śacī'?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Śakra married the daughter of the asura king Vemacitrin, named Śacī.
They asked again:
“Furthermore, for what reason is he named ‘Thousand Eyes’?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“When Śakra was originally a human being, he was exceedingly intelligent; when deciding legal cases, he could settle a thousand matters in a mere instant. For this reason, he is named ‘Thousand Eyes.’”
“Furthermore, for what reason is he named Indra?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Because Śakra dwells in the position of the Heavenly King and adjudicates the affairs of the devas, he is named Indra.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Because he was able to fulfill these seven matters, for this reason the devas called him Śakra.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
36 (Thirty-six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, there was a yakṣa whose form was extremely small, whose complexion was coarse and ugly, and whose body was black; people took no pleasure in seeing him, yet he sat upon the throne of Śakra."
At that time, when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven saw this yakṣa sitting in the place of Śakra, they were all greatly incensed and reviled him with various insults.
Then, the yakṣa’s evil features gradually faded away, his auspicious appearance emerged, and he grew larger and larger by the moment.
The devas reviled him, and their anger increased; the yakṣa’s body then became even larger and his complexion grew more radiant.
The devas went together to the abode of Śakra and said to him:
"There is a yakṣa who is extremely ugly and whose body is very small, yet he sits in the place of Śakra."
"We, the gods, all joined together in reviling him, yet the son of the yakṣa’s complexion grew increasingly fine and his body gradually enlarged.
Śakra said, "There is such a yakṣa who, upon receiving all manner of abuse, has his form and color become even finer; he is named 'One Who Assists Anger'."
At that time, Śakra returned to his seat, bared his right shoulder, held a censer in his hand, and said to the Night Goddess:
"O Great Seer!
"I am Śakra, I am Śakra!
He called out his name three times; the yakṣa then grew smaller, his form and color became increasingly hideous, and he vanished on the spot.
Śakra returned to his throne as Śakra and addressed the devas, saying:
"From this day forward, do not give rise to anger.
If you encounter an adversary, take care never to respond with wrath."
Then he spoke in verse:
"If others come to oppress or deceive you, Do not in turn oppress or deceive them.
Toward those who come to cause you harm, Give rise to a heart of loving-kindness."
One who is without anger and without malice should always be associated with;
such a person is a noble one (ārya), as well as a disciple of the noble ones.
Those who possess anger are obstructed by the mountain of wrath.
"If one who is overcome by anger can exercise even a slight restraint,
this is called a wholesome dharma, like using a bridle to control a wild horse.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Śakra dwells in the position of a celestial king and enjoys all manner of sensual pleasures, yet he is still able to restrain his anger; moreover, he constantly praises those who exercise restraint against anger. How much more so for you, bhikṣus—you who have faith in leaving the home life for homelessness, entering the path, shaving off hair and beard, and donning the dharma robes—how can you fail to restrain anger and praise the abandonment of anger?”
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus.
At that time, the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
37 (37) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, when the morning had arrived, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

Having finished his meal, he washed his feet, folded his sitting mat, and went to the Nyagrodha Grove. After surveying the area thoroughly, he sat down cross-legged at a secluded spot beneath a tree and dwelt in the celestial abodes.

At that time, within the Jeta Vihāra, two bhikṣus arose in mutual anger and contention during a formal legal proceeding of the Saṃgha; one remained small-mindedly silent and patient, while the other was filled with intense rage.
That "blazing" one, seeing his own faults, came to the silent and patient bhikṣu seeking to repent.
However, the silent and patient bhikṣu did not accept his repentance.
In this manner, as the bhikṣus passed the word from one to another, they conversed together until a great sound arose.

At that time, the Tathāgata was dwelling in the celestial abode; with his pure divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, he heard this sound from afar. He immediately rose from his seat, went into the midst of the Saṃgha, and sat down upon a seat prepared before the assembly.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This morning, I put on my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the city to beg for food, until finally I came to sit in meditation within this forest. I heard the bhikṣus shouting and crying out at the top of their voices; what were they doing?"
At that time, the bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
While two groups of bhikṣus were settling a legal matter at the Jeta Vihāra, they became angry and quarreled with one another."
One bhikṣu was small-minded and habitually patient;
the other bhikṣu was fiery-tempered and talkative.
When the fiery bhikṣu recognized his own fault, he returned with sincerity to repent, but the patient bhikṣu would not accept his repentance.
They passed the time together, making a great sound.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"How can one be so foolish as not to accept another's confession?"
"O Bhikṣus!
You should know that in the past, Śakra Devānām Indra, amidst the assembly of devas in the Sudharmā Hall, spoke this verse:
'Just as one uses a ladle To pour ghee to nourish a lamp, [so too does one increase merit]. "
When a fire blazes up and becomes even more intense, it conversely burns the gourd vessel itself.
Anger is just like this: it returns to burn one's own roots of goodness.
I never harbor resentment; once anger has arisen, it is immediately dissipated.
It is not like a swirling current that turns back upon itself endlessly;
though I may be angry, I shall not speak ill of you, nor shall I touch upon what you hold dear.
What you hold dear is like a vital artery; I shall never cause it harm.
Having disciplined the body, one gains immediate benefit for oneself.
One who is without anger and without malice is a noble one (ārya);
they are a disciple of the noble ones and should always be associated with.
For all those who harbor anger, the heavy obstruction is like a mountain.
If, at a time when anger arises, one is able to exercise even a small degree of restraint, this is called wholesome karma;
it is like using a bridle to control a wild horse.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Śakra Devānām Indra, who occupies the rank of king among the gods and possesses sovereign power over the heavens, is still able to practice patience and praise those who possess it; how much more so should you, bhikṣus, who have left the household life and altered your appearance, not practice patience and praise patience?"
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 38 (38) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, Śakra Devānām Indra, leading the hosts of devas, was about to go forth to wage war against the asuras."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to the Asura King Vemacitrin:
"We need not now necessarily lead vast multitudes of followers to inflict mutual harm upon one another; let us instead engage in debate to determine victory and defeat."
Vimalacitra said to Śakra Devānām Indra:
"Kauśika! If there is a victory or defeat in our debate, who shall distinguish it?"
Śakra-devānām-indra said:
"Within our assembly, as well as among the asuras, there are those who are sagacious, wise, and eloquent, capable of discerning good and evil and determining victory or defeat."
Vemacitra said: "Śakra, you speak first. Śakra replied:
"I too am able to speak;
however, you are an elder deity and should speak first.
Vemacitra then spoke in verse:
"Now that I have seen through the transgression of patience, the fool thinks it is the dharma of patience;
because of his fear, he gives rise to patience, and thus considers himself superior."
Śakra Devānām-indra spoke again in verse:
"Following their words brings fear; one's own benefit is supreme.
Among all wealth and various gains, there is none superior to patience."
Vimalacitra spoke again in verse:
"The fool lacks wisdom; he must be restrained and checked, just as that hind cow leaps onto the back of the lead cow."
"Therefore, one must use swords and staves to subdue the foolish.
Śakra Devānām Indra replied in verse:
"I observe that to restrain the foolish through silence and patience is the most excellent way."
When one is met with extreme hatred and anger, if one can endure it, that [anger] subsides of its own accord.
One who is without hatred and without malice is indeed a noble one (ārya);
such a person is also a disciple of the noble ones, and one should always draw near to them.
For all those who harbor ill will, anger is a heavy obstruction like a mountain.
If, when anger arises, one is able to restrain it even slightly,
this is called a virtuous deed, like using a bridle to control a wild horse.
“Those among the hosts of devas and asuras who possessed wisdom deliberated together in detail to weigh their respective strengths and weaknesses.

Since the asuras took strife and combat as their foundation, while Śakra Devānām Indra brought disputes to rest with a mind free from anger and rivalry, the asuras were deemed defeated and Śakra was declared the victor.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Śakra Devānām Indra is sovereign among the devas; throughout the long night he has practiced patience and praised the dharma of patience. You bhikṣus, if you can practice patience and praise those who are patient, you will be in accord with the dharma of renunciation.”
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 39 (39) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, Śakra Devānām Indra was about to engage in battle with the asuras; having completed his preparations, he was fully equipped for war."

"If we, the gods, should achieve victory, we shall certainly bind the asuras with the fivefold bonds and lead them to our celestial palace."

When Vemacitrin saw Śakra, he spoke with anger and abuse, uttering most foul words.
