Then, the charioteer Mātali spoke these verses:
“Māghava, husband of Śacī, are you afraid and powerless? Or have you lost your senses?”
"Vemacitrin reviled me face to face; how can I endure such extreme and wicked words?
At that time, Śakra replied in verse:
"I do not practice patience out of fear, nor because I lack the power."
Yet fearing Vimalacitra, I cultivate patience through superior wisdom.
The fool’s shallow understanding cannot reach mine; his mind is constantly engaged in contention and never ceases.
If I were to restrain him by force, I would be no different from that very fool.
The charioteer spoke again in verse:
"If the infant is left unrestrained, He grows increasingly wild without ceasing;
Like that ox walking behind, He leaps upon the ox in front on the road."
"The strong one uses strength to restrain those who are foolish.
Śakra spoke again in verse:
"In my observation, there is nothing that restrains the foolish more than patient silence."
When hatred is blazing fiercely, only patience can best restrain it.
The fool claims to possess power, yet in truth he is powerless;
the fool does not recognize good from evil, and thus there is no dharma by which he may be restrained.
I possess valor and strength, yet I am able to endure those who are foolish and inferior;
this is called the foremost patience, the most excellent among all forms of endurance.
When one who is weak must not fail to act toward those who are powerful—
This is called the patience of fear; it is not called the patience of reality.
When one who has attained mastery through power is reviled by others, to remain silent and not retaliate—this is called supreme patience.
When one of weak character is intimidated by power and remains silent, unable to respond, this is called fear;
it is not called practicing patience.
When the ignorant and witless inflict harm upon others, [they do so out of ignorance].
Seeing others silently endure, one considers oneself superior.
To the noble ones and the wise, patience is said to be the supreme excellence;
therefore, the assembly of sages and saints constantly praises the merit of patience.
Removing it from oneself and bestowing it upon others, one extinguishes all calamities and fears;
seeing another’s anger raging, one should simply practice silent forbearance.
That anger will naturally subside without the need for the force of swords or staves.
Both parties gain great benefit; one benefits oneself and benefits others.
The foolish claim that patience is cowardice, yet it is praised by the wise and virtuous.
One endures those superior to oneself out of fear of harm and calamity.
"If one endures a dispute with an equal out of fear that both will be harmed,
yet can also endure those who are base and inferior— this is the highest form of patience.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Even Śakra, who is most sovereign among the Thirty-three Gods and practices the dharma of kings, is still able to cultivate patience and praise patience; how much more so should the bhikṣus, who have altered their appearance to enter the Dharma, cultivate patience and praise patience."
"If one can cultivate patience and praise it, this is the dharma of those who have left the household life.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
40. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

"Formerly, when Śakra-devānām-indra wished to go to the pleasure gardens, he commanded his charioteer Mātali:

King Śuddhodana emerged from the Vaijayanta Hall, joined his palms with fingers interlaced, and faced east toward the Buddha.

"O Mātali, you should know this: The World-Honored One of greatest renown, I now give rise to reverent faith toward him; Therefore, I stand here with palms joined."

"At that time, I pay homage to the Supreme One in the world; I too shall follow you in paying respectful homage."
Having spoken these words, he joined his palms in reverent salutation, mounted his carriage, and departed.

“Even Śakra, the Heavenly King who dwells in the realm of Sovereign Freedom, still pays homage and prostrates before the Buddha. When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
41 (41) Thus have I heard:

Entering meditative absorption throughout the long night, Cultivating the supreme holy life,

The great Arhats, who have distanced themselves from desire,
are able to extinguish the darkness of ignorance and sever all fetters; likewise,
those living at home who cultivate goodness and do not commit evil deeds— [all these are the field of merit].

When Śakra had spoken these words, he joined his palms in reverent salutation, mounted his chariot, and departed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Even Śakra, who dwells among gods and humans and possesses sovereign power, is still able to show reverence and pay homage to the Dharma; how much more so should you, bhikṣus, who have shaved off your hair and beards to leave the household life and study the Path, not diligently honor and revere the Dharma?”
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
42 (42) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, Śakra Devānām Indra wished to go to the pleasure gardens and commanded his charioteer Mātali:
'Prepare a chariot drawn by a thousand horses.'"
At that time, Mātali, having finished harnessing the chariot, went to where Śakra was and said to him:
"The chariot is prepared; please know that it is now the proper time."
At that time, Śakra descended from the Vaijayanta Hall and joined his palms facing west.
When the charioteer Mātali saw this, he too was struck with alarm and fear, dropping both the whip and the reins.
Śakra said, "What have you seen that causes you such terror? Mātali replied:
"O husband of Makhali Gosāla!
I now see you facing west with palms joined; because my heart was filled with fear, I lost control of the whip and reins.
All living beings revere you."
All lords of the earth are entirely subject to you;
the gods of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three all pay homage to you.
Who else possesses virtue that surpasses yours?
"Joining my palms together in añjali, I respectfully face the western direction.
Śakra replied, "All pay me honor, just as you have said.
Those whom all devas and humans revere are called the Saṃgha; now I too pay reverence and place my faith in the Saṃgha."
At that time, Mātali spoke in verse, asking:
"The human body is filled with pus and sweat, More loathsome than a corpse exposed in the open;
Constantly afflicted by the sufferings of hunger and thirst— How could one envy such a homeless state?"
For what reason now do you show such profound reverence for him?
What manner of deportment does he possess, and what are his virtuous practices?
I pray that you speak for me; I shall now listen with a sincere heart.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra spoke these verses:
“Because he has no home, I truly envy him;
He likewise has no storehouses, Nor treasuries or grain.”
Free from all worldly affairs, moderate in food to sustain life,
well-guarding the precepts, and eloquently expounding the sublime Dharma;
courageous and without fear, practicing the noble silence.
The devas and asuras are constantly engaged in conflict;
among all human beings, there are likewise mutual feuds and rivalries.
But those whom I now revere have all abandoned the sword and the staff.
All that has been accumulated, he is able to distance himself from it all;
what the world loves and clings to, his mind abandons it all.
To him whom I now pay homage, who is far removed from every fault—
"Mātali! You should now understand this matter.
At that time, Mātali spoke again in verse:
“‘He whom you worship is most supreme; I too shall pay him homage.
He whom Ma-ka worships, I now worship along with you.’”
Having spoken these verses, Śakra departed in his chariot.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If even that Śakra, who dwells in sovereignty over humans and devas, can still revere the Saṃgha, how much more so should you, bhikṣus, who have left the household life to cultivate the Path, each revere the Saṃgha."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Indra and Mahāli—by what cause did the yakṣa obtain his eyes?
How did he attain excellence? Regarding bondage and reverence for the Buddha.

3. First Recitation, Third [Section], 43 (43). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, the asuras assembled their fourfold army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—and having fully equipped them with all the implements for battle, they desired to go to the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa devas to fight with the gods."
At that time, Śakra, hearing that the asuras had arrayed their fourfold army, immediately addressed the devaputra Subhīra:
"I have heard that the asuras have arrayed their fourfold army; you too must array your fourfold army and go forth to fight them."
Sūbhila replied, "This is most excellent. Having said these words,
he became dissolute and attached to pleasure, no longer remembering this matter.
When Śakra heard that the asuras had already emerged from the city, he again summoned Suvīra and said:
"The asuras have now left the city; you should array the fourfold army and go there to fight them."
Subhira replied, "Kauśika!
This is a virtuous matter."
Sūbhāsa remained thus addicted to pleasure and failed to prepare for battle.
The Asuras arrayed their fourfold army and, having already reached the summit of Mount Sumeru, gradually drew closer.
Śakra spoke again:
"I have heard that the asuras are gradually drawing near; you should take the fourfold army and go to strike them.
Subhira then spoke in verse:
"If there is a place of pure leisure and no affairs, I only wish for such a place as this to be granted to me.
Śakra then replied with a verse:
"If there is such a place of leisure and joy, you should take me together to it."
Subhira spoke again in verse:
"I am now indolent and have no desire to rise; though I possess learning and knowledge, I am not adorned.
The light of the five desires of the celestial maidens fills the four quarters; I only pray that Śakra will grant me this wish."
Śakra replied with a verse:
"If there is such a place of indolence, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial maidens,
where one may indulge in the five desires and experience pleasure— if you go there, you shall be with me."
Subīra spoke again in verse:
"O Heavenly King, if there is no place for you to perform service, grant me this pleasure free from suffering."
Śakra replied in verse:
"Suvīra, since you have such [a desire], I shall share this pleasure with you.
Have you ever seen or heard of anyone who, lacking any occupation or work, was able to maintain a livelihood and enjoy happiness?"
If you now possess such a place, you may go there quickly and follow it;
you should fear worldly affairs and delight in secluded places, and you ought to hasten toward Nirvāṇa.
Upon hearing these words, Subrahma immediately assembled the fourfold army and went out to battle the asuras.
At that time, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated and driven back; the asuras, having been variously adorned, returned to their palace.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Śakra Devānām Indra, though he occupies the position of King of Devas and possesses great sovereignty, still exerts himself with diligence and praises diligence; how much more so should you, who have left the home life out of faith and donned the dharma robes, not exert yourselves with diligence and praise diligence?”
"If one can be diligent and praise diligence, such is that which accords with the Dharma of going forth.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
44 (Forty-four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, in a remote forest hermitage far from a village, many sages lived there.
Not far from that sages' abode, devas and asuras were engaged in battle."

At that time, the asura king Vemacitra, adorned with five kinds of ornaments—a celestial crown upon his head, holding a mani-whisk, bearing a flower parasol above him, girded with a jeweled sword, and wearing sandals set with various gems—arrived at the abode of the rishis.
He did not enter through the gate, but passed through the wall; furthermore, he neither spoke with nor exchanged greetings with the various seers, and then departed through the wall once more.
At that time, one seer spoke these words:
"Vemacitra and his followers lack a heart of respect; they do not exchange greetings or converse with the seers, but simply pass through the wall."
Again, another seer spoke these words:
"If the asuras had shown respect and inquired after the well-being of the seers, they would have surpassed the devas; now, they certainly do not."
One seer asked, "Who is this? Another seer replied:
"This is Vemacitra, the King of the Asuras.
The seer spoke again:

"The Dharma and insight of the Asuras are shallow; they lack the teachings of the Dharma and have no heart of reverence. They are like farmers; the gods will surely be victorious, and the Asuras shall be defeated."

At that time, Śakra arrived at the side of the seers; he immediately cast off the five kinds of royal ornaments of a celestial king and entered through the gate. He comforted the seers, went about observing them everywhere, and said to them:
"Are you all peaceful and secure? Are you free from all afflictions?"
Having finished his greetings, he departed through the gate.
Then another seer asked: "Who is this?"
He comforted him with inquiries after his well-being and observed his conduct thoroughly before departing; he possessed profound teachings and was of upright and dignified appearance.
One of the seers replied, ‘This is Śakra.’”
One seer said:
"The devas are exceedingly capable of respectful compliance; because their conduct is harmonious and appropriate, the devas will surely prevail and the asuras will be defeated.
When Vimalacitra heard the seers praising the devas and disparaging the asuras, he became extremely enraged.
Having heard this, the various seers went to where the asuras were and said to them,
"We have heard that you are filled with great rage.
They then spoke these verses:
"We have come here of our own accord, desiring to ask for our wishes;
grant us fearlessness and do not give rise to anger again.
If we have any faults, we pray that you will instruct and reprimand us."
Vemacitrin replied in verse:
"I shall not grant you fearlessness, for you have invaded and insulted me;
you humbly sought Śakra, yet you now utter disparagement against me."
"You seek fearlessness, yet I shall give you fear.
At that time, the sages replied with a verse:
"Just as a person creates for themselves, so do they personally reap the fruit of their retribution."
By performing good, one obtains good for oneself; by performing evil, evil returns as retribution.
It is like sowing seeds: according to what is sown, one receives the fruit.
You have now sown the seeds of suffering; later, you will surely receive them yourself.
"I now beg for fearlessness, yet you instead grant me terror;
from this day forward, I shall cause your fears to be inexhaustible.
Having spoken thus to the asuras face-to-face, the seers immediately ascended into the void and departed.
That very night, Vemacitrin dreamed that he was engaged in battle with Śakra; he was struck with great terror, and it happened likewise a second time.
When he dreamed for a third time, Śakra’s host actually came to seek battle.
At that time, Vemacitrin immediately engaged in combat; the asuras were defeated, and Śakra pursued them until he reached the asura palace.
Thereupon, having achieved victory in various battles and disputes, Śakra proceeded to the abode of the sages.
The various seers were in the east and Śakra was in the west, sitting facing one another.
At that time, the seer Pūrvavāta addressed Śakra with this verse:
"My body has long been that of a renunciant, Yet there is a foul odor beneath my armpits."
"The wind blows toward you; move aside and sit to the south.
Such foul odors as these are not pleasing to the devas.
At that time, Śakra replied in verse:
“Having gathered various flowers to form a crest-ornament upon the head,
with their manifold fragrances, how could one not feel weary and detached?”
"The various sages who have gone forth possess a fragrance like that of flower garlands;
I now receive it upon my head and do not find it wearying or burdensome.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Śakra dwells in the position of King of Devas because he has long venerated those who have gone forth. You bhikṣus, having gone forth out of faith, should likewise show such reverence.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
45 (45) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, his countenance exceptionally sublime and surpassing that of humans and gods, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the middle watch of the night. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, within the Jeta Grove, a brilliant radiance shone forth, surpassing even the light of day.
Then, Śakra Devānām Indra spoke this verse:
"By the cessation of what does one sleep in peace? By the abandonment of what does one sleep in peace?"
By extinguishing what is there no sorrow?
Which single dharma, when extinguished, do you praise, O Gautama?
I pray that you resolve these many doubts for me.
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse, saying:
"By extinguishing anger one sleeps in peace; by extinguishing anger one is free from sorrow.
Having uprooted the thorny poison of anger, you, Śakra, should now know this."
"In this way, anger destroys beauty and goodness; it extinguishes the superior matters praised by the Hearers.
Having heard what the Buddha spoke, Śakra Devānām Indra circumambulated the Buddha three times and joyfully put it into practice.
46. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"On the eighth day of the month, the Four Heavenly Kings dispatch their messengers to traverse the world and observe the realm, examining those who are compassionate and filial toward their parents, respectful and obedient toward their elders, and who serve śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas while practicing wholesome dharmas, as well as those who commit evil deeds. Therefore, you ought to practice wholesome dharmas, eliminate all evils, restrain your emotions, and maintain the precepts."
On the fourteenth day, the Four Heavenly Kings again dispatched their princes to inspect the world.
On the fifteenth day, the Four Heavenly Kings themselves inspected and observed it, doing exactly as they had before.
At that time, having completed their investigation, the Four Heavenly Kings went to Śakra’s Hall of Good Dharma and addressed Śakra, saying:

"Among the gods, the world of humans, and those in the intermediate realms, there are many who are unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, who do not serve their teachers or family elders, and even among them, there are few who maintain the precepts."
At that time, having heard these words, Śakra and the assembly of devas were distressed and unhappy; all the devas spoke thus:
"This will diminish the host of devas and benefit the asuras."

"If, within this world, there are those who are always able to be filial and obedient toward their parents, who make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and who are even capable of observing many precepts."
The Four Heavenly Kings reported this to Śakra, and at that time all the devas were filled with supreme joy, saying:

"Among the people of the world, there are those who practice virtuous deeds; they are most excellent and good, performing what ought to be done, thereby increasing the strength of the devas and diminishing the asuras."
Śakra rejoiced and immediately spoke these verses:
"On the eighth and fourteenth days, as well as the fifteenth,
and during the month of the gods' supernatural powers, one should uphold the pure precepts."
"This person shall be born in heaven, with merit equal to my own body.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What Śakra has said cannot be called well-spoken."
Why is this? If an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted has accomplished what was to be done, he should recite this verse:
"On the eighth and fourteenth days, And likewise on the fifteenth day,"
"And during the month of the gods' power, one who upholds the pure precepts shall obtain supreme victory; their merit will be equal to my own body.
The Buddha and the Arhats should speak these verses; they are called "truthful speech" and "well-spoken."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
47 (47) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the asura king Citta was afflicted by illness and lay in a state of great distress.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra went to his place, and the asura spoke to Śakra, saying:"
"May you cause my illness to subside and bring me peace; may my body become healthy and robust, as fresh and radiant as it was before.
Śakra replied, "If you will teach me the illusory arts of the asuras, I shall cause you to be at peace, your illness to be cured, and your joy to be restored as it was before."
The asura said, "Wait while I consult the other asuras; if it is appropriate, I shall instruct you.
The asura king then questioned the asuras.
At that time, among them was a deceitful and hypocritical asura who said to Vemacitra:
"Śakra has long practiced upright and wholesome conduct, free from all deceit and hypocrisy. You should say to Śakra:
'You have studied the deceitful illusions of the asuras; you shall enter the Lulu Hell.'"
"Should Śakra say to you:
'If I do not learn from those asuras, you need only depart and your affliction will surely be healed,' then the asura king shall follow those words and speak this verse to Śakra:"
“Śakra, the Thousand-Eyed Lord and Consort of Śacī, if he had known this illusory dharma, would surely have fallen into that Raurava hell,
where he would have been burned and boiled for the full duration of an eon.”
At that time, having heard these words, Śakra immediately said:
"Stop, stop! There is no need for illusory arts.
He then immediately made this vow:
"May your illness be cured; may you be at peace and free from affliction.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Even Śakra Devānām Indra, though occupying the rank of a deva, does not act with flattery or crookedness, but conducts himself with truthfulness. How much more so for you who have left the household life, shaved off your hair and beards—should you not abandon all matters of flattery and hypocrisy, and instead practice sincerity and straightforwardness?"
"If one acts with integrity, it accords with the Dharma of renunciation.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
48 (48) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Śakra came to where the Buddha was; as he was about to depart, he requested to receive a single precept.
What is the one precept?
"If I return to my palace and encounter those who harbor enmity or hatred toward me, even if they come to harm me, I shall never inflict harm upon them in return."
When Vemacitrin heard that Śakra was observing such precepts, he took up a sharp sword and waited by the roadside.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, hearing that the asura was waiting by the side of the road with a sword in hand, spoke to the asura from afar: "Stop!
"Stop!
You are now binding yourself," Vimalacitra said to Śakra.
"You have received a single precept from the Buddha, saying:

'If I return to my palace and encounter those who harbor enmity or hatred toward me, even if they should seek to harm me, I shall never direct evil toward them. How could you not accept such a precept?"
Śakra replied: "Although I have received the precepts, I told you, 'Stop! Stop! You are now binding yourself.
Such words do not constitute a violation of the precepts."
Vemacitrin said, "Kauśika, release me! Śakra replied:
“If you swear an oath that you will no longer harbor enmity or malice toward me, I shall release you.
Vimalacitra then spoke this oath:
“May I incur such evil retribution as would come from greed, hatred, lying, or slandering the noble ones.”
At that time, having heard this vow, Śakra immediately said to Vimalacitra,
"I now release you.
Śakra-devānām-indra returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When Vemacitrin heard that I had received the precepts, he immediately took up a sharp sword and waited by the roadside, plotting against me.
At that time, I spoke from afar to the asura, saying:”
"Stop! Stop! You are now binding yourself."
Vemacitra then said to me: "You have received a single precept from the Buddha.
If I return to my palace and see those who harbor enmity or hatred toward me, even if they come to harm me, I shall never inflict evil upon them; how could you not receive such a precept?"
I then replied: "Although I have received the precepts, I merely told you to stop; you are now binding yourself.
Such words do not constitute a violation of the precepts."
Vemacitrin then said to me: "Kauśika!
Release me!"
I then spoke these words:
"You may make a solemn vow that you will no longer harbor hatred or malice toward me; I shall release you.
When Vemacitrin heard my words, he immediately uttered this oath:
"‘May I receive such an evil retribution as this—greed, hatred, lying, and slandering the noble ones.
Hearing his vow, I immediately released him and let him go."
Śakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now that this asura has made this solemn oath, from this day forward, will he no longer harbor enmity or ill will?"
The Buddha told Śakra:
"Even if the asuras did not make a vow, they would still not commit evil; how much less so once they have made a vow?
At that time, having heard what the Buddha said, Śakra leaped for joy and, vanishing from his seat, immediately returned to his celestial palace.
49 (Forty-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Once upon a time, Śakra fought with the asuras.
At that time, the devas were defeated and the asuras prevailed.
Seeing that he was no longer victorious, Śakra immediately turned his chariot and wished to return to the celestial palace."
Along the way, he saw a *khasarpa* tree, upon which was a nest of a garuḍa.
At that time, Śakra commanded his charioteer Mātali, saying:
"In this nest there are two bird eggs; should they be harmed, you must turn the chariot and avoid this tree."
Śakra then addressed Mātali with these verses:
“Behold the nest upon the tree; within it are two eggs.
If the chariot proceeds there now, it will surely collide with them and break them.”
‘If I were to enter the ranks of the asuras with this body and lose my life, I would never harm the bird’s eggs.
Having spoken this verse, he immediately turned his chariot back.
At that time, when the host of asuras saw Śakra turn back, they were seized with great terror and each said:
"Śakra just now feigned a retreat."
"If they turn back now, they will surely destroy my army.
The host of asuras immediately retreated; the devas pursued them in their retreat until they were driven to their city.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“Śakra Devānām Indra, while dwelling in the position of a heavenly king, was still able to cultivate loving-kindness and patience throughout the long night; you, bhikṣus, should train yourselves in this way.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
50. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Śakra Devendra and the asura Bali Vairocana went to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night; their majestic radiance was blazing and intense. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side.
At that time, Śakra and Virūḍhaka illuminated the Jetavana Grove with their radiance, making it appear like broad daylight.
Then, Virūḍhaka sat to one side and spoke these verses:
"When a person is always diligent, Whatever they seek will surely be attained."
"Having already attained the principles of meaning, one dwells in peace and receives happiness.
Śakra also spoke in verse:
"If a person is always diligent, what they seek will surely be obtained."
"Once one has attained one's goal, the cultivation of patience is supreme.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What among what we have spoken is beneficial?
What is without benefit?
The Buddha told Śakra:
"Those who possess skillful discernment all speak well.
You should now listen to what I have to say.
He then spoke in verse:
"All sentient beings seek their own benefit, each according to the desires of their own mind;
likewise, they seek to satisfy their wishes for profit and pleasure. If a person applies themselves with diligence, they will surely attain what they seek;
once a task is accomplished, patience is supreme. Therefore, one should practice patience."
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Śakra and Vaiśravaṇa prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from that place to return to their palaces.
51 (51) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a poor man who was extremely destitute and deeply pitiable; yet, within the Buddha’s Dharma, he conceived pure faith, was able to maintain the precepts purely, recited the sūtras to some extent, and was also capable of giving small gifts.
Due to these four causes and conditions as karmic retribution, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the supreme and wondrous abode of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
These newly born devas possess three kinds of excellence:
first, excellence of physical appearance; second, excellence of reputation; and third, excellence of lifespan.
When the various devas saw this, they all paid him respectful homage together and went to the abode of Śakra, where they addressed Śakra, saying:
"There is a newly born deva who excels all other devas in three respects."
Śakra said:

"I have previously seen that newly born deva; when he was originally a human being, he was poor, destitute, and extremely haggard. Yet, solely through his faith in the Triple Gem, by being able to maintain the precepts purely and practicing giving to some small extent, he has now attained birth here in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
At that time, Śakra spoke these verses:
"If one gives rise to pure faith in the Triple Gem, And one's mind remains firm and unshakable,
Holding the precepts received without violation— Know that such a person is not called poor."
One is called a person whose life is wisdom; because of revering the unsurpassed Triple Gem, one attains birth in the heavens to experience supreme bliss. Therefore, one should train in this way.
At that time, having heard this verse, the devas rejoiced and accepted it with faith; they paid their respects and returned to their palaces.
52 (52) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) in the city of Rājagṛha, each performing their own sacrificial rites.
Among them, if there was a donor who placed faith in the non-Buddhist Cārika, he would say, "One must first make offerings to my teacher, Cārika";
if one placed faith in the non-Buddhist Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, he likewise said, "One must first make offerings to my teacher, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa."
If they believe in the non-Buddhist Gandhara, they all say, "First give a great alms-offering to my teacher Gandhara, and only then to others";
if they believe in the non-Buddhist named San-shui (Three Waters), they say, "One should make offerings to my teacher San-shui";
if they believe in the non-Buddhist named Lao-shengwen (Old Sravaka), they say, "First make offerings to my teacher Lao-shengwen."
If those who believe in the non-Buddhists or the Great Śrāvakas say, "One should also make offerings to my teachers, the Great Śrāvakas";
and if those who believe in the Buddha all say, "One should first make offerings to my teacher, the Tathāgata, as well as the Saṃgha."
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra thought to himself:
"Now the people of Rājagṛha have conceived great wrong views; while the Buddha and the Saṅgha are still in the world, to conceive such wrong views is called unwholesome."

At that time, Śakra immediately transformed himself into an elderly brahmin of handsome appearance; riding in a white chariot drawn by white horses, surrounded on all sides by young brahmin students (maṇava), he proceeded directly toward the monastery grounds.
At that time, the people of Rājagṛha all thought to themselves:
"Where is this old brāhmaṇa going first? We shall follow him.
Then Śakra, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those people, turned the chariot southward toward Vulture Peak Mountain.
Arriving at the place where the various carriages were stationed, he halted there.
Alighting from his vehicle, he proceeded forward to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Śakra spoke these verses:
“The Holy King who turns the Wheel of Dharma, Who can ferry others to the further shore of suffering,
Free from enmity, hatred, and fear— To him I now prostrate in homage.”
If one wishes to cultivate merit, where should one give?
Furthermore, if one desires to seek merit with diligence, one should give rise to pure faith and reverence.
By practicing generosity today, one will obtain a favorable retribution in future lives.
"In what field of merit does even a small gift yield a great fruit?
At that time, while the World-Honored One was on Vulture Peak Mountain, he expounded for Śakra, Lord of the Devas, upon that which is most supreme among sacrifices, answering in verse:
"The four fruits and the four paths, The ones perfected in meditation, clarity, and conduct—"
The power of merit is profoundly deep, like the waters of the great ocean.
This is called the truly supreme;
the disciples of the Tamer can kindle the lamp of wisdom within the great darkness.
Constantly for the sake of all sentient beings, They preach the Dharma and reveal the Path;
This is called the Sangha-field of merit, Vast and without bound.
If one gives to this field of merit, This is called a virtuous gift.
If one makes offerings to this field of merit, it is called a "virtuous sacrifice.
To burn objects as a sacrifice to heaven is merely a waste with no benefit;
it is not called a "virtuous burning."
Having performed various meritorious deeds in youth, one later attains great wealth and benefit;
this is called "well-burnt.
This is known as a noble field of merit; by giving to even a single person among the sequence of the Sangha, [one gains such reward].
One will surely obtain great fruit hereafter.
As taught by the Knower of the World, the Buddha of Immeasurable Merit praised the Saṅgha with a hundred verses.
There is no field of merit superior to the Saṃgha; if a person plants even a small amount of goodness, the reward they obtain will be immeasurable.
One should therefore give to the Saṃgha—those who are able to uphold the Dharma in its entirety.
This is what is called the Saṃgha.
Just as there are many precious jewels, so too is the ocean of the Saṃgha;
it abounds with the jewels of merit. If one can give to this jewel of the Saṃgha, [one will obtain great reward].
Such a person is called a virtuous man.
If one can give with faith, know that such a person will obtain joy during the three times;
because of this joy during the three times, [they shall attain liberation].
Able to cross over the three evil realms, Dispelling all dust and defilement,
and removing the poisoned arrows of affliction;
Benefiting oneself as well as others— One who can establish such a sacrifice, [is truly a field of merit].
Such a person is called a wise one in the world.
With faith already purified, they shall reach the state of the unconditioned;
this is the supreme bliss of the world, where the wise are born.
Having heard these verses, Śakra rejoiced and leaped for joy; he vanished from his seat and returned to his celestial palace.

Not long after Śakra had returned to his palace, the elders and brahmins in the city of Rājagṛha rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"We pray that the World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, will accept our joyful invitation for a great sacrificial feast tomorrow morning."
At that time, the Tathāgata silently granted his consent.

Then, the brahmins and householders of Rājagṛha, knowing that the Buddha had accepted their invitation by remaining silent, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and each returned to their respective dwellings.
When those people had returned home, each prepared various fragrant and delicious foods, arranging them with purity and cleanliness.
Having completed the preparations, they spread out seats in the early morning and provided pure water; then they sent a messenger to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to inform the World-Honored One, saying:
"The time for the meal has arrived."

At that time, the Tathāgata put on his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the assembly of monks with the World-Honored One at their head, proceeded toward that city and arrived at the site of the great shrine.
Having arrived there, the Tathāgata prepared his seat and sat before the Saṃgha; the people of that city then prepared excellent couches and seats for the Saṃgha and sat with them.

At that time, when the various elders observed that the assembly was seated, they each distributed pure water; the brahmins and elders personally served various kinds of fragrant and delicious food and drink with their own hands.
At that time, each of the people urged others to offer more.
Then, the World-Honored One, observing that the assembly of monks had finished their meal, immediately set aside his bowl and entrusted it to Ānanda.
At that time, the people each prepared their own seats and sat before the Buddha, focusing their minds with reverent devotion, desiring to hear the Dharma.
Then, the Tathāgata praised their offerings and spoke these verses:
“Among the scriptures of the Brahmins, The sacrificial fire is supreme.
Among the scriptures of the non-Buddhists, the Veda is supreme;
Among all people in the world, the king is foremost;
Among the hundred rivers and myriad streams, the great ocean is called the greatest.
Among all the stars and lunar mansions, the moonlight is called the foremost;
among all luminous things, the sunlight is the most supreme.
Above, below, and in the four directions, throughout the world and among gods and humans—
"Among all the assemblies of noble sages, the Buddha is the most supreme and honored.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached various teachings to the people of Rājagṛha, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; the people were filled with joy and withdrew from their seats.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Rishi Subila extinguished his anger; on the eighth day of the month he fell ill, yet he maintained a single precept. [There were also] the bird’s nest and Pāli.
The Poor Man and the Great Sacrifice (53). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling by stages through the kingdom of Kosala and arrived at Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard that the Buddha had arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and after exchanging greetings, sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I have heard in the past that you left the household life to seek the Way, vowing to achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Is it true that you spoke such words?
Or is this perhaps a false report spread by others?"
"Is it because of such censure and reproach that you have spoken these words?
The Buddha told King Prasenajit:

"Such words as these are words of truth; they are not reproach, nor are they exaggeration or diminution. They are truly my own words, truly spoken in accordance with the Dharma, and not spoken contrary to the Dharma. No outsider whatsoever would be able to censure or reproach me."
King Prasenajit spoke again:
"Although I have heard such words from you, I am still unable to believe them.
Why do I not believe? "
"From ancient times, there have been many who had long since left the household life—venerable elders and long-established figures among the brahmins:

Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra. Even these venerable elders did not believe that they had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how much less could you, being young and having recently left the household life, have attained it?"
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
There are four things in the world that must not be treated lightly, even if they are small."
What are these four?
First, although a prince is young, he must never be treated with contempt.
Second, although a dragon’s son is young, he likewise must not be treated with contempt.
"Third, although a fire may be small, it must not be treated with contempt.
Fourth, although a bhikṣu may be junior, he must not be treated with contempt.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Though the king be but small, he has fully practiced all arts and skills;
since his birthplace is truly noble, he is not mixed with vulgarity or filth.
Possessing great and beautiful renown, it is heard and known by all."
Thus, although it is called small, its reality should not be underestimated.
One who wishes to protect their own life should not treat even the small with contempt.
Though a kṣatriya may be of low status, by law he is entitled to succeed to the royal throne.
Having already succeeded to the royal throne, one ought to administer punishments according to the Dharma;
therefore, one should act with reverence and obedience, and it is not fitting to give rise to contempt or negligence.
Whether among the various villages or in secluded and quiet places, [one should maintain this].
If one sees a young dragon, though its form is minute and subtle,
it can become large and can also become small;
it can likewise raise clouds and pour down heavy rain.
If one wishes to protect one's own life, one must not treat them lightly, for they are surely capable of unleashing their venomous sting;
for the sake of one's own benefit, one ought to guard oneself against them.
If all conditions are complete, the fierce flames blaze most intensely;
when they encounter a great gale, they can burn down mountains and forests.
Once the woods and fields have been consumed, they will grow back again when the time is right.
One who wishes to protect their own life should not treat even a small fire with contempt.
If one uses harsh words to insult those who maintain pure precepts,
one’s own body, children, and grandchildren will all be subjected to slander.
In future lives, you shall likewise receive the retribution for evil;
therefore, you should protect yourself and not inflict evil upon others.
A Kṣatriya endowed with skillful arts, a son of a nāga, and fire—[these are difficult to overcome].
“A bhikṣu who maintains pure precepts—these four should not be slighted.
For the sake of protecting one’s own life, one should prudently keep them at a distance.

At that time, having heard these words, King Prasenajit’s heart trembled and the hair on his body stood on end. He immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

At this moment, I truly possess transgressions and offenses; I know myself to have violated the precepts, like one who is infantile, foolish, deranged, ignorant, and has performed what is unwholesome.”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will grant me permission to repent.
The Buddha said to King Prasenajit,
"Out of compassion for you, I now grant you permission to repent."
At that time, King Prasenajit, having received this confession, was filled with great joy; he paid his respects and departed.
54 (54) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit was by nature benevolent and filial. When his mother first passed away, he wailed with grief and longing, unable to bear the sorrow.

After cremating his mother, he bathed himself; while his clothes and hair were still damp from the water, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling at midday. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side.
The Buddha said to the king:
"From where have you come?
Your robes and hair are still damp."
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My own compassionate mother was especially revered by me; she has now passed away.”
"I escorted my mother’s funeral as far as the wilderness; once the burial was completed, I bathed thoroughly, yet my clothes and hair are still damp.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"Did you hold your mother in the utmost love and respect?"
The king replied, "I truly do love and revere her.

Should there be anyone capable of restoring my mother to life, I would give them my entire army of elephants, chariots, cavalry, and infantry; I would continue my mother’s life without any regret in my heart."
"Even if he were rewarded with half the kingdom, he would not harbor any resentment.
The King spoke again, saying, "The Buddha’s words are truthful: all who are born must inevitably return to death."
The Buddha said: "It is so! It is so!"
Birth is inevitably followed by death; among the five destinies and four modes of birth, there is none that does not end in death.
Whether one be a king, a subject, a citizen, or a member of the Brahmin class, all must ultimately return to death.
An anointed king of men, possessing sovereign power and ruling over a realm, must ultimately meet his end.
Even a Wheel-Turning Sage King, who rules over the four continents and is endowed with the seven treasures, shall likewise die.
The rishis with the five supernatural powers, dwelling in mountains and thickets, drinking water and eating fruit, also return to death.

The gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, who experience supreme bliss, whose radiance is brilliant and intense, who dwell in celestial palaces and enjoy long lifespans, likewise return to ultimate extinction.

All the Arhats have laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, exhausted all fetters of existence, and achieved mastery over their minds; through right knowledge they are liberated, and even this final body shall return to dissolution.
The various Pratyekabuddhas, solitary and without companion, who always dwell in seclusion and tranquility, shall likewise be dispersed and extinguished.

Even the Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, who possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and who can roar the lion’s roar, have bodies that are impermanent and must ultimately return to dispersion and extinction.
The Buddha said, "Great King!
For your sake, I have made various distinctions: birth is inevitably followed by death."
"To speak briefly, there is no birth that does not end.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"All who are born must die; The span of life inevitably comes to its end."
Receiving retribution according to one's karma, good and evil each yield their respective fruits.
By cultivating merit, one ascends to heaven; by committing evil, one enters hell.
By practicing the Way, one cuts off birth and death, forever entering into nirvana.
Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering into mountain clefts,
is there any place on earth where one can escape and not undergo death.
Even the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Bodhisattvas, and the Śrāvakas— none are exempt.
"If even [the Buddha] will cast off this impermanent body, how much more so must all ordinary worldlings?
At that time, King Prasenajit, having heard what the Buddha had said, his mind opened and his understanding was clarified; he no longer felt sorrowful, but departed with joy.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
55 (55) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit was in a secluded place, reflecting alone and quietly:
"As for those who are human beings, how do they love themselves?
How do they hate themselves?"
He further thought:
"If one engages in wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, and remains far removed from all evils, this is called 'loving oneself.
If one engages in unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, and commits various evil deeds, this is called 'not loving oneself.'"
King Prasenajit, having reflected thus, rose from his secluded place and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While dwelling alone in seclusion, I reflected thus:
"What is meant by 'loving oneself,' and what is meant by 'not loving oneself'?"
"If one can practice virtue through body, speech, and mind, this is called loving oneself;
if one performs unwholesome deeds through body, speech, and mind, this is called not loving oneself.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Great King!
It is indeed so.
If a person acts wickedly through body, speech, and mind, this is called not loving oneself."
Why is this? Those who commit evil, though they may have enemies, do not necessarily cause immediate harm;
however, the destruction wrought by the evil karma one creates oneself is profoundly deep. Therefore, to create evil karma for oneself is called "not loving oneself."
Furthermore, to commit killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct for one's own sake constitutes self-harm.
If a person who practices virtue through body, speech, and mind should form this thought:
"I renounce my beloved home, wife, and children."
This is called not loving oneself, yet it is in truth loving oneself. Why is this?
For such a person, though they may have friends, parents, and brothers whose kindness penetrates to the very marrow of their bones, when they reach old age and decay, none can save them.
"To practice virtue through one's own body, speech, and mind, thereby being able to deliver oneself—that is called 'loving oneself.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"If a person loves themselves, They will not inflict evil upon others."
There is no one who, having committed evil deeds, attains happiness.
If a person loves themselves, they should cultivate various wholesome karmas;
thus they will swiftly obtain all manner of happiness.
Now, one who wishes to love themselves should protect themselves,
just as one would guard a frontier city in a wilderness teeming with bandits.
When encountering times free from calamity, one should remain hidden within oneself.
"If one loses [this] without encountering difficulties, yet encounters difficulties, the suffering will be endless.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
56 (56). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, while in a secluded place, had this reflection:
"What is it to protect oneself?
What is it not to protect oneself?
He then reflected further to himself:
"If a person cultivates goodness, they are said to protect themselves;
if a person commits evil, they are said not to protect themselves.
Having reflected thus, he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
While in a quiet place, I engaged in this reflection:"
"What is self-protection?
What is lack of self-protection?
He then further reflects:
"If one cultivates wholesome conduct, it is called protecting oneself;
if one engages in unwholesome conduct, it is called not protecting oneself.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"It is indeed so!
It is indeed so!
If one surrounds oneself with the fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—that is not called protecting oneself."
Why is this? Because it is not due to external protection.
If a person’s body, speech, and mind are virtuous, then even without the fourfold army, this is called protecting oneself.
Why is this? Because there is internal protection (*adhyātma-rakṣā*).
This internal protection is superior to external protection; therefore, it is called "protecting oneself."
The Buddha then spoke these verses:
"If a person wishes to protect themselves, They should guard their body, speech, and mind;
They should practice wholesome dharmas And possess both a sense of shame and dread of blame."
Those who do not guard their threefold action,
Whose wrong views and slumber obscure all wholesome dharmas, And who follow after Māra,
Bring about their own ruin; Therefore, one should protect oneself.
"Cultivate meditative concentration and wisdom, and always remember the teachings of the Buddha.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
57 (Fifty-seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, while in a secluded place, reflected thus:
"In this world, there are few who can attain wealth, nobility, and prosperity.

Even if they do attain such wealth and prosperity, those who do not indulge in arrogance or luxury, but remain chaste, modest, and content, who restrain their cravings and do not afflict sentient beings—such people are rare."

In this world, there are many people who, having acquired superior wealth and status, become arrogant and self-indulgent; they crave sensual desires and further afflict sentient beings—such people are numerous.
King Prasenajit, having reflected thus in a secluded place, rose from his seat and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In a quiet place, I reflected thus:

"In this world, if there were someone who, having acquired superior wealth and status, knew contentment within their own mind, was able to remain free from arrogance and self-indulgence, did not crave sensual desires, and did not cause harm to others—such people are few."
Furthermore, there are many people who, having obtained superior wealth and estates, become arrogant and self-indulgent, craving sensual desires and further afflicting sentient beings.
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
It is truly so, it is truly so."
Within this world, there are many people who, having received noble titles and emoluments, become arrogant and self-indulgent; they crave sensual desires and inflict suffering upon sentient beings.
"Such a foolish person shall suffer for a long night, undergo great loss and decline, and after the end of his life, he will certainly enter hell.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"

It is like a fisherman and his disciples, who are skilled in the methods and expedient means of catching fish; they cast a fine and dense net across the current and drag it in, whereby fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, and all other aquatic creatures are caught in the net.
Just as these aquatic creatures and others that enter the net are all gathered into the hands of the fisherman, who drags, twists, and turns them according to his will;
so too it is with many people in the world who, having obtained superior rank and emoluments, become arrogant and self-indulgent, craving the five desires and further afflicting sentient beings.
Why is this? Such foolish people enter the net of Māra; captured by that net, their every movement and action revolves around what Māra has wrought.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Recklessly attached to worldly affairs, Deluded and craving the five desires,
They do not know there will be bitter fruits, Like fish entering a dense net."
"Since this karma has already been completed, one will experience extreme and great suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
58 (Fifty-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, while in a secluded place, reflected thus:
"In this world, there are few people who, having obtained superior rank and emoluments, do not become arrogant and self-indulgent, do not crave the five desires, and do not afflict sentient beings."
Within this world, there are many people who, having attained superior status and wealth, become arrogant and self-indulgent; they crave the five desires and further afflict sentient beings.
Having reflected thus, he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now, while in a quiet place, I have had this thought:
"In this world, there are few people who, having attained a superior foundation of merit, do not become arrogant or self-indulgent, do not crave the five desires, and do not afflict sentient beings."
"Many people, having attained superior foundations of wealth and power, become greedy for and addicted to the five desires, further afflicting sentient beings.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
So it is, so it is. It is truly as you have said.
It is like a hunter who digs a pit to capture deer; once they are driven into the pit, he may take them as he pleases.

Within this world, there are many people who, having attained superior foundations of power, become arrogant and self-indulgent; they crave the five desires and likewise inflict suffering upon sentient beings.
"Such foolish people fall into the pit of Māra; following the deeds of Māra, they shall enter hell and suffer for a long night.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Recklessly attached to worldly affairs, Deluded and craving the five desires,"
Not knowing the evil fruits that follow, like a deer entering a deep pit, one undergoes extreme suffering and affliction.
For those who perform such evil deeds, there is the retribution of sorrow upon sorrow; what use is regret once it has come?
"Those who cultivate wholesome deeds will later obtain wondrous rewards;
at the time of death their hearts will be joyful, and thereafter they shall have no regrets.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
59 (Fifty-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There is an elder named Mahānāman; his family is immensely wealthy, possessing abundant riches and treasures.
The Buddha asked the king:
“What constitutes great wealth?

The king addressed the Buddha, saying, “In that householder’s home, gold, silver, and rare treasures number in the hundreds of thousands of millions, beyond measure; how much more so his other riches!”
Though they possess wealth, they are unable to eat fine food; what they consume consists of coarse, gritty grains mixed with husks.
When they prepare a soup, they boil ginger until it is completely disintegrated, and once cooked, they take it out again to sell for their livelihood.
As for what he wears, he dons only coarse cloth; his five garments are all tattered and worn-out, serving as his inner clothing.
He rides an old, dilapidated chariot, using leaves strung together as a parasol.
Never before had he been seen giving alms to śramaṇas, brahmins, or poor beggars.
Whenever he wished to eat, he would first close his doors, fearing that śramaṇas, brahmins, and others might come to him for alms.
The Buddha said,
“Great King! Such a person is not a virtuous man.”

Why is this? Having obtained such wealth, they are unable to maintain a clear and upright mind while enjoying it; furthermore, they cannot provide for or support their wives and children, nor do they bestow gifts upon their slaves and servants, nor do they occasionally practice almsgiving toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, nor do they seek the superior karma that brings the reward of rebirth in heaven.
It is like a salt marsh where there is a small pool of water; because it is salty and bitter, no one can drink from it, and it eventually dries up completely.
The foolish people of the world are just like this.

Having acquired great wealth and property, he is unable to practice giving or enjoy it himself; furthermore, he is incapable of making offerings to his parents, nor to his wife and children, nor to his retinue, slaves, servants, or friends and acquaintances. Failing to bestow anything upon them at all, although he possesses abundant riches and treasures, they provide him with no benefit whatsoever.
The Buddha said, “Great King!

A virtuous man, having acquired wealth and property, is able to use it for himself and experience happiness with integrity; he is also able to make offerings to his teachers and elders, his parents, and his wife and children, as well as to his kinsmen, servants, laborers, and friends and acquaintances, even extending his offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor and destitute, being capable of bestowing gifts upon them all.”
The wealth and treasures acquired by such a virtuous person are called the fruit of superior karma;
they serve as the cause for happiness and the condition for rebirth in heaven. This person’s accumulation of wealth thus accomplishes great goodness.

For example, near a city, village, or town, there is a clear and cool pond from which fine water flows forth; its four sides are level and even, it abounds with trees, and is filled with various flowers and fruits. Soft grass covers the ground everywhere, so that all people may bathe therein and obtain excellent drinking water, while birds and beasts soar and frolic in joy.
"A virtuous and robust man is also like this; he shall even be reborn in heaven and achieve great goodness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as in salty, barren soil, There is a cool, deep pool of water."
Bitter and salty, it is undrinkable; later, it boils down until it is completely exhausted.
So too is the case with the wretched man: though he possesses abundant wealth and treasures, he cannot provide for his own food or clothing, nor does he give anything to others.
This is what is called being "stolid.
For example, on a level and broad ground, there is a fine, clear-flowing pool;
the forest is also lush and verdant, where humans and beasts alike find joy.
"These are called the wise.
Like a great bull-king, they experience happiness upon birth and are reborn in the heavens upon death.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
60. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a great elder in the city named Mahānāman.
Having no male heir, he met with illness and passed away.
At that time, according to the laws of the kingdom, if no son was born, after his death, the family property would escheat to the state.
For this reason, all the property belonging to Mahānāman should now revert to the sovereign.
At that time, King Prasenajit, his body covered in dust, went to where the Buddha was; having prostrated himself in worship, he withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha said to the king,
"For what reason have you come here today with your body covered in dust and your countenance altered from its usual state?
King Prasenajit replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder named Mahānāman who passed away yesterday. Because he had no son, all his wealth and treasures have been confiscated by the palace; it was for the sake of viewing these riches that I braved the wind and dust, and thus my body is covered in grime.”
The Buddha asked the king,
"Is Mahānāman truly very wealthy?
The king immediately replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.
In what way is one greatly wealthy?"
There were gold, silver, and precious jewels numbering in the tens of billions, beyond all calculation, let alone other forms of wealth.

Although he possessed such treasures and vast accumulations, because of his stinginess and greed, he begrudged them and would not consume them; as for what he did eat, it was merely chaff, weeds, and husks, which were extremely coarse and unpalatable.
When preparing soup, once the ginger has been boiled, he takes it back out and sells it for his livelihood.
As for what he wears, he dons only coarse cloth; five pieces of coarse and tattered fabric serve as his undergarments.
He rides in a dilapidated old cart with a parasol made by stringing together leaves;
he has never been seen to practice even a small amount of giving toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or poor beggars.
The Buddha said:
"Such a foolish person is not a virtuous man. Why is this?"

Although he possesses wealth and treasures, he cannot open his mind to receive happiness with integrity; furthermore, he is unable to provide for his parents and wife and children, nor does he bestow gifts upon his slaves and servants, nor does he occasionally give alms to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, nor does he seek the wholesome reward of rebirth in heaven.
The Buddha told the king:
"This Mahānāman, in times past, had already planted a small root of merit under the Pratyekabuddha Tagaraśikhin."

At that time, when giving food and drink, he did not give with a sincere heart, nor did he give with faith; he did not give with his own hands, nor did he give with reverence, but instead tossed it away as he gave.
Having completed the act of giving, he later felt regret and thought to himself:
"How could I have given my food and drink to this shaven-headed śramaṇa?"
"It would be better to give it to the servants in my own household.
Because he gave up his body in that manner, he was reborn into the family of a preeminent and immensely wealthy great householder in Śrāvastī.

Although he was born into the home of such a wealthy householder, because he had previously felt regret over giving the food, he naturally took no pleasure in wearing fine clothes, nor did he enjoy eating exquisite foods; he found no delight at all in saddled horses, carriages, or any articles of adornment.

"Great King, you should know that in a former life, Mahānāman’s family was wealthy and influential. For the sake of wealth, he killed his half-brother; because of this cause and condition, he fell into hell and underwent various sufferings for immeasurable years. It is for this reason that his wealth has repeatedly, seven times over, been confiscated by the government."

Due to the karmic cause of offering food to the Pratyekabuddha Mahānāma at Taugala, Mahānāma’s store of merit was exhausted; like a great criminal who, after casting off his body, enters hell, so too did Mahānāma, upon casting off his body, enter the Great Howling Hell (Mahāraurava).
At that time, King Prasenajit again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Did Mahānāman truly enter the Great Howling Hell after casting off his body?”
The Buddha said, "He has truly entered.
When the king heard this, he wept with tears streaming down his face; he adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and spoke these verses:
"Money, grain, silks, and precious jewels, Slaves, servants, and retinues— None of these will follow, nor anyone who follows them; Not even a small portion can be taken."
When one is overcome by death and abandons the corpse, though all manner of wealth and treasures be arrayed before one,
not a single thing can be stored away, nor can even a small portion be taken along.
What thing follows a person, just as a shadow follows its form?
Good and evil receive their retribution without fail; only this [karma] follows a person like a shadow.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Good and evil follow a person, Just as a shadow follows a form;
Wherever one goes, They are never parted."
Just as one with meager provisions Increases suffering while crossing a perilous path, So too it is with those who practice evil: They cannot reach the auspicious path.
Just as one with abundant provisions Traverses the perilous road in peace and ease,
So it is for one who cultivates merit: they reach a secure and auspicious place.
Just as those long separated from one another, having reached a vast and distant land, safely return home with hearts full of joy and delight.
Wife, children, and kinsmen rejoice in supreme happiness;
so it is for the practitioner of virtue, whom their own wholesome deeds come to welcome.
Just as one who has been separated from kinsmen rejoices upon being reunited with them, so do they rejoice when meeting their virtuous karma.
Therefore, one should accumulate merit for the sake of future lives.
Desiring to obtain blessings in the next world, one should practice right conduct;
thus, one will not be censured now and shall experience happiness hereafter.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
61 (61) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit wished to perform a great sacrifice. He had a thousand bull-kings fed and tied to pillars, along with several thousand gayals, water buffaloes, milch cows, calves, and young bulls;
there were also several thousand goats and rams, as well as various other domestic animals, all tethered at the sacrificial ground.
At that time, various brahmins from other kingdoms, having heard of the king’s great sacrifice, came from afar and assembled in Śrāvastī.

Then, at dawn, a great number of bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city to beg for food. They heard that King Prasenajit intended to perform a great sacrifice, providing for a thousand bull-kings, as well as thousands each of wild oxen, water buffaloes, milch cows, calves, and yearlings;
there were also thousands of goats and rams.
In this manner, various kinds of animals were all bound and tethered at that sacrificial ground.
Furthermore, they heard that Brahmins from other countries, having heard that King Prasenajit was preparing for a great sacrifice, had all gathered together in Śrāvastī.

When the bhikṣus had finished their almsround, they put away their robes and bowls, washed their feet, and went to where the Buddha was. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Today, as we entered the city to beg for alms, we heard of such matters.
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Month after month, one may perform hundreds of thousands of sacrifices, Cultivating these practices in the pursuit of merit;..."
It is not equal to a single moment of faith in the Buddha, even one-sixteenth part thereof.
To perform hundreds of thousands of sacrifices month after month, practicing them in pursuit of merit,
is not equal to a single moment of faith in the Dharma, even one-sixteenth part thereof.
Month after month, performing a hundred thousand sacrifices to seek merit—
this is not worth even a sixteenth part of placing faith in the Sangha. Month after month,
performing a hundred thousand sacrifices to seek merit— this is not worth even a sixteenth part of placing faith in the Sangha.
It is not equal to a single portion—one sixteenth—of a mind of loving-kindness.
To practice this for a hundred thousand sacrifices month after month in pursuit of merit is not equal to having compassion for sentient beings;
it does not match even one-sixteenth part of that.
Month after month, performing a hundred thousand sacrifices to seek merit is not worth a sixteenth part of having compassion for spirits and deities; month after month,
performing a hundred thousand sacrifices is not equal to a single virtuous thought.
Compassion for the class of animals is but one sixteenth part;
Month after month, performing hundreds of thousands of sacrifices, It is not equal to having faith and delighting in what the Buddha has taught,
Which is worth one sixteenth part of that merit.
Even if one performs various sacrifices and practices the rites of fire-worship,
seeking blessings by performing these various offerings throughout the full course of a year,
it is not equal to standing upright with a rectified body.
"One prostration toward the Buddha is one-fourth of the [fourfold] division.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
62 (Sixty-second). Thus have I heard:

At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"A king binds people with iron, wood, and rope;
but the noble sages, observing this matter, know deeply that these are not firm bonds."
If one is attached to wife and children, to wealth and precious jewels—such bonds that fetter a person are more solid than those.
Fools give rise to attachment for wife, children, and wealth; [but these are not as firm as the bond of craving].
"In truth, like a torrential flood, it sweeps away all ordinary people.
