63 (Sixty-three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha led his fourfold army and came to engage in a great battle against King Prasenajit of Kosala.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, defeated the army led by King Prasenajit.
King Prasenajit, riding alone in a single chariot, was the only one who managed to enter the city.

At that time, the bhikṣus entered the city to beg for food; having witnessed this event, they finished their almsround, washed their feet, and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This morning, as we entered the city to beg for alms, we saw King Ajātaśatru and King Prasenajit each arraying their fourfold armies, engaged in a most great battle.”
"King Prasenajit’s fourfold army was defeated by them; only the king himself, riding alone in a single chariot, managed to enter the city.
When the World-Honored One heard of this matter, he immediately spoke these verses:
"To be victorious breeds much resentment; To be defeated brings distress and sleepless nights."
"If there is neither victory nor defeat, one sleeps peacefully in tranquil extinction.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
64 (Sutra 64). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha and King Prasenajit each arrayed their fourfold army, and they engaged in a great battle.
King Prasenajit utterly defeated the army led by King Ajātaśatru and furthermore captured King Ajātaśatru himself.
Having achieved victory, King Prasenajit mounted the same carriage as King Ajātaśatru and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating at the Buddha’s feet.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī—I have harbored no resentment or ill will toward him from the very beginning.”
"He has always harbored hatred and jealousy toward me;
yet, as he is the son of my own dear friend, for this reason I now wish to release him so that he may return to his kingdom."
The Buddha said,
"Great King!
You may release him and let him go."

"If you can release that king, it will bring great benefit for a long night. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "The power that can break another's army Is itself destroyed by that other; The strength that can shatter another's host Is itself shattered by that other. If one can subdue the enemy with one's own power, One will not be harmed by others.

If one can subdue the enemy through one's own strength, One will not be harmed by others. Therefore, one should subdue the enemy with one's own power; One should not be subdued by the enemy's power. If one can subdue the enemy with one's own power, One will not be harmed by others. If one can subdue the enemy through one's own strength, One will not be harmed by others. Therefore, one should subdue the enemy with one's own power; One should not be subdued by the enemy's power."* *Note: The final two lines of the verse are reconstructed based on the standard structure of such Buddhist didactic verses to complete the meaning.*
One who has the power to plunder others will, in turn, be plundered by them.
The fool claims there is no retribution, yet he will surely undergo great suffering;
only at the time of his death will he realize that retribution truly exists.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
65 (65) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, while in a secluded place, reflected thus:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha is exceedingly meaningful and beneficial;
it can bring about immediate retribution, is free from feverish affliction, does not depend on the passage of time, and can lead people to a good destination. He says to all people:"
"Come, you all!
I shall well demonstrate the sublime Dharma to you. For one who is wise, this is to be personally realized and thoroughly understood through deep penetration.

You require a virtuous friend; you require a virtuous companion. You should always befriend such a virtuous friend, and not turn toward evil friends or wicked associates; you must distance yourselves from evil companions."
Having reflected thus, he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In a secluded place, I reflected thus:
"The Dharma taught by the Buddha possesses great benefit and purpose;
it can bring about results in the present life, free from all feverish afflictions, without depending on the passage of time... and even extends to not associating with evil friends."
The Buddha said to the king: "It is so, it is so.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha possesses great significance and benefit;
it can bring about rewards in the present life, and even leads one to refrain from associating with evil companions."
In the past, while I was at the Gṛdhrakūṭa Forest near Rājagṛha,
the bhikṣu Ānanda was alone in a quiet place and reflected thus:
"A virtuous friend is half of the holy life (*brahmacarya*)."
After Ānanda had risen, he came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and spoke these words:
"A virtuous friend is half of the holy life (brahmacarya), and not so a bad acquaintance, a bad companion, or a bad friend."
I said to Ānanda: "Stop! Stop!"
Do not speak such words. Why is this?
For a virtuous friend, a good companion, and a virtuous associate constitute the very embodiment of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Furthermore, as for having virtuous friends as companions, one does not join with evil associates, wicked friends, or evil companions as a faction.
Why is this? It is because, by means of virtuous friends, I have been liberated from birth and death.
"Therefore, you should know that a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) is the entirety of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Such matters should be understood through discernment.

The Dharma taught by the Buddha possesses great benefit and meaning; it can bring about rewards in the present life, and even leads one to avoid associating with evil friends, evil companions, or evil associates.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is supreme.
Those who are heedless are censured by the noble ones."
If one is heedful, one shall attain the station of the Lord of Devas and be supreme among all the gods.
Between that which is done and that which is not done, heedfulness is the most excellent.
"If one is not negligent, sitting in meditation to exhaust all outflows, one shall attain the supreme fruit.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
66 (Sixty-six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, while in a secluded place, reflected thus:
"Is there perhaps any single dharma that can bring benefit in the present life as well as benefit in future lives?
Having had this thought, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is there perhaps a single dharma that can bring benefit in the present life and benefit in future lives?
The Buddha told the king:
"I have a single dharma; if it is practiced and expanded, it will bring great benefit in both the present and the future."
What is called the practice of the dharma of heedfulness brings benefit in the present life and also benefits in future lives.
It is like the great earth, which can produce the hundred grains;
all grasses and trees, as well as all wholesome dharmas, likewise arise because of heedfulness.
Heedfulness increases; heedfulness expands.
Great King!
It is just as with the great earth: all seeds grow because of the earth, and they expand because of the earth.
It is likewise for all sentient beings that they rely upon heedfulness.
Just as among all root-incenses, the black solid incense is the foremost, so too is it with all wholesome dharmas: they depend upon heedfulness.
Among solid fragrances, red sandalwood is the foremost; this matter is likewise so: among all wholesome dharmas, non-negligence is the foundation.
Non-negligence is the cause of the true dharma.
Heedfulness is the source from which all wholesome qualities arise.
Among all flower garlands, the *gandharvī* lute-flower garland is the most supreme;
among all wholesome qualities, heedfulness is the most supreme.
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all water-born flowers, the blue lotus is foremost;
among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above:
"Among all the tracks of animals, the elephant's track is the greatest.
Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Just as in a battle with bandits, one who is able to go out first to fight is called the foremost;
among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is the foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all beasts, the lion is foremost;
among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all palatial towers, the Pāṇaśā is foremost.
Among all wholesome dharmas, non-heedlessness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all the trees of Jambudvīpa, the tree atop the realm of Jambudvīpa is the foremost.
Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is the foremost."
The rest is as explained above.

Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all *pāṭala* trees, the variegated *pāṭala* is the foremost.
Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is the foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all trees, the Pārijātaka is foremost;
among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all mountains, Mount Sumeru is foremost.
Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above:
"Among all golds, Jāmbūnada gold is foremost;
among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above:
"Among all fine garments, those of Kāśī are foremost;
among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all forms, white is foremost.
Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."
The rest is as explained above.
"Among all birds, the golden-winged one is foremost.
Among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is foremost."

"Among all forms of light, sunlight is foremost.
So too is the dharma of heedfulness."

"As for the various virtuous practices mentioned above, heedfulness (*apramāda*) is their root and their cause of origination.
Therefore, Great King, you should now cultivate the dharma of heedfulness and should likewise rely upon the dharma of heedfulness."
If the king is thus, his queen, as well as his consorts and ladies-in-waiting, shall likewise not be negligent;
and the princes, ministers, and all their subordinate officials shall do the same.
If one is heedful, it is equivalent to guarding the inner and outer quarters of the royal palace.
Because of heedfulness, the storehouses become full.
When a king is heedful, he protects himself and protects all others as well.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Non-negligence is supreme; negligence invites much reproach.
By being non-negligent in this life, one attains great benefit in the next."
"Benefiting others in the present and benefiting the world, understanding that both benefit them—such a person is called a hero; this is the conduct of the wise.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
67 (Sixty-seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, while in a secluded place, reflected thus:
“There are three things in the world:
first, that which is loathsome; second, that which is unlovely; and third, that which is not to be remembered.
What is meant by ‘that which is loathsome’?”
This is what is called old age.
What is meant by "unlovely"?
This is what is called sickness.
"What is it that cannot be pursued with longing? It is what is called death.
Having reflected thus, King Prasenajit rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself before the Buddha, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
While in a quiet place, I engaged in this reflection:"
“There are three things in the world:
first, that which is loathsome; second, that which is unlovely; and third, that which is not to be remembered.
What is meant by ‘that which is loathsome’?”
This is what is called old age.
What is meant by being unlovely?
This is what is called illness.
"What is it that cannot be pursued with longing?
It is what is called death.
The Buddha said to the king:
"So it is! So it is! These three kinds of dharmas are indeed as Your Majesty has said."
The Buddha said,
“Great King!
If these three did not exist in the world, the Buddha would not appear in the world, nor would he preach the Dharma.”
"Because these three exist, the Buddha appears in the world to preach the Dharma for the sake of the masses.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The king’s chariot is magnificently adorned, Its ornamentation is most wonderful and marvelous."
Through long duration, form decays; just as the body inevitably returns to old age, so too the true Dharma has no aging, for it is handed down in succession from one to another. Alas!
How evil is the thief of old age! That which was upright and most exquisite in form—
"You are capable of bringing about ruin.
Even if one's lifespan reaches a full hundred years, one must inevitably enter the path of death.
Illness comes to seize away one's strength, and old age delivers one unto death."
"Examine the mind with diligent vigor, Thoroughly understand the limits of birth, And surpass those hosts of Māra’s armies;
Cross over to the far shore of existence and birth-and-death.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
68 (Sixty-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When practicing giving, to whom should one give?"
The Buddha replied to the king,
"One who practices giving should bestow gifts upon others according to their own inclinations and desires.
The king asked the Buddha again:
“Where must one give alms to obtain a great fruit?
The Buddha answered the king,
“Your question is different from the previous one.”
I now ask you; answer as you see fit.

Suppose an army is set out for battle, and there is a Kṣatriya from the east who is robust and strong, yet he is not skilled in the art of war, nor does he know how to properly discipline his body or master the arts of archery. He is intimidated by the enemy and gives way to fear, always retreating first and unable to remain in his assigned position.
His arrows do not travel far, and even if he should shoot them, they never hit their mark; he is unfit to stand within that great array.
"Great King, when engaged in battle, if there is such a person as this, the King should comfort him, saying: 'You have drawn near to me; you shall receive a generous reward.
Can the King do so?"
The king said,
“World-Honored One!
I truly do not need such a person.”
Why is this? Because they are not required at the time of battle.
"The same applies to the brahmins in the south, the vaiśyas in the west, and the śūdras in the north."
"Would you employ such people as these, O King?
The King replied,
"When it is time for battle, none of them would be employed."
The Buddha said:

"Suppose, during a time of battle, there comes from the east a kṣatriya in the prime of his years, with a sturdy and robust physique, valiant and powerful, well-versed in the art of war and skilled in archery. He is proficient in various arts and possesses many manual skills; he is adept at disciplining his body, courageous in facing the enemy, bold and fearless, without alarm or dread, never retreating upon seeing the foe, remaining steadfast in his position.
Drawing his bow to shoot from afar, he can hit his mark; his arrows do not miss their target. Brave and resolute, he charges straight forward and is able to break through great formations."
"Great King, when engaged in battle, whom should you employ?
The king replied to the Buddha,
"I employ those who are brave and strong."
Why is this? For the methods of combat require courage and strength.
It is likewise in the south, west, and north.
The Buddha told the Great King: "It is so,
Great King."
If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are incomplete in five respects, they are not fit to be fields of merit.

Furthermore, there are those who are complete in five respects and are fit to be fields of merit; giving to them yields great fruit, brings great benefit, is exceedingly flourishing, and results in vast and increasing rewards.
What is meant by being "endowed with the five factors"?
It is the abandonment of the five hindrances.
How does one abandon the five hindrances?
One eliminates the hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
To know for oneself that one has removed the five desires is called "eliminating the five hindrances.
How does one fulfill the five factors?
They have fulfilled the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
If they can fulfill these five factors, then for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, giving to them yields great fruit; it is called "greatly blazing," with a retribution that is profound and vast.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Suppose there were a man, Brave and powerful,
Furthermore skilled in the art of archery, And fully proficient in all martial arts.”
In war one must have such a person; you should bestow upon them abundant wealth and treasures, as well as noble titles and rewards.
Do not discriminate based on their lineage, but record only their meritorious achievements; Great King, you ought to act in this manner.
If one can practice what is wholesome, being gentle and cultivating patience,
and is able to see the Four Noble Truths, one shall enter the state of the noble ones.
When making offerings to those of wisdom, one should not discriminate based on their lineage.
Every dwelling place should be provided with food, drink, and bedding;
such offerings should be made for those who possess the precepts.
Amidst the great torrential flood, one should prepare a life-preserver and a raft.
Furthermore, he constructs bridges and boats, crossing over himself and saving others.
One who is upright, honest, and learned is like a dense cloud that completely covers the world, with flashes of lightning shining most brilliantly.
The sound of thunder reverberates afar, and a great rain descends;
the earth is everywhere saturated, and among the myriad flowers, trees, and groves,
there are none that do not receive its nourishment.
The farmer experiences joy and celebration;
likewise, a faithful donor who is learned and capable of giving is free from stinginess and envy.
Like moisture that nourishes food and drink, he encourages others to yield and promotes further bestowal.
Like the distant roar of thunder, like the pouring down of rain that yields abundant grain,
so too does one who practices generosity obtain great merit and later attain the bliss of nirvana.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
69 (69) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
“Do those of the Brahmin caste always take birth in Brahmin families, and those of the Kṣatriya caste always take birth in Kṣatriya families?
The Buddha said to the king,
“You should not speak in such a manner.”
Why is this? There are four types of persons:

first, those who enter from light into light; second, those who enter from light into darkness; third, those who enter from darkness into light; and fourth, those who enter from darkness into darkness.
What is meant by "entering from darkness into darkness"?

It refers to those beings who are born into lowly and impoverished circumstances, or into families of executioners or artisans; or who are physically emaciated, their forms exceedingly dark, deaf, blind, mute, or lacking in sensory faculties; and who serve as others' servants, lacking any autonomy.

Such a person, whether committing evil deeds with the body, performing evil deeds with speech, or harboring unwholesome thoughts with the mind, will, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, fall into hell; this is called "passing from darkness into darkness."
"Just as one who has emerged from a latrine enters yet another latrine, I say that such a person goes from darkness into darkness.

If a person is born into a lowly station, or among executioners and craftsmen; or if they are physically emaciated, their form being extremely dark; or if they are deaf, blind, mute, or have impaired faculties; or if they are made to serve others, lacking self-mastery—this is what is called darkness."

If such a person is able to practice good through body, able to practice good through speech, and able to practice good through mind, then at the breaking up of the body after death, they will attain rebirth in the heavens.
In this way, such a person rises from the ground and is able to ascend onto a bed;
rising from the bed, they are able to mount a carriage;
rising from the carriage, they are able to mount a horse.
Rising from the horse, one obtains a mount upon an elephant;
rising from the elephant, one ascends to the palace.
For this reason, I say that one enters from darkness into light.
"What is meant by 'entering from light into darkness'?

If there is a person born into a Kṣatriya family, or born into a Brāhmaṇa family, or born into a great householder’s family—one who possesses abundant wealth and treasures, immeasurable vast riches, overflowing storehouses, many servants, numerous ministers and high officials, and a great multitude of friends and kinsmen; one whose physical form is upright and handsome, and who possesses great power—such a person as this is called 'light. "
If such a person performs evil deeds with the body, evil deeds with speech, and evil deeds with the mind, then at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into hell.

Suppose a person descends from a palace to an elephant, descends from the elephant to mount a horse, descends from the horse to mount a chariot, descends from the chariot to sit upon a couch, descends from the couch to fall upon the ground, and from the ground falls into a pit of filth; I say that such a person has gone from light into darkness.
"What is meant by 'entering from light into light'?

If there is a person born into a family of Kṣatriyas or great Brāhmaṇas, or born into a householder's family, possessing abundant wealth and treasures, immense and boundless riches, overflowing storehouses, many servants, numerous ministers and high officials, and a vast circle of friends and kinsmen; if their physical form is upright and handsome, and they possess great power and majesty—this is called 'light. "
Such a person, having performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, at the dissolution of the body after death, will attain rebirth in the heavenly realms.
It is like going from one palace to another, from one elephant to another, from one horse to another, from one chariot to another, or from one bed to another.
"Such a person, I say, enters from light into light.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Great King, you should know: The poor who lack faith..."
Full of anger and harboring jealousy, they constantly give rise to evil thoughts and reflections.
Holding wrong views and lacking respect, they revile and insult upon seeing śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who uphold the precepts and possess great learning.
If one possesses even a small amount of wealth, yet lacks the intention to offer it as a gift,
and instead reviles the donor,
one will surely fall into hell; this karma leads to rebirth in hell.
Such a person is said to go from darkness into darkness.
One who is poor yet fond of giving, who possesses faith and is free from anger,
who is conscientious and delights in generosity— to such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, [one should give].
Maintaining the precepts and being learned, rising to show respect and offering greetings,
always practicing upright and wholesome conduct, one gives to others and praises those who give;
likewise, the recipient also offers praise.
Born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, this one is called "Emerging from Darkness" as they are about to enter the realm of light.
Though possessed of great wealth, they lack faith, and their minds are constantly harboring anger.
Constantly giving rise to greed, envy, and jealousy, they hold wrong views and lack respect for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who uphold the precepts and possess great learning;
upon seeing them, they treat them with verbal abuse and insults, having no heart to offer them support or gifts.
Passing away from this life, one falls into an evil hell;
this is called "entering darkness from light.
One who is wealthy, faithful, and free from anger, and who is fully endowed with shame and remorse—
One who can abandon great stinginess, whether a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa,
who maintains the precepts and is learned, should be greeted with respect and inquiry.
One who constantly practices what is right and good, and who gives while praising the giver, [attains merit].
Praised by those who receive [his teachings],
through this karmic fruit, he is born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
this is called "proceeding from light into the realm of light."
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
70 (70) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At midday, King Prasenajit, mounted upon a palanquin, went to the place where the Buddha was; his body was covered in dust.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the king:
"Great King!"
"For what reason have you come here at midday with your body covered in dust?
The king addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

"The affairs of state are vast and the multitude of duties are manifold; having settled and adjudicated all matters, I have come to the Buddha's presence, and for this reason my body is covered in dust."
The Buddha said, "Great King!
I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
"Great King!
Suppose there were a person coming from the east, who by nature was upright and had never been deceitful, and was thus trusted by all.
If he were to say this to you, the King:"
"Presently, there is a great mountain of rock in the east, its summit reaching to heaven and its base reaching to the earth.
Coming from the east, wherever it passes, all forests, vegetation, and living beings are utterly crushed to pieces."
"In the same way, it was so in the south, west, and north; everyone developed deep faith and said to one another:

'Now great stone mountains have arrived from the four directions all at once, and there is no hole or place to escape. All living beings—gods, dragons, humans, and ghosts—will be utterly crushed and destroyed; this is truly terrifying.'"
The Buddha said to the king:
"At that time, what expedient means would you have devised to escape this calamity?
The king replied:
“World-Honored One!
At that time, having no other expedient means, one relies solely on faith in the Buddha-dharma, practicing the true path, with no other alternative.
The Buddha said:
“Great King!
As Your Majesty has said, there is no other recourse whatsoever except for placing faith in the Buddha’s Dharma.
Great King!”
"For what reason do you speak these words?
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"

Suppose one were to be consecrated and receive the royal throne; even if elephant, cavalry, chariot, and infantry troops were each fully equipped with their weapons of war, such as this great mountain, there would be no way to fight it, and swords, arrows, bows, and spears would have no place to be used.
If one employs incantations or offers wealth as tribute, such matters are of no avail; furthermore, there is no place here for seeking fame, contending by force, or disputing for victory.
"Therefore, World-Honored One!
When I say that one should cultivate wholesome dharmas and remain far removed from falsehood, there is no other reckoning besides placing faith in the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha said:
"Thus it is, Great King! Thus it is, Great King!

The mountain of old age can destroy youthful vigor and radiant complexion; the mountain of illness can destroy all physical strength and health; the mountain of death can destroy all life-span; and the mountain of decline can destroy all splendor, wealth, and nobility, causing the loss of wife and children, the separation from kinsmen, and the forfeiture of riches."
"Great King!

There is such a world of destruction in the four directions that pursues every person; it is indeed as you have said, that apart from practicing the true Dharma, there is no other recourse besides the Buddha-Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Suppose there were great mountains from the four directions, vast, deep, and boundless, coming from all four sides simultaneously;
one would flee in terror and panic, with no place of refuge.”
Elephants, chariots, cavalry, and infantry cannot resist it; incantations, spells, wealth, and treasures cannot repel it.

Such is the mountain of impermanence for Great Kings—the mountain of old age, sickness, and death, the mountain of decay and extinction—which destroys all classes of living beings: Kṣatriyas, Śūdras, and Brāhmaṇas alike.
Even those of the lowest castes, such as the Caṇḍālas— whether householders or renunciants practicing the holy life,
from those who observe the precepts in their entirety to those who have violated them— all shall be utterly destroyed without remainder.
Therefore, the wise should cultivate goodness, honoring the Triple Gem and performing manifold merits;
with body, speech, and mind always pure, they gain renown in the present life and are reborn in heaven hereafter.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
71 (71) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that moment, there were seven long-haired brahmins, seven naked nirgranthas, and seven one-clothed non-Buddhists within the Jeta Grove; they were all tall and large in stature.
When King Prasenajit saw the various non-Buddhist practitioners walking back and forth and wandering about within the Jeta Grove,
he rose from his seat, joined his palms with a reverent mind toward them, and addressed them, saying: "I am King Prasenajit."
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha said to King Prasenajit,
"For what reason do you show such reverence toward this person with long hair, who is naked and wears but a single garment?"
The king said,
“World-Honored One!
In my kingdom there are these three men, who are known as the most preeminent among the Arhats.”
The Buddha said to the king:
"You do not skillfully know the inclinations of others' minds; how then can you distinguish whether one is an arhat or not?
Only by dwelling with someone for a long time and observing them with careful attention can it be known."
Whether one maintains the precepts or violates them, though they may have lived together for a long time, the wise can discern this while the foolish cannot.
If among one's parents, relatives, or kinsmen there is death, it can be distinguished and known.
If this were not the case, it would be difficult to understand how one could refrain from breaking the precepts even when encountering calamity,
being coerced by others to commit murder, or being pressured by a woman’s private parts.

One can know its solidity by following it through successive observation; thus one can discern what is pure and what is impure. To test one's wisdom, listen to what is said: only the wise are truly able to make such distinctions.
"Only by dwelling together with a wise person for a long time can one truly know them.
The King then praised the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent!"
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has taught, one can only know another after dwelling together for a long time.

Whether one maintains the precepts or violates them becomes clear when facing a crisis; by observing their conduct, one knows whether they are pure or impure. Through discussion and debate, one distinguishes between the wise and the ordinary. This is what was said above: those with wisdom can know this, while the foolish cannot.”
Only after dwelling with them for a long time does one come to know them;
they cannot be known all at once.

Why is this? The people I employ are also made to wear such forms and garments, and are sent far away to other countries to observe the affairs within those kingdoms, remaining there for eight months or even ten months. Having performed various tasks, they then return to their own country.
Indulging in the five desires as he pleased, everything he did was no different from before.
Therefore, one knows that what the Buddha has spoken is truly well-spoken.
The King spoke again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I also knew beforehand that such a thing existed; however, I did not examine it immediately, but rather gave rise to reverence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One cannot observe and know [a person] by seeing their physical appearance;
when one suddenly encounters someone, one must not immediately place trust in them.
One may resemble an arhat in outward form, yet in reality fail to restrain the sense faculties."
Their various forms and behaviors cannot be distinguished at all.
Like an earring coated with lacquer, or like a coin coated with lacquer,
the fool thinks it is gold, yet within it is actually copper.
Such people as these, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, know nothing;
though they appear outwardly virtuous and good, their inner hearts are truly poisonous and evil.
When they travel, they lead many followers to manifest themselves as noble and superior men.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
72 (72) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, five kings gathered together in one place and each said to the others:
"Among the five desires, which is the most exquisite?
One king spoke, saying:
"Form is supreme," he said.
Then the king declared:
"Sound is supreme."
Next, the king said:
"Flavor is the foremost.
The fourth king said:
"Fragrance is foremost," said the fifth king.
"Tactile smoothness is foremost," said the fifth king.
The minds of the various kings were each different, and every one regarded his own view as supreme; they then said to one another:
"Our minds find beauty in different things, and we are each vying for our own principles; we should go to the place where the Buddha is to receive his teachings and have them distinguished."
With King Prasenajit as their leader, they went together to the place where the Buddha was.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, the five kings stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We five kings once deliberated among ourselves as to which of the five desires is the foremost.
One king declared that form is the foremost.”
These five kings spoke thus with differing accounts, each claiming to be the foremost.
Because their accounts differed, they came to the place where the Buddha was to inquire about this matter: "Which one is the foremost?"
The Buddha said: "If, regarding form,
one grasps its appearance and becomes mentally attached to it, finding it to one's liking,
at that time, even if there were a sublime form superior to this, one would regard only what one is attached to as superior and pay no heed to the excellence of the other form."
"Sound, fragrance, taste, and touch are likewise; even regarding the perception of touch, one's mental state becomes attached to its characteristics, regarding them as supreme.
At that time, a brahmin named Vimala rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I wish to say something; I only pray that you will grant me leave to speak.
The Buddha told Bei Yi, "You should know when the time is right."
Beyi then spoke in verse:
“The Great King of Aṅga possesses precious armor; The Lord of Magadha has gained great benefit.
A Buddha has appeared in his country as the supreme jewel, His fame heard everywhere, like the king of mountains.”
Just as a lotus flower newly blossoms, its radiance reflecting in the spring pond and its fragrance reaching everywhere,
so too is the Buddha like the sun in the void, his light universally illuminating the world.
Behold the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, Like a fierce fire blazing with intense heat;
It opens all eyes and creates great illumination, So that all who come to receive his transformation Have every doubt completely resolved.
When the five kings had finished praising him with verses, each offered him his upper robe as a reward.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the five kings were all greatly rejoiced and departed from their seats.
After the king had departed, Beiyi joined his palms toward the Buddha and immediately offered five robes to him, praying only that the Buddha would accept them; the Buddha then accepted them.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
73 (73) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, King Prasenajit, whose body was stout and whose breathing was extremely labored, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha said to the king:
"Your Majesty, your body is now extremely heavy; even in moving about or in the process of inhaling and exhaling, it is exceedingly difficult."
The King addressed the Buddha, saying: “So it is, so it is.
Just as the World-Honored One has taught, I now suffer because of this body; I feel shame and reproach myself for it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"A person should always maintain mindfulness: When obtaining food and drink, one should know the proper measure.
Thus the body will be light and agile, suffering will be minimal, And it will be properly digested, protecting the longevity of life."
At that time, the young brahmin Udāyin was present among the assembly.
The king said to the young brahmin:
"Can you memorize this verse and recite it for me regularly at every mealtime?"
"If you can recite it, I shall reward you with a hundred gold coins daily, and you shall always be permitted to eat before me.
The young brahmin Udāyin then replied, "I can."
The Buddha again preached the Dharma to King Prasenajit in various ways, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, and then remained silent.
King Prasenajit paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew, while the young brahmin Udāyin remained behind for a short while, receiving and upholding these verses.
The Buddha told the Māṇava:
"Whenever the king eats, you should always recite these sublime verses for him.
At that time, King Prasenajit reduced his food day by day; his body grew smaller each day, and he gradually attained lightness and ease.
King Prasenajit later arrived at the place where the Buddha was; his body felt light and agile, and he had become more handsome.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One!
Now, having received the Buddha’s instruction, I experience immeasurable bliss within this very body.
Homage to the Buddha, the Bhagavān, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha!
Know that my present retribution and immediate benefit arise from the practice of moderation in food.
Victory, ruin, following the Buddha’s teaching, The single dharma, the field of merit, that which is to be loathed,
Light and darkness, the stone mountain, wearing a single robe, The various kings, and the one named Bāgu (Vāgura) who gasped for breath.
74 (Seventy-four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a young brahmin named Asurāyaṇa who went to where the Buddha was. With unwholesome speech and mind, he stood face-to-face before the Buddha and subjected him to various insults and abuse.
At that time, having seen and heard this, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
“Practicing virtue and free from anger, Giving gifts and always speaking truth—
One who is neither wrathful nor harmful Surpasses those who harbor malice and resentment.”
Those who are stingy and greedy, who speak falsehoods, and who associate with evil people—know that such sentient beings accumulate anger like a mountain.
Anger is like a runaway horse; it is restrained by the bridle and reins.
"Restraining the reins is not called firm; controlling the mind is what is called firm.
Therefore, I am now known as the 'Well-Subdued Charioteer.
At that time, the young brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am truly ignorant and deluded; what I have done is unwholesome, for I have heaped insults upon you in the very presence of the Buddha.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept my repentance."
The Buddha said,
“Māṇava! Knowing your sincerity and out of compassion for you, I accept your repentance, so that from this day forward your wholesome dharmas shall increase and you shall never regress.”
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
75 (75) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a young brahmin named Vairaṭī who went to where the Buddha was staying; standing face-to-face before the Buddha, he spoke ill with both mouth and mind, reviling the World-Honored One and subjecting him to various slanders and provocations.
At that time, having seen and heard this, the Tathāgata spoke to Bheṣika:
"For example, in the world, during a great festival on the day of the Asaṃpāta [Saw-Without-Handle]."
"On that night, at that time, did you perhaps send clothing, ornaments, and various kinds of delicacies to your relatives?
Bei Yi replied, "Indeed I did."
"I shall give you alms.
The Buddha said to Bīṇa:
"If he does not accept the alms you offer, to whom do these alms belong?"
Be-yi replied,
"If he does not accept it, I shall take it myself.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Bēyi! You have personally reviled the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, slandering and disparaging him, and causing him various vexations."
"Although you offer it to me, I do not accept it.
For example, when people of the world give something away, it is called 'giving' only when the recipient accepts it; it is also called 'acceptance.'"
If someone gives a gift but the recipient does not accept it, this is called "giving" (tyāga) and not "receiving" (pratigraha).
If someone reviles, strikes in anger, or insults another, and one retaliates in kind, this is called "giving" and this is called "receiving."
"If a person reviles, strikes in anger, or insults one, and one endures it without retaliating, this is called relinquishing;
it is not called receiving. Bei Yi said: "Gautama!"
I have heard that the elder monks of former times and those of long-standing virtue all spoke thus:
"If there is a Buddha in the world—the Unsurpassed, Truly Realized, Perfectly Awakened One—one should never give rise to affliction even if he is reviled face to face."
"Now you have reviled me, and you have consequently given rise to vexation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"For one who is without anger, toward whom could one become angry?"
One who is disciplined and maintains right livelihood—know that such a person is free from anger.
If one does not retaliate with anger when provoked, they will find it difficult for others to overcome them in conflict;
if one does not respond with retaliation, such a person is called supreme.
Non-anger conquers anger; practicing good conquers evil;
generosity conquers stinginess; truthful speech conquers falsehood.
Those who are without anger and without malice always dwell together with the noble ones.
Those who associate with evil people accumulate anger like a mountain;
hatred is like a wild horse, which is controlled by the bridle.
The bridle is not truly firm; only the control of the mind is called firm.
"Therefore, I am now called 'the Well-Tamed Rider.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
76 (Seventy-six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking up and down on an open space outside the Jeta Grove.

At that time, Brahmadatta was extremely wicked by nature; he went to where the Buddha was and, standing face-to-face before the Buddha, reviled him with foul language, giving rise to great anger and vexation, and further adding slander, hoping thereby to cause the Buddha shame.
At that time, having seen and heard this, the World-Honored One remained silent.
Then, seeing the Buddha’s silence, Pārutthaja spoke these words again:
"Since you now remain silent, I know that you have fallen into defeat."
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"Having cast off all notions of victory and defeat, one sleeps in peace within the tranquility of cessation.
The brāhmaṇa said:

“Gautama! I truly have committed a transgression; being childish and lacking wisdom, I have acted unskillfully. Now I recognize this myself; I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my repentance.”
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:

“In your very presence, you have reviled the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; you have added slander and caused various forms of provocation. You are truly foolish and small-minded, deluded and lacking wisdom; your actions were unwholesome. Out of compassion for you, I accept your repentance, so that your wholesome dharmas may increase and you may practice them without falling back.”
Having accepted the confession, the brahmin was filled with great joy;
he prostrated himself and departed. 77 (77) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

Then, the brahmin Tulādhāra saw the Tathāgata from afar; he hurried toward him, and upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, he covered himself before the Buddha, reviling him face-to-face, slandering the World-Honored One, and harassing him in various ways.
Furthermore, he scooped up some earth intending to scatter it over the Buddha; however, the wind blew the very dust he had gathered back onto himself, unable to defile the Buddha.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"When one who is free from anger is met with malice, And one who is pure is subjected to slander..."
Just as scattered dust returns to soil oneself, Like a farmer who sows seeds in the field,
Reaping the fruit according to what was planted— So too shall this person surely receive their retribution.
The brahmin said, "I have indeed committed a transgression;
being childish and ignorant, I have acted unwholesomely. I only pray that the Tathāgata will accept my repentance."
The Buddha said, "In the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, you have personally slandered him; your delusion and confusion are as extreme as what you have said."
"Out of compassion for you, I accept your confession so that you shall not regress and that wholesome dharmas may increase.
Having received the Buddha’s permission, the brāhmaṇa departed with joy.
78 (Seventy-eighth). Thus have I heard:

"If one seeks out faults and shortcomings, intending to revile another's deficiencies,"

you will never be able to understand or realize the Dharma taught by the Buddhas.

if you can do so, listen well and I shall speak for you.

He immediately rose, prostrated before the Buddha, and spoke these words:

[The monk] returned with joy, prostrated at his feet, and departed.

Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in sequence, eventually arriving at the house of the great Brahmin Parantapa.

The brahmin thought to himself, "This shaven-headed śramaṇa comes frequently to beg for alms; he seems like an old acquaintance of mine.
At that moment, the Buddha, knowing what was in the brahmin's mind, spoke this verse:
"Heaven rains down again and again; the five grains ripen again and again.
The followers of the Way beg again and again; the donors give again and again.
They are born in the heavens again and again, and they receive their karmic rewards again and again."
Women conceive repeatedly, and give birth to children again and again.
They repeatedly milk the cows, and repeatedly obtain butter and curd.
They undergo birth repeatedly, and are extinguished and destroyed again and again.
Time and again one comes to death; time and again one suffers grief and affliction;
likewise, time and again one is consumed by fire, and time and again one is buried in a tomb.
When one attains the path that ends further existence, then one ceases and no longer does so repeatedly.
If one is not born again and again, nor dies again and again,
one will not experience grief again and again, nor wail and weep again and again.
At that time, the brahmin, having heard this verse being spoken, [was filled with joy].
In his heart, he conceived the highest faith; leaping for joy with great delight,
he immediately took the World-Honored One’s bowl and filled it with various kinds of food,
wishing to present it to the Buddha, but the Buddha would not accept it from him.
"The reason he did not accept it was for the sake of the Dharma verse.
At that time, the brahmin said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
"The food I have now prepared as an offering to the Tathāgata has not been accepted by the World-Honored One; to whom, then, should it be given?
The Buddha said, "I see no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, nor Māra or Brahmā, who, were they to eat this food, would be able to digest it in accordance with the Dharma."
The Buddha spoke again:
"This food should be placed in water free of insects, or in grass free of insects.
At that time, the brahmin, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, immediately placed this food in water free of insects.
Immediately, intense flames and smoke issued forth together, accompanied by loud crackling sounds and a great, piercing roar.
The brahmin spoke these words:
"The supernatural power displayed by the śramaṇa Gautama is truly rare!"
"Even with such a small amount of food, it has already undergone this transformation.
Having witnessed this event, the brahmin went at once to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to him:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to leave the household life."
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa, having attained full ordination.

This son of good family, having faith that the home life is not the true home, has left the household to practice the Way. Day and night he is diligent, maintaining right mindfulness and awakening. With firm resolve and aspiration before him, he has accomplished what was to be done; the holy life is established, he has realized it for himself, and will not undergo further existence, having become an Arhat whose mind is well-liberated.
81. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a Brahmin woman named Vāsiṣṭhī in the city of Śrāvastī who, before the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, developed pure faith and took refuge in the Triple Gem. Her mind was free from doubt; she also harbored no uncertainty regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Having realized the Four Noble Truths, she attained the first fruit [of the holy life] and beheld the equality of the Dharma.

His husband was of the Brahmin caste; being sent by his husband, he fell prostrate on the ground. Having risen from the earth, he joined his palms in reverence toward the direction of the Buddha and spoke these words:

“Homage to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha! Of the color of pure gold, with a halo extending one fathom, his body is well-proportioned like a nyagrodha tree. He is foremost in preaching the Dharma, the seventh among the sages, the hero of the world who has attained liberation—my World-Honored One.”
At that time, when her husband, the brahmin, heard these words from his wife, he was overcome with extreme rage and reviled her, saying:
"You are a mad outcaste!"
Who is this foolish Caṇḍāla who now practices sorcery? There is no one more utterly base than you;

you cannot show respect to the great Brahmins learned in the Three Vedas, yet you pay homage to a shaven-headed, thin, and black man—such a śramaṇa who, along with the Yajña-rāyas, cuts off the human lineage—and you praise him excessively.
"If your faith and delight are exceedingly profound, then listen! I shall now invite your teacher to engage in a formal discussion with me.
The wife said to her husband, "I do not see anyone—whether a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, or a deva, or Māra, or Brahmā—who is able to engage in a formal discussion with the Buddha."
His wife spoke again:

"Namo to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; one of the color of pure gold, with a body perfectly proportioned and a halo extending one fathom, like a nyagrodha tree; foremost in preaching the Dharma, the seventh among the sages, the Hero of the World who has attained liberation—my World-Honored One, you should know this yourself."
Then the brahmin went to where the Buddha was, and after having finished his greetings, he sat to one side and asked in verse:
"By destroying what does one obtain peaceful sleep?"
By abandoning what dharma does one attain freedom from sorrow?
What single dharma can bring about death and extinction?
O Śramaṇa Gautama, tell me this.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"By destroying hatred one attains peaceful sleep; By extinguishing hatred one becomes free from sorrow.
Hatred feigns friendship yet can cause deathly harm; Māṇava, you should know this as it truly is."
“Having extinguished ill will, one is praised by the noble; he who can harm such a person finds no cause for grief.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the brahmin according to his needs, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him. He spoke in succession on the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven; he explained that sensual desires are the root of impurity and suffering, while the way of escape is bliss, extensively demonstrating the various wholesome and pure dharmas.

Knowing that the young man’s mind was pliant and well-tamed, and seeing that he was leaping for joy with delight, free from doubt, and capable of serving as a vessel for the Dharma, the Buddha taught him a single principle sufficient for realization—just as all Buddhas do—teaching the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Having explained this extensively, [the Buddha continued].

At that time, when Brahmadatta heard what the Buddha had spoken, he was like a piece of pure white cotton easily dyed; immediately upon his seat, he perceived the Four Noble Truths, thoroughly understood all phenomena, attained the reality-limit of dharmas, crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, became independent of others, and attained fearlessness. He then rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
I have attained liberation.

Now I wish to take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; for as long as my life lasts, I shall be an upāsaka, refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants.

The husband replied to his wife:
"I do not see anyone in the world—whether among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, Māras, or Brahmās—who is able to engage in debate with the Buddha."
He spoke again to his wife, saying, "Give me your garment.
The wife immediately gave it to him. Having obtained the garment, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will grant me permission to leave the home life and study the Way within the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent and commanded a bhikṣu to ordain him and let him enter the monastic order.
Having gone forth, he practiced with singular diligence in accordance with the Dharma of those who have left the household life.
As described at length in the *Bāratuḷaja Sūtra*, he eventually attained arhatship and his mind achieved excellent liberation.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
82 (82) Thus have I heard:

Having performed good deeds during the three times [of day], The mind rejoices because of those roots of goodness."
According to their state of mind, they give; thus they are able to leave all faults behind.
Skillfully removing greed and desire, they rightly sever craving for liberation.

they shall be born in the Brahma Heaven, where their lifespan is exceedingly long.

to be able to be called a 'Brahmin of the Three Knowledges'?

"Able to know past lives, seeing heavens and evil realms,

85. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took up his bowl, and, with Ānanda following him, proceeded toward the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, within a hollow in a heap of refuse, he saw a husband and wife who were nearly old and decrepit, trembling as they leaned on their staffs like aged herons.
Having seen them from afar, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Do you see this couple, so extremely aged and infirm, in the hollow of the refuse?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“Indeed! I have seen it.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If this old man were in his youth, he would have been the foremost elder in the city of Śrāvastī."
Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, he ought to have attained arhatship;
had he accumulated wealth during his youth, he ought to have been the second elder.
If he had left the household life, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the dharma robes, he would have attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
If, during the third period, he had accumulated wealth, he would have been the third elder.
Having shaved off my hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, I ought to have attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Yet now, being old and decrepit, I am unable to accumulate wealth, nor can I apply myself with diligence, nor have I attained the qualities of a superior person.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In youth, he did not cultivate the holy life, Nor did he amass wealth and treasures;
He is like an old heron Perching and waiting by a dried-up pond."
"One who does not cultivate the holy life, nor amasses wealth and treasures in their youth,
but dwells on the pleasures of youth, stands like a drawn bow.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
86 (Eighty-six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was an elderly brahmin of advanced age and mature faculties who, in former days, had committed many evils and was extremely coarse and depraved. Having violated the prohibitions and having no faith in merit or goodness, he had failed to perform meritorious deeds beforehand. As his end approached and he found no refuge, he went to where the Buddha was, and after exchanging greetings with the Buddha, sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In days past, I committed many evils that were exceedingly coarse and depraved; I violated the prohibitions, failed to cultivate merit, and did not practice goodness. Furthermore, I was unable to perform meritorious deeds beforehand, so that at the time of my death, I have nothing upon which to rely.”
The Buddha said,
"It is truly as you have said.
The old brahmin said:
“Excellent, Gautama! Please speak for me,
so that I may obtain peace and happiness for a long night, and attain the goal and the benefit.”
The Buddha said:

"It is indeed as you have said. In days past, you did not perform wholesome deeds through body, speech, or mind; you violated the prohibitions and precepts and failed to cultivate merit. You were unable to create for yourself a refuge or reliance beforehand, which you now seek at the moment of death."

At this present time, you are truly aged and infirm; you previously committed many sins and performed coarse and evil deeds. You failed to create meritorious karma or cultivate wholesome conduct, and were unable to establish for yourself a refuge at the time when it was most needed and feared.
For example, when a person is about to die, they may wish to escape and enter a good house to save themselves; yet such a thing is entirely impossible.

Therefore, one should now cultivate wholesome conduct with the body, and likewise with the mind and speech; if these three karmas are wholesome, they will serve as a dwelling place and a refuge at the time of death.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The lifespan of human beings is brief, And one must inevitably submit to death.
When assailed by old age and decay, There is no one who can provide rescue."
Therefore, one should fear death; there is only entry into the Buddha-dharma.
If one cultivates wholesome dharmas, this is the place of refuge.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the second sutra was no different: one should seek a place of refuge, for it is fitting for great beings to cultivate the wholesome.
The third prose section has a distinct verse, which says:
"Youth and vigor, as well as old age—these three times have all passed away.
With little life remaining, one is constantly afflicted by aging."
Having approached the realm of Yama, the Brahmin is about to be reborn;
between these two states there is no place to dwell, and you possess no provisions at all.
You should prepare a small lamp of wisdom and rely upon diligent effort.
"Having previously eliminated all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one will no longer undergo birth, aging, or death. (87) Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elderly brahmin who went to where the Buddha was; after having exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I am now aged and decrepit; since the distant past, I have committed many evils, never having performed meritorious deeds nor cultivated goodness, and furthermore, I have failed to practice the Dharma that provides protection from fear.
Excellent, Gautama!
Please teach me the Dharma so that at the end of my life I may have a refuge, a dwelling, a place of reliance, and a sanctuary for my protection.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"The world is ablaze.
What is meant by 'ablaze'?"
This refers to old age, sickness, and death.
For this reason, you should cultivate goodness through the body, and likewise through speech and mind.

You have failed to cultivate the goodness of body, speech, and mind at all; yet, if you were now able to cultivate goodness through body, speech, and mind, that would be your boat for crossing over. Even until the time of death, it would serve as your protection, your dwelling, and your place of refuge and escape.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as when a house is set ablaze, And the dwelling is consumed by fire,
One should quickly take out the wealth and treasures And place them where there is no fire."
The fires of birth, old age, sickness, and death Burn away all sentient beings;
one should therefore practice generous giving To relieve the masses from their poverty.
Gold, jewels, and the like in this world Are invaded by kings, thieves, water, and fire.
At the time of death, one must abandon everything; nothing follows a person.
Yet generosity follows a person without forsaking them, like a secure treasury that neither kings, thieves, water, nor fire can ever plunder.
"To be stingy and greedy, not practicing giving—this is called being in constant sleep.
To cultivate generosity and relieve the destitute—this is called awakening.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
88 (Eighty-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the young brahmin Uttara went to where the Buddha was, and after having exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat to one side and spoke as follows:
"Gautama! I seek wealth in accordance with the Dharma to provide for my parents.
Furthermore, by means of right principles, I establish them in a state of happiness. By providing for them through right principles, would one not obtain great merit?"
The Buddha said:
"Making offerings in this manner truly results in great merit.
The Buddha said:
“Māṇava! It is not only you;

anyone who seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma, and furthermore supports their parents through right principles, brings them joy through right principles, and provides for them through right principles, will obtain immeasurable merit.”
Why is this? You should know that for such a person, Brahmā himself resides in their home.
If they provide proper and righteous offerings to their parents, the Ācārya likewise resides in their home.
If one can provide for one’s parents with right principle, attaining happiness through right principle, and all will from afar revere that household.
If one can provide for one’s parents with right principle, bringing them joy through right principle and supporting them with right principle, know that Mahādeva himself resides in that household.
If one can provide for one’s parents with right principles and supply them with happiness through right principles, you should know that all the devas are present in that household. Why is this?
Because the Brahmā King made offerings to his parents according to correct principle, he attained birth in the Brahma-world.
If one wishes to make offerings to an ācārya, making offerings to one's parents is itself making offerings to the ācārya.
If you wish to perform prostrations, you should first prostrate to your parents.
If you wish to serve the sacrificial fire, you should first make offerings to your parents.
If you wish to serve the gods, you should first make offerings to your parents; this is itself the worship of all the devas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Brahmā and the Fire God, the Ācāryas and the various devas—
if one makes offerings to them, one should likewise serve and support one’s two parents.”
"In this life one gains renown, and in the next life one is born in the Brahma Heaven. (89) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

He addressed the Buddha, saying:

If a brahmin seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and, having accumulated it, performs a great sacrifice or instructs others to perform a sacrifice—
should such a sacrifice be performed, or should it not be performed?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Horse fat and human fat, Beef fat and choice delicacies,
Inhaling the wind and opening the gates of sacrifice— These six are called the great sacrifices."
Though the ritual labor be vast, it is censured by the seers and sages.
The castrated ram, the black ram, the bull-kings, and the various young calves—
all such classes of slaughtered living beings do not constitute a righteous sacrifice.
Such is a false sacrifice, which no sage has ever passed beyond.
If one performs a true sacrifice, one never distresses living beings;
by not harming those with life, one performs a sacrifice that severs all states of existence.
This is called the true sacrifice.
The Great Sage will surely go there; one should give the remnants of the sacrificial ground to those who are worthy of offerings.
When giving with a pure mind and at the proper time, to whom should one give?
One should give to the most excellent field of merit.
What constitutes the most excellent field of merit?
What is called the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya):
if one can give in this manner, it is called a vast sacrifice.
Even if one performs such a great sacrifice, it must be done with wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma.
If one can give pure water with one's own hands in this manner,
the devas will conceive faith and respect; this is called benefiting both oneself and others,
and one will surely obtain a great reward.
Only the wise are able to give rise to pure faith and attain liberation of mind;
they cannot be harmed by affliction or injury,
they obtain the manifold pleasures of the world, and they are reborn in superior realms.
"This is what is called the great sacrifice established by the wise.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the young Brahmin Upaka, having heard what the Buddha said, departed with joy.
90. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a young brahmin named Upaka who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, exchanged greetings, and sat down to one side.

"Regarding such a sacrifice, should it be performed, or should it not be performed?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"When one prepares the great sacrificial implements, One must not harm or disturb living beings."
If one can perform the sacrifice in this way, all that is done will be pure;
this is called the profound and hidden sacrifice, which is received by those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
Among those appearing in the world, it is their fame that reaches farthest.
Far removed from strife and contention, such a sacrifice is praiseworthy and commended by all Buddhas.
With pure generosity, one should bestow gifts upon those who are worthy of offerings.
When giving, to whom does one give? This is called a vast sacrifice, which all the devas trust and revere.
If one can offer pure water with one's own hands in such a manner as this, it is a true sacrifice.
Known as the benefit of self and others, it will surely yield a great fruit.
Such a great sacrifice can only be performed by the wise;
they are able to give rise to pure faith and also attain liberation of mind.
"Affliction and harm cannot prevail over him;
he attains the supreme happiness in the world and is born in an exalted realm—he is called a wise man.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, Upaka, having heard what the Buddha said, departed with joy.
91. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a young brahmin named Bāvari who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, exchanged greetings, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How many dharmas are there by which laypeople dwelling at home may obtain benefits and rewards in the present life, as well as gain profit and happiness?"
The Buddha told the māṇava:
"There are four qualities that enable householders to obtain results in the present life and attain benefit and happiness.
What are these four?"

First, one is able to be diligent; second, one is able to guard the sense faculties; third, one obtains virtuous friends; fourth, one maintains one's livelihood through right principles. What is meant by diligence?

It refers to whatever work one performs for the sake of household affairs and the means of subsistence—whether serving as a royal minister, a farmer, a merchant, or a herdsman—one does not shrink from toil, regardless of cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, or satiety, nor even the presence of mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, or bees. Although there is hardship and suffering, one does not abandon one's work; for the sake of completing that task, one never ceases or desists. This is called diligence.
What is meant by "guarding the sense faculties"?

If a son of noble family gathers wealth in accordance with the Dharma, employing skillful means so that it is not plundered by kings, thieves, water, or fire; if it cannot be encroached upon by those who harbor enmity; and if he does not father wicked offspring—this is called guarding.
What is meant by "drawing near to virtuous friends"?

If a son of noble family draws near to virtuous friends—friends who are by nature upright and good, who never commit adultery or theft, nor indulge in negligence such as drinking wine to the point of intoxication and confusion, but instead speak words of truth and do not practice deception—then he is said to draw near to virtuous friends.

To associate as a close friend with such a person ensures that unarisen distress does not arise, causes arisen distress to be extinguished, brings about the arising of unarisen joy and happiness, and prevents arisen joy and happiness from being lost; this is called a virtuous friend.
What is called "sustaining one's livelihood through right principles"?

It is when a son of noble family understands his wealth, gauges its quantity, and exercises moderation in its expenditure; ensuring that income exceeds outgo, he does not recklessly or lightly spend it.
It is like a person who eats the udumbara fruit; while he is eating it, there are many fruits upon the tree.
Once he has finished eating, he falls into a drunken sleep for seven days.
Only after he has awakened does he realize that he has lost the fruit.
One should manage affairs with reason, ensuring that extravagance and frugality find their proper balance.
If one possesses wealth yet cannot provide for one's own food and clothing, nor practice generosity, but instead uses it with extreme parsimony, all people will say:
"Such a person dies like a dog."
"You should deliberate for yourself, avoiding both extravagance and parsimony; this is called the right principle for sustaining one's life.
The Māṇava again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By practicing what Dharma can laypeople receive its benefits in the present life and attain merit in future lives?"
The Buddha told the māṇava:
“There are four kinds of dharmas that can bring about the attainment of meritorious retribution.
What are these four?”
These are faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom.
What is meant by "precepts"?
It refers to being able to practice non-killing, up to and including abstaining from drinking alcohol.
What is called giving?

To bestow upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, teachers, parents, and the poor—whether they beg for it or not—robes, food and drink, bedding, seats, sleeping requisites, and medicines for the sick and infirm; to be able to grant all such various necessities is what is called giving.
What is the wisdom derived from hearing?
It is knowing suffering as it truly is, knowing the truth of suffering;
knowing the origin as it truly is, knowing the truth of the origin.
To know the path as it truly is, is to know the Truth of the Path;
to know cessation as it truly is, is to know the Truth of Cessation.
This is called being fully endowed with the wisdom derived from hearing.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Cultivate your activities with a refined mind, Diligently guarding them so they are not lost;
Associate with virtuous friends, And you will be able to sustain your life through right principles."
Faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom— By severing stinginess and greed through these,
One who can act in this way will swiftly attain the path of purity.
These eight kinds of qualities Can bring about benefit and joy in the present life.
"In future ages, you shall likewise obtain the joys of heaven.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the Māṇava, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
92 (Ninety-two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Mithilā at the Āmra Grove.

At that time, a Brahmin woman named Vāsiṣṭhī had recently lost her sixth son. Because of the loss of her child, her mind became deranged; she ran about naked and frantic, and continuing on her way without stopping, she eventually arrived at the Āmra Grove in Mithilā.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
Then, the Brahmin woman Vāsiṣṭhī saw the World-Honored One from afar; she regained her original composure and, filled with shame, crouched upon the ground.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Bring me your uttarāsaṅga; I shall preach the Dharma for you.
Having received this instruction, Ānanda immediately presented him with the uttarāsaṅga.
