The Brahmin woman Vāsiṣṭhī immediately took the garment and put it on, then went to where the Buddha was and prostrated herself at his feet.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded various teachings for the Brahmin woman, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening her; just as the Buddhas of the past had done when teaching the essentials of the Dharma: discourse on generosity, discourse on morality, and discourse on rebirth in heaven; and how sensual desire is the root of impurity and suffering, while the way of transcendence is bliss.

At that time, the World-Honored One extensively expounded the Dharma for her. Knowing that she was sincerely desirous of being freed from the entanglements of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), he taught her the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
This daughter of Vāsiṣṭha was intelligent and possessed of quick understanding; having heard the Dharma, she was able to retain it, just as pure white cotton easily takes on dye.

On that very seat, the daughter of Vāsiṣṭha saw the Four Noble Truths; she saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma, knew the Dharma, crossed over doubt to the further shore, personally realized the Dharma, was no longer dependent on the teachings of others, and attained irreversible faith in the Buddha’s teachings. Having attained fearlessness regarding the Buddha’s Dharma, she rose from her seat, joined her palms in homage to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

I have now attained deliverance from the three evil realms; for as long as my life lasts, I take refuge in the Triple Gem as an upāsikā. For the rest of my life, I shall not kill; with pure faith and devotion, I likewise refrain from stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants.
At that time, the woman, having heard the Dharma with joy, paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
On another occasion, when Vāsiṣṭha lost his seventh son, he felt no sorrow or distress, nor did he grieve; he did not even run about naked and frantic in remembrance of him.
At that time, her husband, Brahmadatta, spoke in verse, asking:
"When you previously lost your son, your remembrance was most bitter;
grief and longing entangled your mind and feelings, so that for a long time you took neither food nor drink."
"Now this seventh son has met with illness and passed away;
you have been his compassionate mother—why do you not feel sorrow for him?
At that time, Vāsisthī immediately spoke a verse in reply to her husband:
"Since immeasurable eons past, I have received bodies without limit;
because of the bonds of affection, my descendants are beyond counting.
Having taken birth in every place, the losses I have suffered are likewise not just once."
Within the vast wilderness of birth and death, one suffers without end.
Having fully understood the nature of birth and death and the destinations to which beings wander,
I now feel no sentiment of sorrow or attachment whatsoever.
Her husband, the brahmin, spoke again in verse:
"What you have said has never occurred before.
From whom did you gain this realization, that you are able to forget your sorrow?"
Then Vāseṭṭha replied with a verse:
"O Brahmin, you should know that in days past,
the Three Buddhas were at Mithilā, within the Āmra Grove."
"He has taught the cessation of all suffering, as well as the path that brings an end to suffering;
by practicing the eightfold noble path, one attains the peace of nirvāṇa.
Then, the brahmin spoke again in verse:
"I too now wish to go to the Āmra Grove to consult that World-Honored One, so as to dispel my grief for my son.
Then, Vāseṭṭha spoke again in verse:
“The Buddha’s body is the color of pure gold, A halo of light extends a fathom in every direction.
Having forever severed all afflictions, He has transcended the stream of birth and death.
Such a Great Teacher Is able to subdue all beings.”
"All sentient beings have received his transformation; therefore, he is called the True Savior.
You should now go quickly to where that World-Honored One resides.

At that time, having heard what his wife said, the brāhmaṇa was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately prepared his carriage and went to that grove. From afar, seeing the World-Honored One’s majestic radiance shining brilliantly, his reverence increased all the more.
Having arrived, he prostrated and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing his mind with the knowledge of others' minds, perceived his profound sincerity; he immediately taught him such dharmas as suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, as well as the Eightfold Noble Path, which lead to nirvana.
At that time, having heard this Dharma, the brahmin realized the Four Noble Truths; having attained the vision of the Dharma, he sought to go forth, and the Buddha immediately granted his permission.
Having gone forth, he practiced with heedfulness and, within three nights, fully attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*).
The Buddha declared that this person had attained arhatship; for this reason, he was thereafter named Sujāta.
Having attained the three types of supernormal knowledge, he commanded his charioteer, Bharadvāja, saying:
"You should mount the precious chariot you are driving and return home; tell Vāseṭṭha:
'You may feel sympathetic joy toward me.'"

Why is this? The Buddha has now taught me the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; furthermore, having been granted ordination, I have attained the Threefold Knowledge. For these reasons, you should conceive pure faith toward me.
At that time, Vāseṭṭha was returning home by carriage. When he saw the carriage returning, he asked the charioteer:
"Did that brahmin see the Buddha?"

The charioteer replied, "The brahmin attained the vision of the Four Noble Truths while still seated upon his mat. Having seen the Four Truths, he sought ordination; the Buddha granted him ordination, and once ordained, within three nights, he realized arhatship."
At that time, his wife said to the charioteer,
"If you can now deliver this good news, I shall grant you the horse and a thousand pieces of gold."
The charioteer replied, "I have no need now for horses or gold coins; I wish to go to where the Buddha is to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.
Vāsiṣṭha said:
"If it be so for you, it is truly excellent.
If you go forth from the household life, you will quickly be able to attain the path of Arhatship.
Vāsiṣṭha said to his daughter:
"You have managed the household well and enjoyed the pleasures of the five senses; I wish to leave the home life.
The granddaughter Śundarī then said to her mother:

"If even my father can renounce the pleasures of the five senses to leave the home life and seek the Way, I too shall now follow him and leave the home life. I shall cast off thoughts of longing for my brothers and kin; just as when a great elephant departs, the young elephant follows, so shall I likewise follow him into homelessness, holding an earthen bowl and going forth to beg for alms."
"I am able to practice the way of being easy to support, and I shall not act in a manner that is difficult to support.
Vāseṭṭha said, "What you desire is truly auspicious and virtuous; your wish shall surely be fulfilled."
"I now observe that before long you will surely bring desire to an end and be free from all fetters and afflictions.
At that time, the brahmins Vāraṇa, Vāsiṣṭha, and Sunda, following one another, all went forth together and simultaneously attained the ultimate end of all suffering.
93 (Ninisan): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Great Forest near the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the Tathāgata put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
Having finished his meal, he set aside his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and sat beneath a tree, abiding in the celestial dwelling (*divyavihāra*).

At that time, there was a brahmin named Ukkaṭṭha Rājagaha who had lost his milch cow. Having searched everywhere for six days without finding her whereabouts, he continued his quest and entered a great forest. From afar, he saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath a tree; his appearance was extraordinary, his faculties were serene and stilled, and his mind was tranquil. He had attained the state of supreme self-mastery, like a golden pavilion, with a majestic radiance shining forth.
Having seen this matter, he went to where the Buddha was and spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"How does a bhikṣu delight in solitude? What is gained by such reflection?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse, saying:
"Regarding all gains and losses, I have no sorrow or anxiety at all.
Do not say of me that I am no different from you."
Then the brahmin spoke again in verse:
"This place is truly a dwelling for Brahmā; it is exactly as the bhikṣu has described.
I wish to discuss matters concerning my own home; I only pray that you will briefly listen to what I have to say."
"O śramaṇa, you who now sit in meditative repose amidst the forest trees,
have likewise not lost your cow; you shall know that for this śramaṇa there has been no suffering from the six days of anxiety,
for he truly dwells in the bliss of tranquility."
You do not plant rice, so why worry about irrigating it?
Nor do you worry about the rice ears, whether they emerge or fail to emerge;
such manifold sufferings as these, you have long since abandoned.
Nor do they plant sesame seeds, nor do they fear weeds and filth;
you likewise have no such toil of weeding and cultivation.
Know that those śramaṇas truly dwell in the bliss of tranquility.
In my home there was a grass mat, which I have spread for seven months;
within it dwell many venomous insects, and the stings of scorpions cause me suffering.
You have no such things; as a śramaṇa, you enjoy happiness.
"You have no seven sons who are stubborn and difficult to instruct,
nor do you owe debts to others from borrowing; since you have no such matters,
you find happiness as a śramaṇa."
Some give birth to a single child, while others remain childless;
some lose their husbands and return home—none of these things occur here.
Know that the joy of the śramaṇa is such that there are no creditors whatsoever.
When at dawn one comes to the gate, there is no such thing as being pursued for debts owed; the śramaṇa lives in happiness.
You have no dilapidated house, nor are there empty vessels everywhere within it.
A field mouse plays in the center, Scratching and touching, it makes a sound;
It disturbs and ruins my sleep, So that all night long I cannot rest.
You have no wicked wife, Ugly, with yellow eyes.
In the middle of the night they are forcibly driven away; at dawn and dusk they are constantly reviled.
Sometimes they speak of the hardships of their homes, or say they owe debts to others.
A śramaṇa has no such concerns; one should know that this is true happiness.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Brahmin, you should know: What you have said is the truth;
No thief has stolen my ox, Which has already been gone for six days.”
There is no such thing as this; true reality is happiness.
I truly have no rice fields, yet I give rise to the thought that they lack water;
nor do I worry about whether the rice stalks will emerge or not.
I have no such suffering; know that this is happiness.
I have no fields of sesame that are overgrown with weeds and desolate;
I have no such matters; truly, this is called bliss.
In truth, I had no grass mats spread out for me throughout the seven months, nor did any venomous insects appear;
there was no suffering from the stings of scorpions upon my family.
I have experienced none of these things; in reality, it was a state of happiness.
I have no seven sons, stubborn and difficult to instruct;
each has incurred debts and is pressed by others.
Nor do I have seven daughters, some of whom have given birth and some who have not.
Having lost my husband and returned home, I have no such suffering as this.
Nor do I have creditors who come at dawn to knock upon my door to demand the repayment of what I owe.
All the empty vessels therein were filled with mice playing within them;
their scurrying and contact produced sounds that disturbed me and brought my sleep to an end,
so that throughout the night I could not rest.
Yellow-eyed and hideous, he forcibly drives one up at midnight;
day and night he constantly reviles, sometimes speaking of the family’s poverty and suffering,
or claiming that one owes debts to others.
There is no suffering such as this; true reality is happiness.
If you do not sever love and hatred, you shall not escape this suffering.
Sever desire and detach from all cravings; only then will you attain happiness.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the brahmin in various ways, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, as extensively described above, until he exhausted all fetters of existence and would no longer undergo future birth.
At that time, the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa, having attained arhatship and the bliss of liberation, leaped for joy and spoke these verses:
"Now I am filled with supreme delight By the Dharma taught by the Great Sage;
Having heard the Dharma and attained realization, I am entirely free from all grasping and rejecting."
Seeing the World-Honored One is not in vain; meeting the Buddha, one attains the fruits of the Path. (94) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the brahmin village of Sālā.
At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl, intending to enter the village of Śālā to beg for food.
Unseasonable clouds arose and the heavens sent down rain; the Tathāgata sought shelter from the rain and proceeded toward that village.
At that time, in the village, the brahmins and elders were gathered at a place of assembly when they saw the Buddha approaching from afar. They all spoke thus:
"What kind of teachings does this shaven-headed practitioner know?"
When the Buddha heard these words, he immediately told him:
"Among you brahmins, there are those who know the Dharma and those who do not know the Dharma;
it is the same for kṣatriyas and householders as well."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One should never cause one's kinsmen or friends to feel humiliated;
a king likewise does not take what should not be taken, nor does he subdue those who should not be subdued."
A wife does not seek to subdue her husband; when parents reach old age, their children should serve them with reverence and care, for it is improper to act with insolence or rebellion.
There is no place where a multitude gathers that is devoid of virtuous and worthy people.
"There is no true man who does not speak the words of the Dharma;
having severed greed, hatred, and delusion, all that he speaks is in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, the brahmins said:
“You are well-versed in the Dharma of the Brahmins; please come and join this assembly.
Immediately, they spread out seats and invited the Buddha to take his seat, saying:
“Please teach us the Dharma; we are eager to hear it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One entered among the assembly, sat upon his seat, and for their sake expounded various teachings to instruct, benefit, and gladden them, speaking in verse:
"If one remains silent and says nothing, No one can know whether they are foolish or wise;
It is only through speech and expression That one may subsequently distinguish between them."
If one speaks the sublime Dharma, teaching the Dharma that leads to Nirvana,
then by means of such speech, one should kindle the lamp of the Dharma.
Having already raised the banner of the Sages, all of this is due to speech.
"Speech itself is the noble banner; therefore, one should not remain silent.
Having spoken thus, the Buddha rose from his seat and departed.
95 (XCV) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Kosala.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Devahita in that country, who had a guest house within his village.
At that time, the Venerable Upamāna was serving as the Buddha’s attendant and was staying in a guest house.
At that moment, the Tathāgata was slightly afflicted by a wind-disorder and suffered from pain in his back.
The Venerable Upamaṇa put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the home of the brahmin Devaśarman.
At that time, Devaśarman was sitting at the gate with his hair being shaved.
Seeing the Venerable One from afar, the brahmin spoke this verse:
“With shorn hair and clad in dharma robes, Holding an alms bowl in your hand, You stand by the side of my gate; What is it that you seek?”
Then, the Venerable Upamāna replied in verse:
“The Great Arhat, the Sugata, the Muni, suffers from back pain;
He requires a small amount of warm medicinal water, And has therefore come to beg it of you.”
At that time, the brahmin immediately took a bowl and filled it with ghee and oil, a chest of black honey, and a cartload of warm medicinal water, and gave them to him.

At that time, having obtained it, the Venerable One carried it to the Buddha’s presence; he then used this oil, along with warm medicinal water, to wash and anoint the Buddha’s body, and [the Buddha] drank black honey syrup, whereupon his back pain was immediately healed.
Then, on the following morning, the brahmin Deva-garbha went to where the Buddha was, greeted the World-Honored One, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin with these verses:
“How is it, O brahmin, that you practice the dharma of a brahmin?”
What gift yields a great fruit?
What is the proper time for giving?
Within which field of merit does one obtain a superior reward?
Then the brahmin replied in verse:
"There are many who have studied extensively, who are learned and capable of retaining all they hear;
whose parents are truly pure and noble, and whose countenances are entirely dignified and handsome."
Those such as these are called Brahmins of the Threefold Knowledge.
If one gives to such a place, One can obtain a great reward.
Giving food and clothing at the proper time— This is called the supreme field of merit.
Then the brahmin again questioned the Buddha in verse:
"O Gautama, what kind of person do you say is called a *brāhmaṇa*?
What constitutes the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*)?"
By giving what does one obtain great fruit?
What constitutes the proper time for giving?
And what is the most excellent field of merit?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Clearly knowing the three periods of time, Beholding humans, devas, and the evil realms,
Having attained the end of birth and death, And having acquired all supernormal powers.”
"When the mind and intellect attain liberation, this is called the threefold knowledge (*trividyā*).
Giving to such a person yields great fruit; this is known as the supreme field of merit.
At that time, the Brahmin Devaśarman, having heard what the Buddha had said, departed with joy.
96. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala and stayed overnight in the Sāla Grove.
At that time, there was a brahmin who lived near the grove and cultivated his fields; having set out early in the morning to work in the fields, he came to where the Buddha was.
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!
Because I recently cleared a forest to farm, I have come to love this grove."
"Do you now also delight in this Śāla grove? Are you not perhaps cultivating it?
At that time, the brahmin spoke in verse:
"Are you desiring to plant and sow, And thus delighting in this grove?"
"Being without companion, you delight in emptiness and stillness; is it because of this forest that you find joy?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"In this forest, I have nothing at all that is done."
Having uprooted its very foundation, all things are utterly withered and destroyed.
Where there was once a forest, now there is no forest;
having already emerged from the forest, I have forever renounced what is pleasurable, and through meditative concentration, I have severed all defiled attachments.
Then the brahmin spoke again in verse:
"You are truly named Buddha, The most honored among all the worlds;
You are well able to extinguish all fetters And are free from all accumulations."
"The most supreme in the world, having reached the ultimate limit of all future existence, you have toppled the flower-bannered standard of desire; therefore, you are called the World-Honored One.
Having spoken this verse, the brahmin departed with joy.
97. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala and was staying in the Sāla Grove.
At that time, there was a brahmin not far from the grove, under whom five hundred māṇavas were studying.

At that time, the brahmin constantly thought to himself, "When will the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, come to wander in this grove? I shall go there to consult him and resolve my doubts and obstructions.
Then the brahmin sent several young brahmin students (*māṇava*) to the grove to gather firewood for a fire sacrifice.

When the young brahmins had reached the grove, they saw the Tathāgata sitting beneath a tree; he was exceptionally handsome and sublime, his countenance serene and radiant, like a tower of pure gold, glowing with brilliant light.
At that time, having seen the Tathāgata, the young brahmins returned carrying their firewood and said to their teacher:
"Preceptor, you have often longed to see the Buddha in the past; now the Tathāgata is nearby in this forest. If you wish to see him, you should know that now is the time."
When the brahmin had heard these words, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings regarding his well-being, and sat to one side.
He then spoke this verse:
"The deep forest is exceedingly lush and flourishing; its interior is truly terrifying."
For what reason do you sit alone in meditation, practicing dhyāna with a fearless mind?
Furthermore, without the music of a multitude, by which you might delight yourself,
why do you find joy in dwelling in seclusion?
This is truly unprecedented.
Are you seeking the Great Brahmā, the sovereign lord of the world?
Or are you seeking Śakra, the venerable lord of the Thirty-three Heavens?
"Why do you delight in dwelling alone in the fearsome deep forest?
Constantly practicing austerities, what is it that you seek?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"Those who are attached to desires harbor many doubts;
regarding countless objects, each gives rise to defiled attachment.
All fetters and latent tendencies arise solely from a lack of wisdom."
I have severed the root of ignorance, vomited out the mire of fetters and desires,
and completely abandoned all seeking. Free from all guile and crookedness,
I have realized and attained purity within all wholesome dharmas.
"Who has rightly attained the unsurpassed path, and who practices dhyāna free from desire.
At that time, the brahmin spoke again in verse:
"I now bow my head in prostration and take refuge in the Honored Muni."
Mastery over all dhyānas, awakened to immeasurable enlightenment;
honored among gods and humans, endowed with the thirty-two marks,
his upright form peerless, like that king of the snowy mountains.
Having attained liberation within the forest, yet not clinging to the forest,
those who are pure and liberated have extracted the poisoned arrow of birth.
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is supreme among all treatises.
His speech is the most supreme;
he expounds the Four Noble Truths, Universally delivering all beings,
having himself escaped great suffering, And likewise delivering the multitudes of living beings.
May all be granted peace and happiness; I pray that you will expound this Dharma.
I now take refuge and pay homage to you, Who have crossed over to the other shore.
O you who are free from all fears, Welcome to dwell in this forest.
"Now that I have encountered the Great Teacher of gods and men,
who is able to eliminate all the sufferings and afflictions of sentient beings.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the brahmin departed with joy.
98 (Ninety-eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala.
At that time, the World-Honored One stayed on the banks of the Sundarī River.
At that time, there was a brahmin living on the opposite bank who went to where the Buddha was staying. After he had finished his greetings, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do you wish to enter this river to bathe?"
The Buddha asked him,
"What benefit is there in entering this river to bathe?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"This river is the place where ancient seers crossed.
If one enters it to bathe, it can eliminate all evils; being pure, fresh, and clean, it is called 'Great Auspiciousness'."
Having heard this, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"It was not because of that Sundarī, Nor by bathing in the rivers Bhidya,
Gaṅgā, Kakṣaput, or Ajiravatī, That one enters these various rivers to bathe."
One can never wash away the evil karma already committed.
Even if one were to bathe together with the powerful Bhaṇḍis and the foolish, the base,
and the lowly within it for as long as a hundred thousand years, [it could not be cleansed].
In the end, they cannot eliminate evil or the defilements of affliction.
If a person’s mind is truly pure, possessing the precepts and constantly observing the *poṣadha*,
and is able to cultivate pure deeds, they will always be fully endowed with the precepts.
Not killing and not stealing, not committing adultery and not speaking falsely—
those who can believe in the retribution of sins and blessings will never envy others.
Washing away the dust and grime with the water of the Dharma, one should bathe in this very place.
Although one may drink from or bathe in rivers such as the Sundarī and the Ganges— all of which are worldly waters—
these cannot remove defilement nor can they eliminate all evil karma.
Of what use is drinking or bathing?
To speak truthfully and with harmony, to abandon anger and refrain from harming living beings—this is the truly pure water.
If one enters the river of pure precepts, one washes away all afflictions.
Though one does not remove external impurities, one can eliminate internal defilements.
Those who are fierce, treacherous, and cruel, the ignorant who commit various evils—
such as these impurities, these filthy, foul, and wicked ones.
"Water thoroughly cleanses the impurities of the body, yet it cannot remove this evil.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
It is truly as you have said.
Now, bathing is able to remove the impurities of the body.
"Those who perform evil deeds cannot have them removed by washing.
99 (99) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling along the banks of the river Sundarī in Kosala.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having newly shaved his beard and hair, stayed by the riverbank.
Rising early in the last watch of the night, he covered his head with his robe, sat upright with his body straight, and fixed his mindfulness before him.

At that time, on the riverbank, there was a fire-worshipping Brahmin who followed the ritual of sacrificing to the fire; he had remaining sacrificial offerings which were to be bestowed upon other Brahmins. As dawn was about to break, he took those remains of the sacrifice and sought out a Brahmin, wishing to give them to him as an offering.
As he passed by the Buddha, at that time the World-Honored One heard the sound of his footsteps and immediately uncovered himself, clearing his throat with a coughing sound.
Once this brahmin had seen the Buddha, he spoke these words:
"This is not a brahmin; he is merely a shaven-headed practitioner."
He then wished to turn back, but again had this thought:
"One who has shaved his hair is not necessarily a śramaṇa; among the brāhmaṇas as well, there are those who have shaved their hair."
"I shall go to him and inquire about the causes and conditions of his birth and his lineage.
At that time, the brahmin went to where the Buddha was and, having greeted him, asked:
"Where were you born?"
"What is his clan?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"One should not ask about the place of birth; one should rather ask about his conduct."
Even a tiny spark can produce fire; from the lowly and base, the wise and accomplished are born.
Likewise, one may give birth to a well-trained mount; through shame and remorse, one performs good deeds.
By diligent self-discipline and compliance, one crosses to the further shore of the Vedas.
With a concentrated mind, collect your thoughts; fully cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya).
In the early morning, you should give away the remains of your sacrificial offerings.
You who are now a brahmin, if you wish to cultivate merit, [act accordingly].
"You should bestow it quickly; such is the way of a virtuous man.
At that time, the brahmin replied with a verse:
"I have now encountered a noble sacrifice; this place is truly a site for the fire-sacrifice."
I now observe you and see that you have truly crossed to the far shore of the Vedas.
In the past, when offerings were made from the remnants of sacrifices, they were always given to others;
never before have we found a recipient as excellent and worthy of gifts as you.
The brahmin immediately offered this food to the World-Honored One, but the Buddha did not accept it, and spoke these verses:
"If one lacks the intention to give before preaching the Dharma, yet gives only after speaking,
such food and drink as this should not be accepted."
The constant law is thus established; therefore, I ought not to eat.
The reason I do not accept [the food] is for the sake of the Dharma verses.
Behold these great beings, who have all extinguished their afflictions.
One should provide various offerings of food and drink;
those who seek a field of merit should likewise give here.
If you wish to cultivate merit, I myself am that field of merit.
Then the brahmin addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"To whom should I now give this food of mine?
The Buddha said:
"I do not see anyone in the world—whether among śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, or gods, or Māras, or Brahmās—who could receive this food and digest it through right principle; such a thing is impossible."
The Buddha said, "It should be placed in that water which is free of insects.
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the brahmin immediately took it and placed it in that insect-free water; smoke and flames rose together, emitting a crackling sound.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the brahmin was seized with great terror and his hair stood on end.
Out of fear and dread, he gathered more firewood to offer as a sacrifice to the fire.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where he was and spoke these verses:
"You have neatly arranged the firewood and kindled it, thinking thereby to attain purity;
yet you, a person of meager merit and lacking wisdom, are merely burning external fire."
A brāhmaṇa should abandon the fire you have kindled;
he should cultivate the fire within his own mind, blazing without interruption.
To increase and expand this fire—this is called the true sacrifice.
Repeatedly giving with faith—this is how you should perform sacrifice.
Now your arrogance is so heavy it cannot be borne by a chariot;
your poisonous anger is like smoke, or like oil poured upon a fire.
The tongue can incite evil speech, and the mind is a hidden storehouse of fire;
if one cannot discipline oneself, how can one be called a true man?
If one takes faith as a river and precepts as the ferry for crossing over, [one may reach the further shore].
Such pure water is praised by the virtuous.
If one enters the cleansing of faith and precepts, it is like the Vedic incantations for you;
it can extinguish all signs of evil and enable one to reach the further shore.
Taking the Dharma as its waters, Gautama is truly one who ferries others across;
with its pure and clear water, it is what the noble man prizes.
All those capable of bathing therein are persons of Vedic merit.
With the body unstained and unmoistened, one attains the further shore.
With truthful speech, one disciplines the sense faculties;
concealing the three karmas and fully cultivating the holy life, patience and a sense of shame are supreme.
"One who is faithful, inclined toward virtue, and upright—this is the true bath of the Dharma.
Therefore, you should now understand it in this way.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin cast aside his fire-offering implements, immediately rose to pay homage to the Buddha, and with palms joined, addressed him:

“I only pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and receive full ordination within the Buddha’s Dharma, so that I may become a bhikṣu, enter the Buddha’s Dharma, and cultivate the holy life.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent, allowing him to leave the household life and receive the full precepts.

At that time, that venerable one diligently cultivated himself with self-restraint, applying himself with single-minded devotion, delighting in seclusion and solitude, remaining free from negligence, and taking no pleasure in associating with either renunciants or householders.

Why is this? Because this son of good family has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and with right faith has gone forth from the household life to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya), so as to realize it through direct knowledge and vision in the present life and personally witness it for himself.

At that time, this bhikṣu cultivated and perfected concentration and wisdom, attained the fruit of arhatship, exhausted all outflows, established the holy life, accomplished what was to be done, and was no longer subject to further existence.
100. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain brahmin with matted hair named Puttalaśa approached the place where the Buddha was; having exchanged greetings, he sat down to one side.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The external hair is all bound in a topknot; Is there internal hair within that topknot?
As for the hair of the world that is bound up, Who is there capable of removing it?"
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"The wise establish the precepts; The mind cultivates wisdom.
With single-minded diligence and tireless study, One who is young shaves off the topknot."
Then the brahmin spoke again in verse:
"With your outer hair all bound in a topknot, do you have a topknot within?
Who is able to sever the hair that binds the world?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, And likewise the mind and mental objects—
When name-and-form are entirely without remainder, The mind is extinguished and enters parinirvāṇa."
If one can act in this way, one shall sever the topknot and hair.
Cāṇḍa, Vasiṣṭha, Lost-Cow, the Assembly Place,
Deva-Respected, Sāla Forest, Fuel-Gathering, and the Two Sundaras.
101. Ekajaṭā (The One-Tufted Lock). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Uruvelā, beneath the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nerañjarā River, not long after his attainment of Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat alone in contemplation and had this thought:

"If a person lacks a heart of reverence and cannot be respectful and compliant toward their elders and superiors, refusing instruction and lacking all sense of awe or restraint, they will indulge their desires and live in self-indulgence, thereby losing all righteous benefit forever."
If it were otherwise, one would be entangled in a multitude of sufferings.

If a person serves their elders with filial piety, honoring and supporting them with reverence and caution, following their will without opposition, their aspirations will be fulfilled and they shall attain great benefit and purpose.
"If this is so, I shall find peace and happiness in all my dealings.
He further thought:

"In all the world—whether among gods or humans, in the realm of gods or the realm of humans, in the realm of Māra or the realm of Brahmā, or among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—among all living beings in the world, if there be anyone whose virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation surpasses mine, I shall approach them, rely upon them, and honor and revere them."

Having observed thoroughly, he saw that among the people, devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas of the world, there was no one who excelled him in ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, such that they could serve as his refuge.
Again, he thought:
"Regarding the Dharma that I have realized, I should now personally attend to it, make offerings to it, revere it, honor it with sincerity, and respect it."

Why is this? All Buddhas of the past have entirely approached, relied upon, made offerings to, revered, and honored this Dharma; likewise, all Buddhas of the future and present also approach and rely upon this Dharma, making offerings and showing reverence, giving rise to a heart of respect.
I, too, shall now approach, rely upon, make offerings to, revere, and honor the Dharma, just as the Buddhas of the past, future, and present have done.
At that time, the Brahma King Mahābrahmā, knowing from afar that the World-Honored One was at the village of Uruvelā, beneath the Bodhi tree on the banks of the Nairañjanā River, had this thought:

"I shall observe the world—whether gods, humans, Māras, Brahmas, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, among all classes of living beings—to see if there is anyone whose virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, or knowledge and vision of liberation surpasses my own, so that I might rely upon them; yet, I do not see anyone at all who can surpass me."

Furthermore, he observes that all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have all personally approached and relied upon the Dharma, making offerings and showing reverence while giving rise to a heart of respect; "I too should now, following the example of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, perform approaching, relying upon, making offerings to, revering, and respecting the Dharma."
Then, the Brahmā Lord again thought to himself:
"I shall pass away from this place and go to where the Buddha is.
Then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, the Brahmā Lord arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is truly as I have thought; it is indeed as I have thought.”
Then he spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgatas of the past and present, And all the Buddhas of the future—
These Perfectly Awakened Ones who can eliminate affliction All take the Dharma as their teacher.”
To draw near to the Dharma and dwell in reliance upon it—this is the teaching of all Buddhas of the three times.
Therefore, those who wish to honor themselves should first respect and revere that Dharma.
"You should remember and keep in mind the Buddha's teachings, and honor and make offerings to the unsurpassed Dharma.
At that time, the Brahma King praised the World-Honored One, gave rise to deep sympathetic joy, paid homage, and departed.
102 (102). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Uruvelā, by the side of the Nerañjarā River, beneath the Bodhi tree, not long after his attainment of Buddhahood.
Seated alone beneath the tree, the Buddha reflected and thought to himself:

"There is but one path that can purify sentient beings, causing them to leave behind suffering and affliction, and likewise enabling them to eliminate unwholesome and evil karma and attain the benefits of the True Dharma. That which is called the Dharma is precisely the four foundations of mindfulness."
What are called the four foundations of mindfulness?

They are the foundation of mindfulness of observing the body, the foundation of mindfulness of observing feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of observing the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of observing phenomena.
If a person does not cultivate these four foundations of mindfulness, they remain far removed from the Dharma of the noble ones and far removed from the Noble Path.
If one departs from the Noble Path, one is far removed from the Deathless (amṛta).
If one is far removed from the Deathless, then one cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.
For such persons as these, I say they will ultimately never be able to escape from all suffering.
If one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, one draws near to the Dharma of the noble ones; if one draws near to the Dharma of the noble ones, one draws near to the Path of the noble ones.
If one draws near to the path of the noble ones, one draws near to the Dharma of the Deathless.
If one draws near to the Dharma of the Deathless, one is able to escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
"If those who are exempt from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—such persons, it is said, have transcended suffering.
At that time, the Brahma Lord, knowing from afar what was in the Tathāgata’s mind, thought to himself:
"I shall now go to the Buddha's presence to express my sympathetic joy and encourage his virtue."
Having reflected thus, in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, he arrived at the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Truly, as the World-Honored One has contemplated in his mind, there is but one path that can purify sentient beings, even enabling them to escape sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction."
Then, the Brahmā Lord spoke this verse:
“This alone is the path that leads out; In this place one may apply oneself with diligence.
If one seeks to be far removed from suffering, There is only this one path.”
Those who traverse this path, like a crane soaring through the sky,
Śākyamuni, the Honored One, has attained the Way of the Buddha.
All Teachers of the Right Path should, by means of this awakening path, [attain the same].
Manifesting this to sentient beings, you should always preach it again and again,
so that all may come to know the limit of existence within birth.
We pray only that you will teach the One Way, out of compassion to rescue all sentient beings.
All Buddhas of the past attained liberation through this path;
The Buddhas of the future and those of the present likewise cross over by means of this path.
What is meant by "crossing over"?
Able to cross the surging torrent, reaching the ultimate limit of the boundless, Tamed and having attained supreme purity;
seeing that the world is entirely subject to birth and death, And understanding all realms,
he proclaims this path clearly for those who possess the eye.
Just as that Ganges River flows on toward the great ocean, so too is the Noble Path; the Buddha has revealed and manifested it.
This path is like that river, leading toward the ocean of ambrosia.
Never before have we heard the sound of the turning of the sublime wheel of Dharma;
we pray only that the Honored One among gods and men, who delivers those subject to old age, sickness, and death—
the one to whom all turn for refuge— will turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
At that time, the Brahmā Lord prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and vanished on the spot.
103 (103) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the Brahma Lord, his radiance twice as great as usual, came to where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side.
The majestic radiance of the Lord of Brahmā illuminated the assembly, shining with brilliant clarity.
Then, from his seat, he spoke these verses:
“The Kṣatriya, the most honored among bipeds, One whose lineage is truly pure—”
"Having perfected both knowledge and conduct, he is the most supreme among gods and humans.
The Buddha addressed the Lord of Brahmā, saying: "Truly so it is; truly so it is."
"A Kṣatriya, the most honored among bipeds, one of true lineage, fully perfected in knowledge and conduct, the most excellent among gods and humans.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the Brahmā Lord leaped for joy; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, vanished from his seat, and returned to his celestial palace.
104 (One Hundred and Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala.
At that time, there was a forest hermitage in that country, where the World-Honored One, together with a great assembly of the bhikṣu-saṃgha, stayed for the night.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised this dwelling place and spoke on the Dharma of dwelling in an araṇya.

Then, the Brahma Lord, knowing that the Tathāgata was traveling through Kosala and staying with the community of bhikṣus in an araṇya dwelling, praised the araṇya dwelling and spoke on the Dharma of dwelling in an araṇya.
The Brahma Lord King thought to himself:
"I shall now go to where the Buddha is to offer praise and sympathetic joy.

At that moment, the Brahma Lord vanished from his place; in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he arrived at the Buddha's location, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Abiding in stillness with one's bedding and requisites, One should sever the fetters of bondage.
If one cannot find joy therein, One should return to dwell among the Saṃgha."
Always maintaining right mindfulness, Taming the senses while wandering for alms,
One who is fully endowed with the precepts Should go to a secluded and quiet place.
Relinquishing all fear, Firmly abiding in fearlessness.
Those who have severed pride dwell with firm resolve in the middle way.
Thus have I heard: one should harbor no doubt;
a thousand arhats shall here bring an end to birth and death.
Two hundred and five seekers, and one thousand one hundred *srotāpannas*,
following the stream and practicing the right path, shall never turn toward a wrong way.
It is impossible to fully declare all those who have attained the fruits of the various paths.
"The reason I am unable to speak is that I fear you will not believe or revere me.
When the Brahma Lord had spoken this verse, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his celestial palace.

105. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Śākya Kapilavastu forest together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats whose taints were exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, completely ended the cycle of further existence, and were liberated through right knowledge, free from all fetters.
Furthermore, there were ten classes of gods of great majesty who came to where the Buddha was to inquire after his well-being and that of the Sangha.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma that accords with Nirvana.
There were four Brahmakāyika devas who each had this thought:

"At present, the Buddha is staying in the Śītagṛha forest at Rājagṛha together with a community of five hundred bhikṣus. They are all great arhats whose outflows are exhausted, who have accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, brought an end to further existence, and are liberated through right knowledge, free from all fetters."

Furthermore, there were ten world-systems of gods of great majesty who came to where the Buddha was, inquiring after the Buddha and the Sangha; the World-Honored One expounded for them the Dharma that accords with Nirvana.
"I shall now go to that place where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, resides.

Having formed this thought, the Brahmakāyika deva immediately vanished from that place; in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he arrived at the Buddha’s location, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Then, a Brahmakāyika deva spoke this verse:
"Now, within this grove, a great assembly has gathered;
for this reason we have come, desiring truly to behold the multitude of monks."
"Do not, with an unwholesome mind, destroy the Saṅgha or break its harmony.
A second Brahmakāyika deva further spoke in verse:
"A bhikṣu with a sincere heart ought to apply himself with diligent effort."
"Just as a skilled charioteer controls the horses to make them docile,
so too should a bhikṣu control his sense faculties.
A third Brahmakāyika deva then spoke in verse:
"Just as a wild horse bound by fetters, By pulling up the pillar and treading over the moat, emerges in safety;

So too are the bhikṣus: having pulled up the pillar of the three poisons and severed the moat of desire, Tamed by the World-Honored One, the Great Teacher, They are able to emerge like these great dragon-elephants."
The fourth Brahmakāyika deva further spoke in verse:
"Those who take refuge in the Buddha Cast off their human forms and attain divine bodies."
At that time, after each of the four Brahmakāyika devas had spoken their verses, they remained within the assembly; with hearts full of reverence and trembling, they paid homage and departed.
106 (106) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the Brahma Lord, his majestic radiance exceedingly bright, came to where the Buddha was.
At that moment, the World-Honored One had entered the fire-light samādhi.
At that time, the Brahma Lord thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata has now entered into samādhi; for me to come here at this moment is most untimely."
At that time, the bhikṣu Kokālika, a close friend of Devadatta, slandered Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Brahmā Sahāmpati went to his location, knocked on Kokālika’s door,
and called out, “Kokālika!
Kokālika!
You should conceive pure faith in Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; those two venerable ones possess minds that are pure and supple, and they are fully endowed with the holy life.
"By making such a slanderous accusation, you will suffer various miseries for a long night in the future.
Kokālika then asked him, "Who are you?"
He replied,
"I am Brahmā, the Lord of the Gods. Kokālika said:
"Has the Buddha prophesied that you will attain the stage of Anāgāmin?
Brahmā replied, "It is indeed so."
Kokālika said, "Anāgāmin means 'one who does not return'; how is it that you have returned?
Brahmā Sahāmpati then thought to himself:
"One should not speak with such persons," and he spoke this verse:
"One who wishes to fathom the immeasurable Dharma / Is one whom the wise should not associate with."
"If one attempts to fathom immeasurable dharmas, one will surely be burned and harmed.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the Brahmā Lord went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
He reported in full to the World-Honored One the causes and conditions as spoken by Kokālika.
The Buddha told Brahmā: “It is so, it is so.”
"One who wishes to fathom the immeasurable Dharma must be able to burn away the state of an ordinary person.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When a person is born into this world, An axe is held within their mouth; It is because of their evil speech..."
One who cuts off one's own body,
who slanders those who should be praised and praises those who should be slandered— such an evil person shall never see happiness.
Kālī falsely slandered the Buddha and the noble ones; because Kālī’s offense was grave, she entered hundreds of thousands of hells.
At that time, Aṅgulimāla also slandered the noble ones; due to the evil of his speech and mind, he entered this hell.
At that time, having heard these verses, the Brahmā Lord paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.

These five sūtras at the end of the fifth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama* (Alternate Translation) and the first five sūtras of the sixth fascicle are absent from the Guo and Song editions but are found exclusively in the Dan edition.
The ninth is the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, and the tenth is the *Subhadra-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Now, upon examining the *Brahmaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, it is found to be a different translation of the same original text as the beginning of the forty-fourth fascicle of the extensive *Saṃyukta Āgama*.

The *Sūtra on Crossing over Subhadra* and the section from the sixteenth fascicle onwards of the thirty-fifth volume of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* are translations of the same original text with different versions.
Thus, the fact that these two editions—the Qi and Song dynasties versions—lack this sūtra is simply due to their being omitted.
Now, based on the Danzang (Dunhuang canon), these have been added and divided into two fascicles.
This is the sixth fascicle of the *Separate Translation of the Saṃyukta Āgama*, whose translator’s name is lost; it is now appended to the Qin records.
107. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were two devas—one named Parittasubha and the other named Parittābha—who wished to come and visit the Buddha.
At that time, when Pakva Brahmā saw these two Brahmās, he asked them:
"Where do you wish to go?
The two Brahmās replied:
"We wish to go to the place where the World-Honored One resides to inquire after his well-being and pay our respects.
At that time, Brahmā Pakuṣāti spoke these verses:
"The four Brahmās are like cranes; The three Brahmās are named 'Gold'."
Seven hundred and twenty-five are named Yūvī.
Behold my golden hue, blazing and magnificent;
all its majestic radiance outshines even the Brahmā heavens.
"Why do you not observe me, yet wish to go to the place where the Buddha is?
At that time, the two Brahmās replied in verse:
"You now possess a minor radiance, which outshines the Brahma heavens."
"You should know that these colors and forms all possess various faults and afflictions;
one of clear wisdom attains liberation and takes no pleasure in such colors and forms.
At that time, after the two Brahmās had spoken this verse, they approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
The two Brahmās addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We wish to come and see the Buddha.”
At that time, Pāka Brahmā asked me,
"Where do you wish to go? We replied:
"I wish to go to the place where the Buddha is.
At that time, Brahmā Pakuṣāti spoke this verse:
"The four Brahmās are named *krauñca* (cranes); The three Brahmās are named *kāñcana* (gold)."
Seven hundred and twenty-five are called the Yavanas.
Behold my golden hue, blazing and intensely radiant;
the light of my body’s brilliance outshines even the Brahma heavens.
"Why do you not observe me, yet wish to go to the Buddha's abode?
We then replied with these verses:
"You now possess a slight radiance that outshines the Brahmā heavens."
"You should know that these colors and forms all possess various faults and afflictions;
the wise attain liberation and take no pleasure in such colors and forms.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
“Brahmā! It is so, it is so.

Although that Brahmā possesses a slight radiance, it outshines the Brahmā-world; you should know that all such radiance has its faults, and the wise, having understood this, should not take pleasure in it.”
The Buddha preached various teachings to the two Brahmās, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
Having heard the Dharma, the two Brahmās rejoiced, prostrated themselves in worship, and returned to their celestial palaces.
108 (One Hundred and Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Brahmā Pakudha gave rise to a wrong view and said:
"This place is eternally firm and indestructible; one shall no longer come and go within the cycle of birth and death. It is impossible for anyone to pass beyond this without coming and going."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of Brahmā Pakāsa, went to that palace of Brahmā Pakāsa in the same instant as a strong man might extend his arm after having bent it.
Then, Pāka Brahmā said to the Buddha:
"Great Seer!
This place is eternal, firm, solid, and indestructible; it is entirely devoid of coming and going."
"If there were anyone who could transcend this and be without coming or going, such a thing is impossible.
The Buddha said to Brahmā:
"This place is impermanent; why do you now falsely conceive the notion of permanence?"
This place is subject to decay, yet you falsely conceive the notion that it is indestructible.
This place is unstable, yet you falsely conceive the notion that it is stable.
This place involves coming and going, yet you now falsely conceive the notion that there is no coming and going.
"There is yet a superior place where there is no coming or going at all; you have merely given rise to the false notion that there is nothing superior.
Then, Brahmā Pakāsa spoke these verses:
"Seventy-two Brahmās who performed supreme merit, All of them have passed away right here."
"All the Brahmās know me; / Only I remain here, never to decline.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"What you call long life / Is in truth but a short duration."
"I know your lifespan to be one hundred thousand *nirarbuda*.
Then, Pāka Brahmā replied with a verse:
"O Bhagavān, World-Honored One!"
Your wisdom is truly inexhaustible; you have transcended birth, old age, and sorrow, and speak for those who possess the eye.
What karma did I previously create, and what ascetic practices did I cultivate, that I am now here in this Brahma Heaven, with my lifespan extended?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"In the past, there was a band of thieves Who plundered and destroyed villages;
They stripped and bound people, Seizing vast quantities of wealth."
At that time, you shall possess great heroic power;
you will rescue and liberate all people, yet without inflicting harm upon them.
Together with those people, you shall practice virtue for the duration of one eon.
Compassionate and kind, you delight in giving, and are further able to maintain the practice of the precepts.
Whether asleep or awake, you should remember what you have practiced.
Furthermore, there was a man traveling by boat upon that River Ganges.
When the evil dragon sought to harm the boatmen with all his venomous power,
you were then a divine seer who rescued their lives.
This was brought about by the precepts you cultivated in days of yore.
Then, Brahmā Pāyāsi spoke these verses:
“You truly do know me, The length of my lifespan,
And furthermore, all other matters— You know them all.”
"Your radiance is exceedingly brilliant, capable of eclipsing all the Brahmās;
there is nothing you do not thoroughly comprehend, and for this reason you are called Bhagavān.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught various dharmas to the Brahmā Bhaga, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. He then immediately vanished from that place and returned to the Jeta Grove.
109 (109). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain brahmin who gave rise to a great false view and spoke as follows:
"I have never seen anyone here who is able to be born within my palace, much less anyone who can surpass me.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered into samādhi, vanished from Jambudvīpa, and appeared sitting in the void above the summit of the Brahma world.
The Venerable Kauṇḍinya, using his purified divine eye, observed where the World-Honored One had gone;
he immediately knew that the Tathāgata was sitting in the open space above the summit of the Brahma-world.
At that time, Kauṇḍinya also entered this samādhi, vanished from this place, and appeared above the crown of Brahmā’s head, situated below the Tathāgata on the eastern side.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, with his purified divine eye, observed where the Tathāgata had gone.

He immediately perceived that the World-Honored One was atop the Brahma-peak; he then entered this same meditative concentration, vanished from that place, and appeared beneath the Tathāgata on the southern side of the Brahma-peak.
With his purified divine eye, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana observed where the Tathāgata had gone;

he immediately perceived that the World-Honored One was atop the Summit of Brahmā. He then entered this meditative concentration, vanished from that place, and appeared atop the Summit of Brahmā, situated below the Tathāgata and manifesting on the western side.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha again used his purified divine eye to observe where the Tathāgata had gone;

he immediately knew that the World-Honored One was atop the Summit of Brahmā. He too entered this meditative concentration, vanished from that place, and appeared atop the Summit of Brahmā, situated below the Tathāgata on the northern side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Brahmā, saying:
"Have you abandoned what you previously perceived?
He further addressed Brahmā:
"You previously thought to yourself:
'I do not see anyone capable of being born into my palace, much less one who could surpass it.
Now, try and observe these celestial bodies; are their features and radiance not superior to yours?"
Then Brahmā said to the Buddha:
“Indeed! I have seen it.”
Now, having seen them—these radiances that were not seen before, but are seen now—these radiances are truly extraordinary and sublime.
"From this day forward, I shall never again dare to say that this place is permanent, eternal, and subject to no change.
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"This place is impermanent; it is empty and lacks self-mastery."
The Buddha preached various teachings to that Brahmā, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; he then entered such a samādhi, vanished from that Brahmā world, and returned to the Jeta Grove.

The Venerable Kauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Aniruddha, and others also preached various teachings to those Brahmās, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; they too entered this meditative absorption, passed away from that place, and returned to the Jeta Grove, with only the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana remaining seated there.
At that time, that Brahmā asked Maudgalyāyana:
"Among the disciples of the World-Honored One, is there anyone who possesses such great majestic power and supernormal faculties as you?
Maudgalyāyana replied:
"Other śrāvakas also possess such majestic power and supernormal faculties.
Venerable Maudgalyāyana then spoke this verse:
"The great arhats, disciples of the Muni, Possess great majestic power and are endowed with the three knowledges (traividya)."
Having exhausted all outflows and knowing the minds of others, they can manifest spiritual transformations for the sake of all living beings;
such śrāvakas are exceedingly numerous, and therefore you should now pay them respect.

Then, after the Venerable Maudgalyāyana had spoken these verses, he taught the Dharma in various ways to instruct, benefit, and gladden them; he likewise entered this samādhi, passed away from that Brahma realm, and returned to the Jeta Grove.
110. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kuśinagara, in the birthplace of the Mallas, within the Śāla Grove.
At that time, when the Tathāgata’s time for parinirvāṇa had arrived, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
“You should prepare a seat for me between the twin trees, with its head toward the north.”
Then, having received the Buddha’s command, Ānanda prepared a seat between the twin trees with its head pointing north.
Once the seat was prepared, he returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have prepared the seat with its head toward the north between the twin trees, and my task is now complete."

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat and proceeded to the place where the twin trees were spread; there he lay down on his right side with his head toward the north, placing one foot upon the other, fixing his mind on clarity, arousing the awakening of mindfulness, and first forming the thought of *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Subhadra in the kingdom of Kuśinagara who had previously resided in that country; he was advanced in years, being one hundred and twenty years old.
At that time, the Mallas of that country made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised this Arhat.
Then, Subhadra heard people say that the Bhagavān was due to enter parinirvāṇa that very night. He thought to himself:
"I have certain doubts regarding the Dharma; only Gautama is surely able to explain them and resolve my uncertainties."
Having formed this thought, he immediately departed from Kuśinagara and went to the Śāla grove.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was walking up and down outside. When Subhadra saw Ānanda, he approached him and said to him:
"I have heard it said that the śramaṇa Gautama shall enter parinirvāṇa without remainder this very day at midnight. I must see him now to resolve my doubts."
Ānanda replied: "Brahmin!
The Buddha’s body is weary; you are now disturbing him."
Subhadra said to Ānanda:
"I have heard that today at midnight the Tathāgata will enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. In the past, I heard the words of ancient seers:
'If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, he is as difficult to encounter as the *udumbara* flower.'"
"I have a slight doubt and wish to consult you for its resolution; I pray that you will grant me an audience.
Thus he requested three times, and Ānanda replied, "Do not disturb the Buddha!"
At that time, the World-Honored One, with his pure divine ear, heard from afar that Ānanda was stopping Subhadra and would not allow him to proceed.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Do not stop that man; let him proceed and ask whatever questions he wishes."

At that time, having heard that the Buddha, out of compassion, had granted him permission to approach, Subhadra leaped for joy. He immediately went to where the Buddha was, and after completing his greetings, sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have a slight doubt; may I ask you about it?"
The Buddha said,
"Ask whatever you wish.
Having received this permission, Subhadra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

There are the six heterodox teachers with their various divergent views: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Keśakambalin, Sañjaya Vairaṭīputra, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra. Each of these six teachers claims for himself that he is already a World-Honored One; have they truly attained all-knowledge?”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Thirty-one years have passed since my renunciation; Fifty years have gone by since then.
Seeking all wholesome dharmas, I have attained clarity through the practice of precepts and meditative concentration."
All those in the various worlds do not know the true direction or location;
how much less could they know the true Dharma?
If one cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path, one can attain the first fruit, and even up to the fourth fruit.
If one does not cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, the first fruit cannot be known,
let alone the fourth.
This lion’s roar of the Dharma is outside such [wrong] teachings.
"Furthermore, there are no śramaṇas, nor are there any brāhmaṇas.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, Subhadra was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, Subhadra adjusted his upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*), joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have now already transcended the three evil realms."
Then Subhadra said to Ānanda: "Excellent, Ānanda!"
"You have attained great benefit by becoming a disciple of the Buddha and serving as his foremost attendant.
I, too, have now gained a wholesome benefit; I wish to go forth into homelessness within the Buddha's Dharma."
Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Buddha,
“Subhadra wishes to go forth into homelessness within the Buddha’s Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Subhadra:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!

As he spoke, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately attained full ordination; having attained full ordination, he then became an Arhat.
Subhadra then thought to himself:
"I cannot bear to see the World-Honored One enter parinirvāṇa; I shall enter it first.
Subhadra immediately entered nirvāṇa first, and the Tathāgata subsequently entered nirvāṇa as well.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who spoke in verse:
“Entering nirvāṇa between the twin trees, The branches and twigs spread everywhere in the four directions.”
Raining down flowers from above and below, they scattered profusely over the Buddha.
As for why these flowers rained down: it was because the World-Honored One had entered *nirvāṇa*.
Śakra-devānām-indra then spoke this verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature to arise and cease. When arising and ceasing have ceased, that is called Nirvana.
At that time, Brahmā Sahampati again spoke in verse:
“In this world, there are living beings who, having cast off their bodies, return to ultimate extinction;
yet now the Great Sage, the Honored One, who is fully endowed with the ten powers—
the World-Honored One who is without equal— now enters into nirvana.”
Then, the Venerable Aniruddha spoke again in verse:
“The Lord of Dharma dwells in mental stillness; The inhalations and exhalations have been severed.
That which the Tathāgata has accomplished— The power of his practice is fully perfected.”
Now entering into nirvāṇa, his mind is free from fear;
having completely relinquished all sensations, like a lamp extinguished when its oil is spent,
he has ceased existence and entered nirvāṇa, his mind and consciousness having attained liberation.
At that time, when the assembly beheld this, the hair on their bodies all stood on end.
Seven days had passed since the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*. Then Ānanda performed the cremation of the Tathāgata, circumambulated him to the right, and spoke these verses:
"O Greatly Compassionate Brahmā-like World-Honored One!"
Possessing great supernormal power, fire issued from his natural body;
though a thousand layers of cotton were used to wrap his body, neither the interior nor the exterior was burned.
1. Second Recitation, First Chapter, 111 (111). The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All of you should diligently cultivate wholesome deeds, gradually increasing them like the waxing moon at its first appearance."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had recently received the precepts; he gradually cultivated a sense of shame and remorse, maintained excellent deportment, and traveled among the people with gentleness and humility, never being stubborn or perverse. He was able to restrain both body and mind, just as a person with clear vision avoids a deep, empty well or a steep mountain precipice.
The bhikṣu is likewise; like the new moon, he gradually increases, his virtuous conduct becoming ever more refined day by day.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:

"In this assembly, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa diligently cultivates virtuous conduct, like the new moon, gradually increasing and progressively refining his sense of shame and remorse. As he travels among the people, he is able to restrain both body and mind; gentle, harmonious, and respectful, he never becomes obstinate or perverse. Just as a person with clear vision can avoid a deep well and stay far away from precipitous valleys, so too is the bhikṣu Kāśyapa."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What kind of bhikṣu is in accord with the Dharma and is fit to go among the households?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is the root of all dharmas, the guide of all dharmas, and that upon which all dharmas rely.
Excellent!”
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound this meaning for our sake; having heard it, we shall receive and uphold it with a sincere heart.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Keep this in mind with a sincere heart.”

If there is a bhikṣu who is free from attachment, who is not bound by love for his home, who does not give rise to increase or decrease, whose mind is without resentment, and who is also without envy.
Seeing others receive offerings and gain, they give rise to joy in their hearts.
Seeing others bestow gifts upon others, they likewise feel no resentment.
Toward those who cultivate merit, they always express sympathetic joy.
Furthermore, he does not praise himself for possessing virtuous conduct; whatever he speaks is always for the sake of all.
When seeing other bhikṣus arrive together with him at another's home, he never disparages them; regarding himself and others, his mind is free from pride or contempt.
"If bhikṣus are able to cultivate a wholesome mind as previously described, they may be said to be compliant, moving about in accordance with the Dharma, coming and going among the people.
At that time, the World-Honored One moved his hand through the air and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now, this hand of mine does not adhere to space, nor is it bound by space; it has no resentment and no anger. Does this hand have any binding attachment, increase, or decrease?"
The bhikṣus then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This hand in space is without binding and without attachment; it neither increases nor decreases."
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"It is so, it is so. If there is a bhikṣu whose mind is free from bondage and attachment, like a hand moving through space, he may enter and exit, go and return among various families, without giving rise to increase or decrease, without giving rise to vexation, and without envy."
Seeing others receive offerings and gain, they feel joy in their hearts.
Seeing others practice giving, even when it does not reach them, they feel no resentment.
Seeing those who cultivate merit, they universally rejoice in them, until their minds are free from all sense of superiority or inferiority.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The bhikṣu Kāśyapa is also like this; as he travels back and forth among humans, his mind is free from bondage and attachment, even to the point that his mind is free from pride or humility.”
The Buddha again moved his hand for a second time in mid-air and addressed the bhikṣus:
"As previously stated, it is even so with the bhikṣu Kāśyapa."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“How does a bhikṣu enter and leave various households and preach the Dharma for people?
How is it that he may be said to preach the Dharma with purity?”
"What is meant by 'impure exposition'?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
The Tathāgata is the root of all dharmas, the guide of the Dharma, and that upon which the Dharma relies.
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
"We pray that you will expound it for us; having heard it, we shall receive and uphold it with a sincere heart.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!"
Listen attentively!
Keep this in mind with a sincere heart.
If there is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma for others, he should form this thought:
"I shall preach the Dharma for that person so that they will develop faith and respect toward me, and be able to provide me abundantly with food, drink, clothing, and medicine for illness."
If one speaks in such a manner, it is called impure.

If there is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma for others, desiring to cause the listeners to realize and understand the Buddha-dharma, to eliminate present suffering, to depart from all feverish afflictions, to guide them toward the good realms regardless of the season, and to manifest this for their sake—even to the point of enabling those who know it to know it themselves without following the teachings of others, so that they may leave behind birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress—and to enable the listeners to hear what is spoken and practice accordingly in accordance with the Dharma.
To cause listeners to obtain the Dharma, obtain its meaning, obtain benefit, and obtain peace throughout the long night—speaking in such a manner is called a discourse of pure compassion.
Out of compassion and for the benefit of others, with the desire that the True Dharma may endure for a long time, preaching the Dharma in such a manner is called "pure.
Therefore, a bhikṣu should reflect thus: when preaching the Dharma to others, one should train in this way.

The third point is also as previously explained: the bhikṣu Kāśyapa is able to speak in this manner in order to cause listeners to realize and understand the Buddha-dharma, and even with the desire to cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time; out of compassion and for their benefit, he speaks thus. This is called purity, and it accords with the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 112 (112). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu is about to go to the house of a donor, he should first form this thought:
'If there is anything to be given, you should give it to me quickly and not let it be delayed; give to me with a sincere heart and not without sincerity; may I receive much and not little.'"
"Be generous with what is refined; do not give what is coarse and harsh.
If one harbors such thoughts and maintains this fixed intention when going to the house of a donor, even if the donor gives, they will not do so with a sincere heart, nor will they give with respect.

Although they provide food and drink, they will not make it abundant; they will give what is coarse and harsh rather than what is refined, and even if they do give, they will do so slowly and not promptly.
Yet because this bhikṣu’s wishes are not fulfilled, he becomes ashamed, sorrowful, and anxious, giving rise to a mind of decline.
This bhikṣu should reflect:
"When I go to the house of a donor, it is not my own home; how could I expect to have my heart's desires fulfilled there?"
"Why do you give rise to the thought, wishing to cause the donor to give quickly without delay, and even to give what is refined and fine rather than what is coarse and rough?
If one forms such a thought, even if nothing is obtained, the mind feels no regret; being free from increase or decrease, there is no resentment or dislike.
