Suppose that donor gives only a small amount, does not give with a sincere heart, gives slowly rather than quickly, and even gives coarse things rather than fine ones; yet, the bhikṣu feels no resentment or malice toward them, nor does he feel shame, for his mind remains without increase or decrease.

The bhikṣu Kāśyapa formed this thought: "I am going to the house of a donor; this is not my own home. How can I express my own wishes and hope for their sincere heart, so that they might give promptly without delay, and even with such refinement that it is never coarse or rough?"
The bhikṣu Kāśyapa thought thus: "When I go to the house of a donor, even if I do not receive an offering, I feel no shame at all, and my mind does not suffer any diminution.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should cultivate such a mind when going to the homes of others.
"You should not give rise to the thought: 'Bestow [this] upon me quickly,' or even 'bestow something refined.
Therefore, you should train yourselves in this way: as when the bhikṣu Kāśyapa went to the house of a donor."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 113 (113). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying in the Vaiśākha Lecture Hall within the old garden grove at Śrāvastī.

Then, during that very night, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa arose from meditative concentration; having arisen from concentration, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You should instruct the bhikṣus, guiding and illuminating them with the methods of dhyāna-concentration, and expound for them the essentials of the Dharma. Why is this?
"I have constantly instructed these bhikṣus; you should do likewise.
I have always expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the bhikṣus; you should do likewise."
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha, "These bhikṣus are unable to accept instruction; they are difficult to teach.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"For what reason do you not preach the Dharma to them now?
Kāśyapa replied again to the Buddha:
"There are currently two bhikṣus here:"
The first was Ānanda’s co-practitioner disciple, named Nanda;
the second was Maudgalyāyana’s disciple, named Abhibhū.
These two disciples disputed with one another over who was superior, each claiming:
"I possess superior knowledge and vision; what I have spoken is superior.
Thus they draw each other out, desiring to resolve their differences regarding knowledge, vision, and verbal expression:
"Is it for me that you speak the sublime, or is it for you that I speak the sublime?"
"Is it for me that the meaning of the phrases is complete, or is it for you that the meaning of the phrases is complete?
At that time, Ānanda was attending upon the World-Honored One, fanning the Buddha with a fan.
At that time, Ānanda said to Kāśyapa:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Venerable One!
Please hear my confession; such a bhikṣu as this has newly entered the Buddha-dharma, being foolish and lacking wisdom, having not yet attained any understanding.
Venerable Kāśyapa spoke to Ānanda, saying:
"Stop, Ānanda! Do not speak words of partiality within the Saṃgha."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"You may go and summon those two bhikṣus.
Then, that bhikṣu, having received the instruction, went to summon them and said to the two bhikṣus:
“The World-Honored One summons you.
Thereupon, the two bhikṣus, receiving the Buddha’s command, immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the two bhikṣus:
"Did you two truly say these words:
'We have recited much; what we know is vast; our spoken words, phrases, and verses are complete and without omission; we wish to settle this contest of victory and defeat'?"
“Is this the case? At that time,
the two bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
“It is indeed so, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha spoke again, saying:

"If you understand these twelve divisions of the scriptures that I have taught—the Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Nidāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, Upadeśa, and Itivṛttaka—and if you recite them until they are mastered, would there be any distinction of superiority or inferiority among these various sūtras?"
At that time, the two bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In these twelve divisions of the scriptures, there is truly no such teaching.”
The Buddha again addressed the two bhikṣus, saying:
"The preaching of the twelve divisions of the sūtras is intended to eliminate disputes, contention, and the desire for victory.
Why do you now speak in such a manner?"
"You foolish people, you hold such an interpretation; could I possibly have spoken in such a way?
To give rise to disputes is not the Buddha-dharma, nor is it the dharma of those who have gone forth."

Within my Buddha-dharma, it is never the case that I am superior and you are defeated; rather, the phrases and meanings of the Dharma I have taught are complete, whereas the phrases and meanings of what you have said are incomplete.
Such a dispute is truly not my teaching.
You two bhikṣus!
Should you engage in such a matter?
Then the two bhikṣus prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to him:
“Having heard what the Buddha has spoken, we recognize our own transgressions.
Truly, we were like infants and fools, possessing no understanding.”
We have done what should not be done; our actions were unwholesome, as we engaged in various contests of victory and defeat. Truly, there is this transgression.
We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for us, will grant permission for our repentance.

The Buddha said, “I know that you have repented with a sincere and earnest heart. You are indeed childish and ignorant, lacking understanding; what you have done is unwholesome and contrary to the Buddha’s teachings, not the way of those who have left the household life. Rather than seeking victory or defeat, you each claimed to possess great knowledge, even asserting that while my words were complete in both phrasing and meaning, yours were not.”
Such contests of victory and defeat truly ought not to be engaged in.
I now accept your sincere repentance, so that your wholesome dharmas may increase and you shall suffer no decline or loss.
Why is this? If one can,
with a sincere heart, truly recognize that there is transgression, and then repent, vowing never to commit it again—
repenting in such a manner causes wholesome dharmas to increase and nothing to be lost.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and departed. 114 (114). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying in the Viśākhā Lecture Hall within the Old Garden.
Then, at sunset, the Venerable Kāśyapa arose from meditative concentration, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You may instruct the bhikṣus; you should preach the Dharma for them. Why is this?"
"I constantly instruct [others], and you should do likewise.
I always preach the Dharma for the bhikṣus, and you should do likewise.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"These bhikṣus are difficult to instruct; they are unable to accept my words.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"What reasons do you see now that cause you not to speak for them?"
Kāśyapa replied:

"If one does not have faith, they will fall away from wholesome dharmas; they will give rise to indolence, lack shame and remorse, be foolish and devoid of wisdom, be greedily attached to the property of others, harbor a mind of malice and harm, be shrouded by the hindrance of sleep, be restless and unable to still themselves, harbor doubts regarding the Dharma, be deeply attached to the view of self, possess a mind defiled by the stains of afflictions, be prone to anger and loss of mindfulness, and lack even momentary concentration. Such various unwholesome and evil dharmas as these are certainly present."
For such persons as these, there is not even the slightest bit of goodness; how much less could they increase their wholesome qualities or remain free from decline?

Furthermore, if there is a person who possesses faith, does not regress from wholesome qualities, is diligent and tireless, is able to practice shame and remorse, is a wise person who fully practices wholesome dharmas, is free from thoughts of greed, stays far removed from anger and resentment, eliminates the hindrance of sloth and torpor, has a mind that does not waver, is without doubt, does not cling to the view of a self, has a pure and undefiled mind, does not delight in malice, is able to abide in mindfulness, and possesses meditative concentration—such that their wholesome qualities do not regress—if such a person possesses these various wholesome qualities as described above, I would not say that their wholesome qualities merely remain stationary, let alone that they do not increase.
"For such persons as these, wholesome qualities will increase throughout the day and night.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "It is so! It is so!"
So it is! It is as you have said.
If one does not believe, they will fall away from and lose wholesome dharmas; even for such persons as these, there is not the slightest bit of goodness, let alone any growth thereof.

Furthermore, if there is another person who possesses faith and does not regress from wholesome dharmas, I would not even say that such a person’s wholesome dharmas remain stationary, let alone that they do not increase.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 115 (115). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying in the Old Garden at the Vaiśākha Lecture Hall.
Then, at sunset, the Venerable Kāśyapa arose from meditative concentration, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.

"I constantly instruct [others], and you should do likewise.
I constantly expound the essentials of the Dharma for them, and you should do likewise.

“World-Honored One!
These bhikṣus are unable to accept instruction; they are difficult to teach.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Why is it that you do not instruct him or preach the Dharma for him?
Kāśyapa replied,
"The World-Honored One is the root of the Dharma, the guide of the Dharma, and that upon which the Dharma relies."
"Excellent!
World-Honored One, we pray that you will expound upon this for us; having heard your words, we shall receive and uphold them with a sincere heart.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Listen well now, receive and keep this in mind; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
“So be it, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"In the past, there was a bhikṣu who personally practiced the conduct of an araṇyaka and praised those who practice the conduct of araṇyakas; he himself practiced alms-gathering and wore rag-robes, and he praised those who practice alms-gathering and wear rag-robes."

Having few desires and being content, they always delight in empty, secluded, and tranquil places; they cultivate diligence with vigor, their minds do not wander, and they constantly rejoice in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*) themselves and praising those who have exhausted them.
For this reason, all the bhikṣus came to attend upon him and inquire after his well-being.
Then that bhikṣu spoke to those who had come: "Welcome, bhikṣus!"
"You may sit here.
What is your name?
Whose disciple are you?"
To practice virtue and goodness is to accord with the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Indeed, those who have left the household life should be like you, acting as true śramaṇas.
If others see you and learn from your conduct, they will before long surely attain their own benefit.
Having witnessed this, a newly ordained bhikṣu would think: "There are bhikṣus who respect one another;

I too should now train in their conduct—practicing the forest-dweller's life myself and praising those who practice the forest-dweller's life, practicing alms-gathering myself and wearing rag-robes, and praising those who practice alms-gathering and wear rag-robes."

Having few desires and being content, they always delight in empty, secluded, and tranquil places; they practice with diligent vigor, their minds do not wander, and they constantly enjoy meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*) themselves and praising those who have exhausted them.
For this reason, all the bhikṣus came to attend upon him, offering consolation and inquiries after his well-being.
Yet this bhikṣu said to those who had come: "Welcome, bhikṣus!"
"You may sit here.
What is your name?
Whose disciple are you?"
You fulfill the conduct of the virtuous and accord with the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
Those who have left the household life should be like you, acting as true śramaṇas.
If others see you, they will learn from your deeds and before long will surely attain their own benefit and purpose.

"If those who are newly trained in the study [of the Dharma] should give rise to such a thought, it will bring them benefit for a long night; they will attain the meaning and attain happiness, which is called 'self-deliverance. They will enable the True Dharma to abide long in the world, and these people, progressing forward, shall never fall back or perish."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“If there is a bhikṣu who is fortunate by birth, and upon first going forth from home, he receives much gain and support—abundant in the four requisites of robes, medicine, bedding, and seats.”
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who, seeing this bhikṣu, approached him, conversed with him, comforted him, and inquired after his well-being.
At that time, this bhikṣu said to that bhikṣu:
"What is your name?"
"Whose disciple is he?
From birth he has been fortunate, receiving abundant offerings of the four requisites—robes, medicinal drinks, bedding, and furniture—all of which are plentiful."
"If there are bhikṣus who associate with you, they shall not lack the four requisites.
When any newly ordained bhikṣu observes this situation, he should think:

"Those bhikṣus who generate merit are mutually respected; I too should now cultivate such conduct, so that the four requisites—robes, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal decoctions—shall also be constantly abundant."

"If a newly ordained bhikṣu forms such an intention and trains in such matters, this is called wasting away through the long night; it is entirely without benefit or ease, contrary to the Dharma of a śramaṇa, and results in various sufferings and afflictions. It is called self-deprecation, where the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is not established, one sinks into the mire, is deceived by evil, and is possessed of fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). One repeatedly undergoes various states of existence, which is called the arising of feverish distress, obtaining bitter retribution, and must inevitably undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
116 (116). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying in the Old Garden at the Vaiśākha Lecture Hall.
Then, as the sun was setting, Mahākāśyapa arose from meditative concentration, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:

"You are now aged and decrepit; your years have reached their decline. You wear these śāṇa refuse-rags, which are soiled, heavy, and thick. You should now return to the Saṃgha, eat the food of the Saṃgha, and wear the robes given by donors—robes that have been cut, torn, and dyed with an unattractive color."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This patchwork robe has been worn by me for a long time, and I have also praised those who wear patchwork robes; how could I possibly discard it?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"What benefit do you see in wearing the patched robe? Throughout the long night, you have worn it;
you have practiced the *āraṇyaka* way yourself and praised those who practice the *āraṇyaka* way; you have practiced begging for alms yourself and praised those who beg for alms."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I see two kinds of benefit for those who wear rag-robes:”
They shall dwell in happiness and security in the present life;
and in future ages, they shall serve as a light of the Dharma for the bhikṣus and become that which later generations study and practice.
People of future generations should give rise to this thought:

"In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, there were bhikṣus of great virtue who had long cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya), who took joy in the Buddha-dharma, who deeply understood the rules and regulations, and who had few desires and were content."
He himself practices the forest-dwelling (āraṇyaka) life and praises those who practice the forest-dwelling life.
He wears rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) and praises those who wear rag-robes.
Next, he practices alms-gathering (piṇḍapātika) and praises those who practice alms-gathering.
“In future generations, many people will give rise to this mind, longing for and admiring this Dharma; you shall act as their deliverer, providing them with benefit, profit, peace, and happiness.
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent!”
Excellent!
If you act in this way, throughout the long night, you will show compassion for the world, bringing vast benefit, providing relief, and establishing its welfare and happiness.
If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who disparage the dhūta practices, they are disparaging me.
If there are those who praise the merits of the dhūta practices, they are praising me.

Why is this? Because, through various causes and conditions and countless skillful means, I have praised the merits obtained through *dhūta* practices, established those who practice *dhūta*, and extolled *dhūta* as the most excellent among all forms of conduct.
"From this day forward, you should always personally practice the *āraṇyaka* way of life and praise those who are able to practice the *āraṇyaka* way of life.
When Mahākāśyapa and the other bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
117. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was dwelling in a remote place, sitting upon a grass mat; his robes were tattered and their dye had faded, and his hair and beard were long. He then approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
When the bhikṣus saw Kāśyapa, they all had this thought:

"That venerable one does not know the proper deportment of one who has left the household life; his robes have turned soiled and discolored, his beard and hair are long, and he lacks the requisite dignified demeanor."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the bhikṣus and wishing to inspire in them a sense of reverence and esteem, saw Kāśyapa from afar and spoke to him, saying:
"Welcome, Kāśyapa!"
He immediately divided his seat in half and commanded me to sit with him, thinking:
"Since you went forth first and I went forth later, I therefore command you to share this seat with me."
Having heard these instructions, Mahākāśyapa was filled with awe and trepidation; he immediately rose, joined his palms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The World-Honored One is my Great Teacher and I am his disciple; how can I sit together on the same seat as my Teacher?”
A second and a third time he spoke these words.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It is truly as you say; I am your teacher, and you are my disciple."
He then commanded Kāśyapa:
"You may sit upon that seat which is appropriate for you.
Thereupon, the Venerable Kāśyapa, having received the Buddha’s instruction, spread out a mat and sat down.

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause those bhikṣus to further increase their sense of revulsion so as to reproach themselves, and wishing to praise the merit and dignity of Mahākāśyapa as being equal to that of the Buddha, addressed the bhikṣus:

"I cultivate the concentration of detachment and enter the first dhyāna, applying my mind with reflection; the bhikṣu Kāśyapa likewise desires to leave behind evil and unwholesome states, and with directed thought and evaluation, enters the first dhyāna, doing so day and night.
It is the same for the second, third, and fourth dhyanas."

If I resolve my mind to enter into a state of loving-kindness—a mind free from resentment, a mind free from malice, a mind that is expansive and thoroughly cultivated as immeasurable—I shall direct this mind toward the eastern direction; likewise, I shall direct it toward the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, desiring to cultivate this mind throughout the day and night.

Mahākāśyapa was also like this: wishing to enter a mind of loving-kindness, a mind free from resentment, a mind free from affliction, and a mind that is pervasive and vast, he cultivated immeasurability well; toward the eastern direction, he formed such a mind, and likewise toward the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
If I cultivate the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, I shall constantly enter these states throughout the day and night.
Mahākāśyapa is also like this; throughout the day and night, he constantly enters these states.

I wish to eliminate affliction and destruction, cast aside perceptions of form, and remove manifold perceptions, entering the sphere of infinite space; furthermore, I wish to constantly enter this meditative absorption day and night, and it is likewise for the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
I, too, wish to enter the meditative absorptions of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), whereby I may manifest a single body as infinite bodies, and again manifest infinite bodies as a single body.

I wish to observe all directions—above and below—and pass through stone walls without obstruction, just like empty space; to sit or lie in mid-air like a king of geese; to walk upon the earth as if on water, and walk upon water as if on earth; and for my body to reach the Brahma-heaven, touching the sun and moon with my hand.

"If I wish to practice this samādhi day and night, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa likewise desires to enter that samādhi of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), by which he can manifest an infinite body from a single body and return an infinite body to a single body; observing the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below, he can pass through stone walls with this very body without obstruction, as if it were empty space; sitting or lying in mid-air like a king of geese; walking on land as if on water and walking on water as if on land; reaching the Brahma-heaven with his body and touching the sun and moon with his hand—and he likewise wishes to constantly enter this samādhi day and night."
“The divine eye, the divine ear, as well as the knowledge of others’ minds, the recollection of past lives, and the exhaustion of outflows—these too are likewise so.
At that time, within that immeasurable great assembly, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa’s merits, honoring him in such a way that his various qualities were equal to his own.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 118 (118). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain, in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the Venerable Ānanda were on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Then, when the time for the meal had arrived, Ānanda said to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa:
"Venerable Sir!"
"The time for alms has arrived; let us go together to beg for food.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa put on his robes, took up his bowl, and together with Ānanda, left Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
Ānanda said to Mahākāśyapa:
"The time is still early; I wish to go to that bhikṣuṇī vihāra to observe the rules and conduct practiced by the bhikṣuṇīs."
Kāśyapa replied,
“So be it,” and immediately they went together to the bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra.
At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs saw the two venerable ones approaching from afar, they immediately prepared seats.
Having finished arranging the seats, they addressed the two venerable ones:
"Please be seated here."
Then the two elders took their seats.
Once the bhikṣuṇīs saw that they were seated, they prostrated at their feet and stood to one side.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa preached the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs in various ways, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.
Within that assembly, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Thullanandā who, upon hearing the essential points of the Dharma, felt no joy in her heart and immediately uttered these malicious words:
"How is it now that the Elder Kāśyapa preaches the essential points of the Dharma for the bhikṣuṇīs in the presence of Ānanda?"
It is like a needle-seller who goes to the gate of a master needle-maker seeking to sell his needles; they can never be sold there.
So it is now with Kāśyapa: how can he preach the Dharma in the presence of Ānanda?
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard those words with his purified divine ear, said to the Elder Ānanda:
“Did you see this bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, who was displeased and lacked joy in her heart, uttering such coarse speech?”
At that time, Ānanda said to Kāśyapa,
"What did he say? Kāśyapa replied:
"He spoke thus:
'How can Kāśyapa preach the essentials of the Dharma before Ānanda Baidālaputra Muni?
For you are like that son of a needle-maker, and you call me a seller of needles.'"
The Venerable Ānanda said to Kāśyapa,
"Stop! Stop!"
“Venerable One!
He is ignorant and of little wisdom; it is not worth holding him fully accountable. I only pray that the Great Virtuous One will accept his repentance.
Kāśyapa then spoke to the Elder Ānanda, saying:

"For the sake of instruction, the Tathāgata, the Bhagavān, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has drawn upon that simile of the moon: it increases day by day and is able to possess a sense of shame and remorse."
Free from shamelessness, enduring insults and humiliation, and restraining both body and mind as you travel among the people, do you act as a guide for me and speak on my behalf, like that moon?
Ānanda replied, "The Tathāgata,
the Hero of the World, has certainly never said that I am equal to that moon.
Kāśyapa spoke again:

"Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the one of equal and perfect enlightenment, knows that I am like the new moon, gradually increasing day by day and capable of possessing a sense of shame and remorse."
"Free from shamelessness, enduring insults and humiliation, restraining body and mind, he frequents various households.
Ānanda replied, "It is indeed so."
The Venerable Kāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"In the presence of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of great assemblies, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, addressed me by name, saying:
'This Great Virtuous One is a person of shame and modesty; his wisdom is profound and far-reaching, resembling my own.'"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"I am now free from sensual desires, unwholesome states, and evil; with directed thought and sustained thought, filled with joy and happiness, and with a unified mind, I have entered the first dhyāna, remaining constantly in such meditative absorption day and night."

The bhikṣu Kāśyapa also constantly remains free from desire, evil, and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained evaluation, with joy and one-pointedness of mind, he enters the first dhyāna, remaining constantly in such meditative concentration day and night.
Ānanda replied, “It is indeed so, Kāśyapa!”

"The second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the four dhyāna-concentrations, the three knowledges, and the six supernormal powers—were likewise thus.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, having uttered this lion’s roar before the great assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, rose from his seat and returned to his dwelling.
119. At that time, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Ānanda and Mahākāśyapa were on Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, there was a famine in the world and alms were difficult to obtain.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda led a group of newly ordained bhikṣus toward a village in the Southern Mountains.

Among the newly ordained bhikṣus, there were many youths who delighted in amusements and games, were addicted to food and drink, failed to restrain their sense faculties, and lacked dignified deportment. During both the first and last watches of the night, they did not diligently practice the Path or recite the scriptures, but instead lay on their left sides upon the ground, indulging themselves in sleep.
Having arrived there, more than thirty monks among the assembly abandoned the path and returned to lay life.

For this reason, the number of followers was diminished. Having completed his travels, he returned to the city of Rājagṛha at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; there, having gathered up his robes and bowl and washed his hands and feet, he went to where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was, prostrated at the Venerable’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda,
"From where have you come?
Your assembly has diminished."

Ānanda replied, “I went to that village in the Southern Mountains, where among my disciples there were more than thirty who had all previously left the home life as *kumārabhūta* (vow-observing youths). Because they have now abandoned the path and returned to secular life, the assembly has diminished.”
Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"For what reason did the Tathāgata establish the rule against eating in a separate group, yet permit three people to eat together in one place?
Such was his intention: he wished to protect all people so that they would not suffer decline."

Furthermore, in order to subdue monks of evil desires who, for the sake of severing their dependence on many followers, invoke the name of the *saṃgha* to seek much, thereby diminishing the households of the laity, destroying the harmony of the *saṃgha*, and causing it to split into two factions—thus preventing monks who act according to the Dharma from receiving offerings of robes, food, and drink, while allowing monks who act contrary to the Dharma to obtain great profit and sustenance.
Having obtained offerings, that bhikṣu of evil desires disputes with those who practice purity.
For what reason, during this age of famine, do you take that newly ordained young bhikṣu as your follower?

Yet this bhikṣu delights in and clings to frivolous play, greedily craves food and drink, has his faculties scattered and distracted, lacks dignified deportment, and indulges in sleep without ever finding satisfaction.

Since you do not diligently practice the Path during the first and last watches of the night, nor recite the scriptures, how is it that this assembly of followers has traveled all the way to that village in the Southern Mountains?
Having arrived there, you will find that those thirty-odd people who were formerly monks as youths have all abandoned the path and returned to lay life;
thus, your assembly is now broken and destroyed.
"You are now without wisdom, just like a small child.
Ānanda replied, "I am already advanced in years; why do you say I am 'just like a small child'?"
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"It was not without reason that I addressed you by name as a 'child.
In these times of famine, it is difficult to obtain alms; why then have you led such a large multitude of people on a journey to that village in the Southern Mountains?"

Among your disciples, there are many youths who delight in play and amusement, are greedy for food and drink, have their senses wandering in distraction, lack dignified deportment, and are insatiably addicted to sleep.

Failing to diligently practice the Way during both the first and last watches of the night, and neglecting the recitation of the scriptures, you have caused more than thirty people to abandon the Path and return to secular life.
Is such conduct not exactly like that of a child?

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā Nandā, hearing Mahākāśyapa reproaching the venerable bhikṣu Ānanda for acting like a child, was displeased in her heart and gave rise to great distress. She immediately uttered harsh words:
"This Mahākāśyapa was originally a follower of other paths; how can he now disparage Ānanda Bhadrika-muni as acting like a child?"
At that time, Kāśyapa, having heard with his purified divine ear these coarse words with which the bhikṣuṇī Diśānandā had reviled him, said to Ānanda:
"The bhikṣuṇī Diśānandā was displeased in body and mind, and giving rise to great suffering and affliction, she uttered these evil words:
'This Mahākāśyapa was originally a teacher of non-Buddhists; why does he revile the Venerable Ānanda Baidharmika-muni for acting like a child?'"
Thereupon Ānanda said to Kāśyapa:
"This bhikṣuṇī possesses the wisdom of a young child, like an infant; I only pray that the Venerable One will grant her repentance."
Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"When I went forth from home, I made this solemn vow:
'If there be any Arhat in the world, I shall take refuge in him.'"
"Since my renunciation, I have had no other inclination, relying solely upon the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed, the Most True, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Previously, when I was still a layman and not yet ordained, I observed that in all the worlds, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, and affliction—this mass of suffering—compete to press upon me with urgency."
At that time, I grew weary of the confinement of the household life, finding no place therein where I could dwell at ease.
I delighted in the way of renunciation, which can leave behind worldly defilements.

I observed that the affairs of the household are as tumultuous as entering a forest of hooks and thorns; one is snagged and pierced by them, marring one’s form and robes, making it difficult to escape.
It is the same for those living at home: bound by worldly affairs and submerged in the mire of desire, they are unable to cultivate the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Day and night I reflected, and I saw no single dharma superior to this: to shave off hair and beard, don the Dharma robes, renounce household affairs, and leave the home life with faith.

When he was about to leave the household life, he selected the lowest garments in his home and obtained a tattered robe; though its value was still worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, he immediately took it as his saṃghāṭī.
He completely renounced his former occupation and entirely abandoned his kinsmen and relatives.
He further thought:
"If there be any Arhats in the world, I shall take refuge in them and follow them into the homeless life."
"At that time, in the center of that great city of Rājagṛha, there was a Lālaka-gandha.
In the center of the Lālaka-gandha, there was the Bahuputra-caitya.

I was upright, magnificent, and exquisite; my faculties were tranquil and composed, and my mind was serene. I had attained the unsurpassed mind of self-mastery, adorned with the marks and signs like a pavilion of pure gold."
Having seen him, my heart leaped with joy, and I immediately thought:
"In the past, I sought a teacher who transcends the world; the one I have now beheld is truly my Bhagavān, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Having formed this thought, his mind was undistracted as he focused single-mindedly on contemplating the Buddha.
He adjusted his robes, circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha is my World-Honored One; I am the Buddha’s disciple."
Thus he spoke three times.
The Buddha also replied: "So it is!"
"Kāśyapa, I am your World-Honored One; you are my disciple.
He spoke thus three times.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If there are disciples of the śrāvaka vehicle in the world who lack a sincere heart, who are not actually the World-Honored One yet claim to be the World-Honored One, who are not actually arhats yet claim to be arhats, and who do not possess all-knowledge yet claim to possess all-knowledge; [they are like those who see a mirage and mistake it for water]."
Such a person’s head shall be split into seven pieces.
Today, I am truly one who knows; I am truly one who sees;
I am truly an Arhat, and I declare myself an Arhat.
I am truly and perfectly awakened; thus I speak of being truly and perfectly awakened.
What I have expounded has a true basis in causes and conditions; it is not without causes and conditions that I teach the essentials of the Dharma.
There truly is a vehicle for transcendence; it is not that there is no vehicle for transcendence.
There truly is an antidote; it is not that there is no antidote.
There truly is diligence; it is not that there is no diligence.
One is able to sever the fetters and outflows; it is not that one cannot sever them. Kāśyapa!

You should now train yourself in this way: whatever you hear of these rules of the wholesome Dharma, you should receive and uphold them with a sincere mind without forgetting, honoring and recollecting them, and abandoning a distracted mind. You should single-mindedly contemplate the increase and decrease of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), constantly contemplating the arising and ceasing of those six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), settling the mind within the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*) so that they become further expanded, realizing the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), maintaining mindfulness bound to the body without ever letting it go, and increasing a sense of shame and remorse.
At that time, the Tathāgata analyzed the essential points of the Dharma for me in various ways, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening me.
During that time, I followed behind the Buddha, never once leaving him.
Every time he had this thought:
"If the Buddha were to sit, I would offer this saṃghāṭī robe, worth a hundred thousand taels of gold, to spread for the Tathāgata."
Because the Buddha knew the thoughts in my mind, he emerged from the path and stood there; I quickly folded my robe and spread it out as a seat for him.
I addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I pray that you will take this seat.
The Buddha then sat upon it; having sat down, he said to Kāśyapa, "This robe is light and soft."
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
“It is indeed so, World-Honored One.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will accept this robe.”
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Can you accept my *nirna* (hempen) robe?
Kāśyapa replied:
“I am able to receive it.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately accepted the great robe worn by Kāśyapa.
At that moment, I personally received this pāṃśukūla rag-robe from the Buddha’s own hands.
Once the Buddha had granted me this, he immediately rose and departed. I followed behind the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, paid homage to him, and then returned to my quarters.
On the eighth day, I attained the three fruits of the path;
on the ninth day, I exhausted all outflows and attained arhatship.
Ānanda, you should know that if anyone were to speak of this correctly and truthfully, they should say:

"I am the eldest son of the Buddha; born from the Buddha's own mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, I uphold the household of the Buddha-Dharma, moving freely and without obstruction through the various gates of dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi."
"Just as the eldest son of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, before he has received the royal throne, indulges himself in the five desires, so too am I now:

I am the eldest son of this Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth, transformed by birth from the Dharma, upholding the house of the Buddha-Dharma, and moving with unimpeded ease through the gates of dhyāna, liberation, and all samādhis."

Suppose the elephant-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch were exceedingly large and tall; could one cover its entire body with a single leaf of a tala tree and expect it not to be visible? Could such a thing be possible?
Ānanda immediately replied,
"Such leaves could never cover the body of that great elephant.
The Venerable Kāśyapa said to Ānanda:
"That [other] may still be overturned, but no one can obstruct or cover my six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā).
If there is anyone who harbors doubts or confusion regarding the power of mental mastery (ṛddhividhi), I am able to expound its meaning for them all, so that they may attain clear understanding."

Regarding the supernormal power of the divine ear, the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, the supernormal power of knowledge regarding birth and death, and the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows—if there should be anyone who harbors doubts or confusion concerning these powers, I am likewise able to expound their meaning for them so that they may attain clear understanding.
Ānanda replied, "Throughout the long night,
I have always revered the Venerable One, and my heart has given rise to pure faith.
When the two venerable ones had finished speaking thus, they departed with joy.
120. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahākāśyapa were both on that mountain.

Then, in that country, there were followers of six teachers of divergent views who came to where the Venerable Śāriputra was; having finished their greetings, they sat to one side and spoke these words:
"Does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, ever say that 'I die here and am born there,' or does he speak in such a manner?"
Śāriputra replied,
"Matters such as these have not been spoken of by the Buddha.
The six heretical teachers then spoke again as follows:
"If this is so," [the interlocutor asked], "do you say that my body is here,
or that it will not be born again?
Śāriputra replied:
“Even the Buddha does not speak of such matters.
The non-Buddhist replied again:
“Do you say that when I die here, I am born there, or that I am not born there?”
Śāriputra said, "The Buddha has not spoken of it either.
The non-Buddhist replied again:
“After my death, am I neither born nor unborn?
Śāriputra replied,
“The Buddha has not said so either.”
The non-Buddhist further said:
"I previously questioned you regarding dying here and being born there, up to neither being born nor not being born; in all these cases, you gave no answer."
If you are truly an elder who has long been ordained, you should have a broad understanding of the meaning; you ought to analyze it for me.
But now, observing that you cannot answer me, you are clearly but a child, an ignorant and foolish man.
When those non-Buddhists had finished speaking these words, they rose from their seats and returned to their respective dwellings.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was not far from Śāriputra; after the non-Buddhists had departed, Śāriputra went to where Mahākāśyapa was and recounted to him what the non-Buddhists had asked:
"For what reason did the Tathāgata remain silent and not answer these four questions?"
Why is this? Why not provide an answer by drawing an analogous comparison for him?
I have heard that in the past, someone asked the Buddha:
"After dying here, will one receive a future existence?"
The Buddha remained silent and did not answer.
Again he asked:
"After death, will you not undergo further existence?"
The Buddha did not answer.
He asked again:
"After my death here, will I undergo further existence, or will I not?"
The Buddha did not answer.
He asked again:
"After my death, will I not experience existence, nor will I not experience existence?"
The Buddha likewise did not answer.
Venerable Kāśyapa said to Śāriputra:
“Could the Tathāgata not say that after form has ceased, it is born into a future existence, and so on, up to being neither born nor unborn?”

The Blessed One has attained liberation through right knowledge at the point where that form is exhausted; yet, there is absolutely no such thing as dying here and being born there, dying here and not being born there, both being born and not being born, or neither being born nor not being born. For this reason, he did not answer.
This meaning is profoundly deep and vast, immeasurable and boundless, beyond calculation, even unto its ultimate cessation.
It is likewise so for feeling, perception, and up to consciousness; for dying here and being born there; and even unto that which is neither born nor unborn.

"This is movement; this is conceit; this is negligence; this is the karma of conditioned activity; this is the fetter of craving. This craving arises, while that craving does not arise; that craving also arises, yet that [other] craving does not arise; it neither arises nor does not arise for that [other]. The Tathāgata, having exhausted craving, has attained excellent liberation. When craving is exhausted, there is no 'arising' of that [existence], nor is there any 'being'."
There is neither "arising therein" nor "not arising therein.
There is also neither "both arising and not arising therein" nor "neither arising nor not arising therein.
There is also neither "it is not that there is no arising therein" nor "it is not that there is no non-arising therein. There is also nothing [beyond these].
This meaning is profoundly deep, vast, and boundless; it is beyond calculation and extends to the ultimate cessation.

Venerable Śāriputra, you should know that for these reasons, when questioned, the Tathāgata does not provide a direct answer as to whether one dies here and is born there, dies here and is not born there, is both born there and not born there, or neither born nor not born.
Thus these two great beings, having praised one another, each returned to their respective abodes. 121 (121). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying in the Śālavatī Grove at the Veṇuvana Monastery in Śrāvastī, in the lecture hall of Viśākhā.
When the sun had set, Mahākāśyapa arose from meditative concentration, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions was it that at the time the Tathāgata first established the precepts, those who were extremely few were the practitioners?”
"For what reason today have the precepts become increasingly numerous, while those who practice them are few?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "It is so, it is so."

There are the impurity of life, the impurity of afflictions, the impurity of sentient beings, the impurity of the eon, and the impurity of views. As sentient beings turn toward evil and the True Dharma reaches its end, the Tathāgata has established many prohibitions and precepts for his disciples. Yet there are few bhikṣus who can comply with the Buddha’s words and uphold these precepts; thus, all sentient beings gradually decline and vanish.

For example, just as genuine gold and jewels gradually diminish until only counterfeit gold appears, so too is it with the True Dharma of the Tathāgata: it gradually declines until the Semblance Dharma emerges.
Because the Semblance Dharma emerges, the True Dharma perishes and disappears.
Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like a ship upon the sea laden with many treasures; the ship will inevitably sink.
The teaching of the Tathāgata is likewise; it gradually fades away and disappears.
The True Dharma of the Tathāgata does not perish because of the earth, nor is it destroyed by water, fire, or wind.
If within my Dharma, one gives rise to evil desires, practices improper conduct, and accomplishes various evils;

if they declare what is Dharma to be non-Dharma, and what is non-Dharma to be Dharma; if they declare what is not Vinaya to be Vinaya, and what is an offense to be no offense, and what is no offense to be an offense; if they declare a light offense to be heavy, and a heavy offense to be light.

Such matters as these that arise in the world all stem from the fact that the phrasing and flavor of the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka) resemble those of the true teaching, causing the Buddha’s True Dharma (saddharma) to gradually fade away and disappear.

Kāśyapa, you should know that there are five causes and conditions that can cause the Dharma to perish, whereby everyone collectively forgets the chapters and verses, and wholesome dharmas (kuśaladharma) regress.
What are these five? They are:

not revering the Buddha, not honoring the Buddha, not making offerings to the Buddha, and being unable to take refuge in the Buddha with a sincere heart, yet still dwelling in reliance upon the Buddha-dharma.
They do not revere the Dharma, do not honor the Dharma, and do not make offerings to the Dharma; they lack sincere devotion toward the True Dharma, yet they abide by it.

They do not respect the precepts, do not honor the precepts, and do not make offerings to the precepts; they cannot maintain the precepts they have received with a sincere heart, yet they abide by them.
They do not show reverence toward the instructor, they do not honor the instructor, and they do not make offerings to the instructor.

Because they lack reverence, honor, and offerings, and because they do not direct their wholehearted attention toward the instructor, they nevertheless continue to dwell in reliance upon this instruction.

Regarding one's fellow practitioners of the holy life who are praised by the Buddha, they do not show them respect, honor, or veneration, nor can they sincerely prostrate, inquire after their well-being, or yet rely upon them for their own dwelling in peace.
Kāśyapa! Due to these five aforementioned causes and conditions, the True Dharma will gradually perish, decline, and be forgotten. “Kāśyapa!”
Furthermore, there are five causes and conditions by which the True Dharma can remain long in the world, neither perishing nor declining, neither being forgotten nor lost.
What are these five?
One should revere the World-Honored One, honor the Buddha, make offerings to the Buddha, and always be able to take refuge in the Buddha with a sincere heart.

Toward the Dharma, the precepts, the instructions, and one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life, one should likewise make offerings, show reverence, honor them, and direct one’s sincere heart toward them. By virtue of these five kinds of wholesome causes and conditions, one can cause the True Dharma to abide long in the world, so that it does not perish, does not decline, and is neither forgotten nor lost.
"For this reason, you should revere the Buddha, the Dharma, the teacher, and your fellow practitioners of the holy life.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
