122. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a master of musicians in that city named Khaṇḍadravya, who went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and spoke these words:
“Gautama! In the past, I once heard from a very old and experienced performer:”

"In a performance arena, theatrical apparatus was set out; hundreds of thousands of people all came to watch as lutes were played, performances were staged, drums and instruments were sounded, songs were sung, and various forms of merriment and laughter ensued."
"Having completed his deeds, after his life ended, he was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Is what has been thus said true or false?
The Buddha told him:
"Stop! Stop! Do not ask about this matter now."
At that time, the master of the musicians asked a second and a third time in the same manner, yet the Buddha did not answer at all.
Then the Tathāgata said to the master of the musicians:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
If there are performers who, upon a stage, set up their instruments and play the lute, sing, drum, and chant, because of these activities, hundreds of thousands of people will all gather there.
These people were originally already bound by craving, hatred, and delusion; if they further engage in acts of negligence, will this not increase their greed, anger, and ignorance?
It is like a person who, bound by a rope, has it further tightened when water is poured over it.

In the same way, these people were already entangled by the three poisons; yet they further perform music and dance upon that stage of performance, which only serves to increase those three poisons until they blaze forth in such a manner.
"Master of performers, it is impossible that one who has performed such deeds as these should, at the end of life, be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

If there were anyone who calculated that by performing various musical entertainments in a theater, they would be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven at the end of life, I declare that such a person is possessed of false views."
"The fruit of wrong view arises in two places: one falls into hell, or else into the realm of animals.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the master musician wept and shed tears.
The Buddha told the master of musicians:
"For this reason, although you have requested three times, I have not spoken for you.
At that time, the master of musicians addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is not merely because I have heard the Buddha’s words that I weep; it is because I pity these musicians and performers, who are infantile, ignorant, and lacking wisdom, and whose actions are unwholesome.”
Throughout the long night, they have held such views that in future lives they shall undergo great suffering, constantly being deceived and held in contempt by others.
If there is a performer who says:
"By performing songs and music on a stage for entertainment, one will be reborn in that Heaven of Radiant Light after death," such words are called a great falsehood.
"It is impossible, World-Honored One, that by means of such karma one could be born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; there is no such place.
From this day forward, I shall never again commit such evil karma."
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"You are now truly sincere; in a future age, you shall certainly be born in a good realm.
At that time, the master musician and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
123. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there was in that city a skilled warrior who served as a village headman. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and after having finished his greetings, sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
In the past, I heard from the elders of old:..."

"When about to engage in battle, one must adorn the weapons one carries, protect oneself firmly, and advance directly with courage and vigor, free from any timidity or weakness; thus one can defeat the enemy before, wound and kill their lives, and cause the remaining troops to all retreat and scatter."
"Having performed these deeds, at the end of his life he was reborn in the Arrow-Adorned Heaven.
At that time, the General asked this question, and the Buddha said to him: "Stop!
"There is no need to speak.
The meaning and intent of what you have asked now is most improper.
A second and a third time, he asked the same question.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"You have already asked me this question with great earnestness three times; if you are able to receive it, I shall explain it for you.
Whenever there are those who go to war, they armor themselves firmly, are well-versed in the arts of combat, stand at the forefront of the ranks, and advance with courage and vigor."
How could such a warrior not apply his mind to skillful means, desiring to harm those enemy forces, and think to himself:
"By what means shall I bind them, harm them, and utterly destroy them?"
"How could one not give rise to such a thought? General!
You have produced three types of evil karma toward sentient beings."
What are called the three types of evil karma?
They are namely those of body, speech, and mind.
If, by means of these three unwholesome karmas, one were to be reborn in heaven after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, such a thing is impossible.
Warrior! If you now hold such a view, it is a false view.
The karma of a false view will inevitably lead to rebirth in one of two places: either in hell or among the animals.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the general wept with flowing tears.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"For this reason, although you requested three times, I did not speak."
"I am now speaking for your sake; why do you weep?
At that time, the general addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
It is not because I have heard this teaching that I give rise to sorrow and distress;

rather, it is out of compassion for those engaged in battle—those who are mired in the ignorance of the long night, like infants lacking wisdom, performing unwholesome deeds and constantly occupied with such matters—who shall undergo great suffering in future lives.
Such evil karma cannot truly lead to birth among the devas.
If one were to be born among the devas of Arrow Adornment (*iṣudhvaja*) by means of such karma, it would be impossible.
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, I shall no longer hold such wrong views.
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
What you have spoken is truly rare.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the general prostrated himself and departed. 124 (124). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the village head who was a skilled horse trainer went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha said to the horse trainer:
"By how many causes and conditions is a horse brought to discipline?"
The horse trainer said:
"Gautama! There are three things by which a horse can be made well-trained:
First, exclusively soft;
second, exclusively coarse;
third, both soft and coarse.
The Buddha said to him,
"If these three matters cannot be mastered through such means, what else should be done?
The horse trainer replied:
"Strike him and let his life end.
The horse trainer then said, "Gautama!"
“You are the unsurpassed teacher who tames; when you tame men, by how many things do you tame them?
The Buddha said, “I also tame through three things:”
First, gentle speech;
second, harsh speech;
third, neither gentle nor harsh speech, by which one achieves subduing.
What is meant by "exclusively requiring moisture"?
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you cultivate the goodness of the three karmas, you will obtain the retribution of wholesome fruits; these are devas, and these are humans."
This is called being tamed exclusively through gentleness.
What is meant by "harsh"?
It is as when one speaks of the three evil realms; these are the retributive fruits produced by the unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind.
What is meant by "coarse yet gentle"?

It refers to the teaching that when there are various wholesome karmas of body, speech, and mind, one attains birth among humans or devas; this is the retributive fruit obtained from wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.

It also teaches that when there are various unwholesome karmas of body, speech, and mind, one shall fall into the three miserable realms; this too is the retributive fruit obtained from [unwholesome] actions of body, speech, and mind.
"This is what is called 'employing both the coarse and the gentle to discipline sentient beings.
The Horse Trainer addressed the Buddha:
"If these three methods fail to subdue them, how should one discipline them?"
The Buddha told him:
"If one uses harsh words with it and it remains untamed, one will suffer deep injury.
The horse trainer replied:
"Now, you śramaṇa, you constantly preach non-killing; why then do you say 'I have caused harm'?
The Buddha said, "Āśvalāyana!..."
"So it is! So it is! That which is called a Tathāgata truly should not be killed; it is something that ought not to be done."
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, employs these three matters to discipline sentient beings; if they are not disciplined, he will never speak with them, nor instruct them, nor direct them.
The Buddha said to Assaji: "What do you think?
If the Tathāgata were not to instruct, nor speak with you, nor provide guidance, would such a thing be called an injury? That would indeed be a true injury."
The horse trainer replied,
"It is indeed so, Gautama."
"If the Tathāgata were not to grant him his word and teach him the Dharma, it would truly constitute an injury more severe than any worldly harm.
The horse trainer spoke again: "Gautama!"
"From this day forward, I shall sever all harmful actions and shall no longer commit evil.
The Buddha then praised him, saying:
"Horse Trainer!"
"What you have said is indeed true and correct.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the horse trainer rejoiced, prostrated himself, and departed. 125 (125). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, a village headman named Duṣṭa went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Suppose there is a person in the world who, having accumulated nothing through cultivation, provokes others and utters provocative words.”
"For this reason, all people unanimously call that person 'extremely wicked.
The Buddha told the village headman:

"Suppose there is a person who provokes and offends another, speaking words of harm and uttering provocative speech; because he causes the other to become angry and resentful, for this reason he is called 'of an evil nature.'"

Because they do not cultivate right view, right action, right speech, right livelihood, right mindfulness, right effort, right intention, and right concentration—and because they do not cultivate right concentration—they cause distress and provocation to others.
Because of being provoked by irritation, they give rise to extreme anger and resentment.
Because of this anger and resentment, they utter words of anger and resentment.
Because they utter such angry words, they are said to be of an evil disposition.
Then the village headman said:
“It is rare, Gautama!
It is truly as you have said; because he causes provocation and offense, he is truly called ‘of evil nature.’”
Because I did not cultivate right view, I was provoked by them.
Because of that provocation, they called me ill-tempered.
All the people of the world have called me ill-tempered, and from that time forth, I have been known as "Ill-Tempered."
The village headman spoke again:
“Gautama! How does one attain freedom from affliction and provocation?”
"Because they are not touched by affliction, they attain speech free from affliction.
Even though they are touched by the afflictions of others, they do not afflict others.
Even though they are addressed with afflictive speech by others, they do not use afflictive speech to afflict them."
Although they may be troubled by others, they do not give rise to a mind of resentment.
Because they do not resent, people of the world all praise them as virtuous ones capable of endurance, and they likewise conceive thoughts of patience and virtue toward those [who trouble them].
If one acts in this way, one is able to cultivate right view.
Because one cultivates right view, one cultivates right action, right speech, right livelihood, right intention, right effort, right concentration, and right mindfulness.
"Because he has cultivated right concentration, when touched by others, he does not give rise to vexation.
Because he does not give rise to vexation, it is called the virtue of patience.
The village headman said:
“Rare indeed, Gautama!
What you have said is most excellent.
It is truly as you have spoken; because I did not cultivate right view, I was tormented by others.”
Because I cause distress to others by uttering words that provoke irritation, worldly people call me ill-tempered; they all conceive an evil notion of me, and thus I am named "Ill-Tempered."
Because they do not cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, when touched by others, they utter words of provocation and distress, eventually leading to anger and resentment.
Because they harbor such thoughts, people in the world label them as being of an evil disposition.
The village headman said,
“Gautama! From this day forward, such an evil nature— sudden and violent, arrogant, and treacherous— I shall renounce.”
The Buddha praised him, saying,
"If you act in this way, it is truly excellent. At that time,
having heard what the Buddha had said, the village headman rejoiced, prostrated himself, and departed.
126 (126). At that time, there was a village headman named Maṇicūḍa who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the past, while I was in the royal palace sitting together with various ministers, the assembly of officials and kinsmen engaged in detailed discussion and debate concerning this: "Is it permissible for one who has become a śramaṇa to hold money and treasures, or is it not permissible to hold gold?"
At that time, one person among the assembly said:
"Even if he were to be seized, what fault would there be?
He ought to be seized."
Another person said:
"One should not take it up;
the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas do not handle gold or jewels."
"World-Honored One!
Regarding these two statements, are they to be called 'speaking in accordance with the Dharma,' or are they not so spoken?
If such words were uttered, would they not be a disparagement of the Buddha and an excessive statement?"
"Is this spoken by the Buddha, or is it not?
The Buddha told the village headman:
"If one speaks in such a manner, it is called slandering me; it is an inaccurate statement and is termed an erroneous exposition."
However, what I have taught is truly different from that.
Why is this? For one who is a bhikṣu, a śramaṇa and son of the Śākyas, it is contrary to the Dharma to handle gold, money, or precious gems.
If one were to grasp gold or other forms of currency and treasure, that would not be the Dharma of the Śramaṇa, the Son of the Śākyas; the Buddha’s teaching is far more excellent and dignified.
Thus the Buddha has said: "One who is a bhikṣu should not grasp gold or other forms of currency and treasure; should anyone grasp them, it is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa."
The village headman said:

"At that time, amidst the great assembly, I also spoke thus: 'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, truly ought not to grasp gold and other precious coins; if there are those who do grasp them, they should indulge themselves in the five desires with unrestrained license.'"
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the village head bowed his head in prostration and departed.
At that moment, the bhikṣu Ānanda was standing by the Buddha’s side, fanning him with a fan.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You may summon all the bhikṣus who reside in this city of Rājagṛha and assemble them all in the lecture hall.
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda, in accordance with the Buddha’s command, exhorted the bhikṣus until they had all assembled in the lecture hall.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had each assembled, Ānanda approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One!”
All the bhikṣus of the Saṃgha who were residing at the Kalandakanivāpa in Rājagṛha have assembled here in the lecture hall; may the World-Honored One deign to know that the time has come.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the lecture hall, prepared a seat before the assembly of monks, and sat down.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“The village headman Makuṭabandhana came to me; having prostrated at my feet, he spoke as follows:”

"In days past, while in the royal palace, I deliberated and discussed with the various ministers regarding the Dharma of the śramaṇas: 'Should one accept and possess gold and other forms of money and treasures, or not? "
At that time, a person among the assembly said:
"Even if a śramaṇa were to hold money, treasures, gold, silver, and the like, what fault would there be?
There is no harm in merely holding them."
Furthermore, some people say:
"According to the dharma of śramaṇas, it is not lawful to hold gold, money, or precious treasures.
Since the words of these two individuals differ, which of their statements accords with the Dharma?
I then replied:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ought not to handle gold, money, or precious gems.
At that time, the village headman spoke these words:

"In the past, among that assembly, I also spoke these words: 'If such śramaṇas may take hold of gold and the like, as well as money and treasures, they should likewise be allowed to indulge freely in the five desires.'"
"At that time, having heard what I had said, the village headman departed with joy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know that the village headman of Maṇiratnaśikhara made a lion’s roar before the assembly, saying:"
“The dharma of a śramaṇa does not permit the acceptance of gold, silver, coins, or precious gems.

Monks, from this day forward, if you have a need and wish to take hold of such things, you should regard them as grass, wood, or excrement; it would be better to grasp filth than to grasp precious objects.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and departed.
127 (127). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the banks of the Kakutthā Pond in the city of Khema in the kingdom of Campā.
At that time, the village head named Rājakeśin approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha said to him:
"In this world, there are many sentient beings who rely upon two kinds of dharmas."
First is the indulgence in sensual pleasure; second is called the practice of what is unbeneficial.
To engage in bodily activities that are unholy is to receive only what is unbeneficial and leads to decline.
To practice such sensual pleasure is termed a base and fettering dharma.
There are three kinds of those who indulge in sensual pleasures. What are these three?

First, there are those who amass unlawful wealth and harm the lives of living beings, seeking pleasure for their own bodies and creating the causes for their own personal enjoyment. This is not called making offerings to one's parents; it is not called giving to one's wife, children, or servants; nor is it toward friends, acquaintances, kinsmen, or those who assist them. Furthermore, it is not called making offerings or providing for śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and other fields of merit.
If it is thus, one does not cultivate the higher path, does not create the causes for happiness, and does not obtain the retribution of happiness; this is called the first kind of sensual pleasure.

Furthermore, even if one experiences sensual pleasure, whether at times it is in accordance with the Dharma or not, whether it involves harm or no harm, one uses it to delight oneself and to provide security and comfort for one’s parents, wife, children, servants, friends, kinsmen, and those who assist one, supporting and supplying them all with true peace and happiness; yet one does not give to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other fields of merit, nor does one cultivate the true path, create the causes for happiness, seek the retribution of happiness, or establish the conditions for rebirth in heaven—this is called the second kind of sensual pleasure.
The Buddha again addressed the village headman:

"If one accumulates wealth and treasures in accordance with the Dharma, yet uses them for harmful purposes—because it is done according to the Dharma and because no cruel evil is committed—one cultivates one's own person and correctly experiences happiness. This is also called providing righteous offerings to one's parents, as well as to one's wife, children, servants, friends, kinsmen, and those who assist one; all these are called providing them with correct peace and happiness and correctly attending to their needs."

From time to time, they make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, cultivate and establish fields of merit, practice the higher path, plant the causes for happiness, seek the retribution of happiness, and create the conditions for rebirth in heaven; this is called the third way of experiencing sensual pleasure.
I now speak thus to all those who experience sensual pleasures:
if they experience sensual pleasures, I call them base;
if they experience sensual pleasures, I call them mediocre.
If one experiences sensual pleasure, I declare that to be superior. What is base and low?

It is when one accumulates wealth through unrighteous means—or even if not through unrighteous means—one seeks only one's own gratification and creates causes for personal pleasure; yet one does not offer support to others, nor provide for one’s wife, children, servants, friends, or kinsmen. Furthermore, one does not seasonably make offerings to the fields of merit such as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; one does not cultivate the higher path, does not create the causes for happiness, does not obtain the retribution of happiness, and does not establish the conditions for rebirth in heaven. This is called "base."
What is called "middling"?

It refers to one who, though enjoying sensual pleasures, does so sometimes in accordance with the Dharma and sometimes not; or who, for the sake of his own bodily pleasure, brings comfort to his parents, wife, children, servants, and relatives, yet does not even create the causes and conditions for rebirth in heaven—this is called middling.
What is meant by "superior"?

It refers to gathering wealth in accordance with the Dharma without causing harm; experiencing happiness through bodily integrity; and providing for one’s parents, wife, children, servants, and friends through righteous means, even to the extent of creating the causes and conditions for rebirth in heaven—this is called superior.
"What are the three kinds of unbeneficial suffering of the body?
They are suffering that is not in accordance with the noble Dharma and is devoid of purpose or benefit; if there is such bodily suffering, the mind has already become corrupted."

When one first violates the prohibitive precepts, the body and mind, both internally and externally, become entirely feverish; one pursues this matter with such intensity that there is not a moment’s respite.

In the present life, being unable to escape this burning affliction, one ultimately cannot attain the Dharma that transcends ordinary men. This is called the first method of fruitlessly tormenting the body.

Furthermore, suppose there is a person who, though not violating the precepts and remaining unchanged in mind, nevertheless aligns their physical and mental actions so that both internal and external are harmonious; yet, while practicing these matters, they do not depart from afflictions in the present life and ultimately cannot attain the state that transcends ordinary humans—this is called the second type of fruitless asceticism of the body.

Furthermore, suppose there is another person who, although not violating the precepts and whose mind does not undergo transformation, nevertheless brings his physical and mental actions into harmony so that both the internal and external are in accord; yet even as he cultivates mindfulness of these matters, he is not free from affliction and distress in the present life. He may achieve a slight degree of progress beyond the common, such as attaining a small measure of wisdom, or seeing the Dharma, or obtaining a small amount of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This is called the third type of fruitless asceticism of the body.

"Headman! I do not say that all fruitless asceticism is of a single kind. There is one kind of asceticism called 'inferior,' another kind of asceticism called 'middling,' and yet another kind of asceticism called 'superior.'"
What is meant by "inferior"?

At the initial moment of violating the precepts, the mind has already become corrupted; body and mind, both internally and externally, are entirely feverish. One pursues this matter with remembrance, never for a moment letting it go, and in the present life remains inseparable from afflictions. Consequently, one can ultimately never attain the Dharma that transcends ordinary men; this is called "inferior."
What is meant by "middling"?

If there is another person who, although not violating the precepts and whose mind remains unchanged, nevertheless finds that their two types of action—body and speech—are in accord with the inner and outer, yet in practicing this matter they do not escape affliction and distress in the present life, nor can they attain the dharmas that transcend the human state; this is called "middling."
What is meant by "superior"?

Suppose there is another person who, although not violating the precepts and whose mind does not undergo transformation, nevertheless accords with both body and mind such that both internally and externally they are in harmony; yet, while practicing this matter, they are currently unable to permanently sever all afflictions, but possess some slight progress beyond the human state, or attain a small measure of wisdom, or attain the vision of the Dharma, or touch the bliss of dhyāna—this is called "superior."
“O village headman!
Avoiding these two extremes, one proceeds toward the path—namely, the three kinds of sensual pleasures and the three kinds of useless asceticism of the body—and proceeds toward the Middle Way.”
What is meant by abandoning the three kinds of objects of sensual pleasure and the three kinds of useless bodily suffering, and proceeding toward the Middle Way?
Village Headman!

Being defiled by craving for sensual pleasure, one harms oneself and also harms others; thus both self and others are harmed. One accumulates various evils in the present and will also accumulate various evils in future lives.
For this reason, one’s mind becomes troubled by grief and sorrow, and one undergoes various sufferings and afflictions.

If, however, one were to exhaust the fetters of desire, there would be no suffering for oneself, nor would one cause suffering to others, nor would there be suffering for either self or others. In the present life, one would not accumulate various sufferings, and in future lives, one would likewise not accumulate any of the manifold sufferings. By virtue of this principle, one attains happiness in the present dharma, is freed from all distress and feverish agitation, and, regardless of the time or season, draws near to Nirvana.

In the present life, one is able to attain the fruits of the Path; the wise person knows this for themselves with clarity and without obstruction, not following the teachings of others—this is called the first Middle Way.
"Village Headman!

Furthermore, there is a Middle Way that is free from affliction and fever, which does not depend on specific times or seasons, brings one close to Nirvana, is known by the wise for themselves, and is not dependent on the teachings of others. That is to say: right view, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right concentration, right effort, right intention, and right mindfulness. This is called the second Middle Way."
When this Dharma was being taught, the village headman Śikhin became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

At that time, the village headman Śikhin knew the Dharma, saw the Dharma, and realized the Dharma; he crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, was freed from uncertainty, no longer followed the teachings of others, and did not accept divergent views. Within the Buddha’s Dharma, he attained sovereign eloquence.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Today I have attained transcendence and take refuge in the Buddha; I likewise take refuge in the Dharma and the Sangha. I uphold the precepts of an upāsaka; from this day forth for as long as life lasts, I take refuge in the Triple Gem."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the village head Kūṭadanta was filled with joy and exultation; he prostrated himself and departed.
128 (128) At that time, the Blessed One was wandering through the village of Madhurā and gradually arrived at the settlement of Uruvilvā, staying in the Mango Grove of the Śuka-yanas.

At that time, the village headman named Assalāyana heard from afar that the Blessed One was traveling through the town of Verañjā and had arrived at the village of Uruvelā in the Mango Grove of the Squirrels. He thought to himself:

"I have heard that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One Gotama can extinguish all present suffering and its origins. I too wish to extinguish all present suffering and its origins; it would be fitting for me to go there to hear this sublime Dharma, for he might explain to me the path to the total extinction of suffering and its origins."
Then, having reflected thus, the one of the donkey clan departed from the village, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have heard the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, which can extinguish the suffering and its origins for sentient beings in the present."
“Excellent!
World-Honored One, out of your compassion and pity, we pray that you will expound upon the meaning of how one can now extinguish the accumulation of suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed him, saying:

"If I were to describe to you the immeasurable sufferings that have already passed away, as well as the Dharma for the cessation of suffering and the origin of suffering, you might at times believe it or not believe it, or find it pleasing or not pleasing."

I now also wish to explain to you the Dharma for the cessation of suffering and the path leading to that cessation, which will eliminate the immeasurable sufferings of the future; yet you may believe it or not believe it, and you may find it pleasing or not.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"I shall now, right here, explain to you the Dharma for the cessation of the accumulation of suffering; you should listen attentively and receive it with a sincere heart."

All sentient beings who experience even minor states of suffering—within which there are various distinctions—these manifold sufferings arise from desire; they are all habituated to desire, with desire as their root and desire as their causal condition.
Then, the village headman spoke again to the Buddha: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"Now my faculties are dull and I do not understand this brief explanation; I only pray that you will show me compassion and expound this meaning in detail, so that I may attain awakening.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
"Suppose all the people in this village of Uruvilvā were bound together, subjected to abuse and insults, and all were executed; would you feel any distress or suffering on their account?"
The village headman said,
"Even though there is grief and distress, it does not necessarily give rise to constant and great suffering.
He then addressed the Buddha again:
“World-Honored One!
Within this village of Uruvilvā, those whom I love are able to give rise to my sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress, such that my mind is not at ease;
as for those who are not loved by me, who are not desired by me, and who are not thought of by me, regarding them I have no sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or distress.”
The Buddha told him:
"Village headman!
Therefore, you should know that the arising of all various kinds of suffering and affliction is entirely due to desire; it is all caused by desire, and desire is their root."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Headman, what do you think?"
If your son had not yet been born, had not yet depended upon his mother, and you had not yet seen or heard of him, would you have felt any desire for intimacy or any heart of affection toward him?
He replied, "There is none.
The Buddha spoke again:
“When your son has been born and raised by his mother, when you see him, do you feel any desire for him or any thought of affection?
He replied, “Indeed I do.”
The Buddha said:

"Suppose your son, having been born from his mother and gradually grown up, were to meet with ruin or be plundered by kings and bandits—if such a thing were to happen, would you not experience suffering, affliction, sorrow, and grief?"
The village headman said:

"If I were to encounter such a situation, at that time my heart would be so consumed by grief and poison that I would either die or be as good as dead; how much more so would it not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress?"
The Buddha spoke again:
"Therefore, you should know that the arising of all various kinds of suffering and affliction is entirely due to desire; it all originates from desire, and desire is its root."
The village headman said:
"How rare, World-Honored One!
What you have spoken is most excellent!"
He skillfully employed various analogies and further addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Suppose my son were in a distant land and I sent a messenger to check on him; if the messenger returned late, both my heart and my mother’s would be uneasy. Worrying over the messenger's delay, we would wonder: 'Will my son not be safe and well?'"
The Buddha said:
“Village headman!

Therefore you should know that the suffering and affliction of sentient beings, their various sorrows and lamentations, all arise because of desire; they are born from desire, and desire is their root.”

If these four cravings undergo decay and transformation, then four kinds of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress arise; if three likewise do so, then three kinds of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress arise; and if there is one craving, then one kind of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress arises.
"If there is no craving, then there will be no sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or distress; one will be free from defilement, like a lotus in a pond that is not stained by water.

When this Dharma was spoken, the village headman Gavāṃpati was freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. He saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, understood the Dharma, and knew the Dharma. Having crossed over doubt and abandoned delusion, he no longer relied on the minds of others nor followed divergent paths; within the Buddha’s teachings, he attained the power of eloquence.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have now attained liberation and take refuge in the Triple Gem. From this night forth, I shall be an upāsaka for as long as my life lasts, giving rise to pure faith."
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and departed.
The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

129 (129). At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus, a thousand upāsakas, and five hundred beggars, was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha, going from village to village and city to city, until he arrived at the Sūnāparantaka city at the Kalandakanivāpa garden, where he stayed.
At that time, the village headman named Mṛṣāvādin was a disciple of the Nirgrantha. Hearing that the Buddha was traveling through Magadha and had arrived at this grove, he thought to himself:
"I shall go and inform my teacher, the Nirgrantha, and afterwards I will go to the presence of Gautama."
Then, the one of the Mūkanta clan went to where the Nirgrantha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the Nirgrantha addressed him, saying:
"Are you able to challenge Gautama with two kinds of arguments?"
Just as two iron hooks catch a fish so that it can neither spit them out nor swallow them, these two types of discourse are likewise able to cause one to neither reject nor accept them.
The village headman said:
"I pray that you will instruct me; I shall go and ask him.
What two arguments can prevent Gautama from being able to either spit out or swallow [the challenge]?"
The Nirgrantha said: "Go to him and speak these words on my behalf:
'Gautama, do you now wish to benefit various households?'"
If you do not bring benefit, what difference is there between you and the common, ignorant folk?
If you claim to bring benefit, why do you now lead twelve hundred bhikṣus, a thousand upāsakas, and five hundred beggars from village to village and city to city, bringing ruin to every household?
Wherever you pass, you will trample upon, destroy, and ruin it, like hail destroying a crop; this is called destruction, not benefit.
At that time, having closed his mouth and received the instruction, he went to the Maṇḍalārāma forest, approached the place where the Buddha was, exchanged brief greetings, and sat down to one side.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "Gautama!
Do you not now wish to increase the benefit and welfare of these families?"
"Do you not always praise those who increase benefit?
The Buddha told him:
"Throughout the long night, I have constantly desired to increase the Dharma of benefit."
Then the village headman spoke these words:

"If you are truly acting for the benefit of others, why is it that now, in this time of famine, you travel from one village to another and from one city to another together with twelve hundred bhikṣus, a thousand upāsakas, and five hundred beggars, bringing ruin upon every household?"
"This is not a method for increasing benefit; rather, it causes diminution, like hail destroying grain. Your destruction of the people is just like this.
The Buddha told him:
"I recall that for ninety-one kalpas, there has never been a single household that suffered diminution as a result of giving cooked food as an offering."

Now, observe for yourself all these households: their abundant wealth and treasures, their retinues and servants, and their elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep—such foundations of prosperity; is there any among them that was not obtained through giving?
It is not solely through giving to me that one obtains this retribution.
There are eight causes and conditions that can ruin a household:

being plundered by kings or thieves; being consumed by fire; being swept away by great floods; losing buried treasures; the birth of wicked sons who do not understand the family business; the forced squandering of wealth; and the irrational expenditure of goods by wicked sons.
All people in the world say:
"Eight things can destroy the household life.
I shall now further speak of the ninth destroyer.
The ninth [reason] is what is called impermanence.
Apart from these nine kinds [of reasons], to say that the śramaṇa Gautama can destroy families is impossible.
If one were to set aside these nine reasons and claim that the śramaṇa Gautama can destroy families and cause them not to prosper, such a thing is impossible.
“Those who do not abandon such speech and do not abandon such desires are like a ball struck by a mallet; they will surely fall into hell.

At that time, having heard these words, the village headman Kṣemaka was struck with fear and alarm; filled with distress and revulsion, his hair stood on end. He rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took refuge in the Buddha, and spoke thus:
“I now sincerely repent before the Buddha!”
I am extremely foolish, like an infant, and have committed what is unwholesome.
Now, before the Buddha, I have spoken that which is false and unreal, a base and vain lie. I only pray that you will take pity on me and accept my repentance!
The Buddha said to him:

"I know your sincerity; you truly recognize your transgression and truly recognize your folly, like that of an infant. You have committed unwholesome deeds and performed a great, false, and base act against the Tathāgata, the Arhat."
Now that you have recognized your transgressions and sincerely repented, your wholesome dharmas will increase and your evil deeds will recede and perish.
Out of compassion for you now, I accept your repentance, so that your wholesome dharmas may increase and never again decline or be lost.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the village headman named Mukhara rejoiced, prostrated himself, and departed. 130 (130) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Sāla Grove in the city of Nālandā.
At that time, the village headman of the Kevaddha clan had this thought:
"I wish now to see the śramaṇa Gautama; however, if I do not first see my teacher, the Nirgrantha, I shall not go there."
He immediately went to where the Nirgrantha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the Nirgrantha said to him:
"I shall now instruct you in two kinds of challenges, so that that Gautama may neither be able to spit them out nor be able to swallow them."
The one of the Closed-Mouth clan then asked him:
"Ācārya! By what two difficulties can you prevent Gautama from being able to swallow?"
He further addressed him, saying:
"You should go to that Gautama and speak these words:
'Do you not act for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings?'"

You also praise the Dharma that brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings; if you were to say it does not bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, what difference would there be between you and the worldly fools?
"If you say that you wish to benefit and bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, why do you not preach the Dharma equally to all?
Why is there anyone for whom you do not preach?
Then, having received these instructions, the village headman went to where the Buddha was, exchanged brief greetings, and sat to one side.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do you truly not wish to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings?
Have you not always praised such a Dharma?"
The Buddha told him:
"Throughout the long night, I have constantly sought to benefit all sentient beings, and I have always praised such a Dharma as this."
The one of the Closed-Mouth clan said:
"If it is so, why do you not preach the Dharma equally for all sentient beings? Why is there some who are not taught?
The Buddha told him:
"I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
For example, among the people of the world there are three kinds of fields:
there is one superior field, fertile and rich in loamy soil, which is exceedingly excellent."
Regarding the second field, it is situated in a suitable location and is excellent.
Regarding the third field, it is in a remote wilderness, consisting of saline and barren soil.
Suppose there are farmers; in which field would they first sow their seeds?
The one surnamed Bìkǒu said:
"One who acts for the benefit of others first plows the fertile field, hoping to reap great rewards.
The Buddha told him:
"If the fertile fields are exhausted, what fields should be sown next?
The man of the Bi family replied,
"Next, sow the middling ones."
"Having sown the middle field, one next sows the lower field;
likewise, one casts the seed with the hope that at a later time there may be some small harvest.
The Buddha told him:

“If you wish to know those who are superior fields, they are my disciples—the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—for whom I have taught the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; which accomplishes one’s own welfare, whose words and meanings are subtle and profound, which fulfills all benefits, which is perfectly pure, and which reveals the holy life.”
When those bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have heard my Dharma, they dwell in dependence upon me, take refuge in me, and rely upon me; I act as their captain and ferry them across.
"I have opened their eyes so that they may see and abide in peace and happiness.
Having heard this, they each said: "The Buddha has spoken for us;
we shall all practice with our whole hearts, which will bring us benefit and happiness for a long night, securing both meaning and joy."

"Among those, the 'middling field' refers to my disciples, the upāsakas and upāsikās, for whom I teach the Dharma that is good in the beginning, middle, and end; which accomplishes one's own welfare; whose phrasing and meaning are subtle and exquisite; which fulfills benefit; which is complete in its purity; and which reveals the holy life."
After those upāsakas and upāsikās have heard my Dharma, they rely upon me, take refuge in me, and depend upon me; I act as their captain and ferry them across.
"I have opened their eyes so that they may see and dwell in peace and happiness.
Having heard this, they each said: "The Buddha has spoken for our sake;
we shall all practice with a sincere heart, which will bring us long-term benefit and lead us to attain the ultimate meaning and happiness."

"If you wish to know what constitutes inferior fields that are saline and barren, they are like the various non-Buddhists; for them as well, I have taught what is good in the beginning, middle, and end, even unto the revelation of the holy life."

Those various non-Buddhists are each able to hear and receive [the teaching], and according to their inclinations, they may even understand the meaning and intent of a single phrase; thus, for them as well, it shall serve as a means of rescue and benefit throughout the long night, so that they may attain both the true meaning and happiness.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the one of the Mṛḍhaka clan spoke these words:
“How rare! Gautama, you have well spoken this beautiful parable.”
The Buddha told him:
"To establish this meaning, I shall provide another illustration.
It is like the three kinds of jars found among people of the world:"
There is one water jar that is solid and intact, without damage, without holes or cracks, and without any seepage.
Its second jar is likewise intact and unbroken, without holes or cracks, though it has slight seepage.
"The third jar is both cracked and leaking.
If that person were to pour water, which vessel should he use first?
He replied:
"First, when the vessel that is neither broken nor leaking has been filled to capacity, one pours it into a second vessel.
Although this second vessel is intact and not broken, it does have a slight seepage."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Once this jar is full, where else would you pour it?
Even though the third jar is cracked and leaking, one should still pour water into it, for it can be used for a short while before it leaks."
The first jar is a metaphor for my disciples—the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—for whom I preach the Dharma, even unto enabling them to attain its meaning and find happiness.
The second jar represents my disciples, the upāsakas and upāsikās; for their sake I preach the Dharma, so that they may attain its meaning and find happiness.

The third jar represents the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); for their sake I preach the Dharma, such that even if they hear and receive it but slightly, I cause them to attain its meaning and find happiness.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the village headman of the Kṣemaka clan felt terror and alarm in his heart; overcome with sorrow and revulsion, the hairs on his body stood on end. He rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these words:
“I now sincerely repent before the Buddha!”
I am exceedingly foolish, like an infant; my actions have been unwholesome, and in the presence of the Buddha, I have uttered false and unreal words—a base and lying speech.
“I only pray that you will have compassion for me and grant me absolution for my repentance!
The Buddha told him:
“I know your utmost sincerity; you truly recognize your transgression and truly recognize your folly, like that of an infant, for the unwholesome deeds you have committed.”
"Before the Tathāgata, the Arhat, you have spoken this falsehood with a base and deceitful mind.
Now that you recognize your transgression and repent with a sincere heart, your wholesome dharmas will increase daily, while evil matters shall diminish."
"Now, out of compassion for you, I accept your repentance; may your wholesome dharmas increase, and may you never again fall back.
At that time, the village head named Mukhara, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly, prostrated himself, and departed.
131. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Sālavana forest near the city of Nālandā.
At that time, the village headman Sañjaya, the compiler of the treatises, had this thought:
"I ought not to go now to see the Nirgranthas; I shall instead go to where the Buddha is.
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the Buddha, and after having exchanged greetings, sat down to one side.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the village head who was a compiler of the treatises:
"What kind of Dharma did that Nirgrantha Jñātiputra teach to his disciples?"
Then, the village headman addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those Nirgranthas constantly make this claim:”
"If one commits the karma of killing, according to the frequency with which it is committed, one will inevitably fall into the evil realms and enter hell.
It is the same for stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so forth; according to how frequently they are committed, one will inevitably fall into hell."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the village headman:
"If it were as the Nirgrantha has said, no sentient beings would ever fall into the evil destinies or enter hell."
Why is this so? As the Nirgranthas say:
"If one commits the karma of killing, according to the duration for which the killing was committed, one will inevitably fall into the evil destinies and enter hell."
Regarding theft, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so forth, it is also like this:
among all sentient beings, the time spent killing is short, while the time spent not killing is long.
If those who spend more time [in virtue] were to enter hell, then since the time spent killing is short and the time spent not killing is long, one should not fall into the evil realms or enter hell.

It is the same with stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so forth: the time spent actually committing these acts is brief, while the time not committing them is vast; thus, one should not fall into the evil realms or enter hell on account of them.
The Buddha again addressed the village headman:
"According to what you have said, there would be no one at all who enters hell.
At that time, the village headman addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is indeed so, Gautama.
The Buddha again addressed the village headman:

"If there is a teacher in the world who is able to produce skillful measurement, who possesses wisdom and discernment, and who, while remaining on the plane of deliberation, uses his own verbal eloquence—this being the plane of ordinary persons—to teach such a Dharma to his disciples."
If one takes life, they will all fall into the evil realms and enter hell; according to the duration for which the karma was committed, by means of that manifold karma, they are dragged into hell.
It is likewise when one commits theft, sexual misconduct, or false speech; according to the duration for which such actions were performed, one falls into the evil destinies and enters hell.
Those disciples, with single-minded faith and delight in what their teacher had spoken, received and upheld it with utmost sincerity, saying:
"Our instructor and master knows those objects before him; he sees what is seen."
These disciples, in turn, had their own disciples who said to them:
"My teacher and instructor has declared that if one commits the act of killing, the more frequently one kills, the more one will fall into the evil realms and enter hell."
That grandson-disciple thought to himself:
"I have previously committed killing; I will certainly fall into hell.
When I committed theft, sexual misconduct, and lying, I will certainly fall into the evil realms and enter hell."
"Based on this, one forms a view; having attained such a view, it is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Not abandoning this view, not resolving one's doubts, and not repenting for the causes of the evil karma one has committed, one continues to perpetrate such evil karma as before, refusing to reform one's mind and unable to reach fulfillment."
Their liberation of mind is not yet fulfilled,
nor is their liberation by wisdom fulfilled.
Because their liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom are not fulfilled, they slander the noble ones.
"Because one slanders the noble ones, this is precisely wrong view.
The Buddha further addressed the village headman:
"Suppose there is a person who holds such a wrong view; they will fall into the evil realms and enter hell."
All sentient beings possess the defilements of the mind caused by karmic conditions; for this reason, all sentient beings acquire the fetters of karma and afflictions.

Even if a Buddha were to appear—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha—that Buddha would likewise, through various causes and conditions, censure the taking of life, stealing, sexual misconduct, and false speech. It is just so.
He further praised that supreme Dharma with resolute faith and understanding.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:

"My World-Honored One possesses true knowledge and vision; through your various teachings, you have enabled me to preach such a Dharma to my disciples, using various causes and conditions to censure the taking of life and to praise abstaining from killing."
Through various causes and conditions, I have praised abstaining from false speech, sexual misconduct, and theft.
In the past, I myself had committed killing, theft, sexual misconduct, and false speech; because of these causes and conditions, I have constantly reproached myself.
Although one may repent and reproach oneself, this is what is meant by not committing sinful karma.
Therefore, by deeply repenting and reproaching oneself, such evil karma is entirely eliminated through confession, and wholesome karma is increased.

Furthermore, they shall refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so forth; they shall repent and reproach their previous deeds and henceforth never again commit various evil karmas.
For this reason, the mind attains fulfillment and achieves liberation; it is also able to fulfill the liberation through wisdom.
Because both mind and wisdom are fulfilled, one does not slander the noble ones.
"Because one does not slander the noble ones, one attains right view.
The Buddha told the village headman:
"By virtue of being able to cultivate the conditions for right view, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one goes to a good destination and is reborn in the heavens."
Because they are able to repent with right view, they can purify the minds of all sentient beings, and can also purify the karmic bonds, afflictions, and defilements of sentient beings.
When a noble disciple hears this matter, they immediately begin to practice and study it.

Whether at the proper time, during the specific divisions of time, or within the intervals between those divisions, as the day and night pass by—during such times, is the time for killing more frequent, or is the time for not killing more frequent?
Inferring by way of this principle, the time spent killing is short, while the time spent not killing is long.
That I intentionally committed killing at those times was truly unwholesome; my actions were irrational.
From this day forward, I shall never kill again.
Toward all beings, I shall no longer give rise to aversion, nor resentment, nor jealousy; instead, I shall give rise to profound joy.
Because joy arises, a deep sense of affection and delight is produced.
Because affection and delight arise, a profound sense of pliancy and ease is attained.
Because profound pliancy and ease are attained, one experiences happiness.
Because he experiences happiness, his mind attains concentration (*samādhi*).
Because the mind of the noble disciple has attained concentration, it becomes endowed with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Being endowed with loving-kindness, he is free from enmity, resentment, and hatred; he becomes free from jealousy, and his mind becomes vast, expansive in its aspirations, immeasurable, and boundless.

Because he has skillfully cultivated loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he harbors no resentment or aversion toward any sentient beings in the eastern direction; it is likewise so for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. He universally gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all worlds, forming this mental resolve: "I shall cultivate and establish such a virtuous mind, and abide within that virtue."
At that time, the World-Honored One took a small amount of earth from the ground, placed it upon his fingernail, and asked the village headman of the Koṭṭhila clan:
"Is the soil of the great earth more abundant?"
"Is the soil on my fingernail more?
The village headman replied, "The soil on my fingernail is extremely scant; it cannot even be compared [to the earth]."

“Compared to the soil of the great earth, it cannot be compared by even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-billionth part; no calculation or analogy can measure them against one another.
The Buddha told the village headman:
“All sinful karma is like the soil on a fingernail; the soil of the great earth cannot be measured by calculation or analogy.”
The village headman said: "So it is, so it is.
By comparison with evil karma, one can see that such a small amount of karma cannot drag a person down into the evil realms, nor can it cause them to remain there; it is not even calculable."
Now, the merit obtained by one who practices loving-kindness is like the soil of the great earth;
the sin of killing is like the soil on a fingernail.
The merit of compassion is like the soil of the great earth.
The sin of stealing is like the soil on a fingernail;
the merit of rejoicing [in others' virtue] is like the soil of the great earth;
the sin of sexual misconduct is like the soil on a fingernail.
“The merit of abandoning [false speech] is like the soil of the great earth;
the fault of lying is like the soil on a fingernail.

When the Tathāgata was thus distinguishing these dharmas, the village headman of the clan of Kṛtaka, having heard what the Buddha taught, became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. He realized the Dharma, witnessed the Dharma, knew the Dharma, reached the limit of the Dharma, crossed beyond all doubts, no longer followed the faith of others, and immediately attained the state of having completed what was to be done.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have already attained deliverance!"
I have attained deliverance!
I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma and the Sangha, and become a lay follower (*upāsaka*), maintaining pure faith for as long as my life lasts.
The village headman spoke again to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
For example, if one utters evil abuse for the sake of gain and profit, it becomes increasingly worse day by day; such a person loses even their own wealth, let alone obtain any profit.”
I am likewise; for the sake of gain, I have drawn near to the foolish and unwholesome Nirgranthas.
Driven by delusion, I have associated with them, honoring and revering them. Yet from them I have gained no wholesome benefit; rather, I have been ensnared by them and am about to fall into hell.

"Blessed One, you have rescued me, enabling me to escape the evil realms. I now return once more to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; for as long as life lasts, I shall be a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
I hereby renounce all my former faith, affection, and reverence for that foolish Nirgrantha."
"For a third time, I now again take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. For as long as my life lasts, I shall be an upāsaka and never give rise to lack of faith.
At that time, the village headman named Kṛtaka, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced, prostrated himself, and departed.
Agitation and strife; training horses and the ill-tempered one with a topknot, as well as the Sage;
the king’s hair and the donkey-bred one, famine and agriculture—what ten discourses are taught?

132 (One Hundred and Thirty-Two). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice as bright as usual, came to the place where the Buddha was during the night. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat down to one side.
At that time, the radiance of this deity was exceedingly brilliant, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove until it was all clearly lit.
Then, the deity withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
"Abiding in a forest hermitage, Practicing the holy life in tranquil extinction."
"Eating but one meal a day, his complexion is exceedingly serene.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"He does not grieve over the past, nor does he seek the future."
Now, with right wisdom as his sustenance, he merely seeks to preserve his body.
Because he desires to recall past events in future lives, all six sense-faculties are delighted;
therefore, his countenance is harmonious and serene.
"Just as newly grown reeds, when cut and placed in the sun, wither and dry up of their own accord;
such is the nature of ordinary people.
The deva further spoke in verse, praising him:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain *nirvāṇa*;
having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he was able to cross over the world's craving.
When this deva had spoken this verse, he returned to his palace with joy.
133 (133). Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice as bright as usual, came to the place where the Buddha was during the night. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat down to one side.
At that time, the radiance of this deva was exceedingly intense, illuminating the Jeta Grove so that it was entirely filled with great light.
Then, this deva withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
“Those people who are possessed of pride Can never be disciplined.”
"Feigning the practice of meditative concentration, One remains negligent in the empty forest;
Because of such negligence, One cannot cross over the shore of death.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Abandoning pride and constantly entering meditative concentration, exhausting all conceptual thoughts through the knowledge of phenomena,
liberated in every respect, one dwells heedfully in the empty forest;
by virtue of this heedfulness, one is able to cross over to the further shore of death.”
The deva praised him with these verses:
“In the past, I have already seen a brāhmaṇa attain nirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.”
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy.
134 (134) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain deity, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat down to one side.
At that time, the radiance of this deva was exceedingly brilliant, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove until it was all clearly visible.
Then, this deva withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
"How may one’s meritorious deeds constantly increase throughout the day and night?"
"Who, by maintaining the precepts in accordance with the Dharma, proceeds to the heavenly realm?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"One who plants gardens and groves, and places bridges and boats across great torrents,"
One who digs a fine well in the wilderness, or builds a guesthouse on a main road,
will find that their meritorious deeds constantly increase day and night.
By upholding the pure precepts of the True Dharma, one thus proceeds toward the heavenly realms.
The deva praised him with these verses:
“In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain Nirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.”
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy.
135 (135) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice as bright as usual, came to the place where the Buddha was during the night.
The light of this deva was so exceedingly intense that it illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, making it all brilliantly clear.
At that time, this deva withdrew to sit to one side and spoke in verse:
"How may one obtain great power, And likewise acquire a wondrous form?"
By giving what does one obtain peace and happiness?
By what cause does one obtain the pure eye?
What constitutes the giving of all things?
"I pray that you will explain this to me.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"By giving food and drink, one gains strength; by giving clothing, one gains a radiant complexion."
By giving vehicles one obtains peace and happiness; by giving lamps one obtains clear vision;
by giving dwellings as an all-encompassing gift and instructing disciples according to the Dharma—one who can practice such giving is said to bestow nectar.
The deva praised him with this verse:
“In the past, I have already seen a brahmin enter nirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.”
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy. 136 (136).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night; his majestic light was so blazing and intense that it illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, making it all brilliantly bright.
At that time, this deva, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side and spoke in verse:
“Among the gods and humans in the world, Food and drink give rise to joy;
Yet there is nothing in the world That does not produce joy through food and drink.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If there are those who can practice faithful giving, Causing the mind to become utterly pure,
Then in this life or in future lives, The merit of food and drink will follow them."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, this deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is truly rare!”
"You have well spoken this verse.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
I recall that in the past there was a king of men named Dandapani; that king provided food and drink at his four city gates, as well as within the city and in the marketplace.
At that time, the king’s consort said to the king:
"Your Majesty is now performing meritorious deeds; we pray that you will allow us to assist you in creating merit.
When the king heard her words, he took the food that had been offered at the eastern gate of the city and gave it to the consort instead.
The king’s crown prince also said to his father,
"If my parents practice the cultivation of merit, I too would delight in practicing it.
When the king heard these words, he diverted the food that had been given as alms at the southern city gate and bestowed it upon the crown prince.
The minister came later and addressed the king, saying:

"Your Majesty now cultivates goodness, and both the queen and the crown prince cultivate meritorious deeds; I only pray that you will permit me to assist in the cultivation of these meritorious deeds."
When the king heard these words, he diverted the food that had been set aside for the western city gate and gave it instead to the minister.
At that time, various ministers again addressed the king, saying:
"The queen, the crown prince, and the minister are all cultivating merit; we now also wish to assist them in their cultivation."
When the king heard these words, he immediately diverted the food intended for the northern gate and gave it to his ministers.
At that time, the people of the kingdom again addressed the king, saying:
"The queen, the crown prince, and the chief minister are all cultivating merit; we pray that you will allow us to assist them in performing meritorious deeds."
When the king heard these words, he again diverted his acts of giving and bestowed them upon the people.
At that time, the official in charge of almsgiving addressed the king, saying:

"Whatever the king possessed—whether at the four city gates or through acts of charity—has been entirely diverted to the queen, the crown prince, the prime minister, the great ministers, and the people of the kingdom. The king's giving has been cut off, and furthermore, the treasury is exhausted."
The king then replied:

"That which was previously granted has already been exhausted; from this day forward, whatever tribute is offered by small kingdoms of other regions shall be divided, with half entering the treasury and half used for the cultivation of merit."
"World-Honored One!

At that time, I cultivated merit throughout the long night; throughout the long night, I obtained supreme retribution, always harboring joy and bliss. The blessings and rewards I received were inexhaustible, and their limit could not be seen."
"Just as I have received [the fruits of my actions], I have obtained this great reward; thus I know that the World-Honored One has well spoken this verse.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Devaputra Cihuan (Slow) leaped for joy, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to his celestial palace.
137 (One Hundred Thirty-Seven) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during that night. His brilliance was so intense that it illuminated the entire Jetavana. Standing to one side, he spoke this verse:
"Just as when one travels far to another land, who is there to be relied upon?
Within that foreign household, whom does one regard as kin?
Amidst its wealth and possessions, whom does one regard as a friend?"
"When one reaches a future life, whom else can one rely upon as kin?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered with a verse:
"If one travels far to another land, one's traveling companion is called a kinsman."
Within one's own household, the compassionate mother is the most intimate;
in the pursuit of wealth and profit, kinsmen are the companions.
Those who are able to cultivate merit and virtue—these are called true kin in the world beyond.
The deva praised him with this verse:
“In the past, I have already seen A brahmin enter parinirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, He is able to cross over the world’s craving.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, this deva departed with joy.
138 (138) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night. His majestic light shone brilliantly, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove until it was all clearly visible. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
“The lifespan of humans is uncertain; Day by day they tread the path toward death.
Assailed and robbed by impermanence, Their life span is exceedingly brief.”
"Old age invades the vigor of youth; there is no one to provide rescue or protection.
Terrified and fearing death, one should cultivate merit to attain the joy of the higher realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"The lifespan of human life is uncertain; day by day one approaches the path of death.
Seized and robbed by impermanence, the duration of life is exceedingly brief.
Old age invades the vigor of youth, and there is no one to provide protection."
Trembling with fear as death approaches, And desiring to attain the bliss of nirvana,
One should renounce the five worldly desires And ought not to give rise to deep attachment.
The deva praised him with this verse:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain *nirvāṇa*;
having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he was able to cross over the world’s craving.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, this son of heaven departed with joy.
139 (139). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice as bright as usual, approached the Buddha during the night. His majestic light shone brilliantly, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove until it was completely bright. He withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
"The four seasons do not pause for a moment, and life likewise exhausts itself day and night;
youth does not remain long, and the terror of death approaches.
For the sake of Nirvana, one should diligently cultivate merit."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"The four seasons do not pause for a moment, And life is exhausted day and night.
The prime of youth does not endure long; Terror, death, approaches."
"Seeing the suffering of birth and death, one gives rise to great fear;
abandoning the pleasures of the five worldly desires, one should seek nirvāṇa.
Thus the deva praised him with these verses:
“In the past, I have already seen the Brahmin who has attained *nirvāṇa*;
having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over the world’s craving.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, this deva departed with joy.
140. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, during the night, a certain devaputra, whose radiance was twice as bright as usual, approached the place where the Buddha was. His majestic light was so brilliant that it illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, making it all clearly visible. He then withdrew to one side and spoke this verse:
"One should reflect: 'What dharmas should be contemplated? What dharmas should be abandoned?
What sublime practice should be cultivated? What state should be accomplished?
One who can cross over the swift-flowing stream is called a bhikṣu."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"One who can sever the five hindrances, Abandon the five desires,
Cultivate the five faculties with superior effort, And accomplish the fivefold qualities of the Dharma— ”
One who can cross the swift-flowing stream is called a bhikṣu.
The deva praised him with this verse:
“In the past, I have already seen a brāhmaṇa attain nirvāṇa;”
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, this deva departed with joy.
141 (141). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the place where the Buddha was during that night. His majestic light shone forth, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove with a brilliant brilliance. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
"Who is asleep while called awake?
Who is awake while called asleep?
How does one become defiled by the dust and grime?"
"How does one attain purity?
The Buddha answered in verse:
"If one upholds the five precepts, though asleep, they are called awake."
If one commits the five evils, though awake, one is called asleep.
If one is shrouded by the five hindrances, one is said to be defiled by dust and grime.
The body of the fivefold aggregate of one beyond training is pure and free from dust and grime.
The deva further spoke in verse, praising him:
“In the past, I have already seen a brahmin attain nirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over the love of the world.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, this deva departed with joy.
How does one dwelling in *āraṇya*, free from pride, and cultivating merit day and night obtain great power? What thing gives rise to joy?
From afar they come, and through forceful intimacy they press upon one;
day and night there is loss and diminution—both in thought and in sleep. (142) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night. His majestic light was so brilliant that it illuminated the Jetavana, shining with great clarity. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
“If a person has sons and grandsons, Then they give rise to joy.”
Wealth, treasures, and the six domestic animals—when these exist, all are joyful.
When a person receives a body, they likewise give rise to joy.
But if one sees that which is bodiless, then there is no heart of delight.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"If a person has children and grandchildren, They will give rise to sorrow and affliction.
