Wealth, treasures, and the six domestic animals— These are the very roots of suffering and distress."
"If one again receives a body, it becomes a source of sorrow, affliction, and distress;
if one does not receive a body, that is called the bliss of quiescent extinction.
The deva further spoke in verse, praising him:
“In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain *nirvāṇa*;
having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he was able to cross over the world’s craving.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, this deva departed with joy.
143 (One Hundred Forty-Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the world there are three kinds of ill-behaved horses that all people of the world clearly recognize.
There may be a horse whose gait is swift and fleet, yet it lacks a beautiful color; this is called 'the deficiency of the mount. "
Furthermore, there may be a horse that is swift in its gait, yet lacks a beautiful color; this is also called an incomplete vehicle.
Alternatively, there may be a fine horse that is both swift in its gait and possesses a beautiful color; this is called a complete vehicle.
There are likewise three kinds of persons, like those three kinds of untrained horses.
These three types of persons are known and seen within the teachings of the Buddha.
What are the three?
There is a person who possesses both speed and vigor, yet lacks beauty and a mount;
or again, there is a person who possesses both speed and vigor and possesses beauty, yet lacks a mount.
Furthermore, there may be someone who possesses both swiftness of speed and a beautiful color, as well as a suitable vehicle, all fully complete.
"What is it to have swiftness complete, but the color incomplete and the vehicle incomplete?"

A person who is in accordance with the Dharma knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering as it truly is, knows the cessation of suffering as it truly is, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. Having known and seen thus, they abandon the three fetters, namely: the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt.

Having severed these three fetters, one attains the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer); no longer falling into the evil realms, being certain of the path, and undergoing at most seven more births among humans and devas, one reaches the end of suffering—this is called being endowed with swiftness.
What is meant by "incompleteness of form"?

If, when questioned or challenged regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, one is unable to provide a skillful response; if, regarding profound questions and challenges, one cannot achieve full comprehension; if one cannot explain the words and meanings in their proper sequence; and if one cannot provide a thorough explanation in accordance with the truth—this is called incompleteness of form.
What is it that constitutes the non-perfection of the vehicle?

It is when one has little merit such that, in whatever place one is born, there is no merit; consequently, one does not obtain gain, clothing, food and drink, bedding, or medicinal requisites—this is called the non-perfection of the vehicle.
This is called being endowed with swiftness, but not endowed with beauty of form, and not endowed with a vehicle.
"What is meant by being endowed with swiftness, endowed with beauty of form, but not endowed with a vehicle?"
What is meant by being endowed with swiftness?

It is when a person among those who follow the Dharma knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering as it truly is, knows the cessation of suffering as it truly is, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is; having known and seen this, they sever the three fetters, namely: the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt.

Having severed the three fetters, one attains the stage of *srotāpanna*; not falling into the evil destinies, being certain of the path, and undergoing at most seven more births among humans and devas until the end of suffering—this is called "endowment with swiftness."
What is meant by the perfection of form?

If, when questioned or challenged regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, one is able to explain them skillfully, with words and meanings that correspond to one another, and by expounding them clearly in accordance with reason, this is called the perfection of form.
What is meant by "incompleteness of the vehicle"?
It refers to having little merit such that one cannot be born with great merit, and thus fails to obtain gains, robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
This is called having excellence in speed and appearance, but a lack of excellence in the vehicle.
What is meant by having excellence in speed, appearance, and the vehicle all together?
What is swift?

It is knowing suffering as it truly is within this Dharma, knowing the origin of suffering as it truly is, knowing the cessation of suffering as it truly is, and knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.

Having thus known and seen, one severs the three fetters and attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); being reborn seven times among humans and devas, one does not fall into the evil destinies—this is called being endowed with swiftness.
What is meant by "perfection of form"?

If one is questioned or challenged regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, and is able to provide a thorough explanation such that the phrasing and meaning are consistent, and one expounds clearly in accordance with the principle—this is called the perfection of form.
What is meant by "being fully endowed with the vehicle"?
It refers to one who possesses great merit and is thus fortunate from birth, able to obtain gains, clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
"This is called being fully endowed with the vehicle; this is called the third excellence—being fully endowed with speed, color, and the vehicle.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
144 (144). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“In the world there are three kinds of horses, all excellent and well-trained.
There may be a horse that is fully endowed with speed and swiftness, yet lacks beauty and stature.
Or again, there may be a horse that is fully endowed with both speed and beauty, yet lacks stature.”
Furthermore, there may be horses that possess all three qualities,
while humans likewise have three grades, just like those three types of horses.
Among these three kinds of people within the Buddha’s teaching, as is currently known and seen, some are fully endowed with swiftness, yet lack beauty and a suitable mount.
There are those who possess two [factors] but do not possess one;
there are those who possess all three factors.
Which ones possess one but do not possess the other two?

Just as in the Buddha’s Dharma, one knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering as it truly is, knows the cessation of suffering as it truly is, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is; having severed the five lower fetters and attained the stage of non-returning (anāgāmin), such a person does not return to this world and will not fall into the evil destinies.
What is meant by "incompleteness of form"?

If, when questioned or challenged regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, one is unable to provide an explanation, and is unable to recite the words and meanings in accordance with the principles, this is called incompleteness of form.
What is meant by "incompleteness of the vehicle"?
To have little merit such that one cannot be born with great merit, and to fail to obtain gains, robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites—this is called incompleteness of the vehicle.
What is the second case, where two matters are fulfilled but one is not?
This person, within the Buddha’s Dharma, perceives the Four Noble Truths and even severs the five lower fetters, thereby attaining the stage of Anāgāmin.
If there are those who pose questions or challenges regarding the Abhidharma or the Vinaya, he is able to explain and expound upon them for them; the rest is as stated above.
Regarding the lack of one [of the two], it is also as stated above. This is called the second [type]: being complete in two, yet incomplete in one.
What is the third [type of person] who is endowed with three things?

This person, having understood the Buddha’s Dharma as it truly is and having seen the Four Noble Truths, attains the stage of Anāgāmin; furthermore, possessing great merit, they receive offerings and gains. This is called the third [type of person] who is endowed with three things.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 145 (144) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"For example, there are three kinds of excellent riding horses in the world, and people are likewise of three kinds.
There are three types of persons; the first of these is one who is fully endowed with swiftness, color, and carriage."

If there is a person who, within the Buddha’s Dharma, knows and sees the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, has already severed the three outflows—namely, the outflow of sensual desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance—and is fully endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation; having exhausted all fetters of existence, attained mastery over the mind, brought an end to birth and death, established the holy life, accomplished what was to be done, and accepted no further existence, thereby attaining arhatship—this is called being "endowed with swiftness."
The rest is as explained above.
What is the second?
It is when two factors are fully present, but one is not.
Within the Buddha-dharma, having known and seen the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, one attains the state of an Arhat;
if there are questions or challenges regarding this, it is as explained above.
What is the third?
It is the fulfillment of three matters.

When a person, within the Buddha’s Dharma, has known and seen the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, and even possesses merit such that they are able to receive offerings and sustenance—this is called the fulfillment of the three matters.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
146 (146). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"These three kinds of well-trained riding horses are fit for kings and princes to ride.
What are the three? "
These are known as being endowed with swiftness, endowed with color, and endowed with the vehicle.
There are three kinds of bhikṣus who are like those three horses.
If a bhikṣu is endowed with these three qualities, he should be worthy of prostration, offerings, and praise with palms joined; this is called being endowed with the three qualities.
What is the perfection of physical form?
It is to fully maintain the prohibitive precepts, to skillfully guard and uphold the Prātimokṣa, and to possess all dignified deportments in coming and going, entering and exiting.
To feel great dread regarding even minor transgressions, to firmly uphold the prohibitive precepts without any violation—this is called being endowed with form.
What is meant by being endowed with power?
Regarding unwholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, he causes them not to arise; regarding those that have already arisen, he employs skillful means to extinguish them.

Regarding wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen, he employs skillful means to cause them to arise; regarding those that have already arisen, he employs skillful means to increase and expand them.
This is called being endowed with power.
What is meant by being endowed with swiftness?
If, within the Buddha-dharma, one knows and sees the Four Noble Truths as they truly are, this is called being endowed with swiftness.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
147 (147) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of excellent horses upon which a king should ride.
What are these four?

Well-tamed, swift, capable of endurance, and dwelling well without fighting—a bhikṣu who has thus accomplished these four qualities should be taken as a refuge, honored with offerings and prostrations, and revered with palms joined; he is the unsurpassed field of merit within the world.
"What are the four? They are:
being well-trained and swift, being able to remain well-settled, and not fighting.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
148 (148). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of horses that a wise person should mount; these are all found in the world. What are the four?
The first is one who, upon seeing the shadow of the raised whip, immediately becomes alarmed and follows the driver's will."
The second kind, when the whip touches the hair of its body, immediately becomes startled and alarmed, yet complies with the driver's will.
The third kind, when the whip touches the flesh of its body, only then becomes startled, yet follows the driver's will.
As for the fourth type, one must whip until the flesh and bone are pierced before they are startled and act according to the driver's will.
The carriage of a man likewise has four types.
What are the four? The first is this:
one hears that in another village, whether a man or a woman, has been afflicted by illness and is so severely debilitated that they are on the verge of death.
Having heard these words, he developed a profound sense of weary detachment toward worldly phenomena.

Because of this detachment, he cultivated goodness with a sincere heart; this is called the "well-tamed vehicle of the man," like one who, upon seeing the shadow of the whip, accords with the driver's intent.
As for the second, he sees within his own village a man or a woman who has contracted a grave illness and, having reached a state of extreme debility, passes away.
Having witnessed these matters, one develops a deep sense of weary detachment.

Because of this weary detachment, one cultivates goodness with a sincere heart; this is called the "well-tamed vehicle of the man," which, like the hair on the body being touched, accords with the will of the driver.
As for the third type, although they see those in their own village who fall ill and die, they do not give rise to a sense of revulsion.

Only when they see their own kinsmen and those who have assisted them fall gravely ill and eventually reach the end of their lives are they able to develop a mind of revulsion toward worldly phenomena.

Because of such revulsion, one diligently cultivates wholesome conduct; this is called the "well-tamed vehicle of a man," which, like touching the hair or flesh [of a horse], accords with the driver's intent.
As for the fourth type, even when he sees his own kinsmen or those who assist him fall ill or pass away, he still does not give rise to a mind of revulsion.
If one’s own body falls ill, becoming extremely grave and severe, and one undergoes great suffering and distress with a deeply unhappy mind, only then does the thought of revulsion arise.

Because of this revulsion, one cultivates various wholesome deeds; this is called the "well-tamed vehicle of a man," which, like seeing a whip touch the flesh and bone, follows the will of the driver.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 149 (149) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are eight kinds of horses that transcend what is known in the world and can be seen in the present.
What are these eight?

First, suppose a horseman, holding the reins and grasping the whip, is about to set out on a long journey, when that wicked horse bites the bit and leaps about, suddenly snapping the harness and breaking the riding gear, thereby injuring its own body; this is called the fault of the horse.
As for the second, when the driver mounts it, it refuses to move forward; this wicked horse leaps and bounds beyond control, shattering its harness and equipment.
As for the third, when the driver mounts it, it refuses to stay on the road, but merely leaps over ditches and moats.
As for the fourth, when mounted, it refuses to move forward and instead retreats backward.
As for the fifth, it has no fear at all of the person who drives it or the pain of the whip.
The sixth [figure] is a horseman who, using a whip and a goad, employs skillful means to make the horse stand on its two hind legs.
The seventh is a horseman who, desiring to gallop, instead lies prostrate on the ground and refuses to advance upon the path.
The eighth is this: when a horse-rider intends for the horse to go forward, it instead comes to a halt.
Within the Buddha-dharma, there are likewise eight such faults and afflictions for those men who practice and study.
What are the eight?
If a bhikṣu has been touched by the awareness of a matter—whether seen, heard, or suspected—concerning his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he should immediately say to them:
"You are currently immature and lacking wisdom; you are unskilled and ignorant. You ought to be aware of others; why do you wish to provoke me?"
"You have faults yourself, yet you instead raise the matters of others.
Such a person is like the first horse.
As for the second, when he sees that another bhikṣu has committed an offense regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected, he immediately speaks to that fellow-practitioner of the holy life:
Suppose there is a guilty person who says, "You have now committed such a crime.
Then another guilty person replies to him:
"If you first confess and repent for the very same crime that you yourself have committed, only then may you accuse me of my crime."
Such a person is like the faults of the second horse. As for the third:

if there is a bhikṣu who, having committed an offense based on what was seen, heard, or suspected, is accused by another, yet speaks evasively, following his own attachment, aversion, or fear, and gives rise to anger through a deluded mind—such a person is like the faults of the third horse.

The fourth [case] is when a bhikṣu has likewise committed an offense regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected, and having been accused by another, he immediately says to that person who raised the charge:
"I do not recall committing such an offense at all."
"You should know that this person shares the faults of the fourth horse.
As for the fifth: if there is a bhikṣu who likewise commits an offense regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected, and his fellow practitioners in the holy life come to reprove him."

At that time, the offender immediately takes up his robes and bowl and departs as he pleases, his mind entirely devoid of fear or respect for the Sangha or those who have raised the matter against him.
It should be understood that this person shares the faults of the fifth horse.

As for the sixth: suppose there is a bhikṣu who has likewise committed an offense regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected, and his fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) raise the matter against him.
At that time, the offender immediately sits upon a high place and disputes the principles with the elder bhikṣus, raising his hands and shouting loudly, saying:
"All of you yourselves have committed offenses regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected, yet you further say that I have committed such an offense!"
"You should know that such a person shares the faults and afflictions of the sixth horse.

As for the seventh: if there is a bhikṣu who likewise commits an offense regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected, and a pure bhikṣu rebukes him for that matter, yet that guilty person remains silent and says neither 'I am guilty' nor 'I am innocent,' thereby vexing and disturbing the Saṃgha."
It should be known that such a person commits the same transgression as the seventh horse.

As for the eighth: if there is a bhikṣu who likewise commits an offense regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected, and a pure bhikṣu brings this matter to his attention, that offender immediately abandons the precepts, loses his roots of goodness, and deserts the path to return to lay life.
Having finished his discourse on the Way, he stood to one side by the gate of the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"I am now returning to lay life; has I fulfilled your wishes or not?"
"Are you now joyful and exceedingly happy?
"You should know that such a person shares the faults and afflictions of the eighth horse.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
150. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are eight kinds of horses that are ridden by the noble ones.
As for those 'noble ones,' they are the wheel-turning sage kings (cakravartin).
What are these eight?
Born from the lineage of noble steeds, this is called the first mark of an excellent horse.
The second is that it is exceedingly well-tamed and never provokes or harms other ordinary horses; this is called the second mark of an excellent horse.

As for the third horse, it consumes whatever grass is offered without discriminating between good and bad, eating it all completely without leaving anything behind; this is also called the mark of a noble steed.

As for the fourth, when confronted with foul and filthy things that give rise to impure impressions—such as places where excrement and urine have been deposited—it never stops there to dwell or lie down; this is called possessing the fourth mark of a noble steed.

The fifth is that it can point out the faults of the unruly horse to the charioteer and can instruct the charioteer on how to remedy all the horse's ailments; this is also called the mark of a noble horse.
The sixth is that he can endure heavy burdens without seeking light ones, constantly thinking:
"Whenever I see other horses carrying loads, I shall cut them down."
This is called the sixth characteristic of an excellent horse.

As for the seventh: it always remains on the path and never strays from it; even if the path is narrow or shallow, it clearly understands it. This is called the seventh characteristic of an excellent horse.

The eighth is that although his illness may be grave and he approaches the end of his life, his physical strength and faculties remain no different from before; this is called the eighth mark of the noble steed of a Great Man.
There are also eight qualities of the noble steed of a Great Man.
What are the eight? The first is this:

if there is a bhikṣu who well maintains the prohibitive precepts and is fully endowed with dignified deportment, moving through the human world without committing any transgression; and even if he should inadvertently commit a minor offense, his mind gives rise to great fear.
One who upholds the precepts they have received is like a blind person protecting their remaining eye.
It should be known that such a person is like that first horse, which is born into the station of the noble vehicle.

As for the second type: if there is a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with wholesome qualities, he never causes disturbance or offense to his fellow practitioners of the holy life; they dwell together in peace and happiness, like water mixed with milk.
It should be known that such a person is like the second horse, born in a noble place.
As for the third, there is a bhikṣu who, when receiving food and drink, does not discriminate between the fine and the coarse, eating everything without remainder.
It should be known that such a person is like the third horse, born in a noble place.

As for the fourth: if there is a bhikṣu who, upon seeing various unwholesome dharmas that are impure, gives rise to a mind of weary aversion and completely distances himself from the unwholesomeness of the three karmas, censuring those evil dharmas as base, vulgar, and lowly.
It should be known that such a person is like the fourth horse, born in a noble place.

As for the fifth: if there is a bhikṣu who, having committed an offense, personally confesses his transgression before the Buddha, and likewise declares his own flaws in the presence of those practicing the holy life (brahmacarya).
It should be known that such a person is like the fifth horse, born in a noble place.

As for the sixth: if there is a bhikṣu who is fully endowed with the training of the precepts, and seeing fellow bhikṣus practicing the same holy life who have committed an offense against the precepts, he constantly reflects in his mind:
"I shall practice and train so as not to commit any transgression."
"You should know that such a person is like the sixth horse, born in a noble place.
As for the seventh, it is a bhikṣu who practices the Eightfold Noble Path and does not follow deviant ways."
It should be known that this person is like the seventh horse, who does not travel on wrong paths and is born in a noble place.

As for the eighth: if there is a bhikṣu whose illness is so grave as to border on death, he remains diligent and untiring, his will firm and unshakable, constantly desiring to advance in the pursuit of all sublime and wondrous dharmas, his mind free from weariness.

"You should know that such a person is like the eighth horse: he exerts his full strength until death and is reborn in an auspicious place; within the Buddha’s teaching and discipline, he is able to attain the truth.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
151 (One Hundred and Fifty-one). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Nādikā at the Koṭiṣaṇḍa Monastery.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākātyāyana:
"Stabilize your mind and do not let it be distracted; you should be like a well-bred horse that trains and governs its faculties, rather than like a wild horse whose senses run wild and scatter.
Just as a wild horse tied to a manger thinks only of water and grass and knows nothing else."
If one does not obtain food, the tethering ropes will be severed.

It is also like a person who is strongly bound by the fetter of desire; because of this greed and desire, they harbor much resentment and give rise to many thoughts of sensual craving. Because these thoughts of desire arise, various afflictions and harms are produced, and from this, all manner of evil thoughts emerge.
Because of these matters, one does not know the essential way out and ultimately cannot recognize the true nature and characteristics of desire.
Furthermore, if there is a person who is addicted to sleep, because they constantly sleep, many distracted thoughts arise, and various afflictions grow from them.
For this reason, they do not know the essential means of deliverance or the methods of antidote.

Furthermore, if there is a person who frequently gives rise to agitation and regret, because such a mind of agitation and regret constantly arises, they are unable to discern the characteristics of all phenomena with clarity.
One should know that restlessness and regret are causes of distraction; by reason of these, one does not understand the essential way out or the methods of antidote.
Furthermore, if there is a person who frequently gives rise to doubt, because of this doubting mind, they will remain hesitant and lack clarity regarding all phenomena.
For this reason, they do not know the essential means of deliverance or the methods of remediation.
It is like a well-trained horse tied to a stall; its mind thinks not at all of water or grass, nor does it break its tether and bridle.

For example, suppose there is a person whose mind is free from the fetters of desire and possesses only pure thoughts; because they do not become attached to these thoughts of desire, they likewise do not give rise to the hindrances of restlessness, regret, doubt, or sleep. By the power of the causes and conditions of this mind that does not produce the five hindrances, they come to know the methods for renunciation and their antidotes.

Monk, in this way, one does not rely on earth, water, fire, or wind; nor does one give rise to the dharma of meditation by relying on the four formless attainments. One does not rely on this world, nor on another world; nor does one rely on the sun, moon, or stars; nor on what is seen or heard; nor on consciousness that cognizes; nor on wisdom that knows; nor on the pursuit of the objects of mind and consciousness; nor does one rely on perception and cognition. Thus, one attains the meditation that is without any basis for reliance.

If there is a bhikṣu who, by not relying on such meditative methods of the various stages, attains profound concentration, then Śakra Devānām Indra, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and all the Brahmā assemblies will all join their palms in reverent respect and take refuge in that person.
"We do not know by what dharma or rule we should now attain meditative concentration.
At that time, the Venerable Bakula was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him with a fan, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does a bhikṣu cultivate the various dhyānas so that he does not rely on the four great elements or the four formless states, and even does not rely on the perceptions of vitarka and vicāra?
If it is thus, how do the bhikṣus attain such dhyāna?
Śakra Devānām-Indra and the great assembly joined their palms in reverent respect, honoring and praising those who have attained this samādhi, and spoke these words:
"This son of good family is the most eminent among men; upon what does he rely to cultivate these various dhyānas?"

The Buddha told Bakkula: "If there is a bhikṣu who deeply cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he contemplates that this great earth is entirely false and deceptive, and does not perceive at all the notion of a real earth. It is the same for the elements of water, fire, and wind, as well as the four formless realms; for this world and other worlds, the sun, moon, and stars; for what is known through consciousness, seen, or heard; for the investigation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); for the spheres of mind and mental objects; and even for those states beyond the reach of knowledge—it is likewise entirely false and deceptive, with no real dharma existing. They exist merely as provisional designations, arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions, possessing various names. Contemplating this emptiness and stillness, he perceives neither a dharma nor a non-dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“You now, Pāṭali, should understand thus:
Practice the method of seated meditation And contemplate that nothing exists.”
Kauśika, Lord of Devas, together with the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens,
the Great Brahmā King, and other world-ruling lords,
join their palms in reverent worship; they bow their heads to the Honored One among Men.
They all uttered these words:
"Homage to you, O virtuous man!
We do not know by what dharma you rely, [that you have attained such mastery]."
"And yet I have attained this profound meditative concentration, which others do not understand.
When he spoke these words, Mahākātyāyana was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The bhikṣu Bakula’s afflictions were forever extinguished; he would not undergo further rebirth, having exhausted all fetters of existence.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The unruly horse and the well-tamed horse; the noble vehicle, the three and four [types], the shadow of the whip, and the tamed mount;
those with faults, the eight kinds of evils, and Kātyāyana free from defilement—these ten matters are all fully concluded.
152 (152). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove.
Then Śreṇika Bimbisāra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of the term ‘upāsaka’?
We pray that the Tathāgata will expound it for us.”
The Buddha told Śreṇika Bimbisāra:
“A layperson in white robes who takes refuge in the Three Jewels is, for this reason, called an upāsaka; you are such a person.”
At that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is called the faith of an upāsaka?"
The Buddha told Śreṇika:

“To have deep faith in the Tathāgata, to abide securely within that faith, and never to be corrupted by the lack of faith of those śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, Brahmās, or humans—this is called the faith of an upāsaka.”
Then Śreṇika Bimbisāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is the Upāsaka precept?
The Buddha told Śreṇika Bimbisāra:
"Not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not deceiving, and not drinking alcohol—these are called the precepts of an upāsaka.
He asked again:
"What is the perfection of giving?"
The Buddha told Śreṇika Bimbisāra:

“The dharma of an upāsaka requires that he abandon stinginess and greed. All sentient beings are entirely shrouded by such greed and envy; for this reason, one should distance oneself from stinginess, greed, and envious intent, giving rise to a mind of relinquishment. To personally bestow gifts without weariness or fatigue is called the perfection of giving.”
He asked again:
"What is meant by being fully endowed with wisdom?
The Buddha told Śreṇika:

“A lay follower knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering as it truly is, knows the cessation of suffering as it truly is, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is. Knowing these Four Noble Truths with certainty and clarity is called being endowed with wisdom.”
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 153 (153) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove.
At that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra went with five hundred upāsakas to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

According to the meaning of the term *upāsaka* as explained by the Buddha, how can one who is a layperson in white robes, possessing the resolve of a man, who has taken refuge in the Triple Gem and declares himself an *upāsaka*, attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*?
"Up to the stage of Anāgāmin?
The Buddha told Śreṇika: "One eliminates the three fetters:
the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the net of doubt (*vicikitsā*)."

Having severed the three fetters, one becomes a *srotāpanna*, no longer receiving a body in the three miserable realms; having developed resolute faith in the unsurpassed path, one returns among humans and devas seven times at most before exhausting the limits of all suffering and entering *nirvāṇa*. This is called an upāsaka who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
He asked again:
"How does one attain the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"Having severed the three fetters and attenuated lust, anger, and delusion, one is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
He asked again:
"How does one attain the fruit of Anāgāmin?"
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
“If one can sever the three fetters and the five lower fetters, one becomes an Anāgāmin.
When Mahānāman and the five hundred upāsakas had heard this Dharma, their hearts were filled with joy, and they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is most rare!
That all householders have obtained such benefits; everyone should indeed become an upāsaka.”
When Mahānāma and the other upāsakas had spoken these words, they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
Having heard what the Buddha had taught, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
154 (154) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove.
Then Śreṇika Bimbisāra went to where the Buddha was, and having completed his respectful salutations, sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by an upāsaka possessing the resolve of a true man?
[The full explanation is as above.]
"Furthermore, how should one fulfill all practices?
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"Though a lay follower may be fully endowed with faith, if he is not yet fully endowed with the prohibitive precepts, this is called having faith but not being endowed with the precepts."
"One who desires to be endowed with faith and precepts should diligently apply skillful means to seek their fulfillment; such a person is called an upāsaka who is complete in faith and precepts.
The Buddha further addressed Mahānāman:

"Even though an upāsaka may possess faith and precepts, if his renunciation is incomplete, he should diligently cultivate skillful means for the sake of its fulfillment, so that it may become complete."
Then Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At this time, I am endowed with faith, precepts, and relinquishment; I possess these three factors.”
The Buddha told Mahānāman:

"Although one may possess these three things, if one does not frequently go to monasteries and vihāras, for this reason one is said to be incomplete; you should diligently apply skillful means and go frequently to stūpas and temples."
Then Mahānāman said to the upāsakas:
"I should now, being fully endowed with faith, precepts, and a mind of renunciation, go to the stūpas and monasteries."
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"If one can be fully endowed with faith, precepts, and a mind of renunciation, frequently visiting stupas and monasteries, and drawing near to the Saṃgha, this is called being fully endowed."
The Buddha told Mahānāman:
"Even if one is fully endowed with the four aforementioned matters, if one does not listen to the Dharma, it is called being incomplete.
Mahānāman said:
"I am able to listen to the Dharma.
The Buddha again addressed Mahānāman:
"Though one may be able to listen to the sūtras, if one does not receive and uphold them, it is still called being incomplete."
Although one may be able to receive and uphold [the teachings], if one does not understand their meaning, this is also called being incomplete.
Although one may understand the significance of the meaning, if one is unable to practice according to what has been taught, this is also called being incomplete.

If one can be fully endowed with faith, precepts, and a mind of renunciation; if one frequently visits stupas and monasteries to listen to the Dharma, upholds it, understands its underlying meaning, and practices according to the teaching—this is what is called the practice of fulfillment.

Although Mahānāman was fully endowed with faith, precepts, and a mind of renunciation, and frequently visited stupas and monasteries to attend upon the Saṃgha, he was still unable to listen to the Dharma with single-minded concentration; this, too, is called being incomplete in practice.
For this reason, one should skillfully and single-mindedly listen to the Dharma.
Although one may be able to listen to the Dharma, if one does not receive and uphold it, it is still called incomplete; therefore, one should receive and uphold the True Dharma.

Although one may be able to receive and uphold [the teachings], if one does not understand their meaning, this is also called being incomplete; therefore, one should understand the purport of their words.

Although one may understand the flavor of the meaning, if one further cannot practice according to what has been taught, this is also called being incomplete; therefore, one should practice according to what has been taught.

If one can be fully endowed with faith, the precepts, and a mind of renunciation, and frequently visit monasteries to listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion, receiving and upholding it without forgetting, and understanding its meaning and intent; and if, through faith, the precepts, and a mind of renunciation, one visits stupas and temples to hear and receive the sutras and teachings, receiving and upholding them without forgetting, and understanding their meaning and intent.
Furthermore, if one is unable to practice according to what has been taught, this too is called being incomplete.
Mahānāman! Because of their faith, upāsakas are able to uphold the precepts.
Because of maintaining the precepts, one is able to possess a mind of relinquishment.
Because of possessing a mind of relinquishment, one is able to go to the monastic quarters.
Because of going to the monastic quarters, one is able to listen to the Dharma with a concentrated mind.
Because one listens to the Dharma with single-minded concentration, one is able to receive and uphold it.
Because one is able to receive and uphold it, one understands its meaning and intent.
Having understood its meaning and intent, one is able to practice according to what has been taught.
"Because one is able to practice according to what has been taught, one exerts oneself in skillful means and is able to bring [the practice] to fulfillment.
At that time, Mahānāma again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How many factors must an upāsaka fulfill to benefit himself but not yet benefit others?
The Buddha told Mahānāma:
"By fulfilling eight factors, one can benefit oneself but not yet benefit others."
What are the eight?
An upāsaka may possess faith himself, yet be unable to instruct others;
he may maintain pure precepts himself, yet be unable to teach others to observe the prohibitions.
One practices equanimity oneself but cannot teach others to practice generosity;
one visits stupas and monasteries and associates with bhikṣus oneself but cannot teach others to visit stupas and monasteries and associate with bhikṣus.
One may be able to listen to the Dharma oneself, yet be unable to teach others to listen to the True Dharma;
one may be able to receive and uphold it oneself, yet be unable to teach others to receive and uphold it;
one may be able to understand its meaning oneself, yet be unable to teach others to understand its meaning.
One is able to practice according to the teaching oneself, but does not teach others to practice according to the teaching.
This is called being complete in the eight branches; it can only benefit oneself and cannot benefit others.
Then Mahānāman again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By possessing how many qualities can one benefit oneself and also benefit others?
The Buddha told him:
"If one can be fully endowed with these sixteen factors, such a person is able to benefit both self and others.
They give rise to faith within themselves and teach others so that they may attain it."
One personally undertakes and maintains [the precepts], and teaches others to undertake and maintain them.
One personally cultivates a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and likewise teaches others to practice a mind of equanimity.
One personally goes to monasteries and stūpas, and likewise teaches others to go to monasteries to draw near to the bhikṣus.
They themselves are able to listen to the Dharma and also teach others to listen to the True Dharma.
They themselves are able to receive and uphold it and also teach others to receive and uphold the Dharma.
They themselves understand its meaning and intent and also teach others to understand its significance and flavor.
To practice according to what one has taught, and likewise to instruct others to practice according to what has been taught—
if one can fulfill these sixteen factors, this is called benefiting oneself and benefiting others.

Such a person, whether among the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brāhmaṇas, the assembly of householders, or the assembly of śramaṇas—wherever they may go—is able to act as a great illumination for that assembly, just like the light of the sun that dispels all darkness; you should know that such a person is truly rare.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Śreṇika Vatsagotra prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 155 (155) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This city of Kapilavastu is prosperous, peaceful, and abundant with joy.
I have always dwelt within it, and I often reflect to myself:

"Should a mad elephant, a runaway chariot, a bolted horse, or a person running wildly come to strike me, at that moment I might forget the mind of mindfulness toward the Buddha, or perhaps forget the mind of mindfulness toward the Dharma and the Sangha."
Again, he thought to himself:
"If I were to lose the mind directed toward the Three Jewels, at the time of my death, where would I be reborn?
Into which realm of existence would I enter?"
"What kind of retribution will you receive?
The Buddha told him:
"At that time, do not give rise to fear; after your life ends, you shall be born in a good realm, not falling into the evil destinies, nor receiving an evil retribution."
For example, when a great tree first begins to grow, it always leans toward the east. If someone were to cut it down, in which direction would it fall?
One should know that this tree would necessarily fall toward the east.
"You are likewise; it is impossible that you, having cultivated goodness throughout the long night, would fall into an evil realm and undergo an evil retribution.
When Śreṇika Bimbisāra heard what the Buddha had said, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his dwelling.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 156 (156) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bhikṣu who is still on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), whose task is not yet accomplished, and who constantly desires to advance toward the fruit of arhatship and enter nirvāṇa—how many dharmas must this bhikṣu cultivate so that he exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*), attains a mind free of outflows, attains liberation of mind, attains liberation by wisdom, realizes the fruit in the present life, and acquires untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*), knowing with certainty for himself: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence"?
The Buddha told Mahānāma:

"If there is a bhikṣu who is still on the stage of training (śaikṣa) and has not yet attained the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), and whose mind constantly strives and seeks, desiring to attain nirvāṇa, he should always cultivate the six recollections."
Just as a person whose body is emaciated desires to eat fine food for their own pleasure, so too it is with the bhikṣus: they cultivate the six recollections for the sake of nirvāṇa.
What are the six?

First, mindfulness of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, the Bhagavān.
At that time, there will be no greed, hatred, or delusion, but only a pure and upright mind.
Because of this upright mind, one attains the Dharma and its meaning, draws near to the Buddha, and the heart gives rise to joy.
Because of joy, the body attains pliancy and bliss.
Because of physical bliss, the mind attains concentration.

Because of attaining concentration, one harbors no thoughts of enmity or hatred toward either enemies or one's own kinsmen; with a mind always equanimous, one dwells in the flow of the Dharma, enters the concentrated mind, cultivates the mind that recollects the Buddha, and proceeds toward Nirvana—this is called the recollection of the Buddha.
Second is the mindfulness of the Dharma.

What is called the Dharma refers to all the merits of the Tathāgata—the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the certain progression toward Nirvāṇa. One should observe this Dharma with a sincere heart; the wise know it for themselves, and the noble disciples should cultivate the mindfulness of the Dharma.
At that time, being free from greed, hatred, and delusion, there remains only a pure and upright mind.
Because of this upright mind, one attains the meaning and the Dharma; by drawing near to the Dharma, joy arises in the heart.
Because of this joy, the body attains pliancy and bliss.
Because of attaining pliancy and bliss, the mind achieves concentration.

Because of achieving concentration, the mind remains equanimous toward those who are hostile or hateful; free from both attachment and aversion, it dwells in the flow of the Dharma and enters a state of meditative absorption.
To cultivate the contemplation of the Dharma, tending toward Nirvana—this is called mindfulness of the Dharma.
Third is mindfulness of the Sangha.

As for the Sangha, they are the disciples of the Tathāgata who have attained the outflow-free Dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*) and are able to serve as a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for the world.
What are called the excellent fields of merit?

There are those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala-pratipannaka), those who have attained stream-entry, those who are candidates for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala-pratipannaka), those who have attained once-returning, those who are candidates for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala-pratipannaka), those who have attained non-returning, those who are candidates for arhatship (arhat-phala-pratipannaka), and those who have attained arhatship.

These are called the excellent field of merit that provides blessings; they possess precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—one should join one’s palms in reverence toward such persons.
By virtue of mindfulness of the Saṅgha, one attains the Dharma and its meaning, gains proximity to the Saṅgha, and gives rise to joy in the mind.
Because joy arises, one then attains happiness.
Because he has attained happiness, his mind attains concentration (*samādhi*).

Because he has attained concentration, toward those who are hostile or hateful, his mind is equanimous; it is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, possessing only a pure and upright mind that dwells in the flow of the Dharma and enters the state of concentrated mind.
To cultivate the contemplation of the Sangha and incline toward Nirvana is called mindfulness of the Sangha.
What is mindfulness of the precepts?

It refers to the indestructible precept, the unimpaired precept, the unmixed precept, the stainless precept, the fearless precept, the precept free from the theft of virtue, the pure precept, and the precept endowed with goodness. When one mindfully contemplates such various prohibitions and precepts, one immediately becomes free from greed, hatred, delusion, and false views.
Because one is free from all evils, one attains the Dharma and its meaning, attains the precepts through close adherence, and the mind gives rise to joy.
Because the mind is joyful, one then attains happiness.
Because the mind has attained happiness, that mind attains concentration (*samādhi*).

Because concentration is attained, toward those who are hostile or hateful, the mind becomes equanimous, pure, and upright; it abides in the flow of the Dharma and enters the state of a concentrated mind.
To cultivate the perception of mindfulness regarding precepts is called "mindfulness of precepts.
What is "mindfulness of giving"?

It is to reflect upon one's own acts of giving and the attainment of wholesome benefits: "While all the world is shrouded by stinginess and envy, I have now succeeded in being free from such stains of greed; abiding in a mind of equanimity, I harbor no parsimony toward any object, but hold it forth to practice generosity."
Once one has practiced giving, the mind should rejoice.
It is like a great sacrifice where one’s own wealth and possessions are divided and bestowed upon others.

If one can cultivate such a mind of generosity, in this very life one will attain the Dharma and its meaning, and achieve the gift of intimacy; free from greed, hatred, and delusion, possessing only a pure and upright mind, one should give rise to joy.
Because of joy, the body attains happiness.
Because the body is happy, the mind attains concentration.
Because the mind is concentrated, toward those who are hostile or hateful, the mind is free from partiality; it dwells in the flow of the Dharma and enters a state of meditative absorption.
To cultivate the perception of generosity is called mindfulness of generosity.
What is mindfulness of the devas?

It refers to the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Regarding these various devas, if they were born in those heavens by virtue of the power of faith and causal conditions, I too possess faith, precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom, and am likewise so.
"By this merit, those who are born in the heavens—I too possess such merit and shall likewise be born in that heaven.

Contemplating such a heaven, because of that recollection of the heavens, one becomes free from greed, hatred, and delusion; possessing only a pure and upright mind, one attains the Dharma and its meaning in this present life, gains proximity to the devas, and the heart gives rise to joy.
Because the mind is joyful, the body attains happiness.
Because it attains happiness, the mind achieves concentration.

Because the mind achieves concentration, regarding those who are hostile or hateful, the mind is free from fluctuation; it dwells in the flow of the Dharma and enters a state of meditative absorption.
To cultivate the perception of the devas is called "mindfulness of the devas. Mahānāma!

If there is a bhikṣu dwelling on the stage of training who has not yet accomplished his task, and who constantly desires to advance toward the fruit of arhatship and enter nirvāṇa, he should with a sincere mind cultivate these six recollections.

By being able to cultivate these six recollections, one exhausts all outflows (āsrava), attains liberation of mind, attains liberation by wisdom, and realizes the fruit of their attainment in the present life.
Having realized this, he uttered these words:
"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence."
When Mahānāma and the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(157) At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu for the summer retreat.
At that time, at the end of the summer retreat, a great number of bhikṣus were sewing robes for the Buddha in the lecture hall.
When the bhikṣus had finished sewing the robes, they reflected thus:
"We have now finished sewing the robes; we should follow the Buddha on his journey."

At that time, having heard that the bhikṣus had finished sewing their robes and were about to travel with the Buddha, Śreṇika Mānava went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At present, my body and mind are extremely heavy and dull; I am disoriented regarding the directions, and though I listen to the Dharma, my heart finds no joy in it. Why is this?
Upon hearing that the bhikṣus have finished sewing their robes and are about to travel with the Buddha, the thought immediately arose in me:
"When shall I ever again behold the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus who cultivate their minds?
The Buddha told him:

"Although I and the bhikṣus have gone elsewhere, if you constantly desire to see the Tathāgata and the bhikṣus, you should observe them with the Dharma-eye and a sincere heart, always practicing five things."
What are these five? They are:
because they possess faith, they are able to accord with the teaching; it is not those who lack faith who can accord with the teaching.
Because they uphold pure precepts, they are able to accord with the teaching; it is not those who violate the prohibitions who can accord with the teaching.
Because of extensive learning, one is able to accord with the teachings; it is not through meager learning that one can accord with the teachings.
It is not through stinginess that one is able to practice giving; it is through a mind of relinquishment that one is able to practice giving.
It is not through folly that one can cultivate wisdom; it is by means of the wise mind that one can discern the characteristics of phenomena.
Therefore, Mahānāman!

If you wish to see the Buddha and the bhikṣus, you should constantly practice these five things along with the method of the six recollections. If you do so, I and the bhikṣus will always be before you.
"What is called the Saṃgha is named 'harmony.
At that time, Mahānāma, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced, prostrated at his feet, and departed. (158) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one attains liberation by virtue of obtaining a concentrated mind.
If this is so, does one first attain concentration and subsequently attain liberation?
Does one first attain liberation and subsequently attain meditative concentration?
Or do concentration and liberation arise simultaneously?
That which has never been attained, never practiced, and has never arisen in the past or future, does not exist in the present either.
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer; when asked a second and a third time in the same manner, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not answer at all.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending to the Tathāgata’s side, fanning the Buddha with a fan.
Then Ānanda thought to himself:

“Now Śreṣṭhī Mahānāma has questioned the World-Honored One regarding this most profound meaning. However, the World-Honored One has only recently recovered from his ailment; his strength is still slight and he is not yet able to preach the Dharma. I should briefly explain a small portion of the Dharma for him, so that he may return.”
Then, having formed this thought, the Venerable Ānanda spoke to Śreṇika:
“That which the Tathāgata has spoken concerns the training precepts, and he has also spoken concerning those precepts of one beyond training.”
He speaks of the concentration of those in training, and also speaks of the concentration of those beyond training.
He speaks of the wisdom of those in training, and also speaks of the wisdom of those beyond training.
He speaks of the liberation of those in training, and also speaks of the liberation of those beyond training.
Then Mahānāma said to Ānanda:

"In what way does the Tathāgata speak of the training in morality and the morality beyond training; the training in concentration and the concentration beyond training; the training in wisdom and the wisdom beyond training; and the training in liberation and the liberation beyond training?"
Ānanda said:

“The noble assembly of the Tathāgata dwells in the precepts and upholds the Prātimokṣa; they are complete in dignified conduct and act according to what should be done. Even regarding minor transgressions, they give rise to great fear; they fully maintain the prohibitive precepts—this is called being complete in the observance of ethical discipline.”

Being weary of sensual desires, evil, and all unwholesome states, one attains the joy and happiness born of seclusion and enters the first dhyāna, continuing up to the fourth dhyāna; this is called dhyāna.

Knowing suffering as it truly is, knowing the origin of suffering as it truly is, knowing the cessation of suffering as it truly is, and knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is—through such knowledge and vision, one severs the five lower fetters: the view of a self, attachment to precepts and rituals, doubt, sensual desire, and ill will.

Having severed the five lower fetters, he attains rebirth by transformation and achieves nirvana in that very place; he is called an Anāgāmin, for he will never again return to this realm of desire. This is what is meant by training in the precepts, training in concentration, training in wisdom, and liberation.

Furthermore, at another time, having exhausted all taints (*āsrava*), he attained the state of being untainted; his mind was liberated and his wisdom was liberated. He realized the goal in this very life, attained the unborn, and knew for himself: "Birth and death are ended, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
At that time, one attains the precepts of no-more-learning, the concentration of no-more-learning, the wisdom of no-more-learning, and the liberation of no-more-learning.
Mahānāman! For this reason, the Buddha speaks of those in training and those beyond training.
When Mahānāma heard what had been said, he rejoiced, prostrated himself, and departed.
Not long after Mahānāma had left, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Do the bhikṣus of this city of Kapilavastu ever engage in discussions with the Śākyas regarding such profound and far-reaching meanings?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“These bhikṣus of Kapilavastu frequently engage in discussions on such profound meanings with the Śākyas.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The bhikṣus of Kapilavastu and the Śākyas have attained great and wholesome benefit, for they are able to understand such a noble and holy eye of wisdom.”
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 159 (159) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove at Kapilavastu.
Then the Śākya Lūhako went to Mahānāma and said to him:
"The Tathāgata speaks of the srotāpanna; how many kinds of indestructible faith does he possess?"
Mahānāma the Śākya replied:
“Regarding the person of srotāpanna spoken of by the Tathāgata, there are four limbs of indestructible faith. That is to say:
indestructible faith in the Buddha, indestructible faith in the Dharma, indestructible faith in the Saṅgha, and the attainment of indestructible faith in the precepts bestowed by the Noble Ones.”
The Śākya Lūhahasta said:
"You should not now say that the Tathāgata taught the four indestructible faiths. Why is this?"
“The Tathāgata speaks only of three unbreakable faiths, namely, the attainment of unbreakable faith toward the Triple Gem.
A second and a third time he spoke thus, and Mahānāma likewise replied:
“Do not say that there are three unbreakable faiths; rather, the Tathāgata has truly spoken of four unbreakable faiths.”

The two men disputed, each contending for their own view and unable to reach a resolution; they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and requested that he resolve their doubts.
At that time, Mahānāma addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
That Śākya named Karkaṭaka came to my place and spoke these words:"
“When asked, ‘How many kinds of indestructible faith does the Tathāgata teach? I replied:
‘The Tathāgata teaches four kinds of indestructible faith, namely: faith in the Triple Gem and faith in the precepts bestowed by the Noble Ones.’”
The Śākya Rūpa-hasta said:
"The Tathāgata has spoken only of the three indestructible faiths; why do you speak of four?
These are what are called the Three Jewels."
A second and a third time he spoke thus, and a second and a third time I replied:
"The Tathāgata speaks of four; he does not speak of three."
"What he has said, I cannot understand;
what I have said, he likewise does not understand.
At that time, the Śākya Raudrākṣa rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Even if the Buddha did not instruct me, and the Saṃgha did not instruct me, and neither the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, nor gods, Māras, or Brahmās—none of these people instructed me—I would still single-mindedly dedicate myself toward the Buddha, and likewise toward the Dharma and the Saṃgha.”
The Buddha said to Mahānāman:
"When the Śākya Lohitya spoke those words, how did you respond?
Mahānāman replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If it is thus, I have no further answer.
Apart from the Buddha-dharma, there is no other place of goodness.”
"Apart from the Buddha-dharma, there is no other place that is truly real;
there is no other place that is good, and no other place that is true.
The Buddha spoke again to Mahānāman:

“From this day forward, you should understand it thus: being fully endowed with four things is called ‘unwavering faith,’ namely, [faith] in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts cherished by the noble ones.”
Because the Śākya Karkaṭaka did not understand, he spoke these words; however, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, he immediately attained comprehension.
Then Mahānāman and the Śākya Karkaṭaka, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced, prostrated themselves, and departed.
160. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Grove in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
At that moment, the Śākyas of that country had gathered at their debating hall; once they were seated together, they engaged in various discussions among themselves and said to Mahānāman:
"There is no one before or after you; in your opinion, who do you consider to be the last?"

Regarding the Śākya named Karkaṭaka (Rough-Hand): the Tathāgata prophesied that he would attain the stage of Srotāpanna, undergo seven births and seven deaths among gods and humans, and reach the end of suffering.
Although that Śākya Karkaṭaka violated the prohibitions and drank fermented liquors, the Buddha still prophesied that he would attain the stage of Srotāpanna.
"If it is thus, what priority or sequence could there be?
He then spoke again to Mahānāman, saying:
"You should go to the place where the World-Honored One is and inquire about this matter."
Then Mahānāma the Śākya, following those words, immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At the assembly hall where the Śākyas of Kapilavastu gathered for debate, they engaged in such discussion among themselves, saying to me:
"Who is senior and who is junior?

At that time, the Śākya Karkaṭaka had just passed away; the Tathāgata prophesied that he had attained the stage of Srotāpanna and would undergo seven births and seven deaths among gods and humans before reaching the end of suffering.

If one were to predict that the Śākya Lohapāṇi—who has violated the precepts and drunk the intoxicating liquor of negligence—has attained the stage of srotāpanna, you should know that there would be no distinction between before and after.
The Buddha told him: "All call me 'Sugata.
When the World-Honored One speaks these words, he is also called Sugata.
Because he is called Sugata, the mind of a Sugata arises; the noble disciple gives rise to upright vision and thus addresses him as Sugata."

Furthermore, Mahānāma! A disciple of the Tathāgata single-mindedly takes refuge in the Buddha, and likewise takes refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha—the Three Jewels. Having attained swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, the wisdom of disenchantment, and the wisdom of the path, they do not fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, the animal realm, or other evil destinies. They attain the eight liberations and achieve bodily realization; being endowed with the eight liberations and dwelling in perfect ethical discipline, they exhaust all taints through the vision of wisdom. This is what is called an Arhat who has attained liberation through both parts.
Furthermore, Mahānāma!
The noble disciple, as described above, is a wisdom-liberated (prajñāvimukta) arhat who does not attain the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa).
Furthermore, Mahānāma!
He is single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha; the rest is as explained above. He is a body-witness of an Anāgāmin, who has accomplished the eight liberations but has not yet exhausted all outflows.
Furthermore, Mahānāman!
They take exclusive refuge in the Buddha; the rest is as explained above. They do not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, nor do they fall into the evil destinies.
They accord with the Tathāgata’s teaching and do not oppose it; this is called "one who has seen the truth" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Furthermore, Mahānāma!
A noble disciple takes refuge single-mindedly in the Buddha.
The rest is as explained above.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha is that which accords with liberation; this is called "liberation through faith" (*saddhāvimutta*).

Furthermore, Mahānāma, if one has faith in the words of the Buddha, delights in and practices them, and endures and takes pleasure in the five qualities—namely, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—this is called a noble disciple who does not fall into the three miserable realms; this is called the "steadfast dharma."

Furthermore, when a noble disciple accepts the Buddha’s words with faith, yet does so with limitations—tolerating and delighting in the five dharmas as described above—this is called a noble disciple who does not fall into the three miserable realms; this is called firm faith.
Mahānāma! It is impossible that the sāla grove could understand the meaning and flavor of my teaching.
Even if it were to understand the meaning, I would still declare that it has attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
For this reason, I did not declare that the Śākya Karkaṭaka had attained the stage of Srotāpanna. Why was this?

That Śākya Karkaṭaka did not violate any of the fundamental grave offenses (ānantarya), but rather violated the prohibitory precepts (pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada); however, at the time of his death, he felt remorse and reproached himself for what he had done.
Because he felt remorse and reproached himself, his precepts were restored in their entirety, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
If a person has committed a minor offense and restores their integrity through remorse and self-reproach, why was it not recorded that the Śākya Mṛgaśiras attained the stage of Srotāpanna?
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Mahānāma the Śākya rejoiced, prostrated, and departed.
What is the lay follower who has attained the fruit,
whose all conduct is self-effacing, and his dwelling place— eleventh and twelfth?
Vimukti and Śāla; Rūkṣahasta is the tenth.

it is the dwelling place of those devas.

"When birth and death have ceased, Nirvana is indeed bliss.
The deva further praised him with a verse:
"In the past, I have already seen A Brahmin attain Nirvana."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy.

Now that we have encountered great hardship, we pray that you become our refuge.

"May that Rāhula naturally release me.

A great radiance shines forth, pure and white, all clearly perceived.

"Do you not dwell in prison, nor even suffer confinement?

"Chains, fetters, bonds, and confinement— All these have been forever extinguished.

The deva again asked in verse:

And what are 'restraints'?"
"What is meant by 'being bound and confined'?
The Buddha answered again in verse:

A son is called a tether and a bridle; love is called a bond and confinement.
I have no mother’s cangue, nor do I have my wife’s shackles;
I am without a son’s tether and bridle, and furthermore, I am without the bonds and confinement of love.
The deva spoke again in verse:
"Excellent! You have escaped the cangue;
there are likewise no fetters."
"Excellent is being without fetters!
It is also excellent to be without bonds or confinement.
The deva then praised him further with a verse:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain *nirvāṇa*;

169 (169). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the village of Mahānāma in the Śākya country.
At that time, not long after the World-Honored One had shaved off his hair and beard, he rose early in the morning and sat with body upright and mind composed, covering his head with his robe.

"You feel not the slightest joy, sitting alone in the forest wilds;

I have no joy, nor do I delight in what is not agitated."
"O Devaputra, you should know that for this reason he is able to dwell alone.

"Why is it that you dwell alone in the forest and wilds without joy, and are not obscured or hindered by that lack of delight?

The deva then spoke in verse:

you are free from all afflictions and yet without worldly joy. Excellent is this freedom from joy!
