174 (174). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, making it brilliantly bright. He withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
"Leaving the household life is exceedingly difficult; it is most difficult and hard to perceive.
When fools become śramaṇas, they encounter many difficult matters.
Those who are fearful and indolent will never possess a joyful heart."
How can one practice the Dharma of the śramaṇa?
If one cannot restrain the mind, dissatisfaction arises repeatedly.
Desiring to attain mastery over one's thoughts, how can they be eliminated?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“A bhikṣu who covers over evil thoughts Is like a tortoise withdrawing its six limbs.
The bhikṣu has no dependence, Nor does he cause harm to others.”
"When the bhikṣu enters nirvāṇa, there is no longer any ground for censure.
The deva further praised him in verse:
"In the past, I have already seen a brāhmaṇa enter nirvāṇa."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy.
175 (175). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the place where the Buddha was during that night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, making it brilliantly bright. He withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
“Sleeping and reclining with frequent stretching, stretching frequently without finding joy,
irregularity in food and drink, and a narrow, inferior state of mind—
these five things come as veils and obstructions, preventing one from seeing the path of the noble.”
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"If a person is weary of sleep and reclining, yawns frequently and finds no joy,
their diet is unwholesome, and their mind is likewise base and inferior,"
"By diligently abandoning these five things, one will surely perceive the Noble Path later on.
The deva further praised him with a verse:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain Nirvana."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy.
176 (One Hundred and Seventy-Six) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a deva, whose radiance was twice his usual brilliance, came to the place where the Buddha was during the night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, illuminating it with a brilliant and great brightness. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
"How does the water of the pond dry up?
What flow returns again?
Where do the suffering and pleasure of the world completely vanish?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Eye, ear, nose, and tongue, Together with body and mind—
When name-and-form are entirely extinguished, The pond is thus dried up.”
"All fetters and karmic actions, as well as the suffering and pleasure of the world, are here exhausted without remainder; there shall be no returning.
The deva again praised him with a verse, saying:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain *nirvāṇa*;
having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he was able to cross over the love of the world.
When this deva had spoken this verse, he returned to his palace with joy.
177 (177). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice as bright as usual, came to the place where the Buddha was during the night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, making it brilliantly clear. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
“The Sage, the Hero of the World, is like an elephant of the Eṇeya breed;
eating little and disdaining flavors, he sits in silence within the forest.
Now I have a slight doubt, which I wish to ask of Gautama.”
From whom does suffering arise?
How is one liberated from suffering?
In what place is suffering exhausted?
"I pray that you will resolve my doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"In the world there are five desires, with the mind as the sixth manifestation."
Having severed the desire for delight and being far removed from all suffering—this is called the essential way out of suffering, and it is also called liberation from suffering;
this state is named the extinction and cessation. You should know this matter.
The deva further praised him with a verse:
“In the past, I have already seen A brāhmaṇa attain nirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, He is able to cross over worldly craving.”
At that time, having spoken these verses, the deva returned to his palace with joy.
178 (178) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a deva whose radiance was twice that of usual, who came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, making it brilliantly bright. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke in verse:
"With nothing to grasp as an object, And no place to rest the feet, In the midst of this profound torrent— Who could avoid being submerged?"
"Who is it that possesses diligent vigor, capable of crossing the torrential flood?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Purely upholding the prohibitive precepts, cultivating wisdom and meditative concentration,"
Observing mindfulness of the internal body, one who was difficult to deliver has attained deliverance.
Having become free from the fetters of desire and transcended the latent tendencies of the realm of form, one exhausts the existence of delight; thus one is able to tread upon the profound.
Yet he does not sink or drown, And is able to cross the torrential current.
The deva further praised him with a verse:
“In the past, I have already seen A brahmin attain nirvāṇa;”
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deity returned to his palace with joy.
179. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual and who shone with a brilliant light that pervaded the entire Jeta Grove, approached the place where the Buddha was. Having prostrated at his feet, he sat down to one side.
He asked: "Gautama!
Are you now able to know all that sentient beings are attached to and bound by, as well as those sentient beings who have attained liberation, and furthermore, is their liberation pure?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the deva, saying:
"I truly know all that binds and attaches, as well as liberation, complete liberation, and pure liberation."
The deva asked again:
"Gautama! How is it that you are able to know how all sentient beings who are bound and attached attain liberation, complete liberation, and pure liberation?"
The Buddha spoke again, saying:

"I have fully perceived all that exists; you, O deva, should know this. Now my mind has attained noble liberation. Because I have attained liberation, I am able to know the bondage and attachments of sentient beings. I also fully know their liberation, their complete liberation, and their pure liberation."
The deva immediately praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Gautama!
You know bondage and attachment, even unto the ability to know the attainment of pure liberation.
The deva further praised him with a verse, saying:
“In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain *nirvāṇa*;
having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.
When this deva had spoken this verse, he returned to his palace with joy.
180. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during that night. His majestic light shone forth, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove with a brilliant and vast brilliance. He withdrew to sit to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! Are you able to cross over the violent torrent?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied:
"It is truly so!
the deva said: "Gautama!
That one is able to cross over such a swift current—so deep and vast, with no foothold on either side and no place to rest in the middle—is truly most extraordinary.
The Buddha said,
"It is indeed so.
The deva asked again:
“Gautama! How is it that you are now able to cross this swift current, where there is nothing to grasp and no place to set foot?
The Buddha answered the deva:
"If I am indolent, I will surely sink;
if I sink, I will surely be swept away.
If I am diligent, I will certainly not sink."
If one does not sink, one will not be carried away by the current.
Within such a great torrent, where there is nothing to grasp and no place to set foot, I have nonetheless been able to cross over this great, swift flow.
The deva immediately praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“It is truly rare that a bhikṣu, amidst this swift current, is able to cross over without any support or grasping!
The deva further praised him in verse:
“In the past, I have already seen A brāhmaṇa attain nirvāṇa;”
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy.
Mouqiang and the celestial maidens, the four wheel-turning kings, Jixian with his topknot hair,
and Yijian; the Eneyan, the swift-flowing river,
and those unbound who attain liberation— may they all be able to cross over to salvation.
181 (181). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice his usual brilliance, approached the place where the Buddha was. The light from his body shone forth, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove with a brilliant and great splendor. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
“The world is constantly filled with alarm and fear, and sentient beings are perpetually afflicted by anxiety and distress.
Whether they have not yet obtained wealth and profit, or have already obtained them,
one who can remain free from joy and fear amidst both gain and loss— ”
"Such matters as these, I pray that you will explain to me.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"If there is one possessed of wisdom, who practices austerities and restrains all the sense faculties,"
Abandoning all worldly affairs— apart from such persons as these,
there is no way to transcend birth and death.
Constantly dwelling within birth and death, one is startled, terrified, and oppressed by fear.
Afflicted by the various afflictions such as sorrow, And constrained by the torments of suffering;
If one relinquishes all these, One can eliminate the aforementioned ailments.
Then, being free from birth and death, One escapes all evils such as grief and fear.
The deva further praised him with a verse:
“In the past, I have already seen a brahmin attain nirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he was able to cross over the world’s craving.”
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy. 182 (182).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a deity whose radiance was twice that of usual who, during the night, came to where the Buddha was. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, making it brilliantly bright. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke in verse:
"Who has attained the most excellent form?"
Who travels by means of harmony?
Where should one dwell? What practice should one cultivate?
Of what kind must one be to be able to make offerings to the devas?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Those who uphold the precepts and possess wisdom, Who are skillful at cultivating themselves,
And who practice dhyāna with mindfulness and heedfulness, Eliminate the four kinds of burning afflictions."
Through right Dharma and liberation of mind, one thus attains a sublime appearance;
obtaining what is beautiful and most excellent, one unites with this path of the vehicle.
Taking on a corresponding form, one dwells in that place, training in the wholesome Dharma.
"If there is such a person as this, he is called one who knows how to make offerings to the devas.
The deva further praised him in verse, saying:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin enter Nirvāṇa."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deity returned to his palace with joy.
183. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, approached the Buddha during the night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, making it brilliantly bright. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
The merchants of the kingdom of Rāṭha possessed immense wealth;
each was greedy for profit, seeking gain without ever being satisfied.
They fought and quarreled over their property, drifting along the current of the fetters of craving and desire.
"Who among such as these could abandon desire and love?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Having cast aside all worldly conditions, including wife, children, and domestic animals,"
Having removed desire, greed, and delusion from all that is cherished and loved,
one renounces desire and leaves the household life;
this can sever the fetters of desire and forever abandon all drifting, drowning, and strife.
At that time, the deva again praised him with a verse:
“In the past, I have already seen The Brahmin attain Nirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, He is able to cross over worldly craving.”
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva returned to his palace with joy.
184 (184). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there were five hundred wagons traveling together as a caravan through a wilderness of perilous difficulties, where there was neither water nor grass."
Five hundred bandits were pursuing his chariot, intending to plunder it.
At that time, there was a celestial deity dwelling in the wilderness who, knowing the bandits intended to commit robbery, thought to himself:
"I shall now go to where that chariot is; I will question him, and if he can answer, I shall provide protection."
"If there should be anything I do not understand, I shall set it aside.

Having reflected thus, he immediately approached the traveling carriage; his bodily radiance shone everywhere, so that all five hundred carriages were filled with great brilliance. He then addressed the merchant in verse:
"Who is it that, while awake, is called 'asleep'?"
"Who among those who sleep is called 'awakened'?
Who is able to understand and penetrate such a meaning? You should know that this is the time; you ought to answer me.

At that time, among the merchants, there was an upāsaka who had attained deep pure faith in the Triple Gem, having taken refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and having reached a state of certainty regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, free from all doubt.
Furthermore, he was free from doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Having already realized the truths, he attained the first fruit of the path.

Rising early in the morning, he sat upright with his body straight, binding his mindfulness before him, and recited the scriptures aloud, chanting verses from the *Dharmapada*, the *Pārāyaṇa*, and various other sūtras and gāthās.
That upāsaka replied with a verse, saying:
"I call the awakened one asleep; I call the sleeping one awakened.
I know this matter entirely and clearly; therefore, I now answer you with a verse."
At that time, a celestial deity asked in verse:
"Why do you now speak these words:
'I call the awakened one asleep, and I call the sleeping one awakened'?"
"How can you answer me in such a manner?
The upāsaka replied in verse:
"Having severed greed, hatred, and delusion, With all outflows extinguished, an Arhat."
They call that waking, while I call it sleeping;
they do not know suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path. To them who are thus asleep, I am called the awakened one—O Deva, you should know this now.
The celestial deity spoke again in verse, asking:
“Excellent! To be awake yet called ‘asleep’—you have skillfully answered my question.”
Having not seen you, my Dharma-brothers, for a long time, I am now filled with great joy to see you again.
Now that you and all your companions, for your sake, Have returned safely and in peace.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
185 (185) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, there was a residence of upāsakas in the city of Śūrpāraka. All those upāsakas gathered together in their hall and censured the faults of desire:
'Desire manifests its outward form like bare white bones exposed by the dew;'"
Furthermore, it is like a piece of meat, which various birds vie to pursue;
desire is like excrement and poison, both stinging and defiling;
it is also like a pit of fire, or like a person with scabies who, seeking relief from the itch by approaching the fire, only increases his affliction.
Furthermore, it is like holding a torch against the wind and running backward; if one does not let go, one will surely be burned.
It is also like a dream or an illusion, like something borrowed, like fruit on a tree, or like a spear or a halberd.
Desire is impure, filled with filth and evil.
It is like undigested food that causes foul-sounding belches and is loathsome;
though they gather together to engage in various discourses condemning the faults of desire, when they return home, each of them again gives rein to their own dissipation.
At that time, the deity presiding over the hall where the upāsakas had gathered thought to himself:

"These upāsakas have assembled in this hall to discourse on the faults of sensual desire; yet when they return home, their craving for desires increases all the more. They cannot be called pure, nor do they act in accordance with the Dharma."
"I shall now cause him various disturbances so that he may awaken.
Having formed this thought, at the time of the assembly of the upāsakas, the deity of that hall spoke these verses:
"The upāsakas gather for discussion, Proclaiming that desire is impermanent."
You yourselves have brought this upon yourselves, sinking into the flood of desire.
Like a deep mire where an old ox has fallen,
so do I now observe that the number of upāsakas is vast.
Though he is widely learned and upholds the precepts, he speaks only of the faults of desire,
saying that desire is impermanent; yet his words are merely empty,
for he truly lacks the resolve to abandon desire, remaining greedily attached to the forms of men and women.
"Attached to what is unrighteous, you should abandon it;
within the teachings of the Buddha, you should practice according to the Dharma.

When the deva had spoken this verse, all the upāsakas, having heard it, attained full understanding. They grew weary of desire, shaved off their hair and beards, and with faith left the household life for the homeless state to study the Path. Practicing with diligent effort, they cultivated morality, concentration, and wisdom, and all of them attained the fruit of arhatship.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
186 (186) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the elder Sudatta had some minor business and traveled from Śrāvastī to Rājagṛha. He went to the house of the elder Ghoṣila and saw that within the house they were not sleeping at all throughout the night; they were splitting wood, kindling fires, preparing various offerings, setting up high seats, and arranging couches and mats.
Having witnessed this, the elder Sudatta reflected:
"Is this householder preparing these offerings for a wedding feast or a joyful banquet?"
"Is it because he wishes to humble King Bimbisāra and his ministers?
He further reflected:

"If the king and his officials were invited to a wedding feast, this householder would not personally attend; yet here he is, busily occupied and performing manual labor himself, lighting fires and preparing food."
"There must be someone superior; I do not know who it is.
I shall now ask.
Having reflected thus, he immediately asked the elder about what he had been thinking.
Then the householder Ghoṣila replied to him, saying:
"I am not holding this assembly for the sake of a marriage celebration, nor have I invited King Bimbisāra and his ministers for this gathering."
"Tomorrow, I intend to invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, and for that reason I have prepared this offering.
When the elder Sudatta first heard the name "Buddha," the hair on his body stood on end; filled with wonder and joy, he asked:
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?"
Purṇa replied:
"One from the Śākya clan has left the household life, shaved off his hair and beard, and attained the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path; he is titled 'Buddha.'"
Sudatta asked again,
"What is meant by 'Saṃgha'?
The elder replied:
"If a son of the kṣatriya caste shaves off his hair and beard and follows the Buddha to leave the household life;
or those of the brāhmaṇa, gṛhapati, or śūdra castes who likewise, with faith, leave the home for the homeless life following the Buddha—these are called the Saṃgha."
"I have now invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha. Sudatta asked,
"Can the Tathāgata be seen today?"
Pūrṇa replied, "The Tathāgata is currently staying nearby in the Kalandaka Grove; wait a moment, and the Buddha will come in person to accept my offerings."

At that time, Sudatta’s heart leaped with joy as he longed to behold the World-Honored One; he fell into a brief sleep, and upon waking, though the sky was not yet light, he thought it was dawn. He rose early and hastened toward the city gate.
However, the gates of that city were always open during two periods: the first watch of the night and the last watch of the night.
When Sudatta arrived at the foot of the gate and saw it was open, he thought the day had already dawned; he immediately went outside the gate, intending to go to where the Buddha was.
First, because he had practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, a radiance came to illuminate his body.

Once he had reached the outskirts of the city, he saw a temple to a deity; he immediately circumambulated the temple and paid reverent homage. It then became dark once more, and he thought to himself:
"It is pitch black; perhaps some human or non-human being might harm me. I should return to the city."
At that time, the deva Śiva emitted a light that illuminated everything, so that even the Jetavana was filled with great radiance.
The deva then spoke to Sudatta, saying:
"You should proceed forward; it is not fitting for you to turn back."
At that time, a celestial deity spoke in verse:
"Even if one were to take a hundred horses, Filled to capacity with all manner of rare treasures,
Along with a hundred golden men, And offer them as a gift in alms,"
If one were to practice such successive acts of giving until they filled the entire Jambudvīpa,
and were to take that mass of merit as but a single portion—
this would not equal a single person who resolves their mind and proceeds toward the Buddha’s abode.
Raising one's foot to take a single step is but one part in sixteen.
Even if there were a full hundred mighty elephants from the Snowy Mountains,
their bodies adorned with gold and jewels, [they could not equal the merit of that step].
Its body is exceedingly beautiful and vast, its movement is extremely swift,
and it is twice as powerful in its wild vigor; though one were to fill it with various treasures and offer them in alms,
this would not equal going to the presence of the Buddha.
The merit of a single step is but one part in sixteen.
Even if there were a hundred jewel-like women from Kāmāhi,
their count complete, with countenances most upright and dignified—
Adorning the body with necklaces, wearing pure gold as head ornaments,
and placing jeweled beads upon the head— though one might give these away as alms,
the merit thereby obtained is not equal to that gained by going before the Buddha.
"Raising your foot to take even a single step is but one-sixteenth part [of the journey].
Therefore, I exhort you: do not turn back from here.
At that time, Sudatta asked him:
“Who are you? The deva replied, “I am your former acquaintance, the young brahmin Suvīra.

At the time of my death, I felt a heart full of joy in the presence of Śāriputra and Mahāmoggallāna; having passed away, I was reborn in the heavens as a son of Vaiśravaṇa, the Northern Heavenly King.”
"If even I, by merely giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward a disciple of the Tathāgata, obtain such merit, how much more so for the Buddha himself?
At that time, Sudatta further thought to himself:
"Now that this celestial deity praises him to such an extent, by this measure I know for certain that that person's merit must be most sublime."

At that time, the World-Honored One was walking back and forth in the open air. The elder Sudatta went to where the Buddha was; upon first seeing the World-Honored One, he did not know how to pay his respects and instead went straight forward and sat down.
At that time, that deva transformed himself into a brāhmaṇa, approached the Buddha’s dwelling, circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated with reverence, and then took his seat.
When Sudatta had seen this, he followed their example, prostrating in reverence and sitting down; he then inquired after them, saying:
"I wonder if your holy body is at ease and well?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"In all matters secure and at ease, The Brahmin has attained Nirvana;
Unstained by desires, He is liberated from all states of existence."
"With the mind severed from all desires, with the mind cleared of the disease of feverish affliction, that mind attains purity;
thus one sleeps in peace within tranquil extinction.
At that time, the World-Honored One led the elder Sudatta into the room, where he spread out a seat and sat down.
Then Sudatta, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side.

The Buddha preached the Dharma to him in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him with discourses on generosity, morality, and rebirth in heaven; he explained that sensual desires are impure and that the renunciation of them is bliss.

The Buddha, knowing that Sudatta’s mind was single-minded and upright, felt leaping joy. He preached the Four Noble Truths for him, and Sudatta perceived the Four Noble Truths while still seated upon his mat. Just as a fresh, clean cloth easily takes dye, so too was Sudatta’s easy realization; he saw the Dharma and realized the Dharma, severed eighty billion deep-seated fetters, and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
He immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My name is Sudatta. Because I provide for those who are poor and destitute, people call me ‘The Solitary Giver’ (Anāthapiṇḍada).”
The Buddha asked:
"Of what country are you?
From what lineage were you born?"
Sudatta addressed him, saying:
"I was born in the kingdom of Śrāvastī; I only pray that the World-Honored One will travel to that country, and I shall provide offerings for as long as I live."
The Buddha asked Sudatta,
"Does that country have monasteries?
Sudatta replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you need only go there; I shall construct it so that the bhikṣus may come and go.
At that time, the Tathāgata accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
At that time, Sudatta, having heard what the Buddha had said and accepted his invitation, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed with joy.
(187) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the elder Sudatta fell gravely ill.
When the World-Honored One heard that his illness was severe, he immediately dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and went to his house.
When the elder Sudatta saw the Buddha approaching from afar, he moved his body to rise; the Buddha said to the elder, "There is no need for you to rise.
At that time, the World-Honored One prepared a separate seat and sat down, and the Buddha addressed the elder:
"Is the suffering you are afflicted by bearable?
Has the medical treatment brought relief, and has it not increased?
The householder replied to the Buddha:
"The affliction I currently suffer is exceedingly difficult to endure; the pain I experience continues to increase, and this pressing agony is truly loathsome."

It is, for example, like a strong man who binds a weak person by the head with a rope, twisting, pulling, and jerking it, and pressing down upon the head; my suffering from headache is just like this.
It is as if a butcher, using a sharp blade, were to slit open a cow’s belly and stir its five internal organs; my suffering from abdominal pain is just like that.
It is as if two powerful wrestlers were to seize a weak and extremely ill person and roast them over a fire; my suffering from bodily fever and agonizing pain is just like that.
The Buddha told the householder:
"At this time, you should give rise to indestructible faith toward the Buddha; you should likewise do so toward the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts."
The householder replied,
“As the Buddha has taught regarding the four indestructible faiths, I too have fully attained them.
The Buddha said to the householder:

"Relying on the four kinds of indestructible faith, you should now cultivate the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). You should recollect the Buddha’s manifold virtues and remember the ten titles of the Buddha: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān. This is called the recollection of the Buddha."
What is the recollection of the Dharma?

It is the sublime and wondrous Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, which is equally auspicious and virtuous, providing benefit in the present and leading to realization; it frees one from all burning afflictions, is independent of time or season, and enables one to proceed toward the higher realms.
Now it is revealed, even unto the point where the wise know for themselves; this is called mindfulness of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*).
What is mindfulness of the Saṃgha (*saṃghānusmṛti*)?

One should constantly recollect the virtues of the Saṃgha: the noble Saṃgha of the Tathāgata, who has attained the fulfillment of the stages of practice, who dispenses medicine according to the illness, who is rightly and truly directed toward the Path, whose conduct follows the proper sequence without transgressing its limits, and who is able to follow the Buddha.

The dharmas they practice—namely, the fruit of stream-entry and the stage of being a candidate for stream-entry; the fruit of once-returning and the stage of being a candidate for once-returning; the fruit of non-returning and the stage of being a candidate for non-returning; and the fruit of arhatship and the stage of being a candidate for arhatship—these are called the Tathāgata’s community of śrāvakas.

Those who are fully endowed with the precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; those who have been invited by others; such as these members of the Saṅgha—one should pay them homage and join one's palms toward them. This is called mindfulness of the Saṅgha.
What is the recollection of the precepts?

It is to reflect upon one’s own practice of the fulfilled precepts: the pure precepts, the flawless precepts, the unimpaired precepts, the unpierced and leakless precepts, the pristine precepts, the stainless precepts, the precepts not sought for wealth or goods, the precepts cherished by the wise, and the precepts beyond reproach.
Next, one should reflect upon this; this is called mindfulness of precepts (*śīlānusmṛti*).
What is mindfulness of giving (*tyāgānusmṛti*)?
Regarding the gifts I have practiced, I have obtained wholesome benefit; I should abandon stinginess and greed, practice giving, remain unattached in mind, and be able to relinquish everything.
When giving, one bestows with one's own hands; the mind always delights in giving without weariness or fatigue, being fully endowed with a spirit of renunciation.
Whenever there are those who beg, one always sets aside a portion for them; this is called mindfulness of giving.
"What is the recollection of the devas?
One should constantly protect the mind and recollect the six heavens of the desire realm, and recollect the srotāpannas and sakṛdāgāmins who are born in those six heavens.
Sudatta addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The appearance of a World-Honored One in the world is difficult to encounter.

The Lord of Dharma resides therein; I now give rise to joy and bliss.

it is not through lineage or wealth that one can attain this state.
Śāriputra, endowed with wisdom, remained tranquil while upholding the precepts.
"Delighting in the seclusion of emptiness, it is most supreme and peerless.

"So it is. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the devaputra Susīma rejoiced and prostrated himself. He vanished from his seat and returned to his celestial palace.
At that time, before dawn, the World-Honored One entered the lecture hall, prepared his seat, and sat down. He addressed the bhikṣus:

"Just now, there was a certain deva whose radiance was twice that of usual who came to where I was. His brilliant light shone forth, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove until it was all clearly visible."

"That Sudatta, having been reborn in the heavens, came to my presence and spoke these verses.

"By subduing the mind of greed and envy, one attains rebirth in the Heavens Free from Heat.

"Purifying the body and guarding speech and mind, having reached the final existence—

Having well cultivated body, speech, and mind, they now abide in their final existence.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that deity rejoiced, prostrated, and departed.

190 (190). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I have a slight doubt and wish to inquire about it.
If you are one of great learning, I pray that you will deign to listen and examine my question.
The Buddha said to the Vatsiputriya:
"If you have any doubts, ask whatever you wish. Vatsagotra asked:
"Is the body one and the self another?"
The Buddha said,
"Matters such as these are not answered by me.
He asked again:
“Is the body different from the self?
The Buddha said,
“Regarding such a matter, I do not answer.”
The Vatsa replied again:
"Now I ask you: Is my body one?
You do not answer me."
"Is the body different from the self?
To such questions you likewise do not answer.
Since you cannot even provide answers to these, how can you declare that your disciples die here and are reborn there among gods or humans?
If you were to declare that one dies here and is born there, would it not be the case that the body remains here while "I" go to those five realms?
If this were so, then the body and "I" would be distinct from one another.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I say that where there is grasping, there is the prediction of rebirth;
if there is no grasping, then there is no rebirth."
"Furthermore, Vātsīputra, it is like that fire: if there is fuel, it burns;
if there is no fuel, the fire does not burn.
Vātsīputra said:
“Gautama! I also see fire burning without being grasped.
The Buddha told Vatsagotra:
"What fire do you see that burns without being grasped?
Vatsa replied again:
"It is like seeing a great fire that is exceedingly fierce; when a violent wind cuts off the flames, one sees it burning even apart from the fire."
The Buddha told Vatsa:
"In this same way, even this severed flame has appropriation. Vatsa said:
“Seeing the fire burning apart from the fuel, by what means is it grasped?
The Buddha said:
“When such a flame is extinguished, it burns because of the wind; because it is grasped by the wind, the flame is able to persist for a brief moment.”
"Due to the power of the wind, the flames can be seen to be severed," said Vatsagotra.
"Gautama! he continued.
Fire may be thus, but humans are not so.
Why is this? When the body dies here and the mind is born there, who is it that takes [the mind] during that interval?
The Buddha said:
"At that time, craving becomes grasping; through the causal condition of craving and grasping, sentient beings undergo birth.
All in the world delight in grasping; all are loved and delighted by grasping; all take grasping as their cause."
Sentient beings find joy in the grasping for views, and all sentient beings enter into such grasping.
Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, is without grasping, he has attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
The son of the cow said,
"I have much business to attend to now and wish to return to my dwelling.
The Buddha said:
“Brahmin! You should know that the time has come.
At that time, Vatsa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
191. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the brahmin Vatsa went to the place where the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was.
Having arrived there, he greeted the Venerable One and sat down to one side.
At that time, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha asked Maudgalyāyana:

"For what reason, when śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas come to question the Buddha regarding whether one dies here and is born there, or even as to whether one neither is born nor is not born, does he remain silent and not answer?"
As for other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, when they see someone come to pose difficult questions, they explain them as they please.
Yet in the past, when I questioned the śramaṇa Gautama regarding death here and rebirth there, he remained silent and gave no answer.
"Does one die here and not arise there? Does one die here and also arise there? Or does one neither arise there nor not arise there? To all these questions, he gave no answer.
Regarding such a matter, all other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas would surely answer;
for what reason, then, does the śramaṇa Gautama remain silent and not answer?
Maudgalyāyana replied:

"The other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not know that form arises from causes; they do not know the cessation of form, they do not know the gratification of form, they do not know the danger of form, and they do not know the escape from form."

Because they cannot understand such meanings, they become attached to form, thinking: "I produce that form," or "I do not produce that form," or "I both produce and do not produce that form," or "I neither produce nor do not produce that form. They thus become attached to form.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.

The Tathāgata knows truly and as it is that form arises from causes and form ceases from causes; he knows the gratification of form, he knows the danger of form, and he knows the escape from form. Because the Tathāgata knows them truly and as they are, when form arises, his mind has no grasping or attachment; even regarding form as neither arising nor not arising, he likewise has no grasping or attachment.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise thus.
This meaning is profoundly deep and immeasurable, without limit; it cannot be known through calculation, has no location, and is without coming or going—quiescent and signless.
At that time, the brahmin Vatsa, having heard what the Venerable Maudgalyāyana had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 192 (192) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the brahmin Vatsa went to where the Buddha was, and after having exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

For what reason, when other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas ask me anything, I always answer in accordance with the truth: "After death, I am born here"; "After death, I am not born there"; "After death, I am both born there and not born there"; "After death, I am neither born there nor not born there."
The Vatsa spoke again:
"Gautama! Why is it that you cannot answer such a difficult question in accordance with its meaning?"
The Buddha told him:

"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not know that form arises from causes; they do not know the cessation of form, they do not know the danger of form, they do not know the gratification of form, and they do not know the escape from form."

Because they do not understand that form arises from causes, and so on, up to not understanding the escape from form, they become attached to form in all these ways: "I die here and am born there," "I die here and am not born there," "I die here and am both born there and not born there," and "I die here and neither am born there nor am not born there. They grasp at all of these.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
He further addressed Ghoṭaka:
"The Tathāgata is not so; he knows the cause of form, he knows the cessation of form, he knows the gratification of form, he knows the danger of form, and he knows the escape from form."

Knowing it as it truly is, the Tathāgata knows, according to reality, the cause of form, the cessation of form, the danger in form, the gratification in form, and the escape from form; he knows form, and regarding "I shall die here and be born there," up to "neither being born nor not being born there," he is entirely unattached.
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
The Buddha told Vatsagotra:
"Therefore, this meaning is extremely profound and vast, immeasurable and boundless, beyond the reach of calculation."
He further addressed Ghoṭaka:
"For this reason, other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, failing to comprehend the underlying meaning, offer forceful answers according to whatever they are asked."

If one were to ask the Tathāgata whether my form is born there, not born there, both born and not born there, or neither born nor not born there, he would set it aside and not answer, as these propositions lack logical consistency.
"I have already been born there, up to and including 'neither born nor not born'—
I do not answer any of these. Vatsagotra said,
"How extraordinary!"
"Gautama!
You and your disciples are equal and without distinction in their meaning, their phrasing, their word-meanings, and the matters you have spoken.
Vatsa spoke again:

"At another time, I went to the place where the śramaṇa Maudgalyāyana was. At that time, I questioned Maudgalyāyana regarding these words and phrases, and he answered me with these very meanings, words, and phrases."
"Gautama!
What you have now proclaimed is no different from that; therefore, I now call it marvelous.
Such a teaching as this has never existed before, nor has it ever been spoken; its principles are consistent and it provides an excellent answer to this question."
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha departed with joy.
193 (193) At that time, the Venerable Sañjīva Kaccāyana was staying at the residence of Cunda in the city of Nādikā.
At that time, the brahmin Vatsa, on account of some business, went to that city.
Having arrived there and finished his affairs, he proceeded to where the venerable Saṃtigacātyāyana was; after exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side.
He addressed the Venerable One, saying:

The Venerable One replied:

The young man asked:

"For what reason is it that when others come to ask other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whether one dies here and is born there, or dies here and is not born there, or even neither born there nor not born there, they are all able to answer;

yet when the śramaṇa Gautama is asked this same question regarding whether form dies here and is born there, or even neither born there nor not born there, he sets it aside and does not answer because it lacks logical consistency?"
The Venerable One said:

What do you think?"

Whether it be causes or conditions, whether it be formations or their root, whether it be that from which formations arise, whether it be form or the formless, whether it be with perception or without perception—by means of these causes, these conditions, these formations, this root, and that from which these formations arise—if there is the remainderless cessation, the state of the exhaustion of perception, or such states as being without causes and conditions, without formations, and without characteristics, as well as the dharma of total extinction, how could the Tathāgata possibly say that one dies here and is born there, or even say that one is neither born there nor not born there?
The young man said: "Kātyāyana!

Such causes, such conditions, such formations, such roots, and such origins from which these formations arise—whether they be material or immaterial, with perception or without perception—all such dharmas reach a state of total extinction without remainder. When perception is extinguished and all these dharmas have ceased, there are no longer any causes or conditions; how then could the Tathāgata speak of them?"
Having heard this, the young man was filled with joy and asked the Venerable One:

The Venerable One replied:

The young man said,
"I now have business to attend to and wish to return to my dwelling.
The Venerable One said:
“You should know that this is the time.
