The translator's name has been lost; it is now appended to the Qin Records.
199. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Ujjaya who came to where the Buddha was. Having exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat down to one side.
He then asked the Buddha:
"Gautama! Is the entire world finite?"
"Or is it infinite?
The Buddha told Upatiṣya:
"Regarding such questions as these, I do not answer at all."
Udāyin said: "Gautama!
When I asked whether the world is finite or infinite, you gave no answer at all."
"If that is so, when you constantly preach the Dharma and explain difficult questions,
what do you answer?
The Buddha said, "Utpalaka!"
Having fully and thoroughly understood all phenomena, I distinguish the true path for my śrāvaka disciples, eliminating all suffering and bringing it to its ultimate end.
Udayin said: “Gautama!
You have thoroughly understood all phenomena; for the sake of your śrāvaka disciples, you preach the right path to eliminate all suffering and reach its ultimate end.”
"If this is so, does everyone practice the path you have attained, or do only some practice this path?
At that time, the Tathāgata remained silent and did not answer.
A second and a third time he asked the same question, yet the Tathāgata remained silent and did not provide any reply.
At that time, Ānanda was attending the Buddha, fanning him with a fan; having heard what Upatiṣya had inquired, he immediately said to him:
"What you have asked later is no different from what you asked before; for this reason, the World-Honored One remains silent and does not answer you."
I shall first provide you with a simile from one quarter.
It is like a frontier-guarded city, whose walls and foundations are solid and firm, and whose railings, windows, and lattices are all likewise secure.
The streets, lanes, alleys, government offices, and marketplaces were each demarcated by surrounding barriers and arranged so as not to interfere with one another;
yet within this city, there was but a single gate.

At that time, the gatekeeper was intelligent and wise, possessed of great power of mindfulness, and skilled at distinguishing between guests and long-term residents; he would allow those he recognized to enter and bar those he did not know.

At that time, those within the city who wished to go out did not know the way out; they looked all around in every direction but saw no other opening, and could only seek escape through this single gate.
Now, this wise gatekeeper, although he does not know all the various types of people within the city, knows that whoever is about to leave the city must all pass through this gate.
In this way, O Uḍra, it is with the Tathāgata as well: although he does not engage in exhaustive deliberation and discrimination, he knows that both entry and exit occur through this very gate.
So too does the Tathāgata know the limits of suffering in the past, the present, and the future; all are reached through this path, whereby suffering is brought to its end.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Udāyin departed with joy.
200 (Two Hundred). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa was on Vulture Peak Mountain. Many heterodox practitioners, non-Buddhists, and brahmins came to his dwelling, greeted the Venerable Pūrṇa, and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Venerable Pūrṇa, saying:
"We have all heard the Śramaṇa Gautama say that sentient beings are severed and will no longer undergo rebirth.
What is the meaning of this?"
The Venerable replied:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the Buddha never says that after beings have died, they do not die again nor are they reborn here or there; for the Buddha truly does not perceive the characteristic of a 'being'."
Why is this so? Because ordinary people harbor delusions and possess pride, they speak of the existence of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata has severed pride and praises its severance; therefore, he has no conception of sentient beings.
When the non-Buddhist practitioners heard the Venerable’s words, they felt neither joy nor resentment, and they immediately returned home.
Not long after they had departed, Pūraṇa went to the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
He reported in full to the World-Honored One what the various non-Buddhists had asked:
"These non-Buddhists all say:
'The World-Honored One teaches that sentient beings are annihilated and will not undergo rebirth.'"
"What does this mean? I then replied:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the Buddha never says that after sentient beings have died, they do not die again or are reborn here from there; for the Buddha truly does not perceive the notion of 'sentient beings'."
Why is this so? Because ordinary people harbor deluded thoughts and give rise to the notion of "sentient beings" due to their pride;
the Tathāgata has severed pride and praises the severing of pride, and for this reason, he does not give rise to the notion of sentient beings.
Pūraṇa spoke again:
"I have made such a statement for the sake of the non-Buddhists; will this not contradict the Dharma taught by the Buddha, leading to slander and the production of exaggerations or denigrations?"
Is it as taught by the World-Honored One, or is it otherwise?
Is it a teaching in accordance with the Dharma, or not in accordance with the Dharma?
Is it a teaching that resembles the Dharma, or one that does not resemble the Dharma?
"Will you not be censured by those who share the Buddha-dharma?
The Buddha told Purna: "What you have said is true;

it is not slanderous, neither adding nor subtracting. It is exactly as I have taught, equal and without distinction. This is a discourse in accordance with the Dharma, not a discourse contrary to the Dharma; there is no one who shares the Buddha-dharma who can censure you."
Why is this? From the very beginning, all things have been harmed by the conceit of "I am"; the afflictions of sentient beings all grow and flourish because of this conceit of "I am."

Delighting in the conceit of "I" and being ignorant of that conceit, because of this ignorance—just as one might circle around without knowing the starting point, or like tangled threads whose beginning cannot be discerned, or like a ball of hemp, or like a military host in disarray fleeing in confusion when defeated—sentient beings are thus agitated and unsettled; they rush hither and thither through this world and the next without ceasing, wandering through the cycle of birth and death, unable to escape.
He further addressed Pūrṇa:
"In this way, my pride—and that of all sentient beings—is inexhaustible, yet it is extinguished in signlessness; reaching its ultimate extinction, it is entirely dispersed and destroyed."

If one knows thus, then within the great assembly of the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of Māras, the world of Brahmās, and among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans, one will attain the ultimate benefit through the long night and achieve liberation and happiness.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
201 (Two Hundred and One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.

At that time, during the night, the Venerable Ānanda went to the Tāpoda River; he removed his robes, placed them on the bank, entered the river to bathe, put on a single bathing cloth, and immediately emerged from the water to wait for his body to dry.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Kūṭadanta who went to that river.
Venerable Ānanda heard the sound of his footsteps and the sound of his coughing, and the non-Buddhist likewise heard the Venerable’s voice.
The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?
Ānanda replied:
"I am a śramaṇa. "There are many śramaṇas; what kind of śramaṇa are you now?
Ānanda replied:
"I am a son of the Śākyas.
The non-Buddhist said, "I wish to pose a difficult question; if you have the leisure, please listen to my inquiry."
Ānanda replied, “Ask whatever you wish; once you have heard it, you shall understand.
The non-Buddhist asked:
"Will I die here and be born there?
Ānanda replied,
"The Tathāgata has not spoken on this."
He asked again:
"When I die here, will I not be born there? Will I both be born and not born there? Or will I neither be born nor not be born there?
Ānanda spoke again:
“Regarding such questions as these, the Buddha does not answer at all.
The outsider said:

“I have now questioned you concerning dying here and being born there, up to the point of neither being born nor not being born; yet you do not answer any of them. Do you perhaps not know such matters?”
Ānanda said, "I know and see such matters; it is not that I do not know or see them.
The non-Buddhist said:
"What do you know and see? Ānanda replied: "What I know and see is that I see those places and I see the conduct of sentient beings;

I even know and see from where they arise, and I know and see their fetters and karma, their movements and actions. I see the knots of affliction gathered like ink; the ignorant and foolish who lack learning are associated with the fetter of views, following toward the future and dwelling long in birth and death."
"What I know and see is of such a nature; how could it be said that I do not know or see?
The outsider Kokanada then asked him, "What is your name?"
Ānanda replied, “My name is Ānanda.
The outsider spoke again:
“Excellent, excellent!
Disciple of the Great Teacher, although we have now engaged in mutual discussion, I did not know that you were Ānanda. Had I known it was you, I would never have been able to oppose you.”
At that time, having heard what Ānanda had said, those non-Buddhist practitioners departed with joy. 202 (202) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Sudatta, desiring much to go to the Buddha to attend upon and make offerings to him, had this thought:
"If I go there now, it is still too early; the Tathāgata has not yet arisen from his meditative concentration. I should first go to where those followers of external paths reside."
He immediately went to that place; having arrived there, they exchanged greetings and sat down to one side.
The heterodox followers asked Sudatta:
"You may tell me: what views does that śramaṇa Gautama hold?"
Sudatta replied, "That which the Tathāgata has spoken exceeds what I am able to reach through my knowledge and vision; it lies beyond my capacity.
The non-Buddhist said:
"If you do not know what the Buddha perceives, perhaps you can at least know what the bhikṣus perceive?
Sudatta replied,
"As for such matters, I too do not know."
The non-Buddhist further said:
"If it is as you say, what exactly do you perceive?
If there is even a slight perception, I request to hear its explanation."
Sudatta spoke again:
"You should first state what you have seen, and then I shall speak of what I have seen myself.
At that time, the non-Buddhist said to Sudatta:
"What I perceive," he said, "is that the categories of sentient beings are permanent and real; all else is false speech.
Furthermore, another non-Buddhist said to Sudatta:
"What I perceive is that everything is impermanent; only this is real, and all else is false speech."
Furthermore, there were those who said:
"It is both eternal and non-eternal, neither eternal nor non-eternal; only this is true, and all else is false speech.
The world is finite, the world is infinite, it is both finite and infinite, and it is neither finite nor infinite."
The body is identical to life, and life is identical to the body; the body and life are distinct and separate.
Regarding the *ātman* of sentient beings: it dies here and is born there; it dies here and is not born there; or it both dies here and is born there, and also dies here and is not born there.
"In this way, householder, as I see it, when one dies here, one is neither born there nor not born there.
When the various non-Buddhists had each spoken of their own views, they said to Sudatta:
"Virtuous sir, you should speak now."
Sudatta replied, "As I see it, all sentient beings are entirely conditioned; they exist through the combination of various causes and conditions."
What is called "causes and conditions" is precisely karma.
If something exists through the provisional conjunction of causes and conditions, it is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; and that which is suffering is non-self.
For this reason, my mind has no attachment to any views.
You non-Buddhists say such things as:
"All phenomena are eternal; only this is true, and all else is false."

Such a reckoning is the very root of all suffering. Because those who are greedily attached to these various false views are conjoined with suffering, they are able to endure great suffering and undergo inexhaustible suffering within the cycle of birth and death—all of which arises from the reckoning that the world is eternal, up to and including the view that after death one neither is reborn there nor is not reborn there.
Such views as these are truly conditioned phenomena, produced by the convergence of causes and conditions through the accumulation of karma.
Inferring from this, one should know that they are impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; and that which is suffering is non-self.
Furthermore, another non-Buddhist said to Sudatta:
"Householder!

If sentient beings exist through the gathering of karma and the conjunction of causes and conditions, they are all impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; and that which is suffering is without self."
"If it is so, you too are now creating the root of all suffering and are conjoined with suffering; within the cycle of birth and death, you shall undergo endless misery.
Sudatta replied, "I have already stated that my mind has no attachment to any views; therefore, I likewise do not cling to such a view as this."
At that time, those non-Buddhists praised Sudatta, saying, "So it is, O Householder; you too should speak in this manner.

Then, amidst the assembly of non-Buddhists with divergent views, Sudatta let out a lion’s roar, causing the minds of all those non-Buddhists holding wrong views to be completely stilled. He then proceeded to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. He recounted to the Tathāgata the discussion he had held regarding his own insights with the non-Buddhists.
The Buddha then praised him, saying: "Excellent!
You should thus defeat the various non-Buddhists, causing them to fall into positions of defeat, and you should cause the discourse of the True Dharma to blaze forth."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
203 (Two Hundred and Three) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the brahmin Dīrghanakha went to where the Buddha was, sat to one side, and spoke these words:
"As for me now, I do not accept or tolerate any dharma whatsoever."
The Buddha said to the brahmin Dīrghanakha:
"Regarding all dharmas, you do not accept any of them; do you, however, accept this [view]?
Dīrghanakha replied:
“Such a view as this, I too cannot endure.
The Buddha said to the brahmin Dīrghanakha:
“If you cannot endure such a view, for what reason do you say:”
"I do not tolerate any phenomena whatsoever.
"Who has caused you to utter such words of intolerance?
The Buddha spoke again to the great clansman:
“If you know or see this, and you do not tolerate this view, you shall immediately sever this view and abandon it.
It is like a person who, having already vomited, does not subsequently take up other views; thus they do not grasp them, and they do not give rise to them.”
The brahmin Dīrghanakha further thought:

"As for what you have said—that I have already severed this view and abandoned this view—it is like a person who has vomited; regarding all views, there is no longer any sequence, nothing is grasped, and nothing arises."
The Buddha told Dīrghanakha:

"If it were so, there would be many sentient beings who share your view and likewise propound such arguments. Yet, among the various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of other paths, those who abandon this view and no longer accept any alternative view are called 'of little wisdom,' extremely meager in understanding, and are also termed 'foolish.'"

Brahmin, you should know that all sentient beings in the world rely upon three views: the first says, "I tolerate everything"; the second says, "I do not tolerate anything"; and the third says, "I tolerate a little and do not tolerate a little."

When a noble disciple observes and examines [the aggregates], they see that they can give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion; they are constantly bound by these three poisons and cannot remain far removed from them. These can produce affliction and harm, can produce fetters and latent tendencies, and prevent liberation. To take delight in sensual desires and to guard and cling to them—this is called patience (*kṣānti*).

If one does not exercise patience, one can give rise to greed, anger, and delusion; constantly entangled by these three poisons, one is unable to distance oneself from them or attain liberation. Delighting in sensual desires, one is perpetually bound by craving and grasping, guarding and clinging to them; this is called "lack of patience."
If one perceives even a slight degree of patience or a slight degree of impatience, it is likewise so.
Patience is as explained in the section on "Patience" above; impatience is as explained in the section on "Impatience" above.
If a noble disciple speaks of patience, they are thereby disputing with those two views.
If one says that there is no tolerance, one likewise disputes with those two views.
If one says that there is slight tolerance and slight intolerance, one also disputes with those two views.
Because one's own view contradicts that of others, one consequently gives rise to contentious debate.
If contentious debate arises, there will inevitably be mutual disparagement and harm.

Because such debate gives rise to disparagement and harm, and because one perceives these faults as being produced by various contentious debates, one then abandons that view and does not accept other views.
For this reason, one is able to sever these views and abandon them, just as a person spits out [something]; among all views, there is no sequence, no grasping, and no arising.
If a noble disciple speaks of patience or impatience, or of slight patience and slight impatience, there is likewise this fault.

In this way, O Brahmin, this form appears as composed of the four great elements; when a noble disciple sees this body as impermanent, and having seen its impermanence, is able to become free from desire.
Seeing the destruction of this body, one immediately abandons it.

If one sees that the body is impermanent, one becomes detached from desire for the body, detached from craving for the body, detached from the body as a dwelling place, and eliminates the fixed notion of the body.
"Brahmin, you should know that there are three kinds of feeling: painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is the cause of these three feelings?"
What is its cultivation?
By what cause does it arise?
From where does it emerge?
With contact as the cause, conditioned by contact, habitual tendencies arise; habitual tendencies are born from contact and produced by contact.
If contact ceases, then feeling ceases; one leaves behind the heat and attains coolness.

It is, for example, like the setting sun: when experiencing the limit of the body, one knows it is the limit of the body; when experiencing the limit of life, one knows it is the limit of life. One knows this according to reality, without error.
When a noble disciple experiences a pleasant feeling, he knows that the body will inevitably perish;
when he experiences a painful feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows that the body will inevitably perish.
It is the same for experiencing pleasant feeling, unpleasant feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, or even non-concordant feeling.
What is meant by "non-concordance with feeling"?
That which is called greed, hatred, and delusion do not coalesce with birth, aging, sickness, and death, nor with sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair—the accumulation of all forms of misery.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having been ordained for half a month, was attending upon the Tathāgata’s side, fanning the Buddha with a fan; at that moment, the Tathāgata preached for him the Dharma of severing desire.

At that time, Śāriputra, observing thus that all phenomena are impermanent, immediately became free from desire and attained realization; he cast aside all views, his outflows were exhausted through non-arising, and his mind attained liberation.
The brahmacārin Dīrghanakha attained the pure eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena, as previously described.
Having gained faith, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to go forth."
At that time, the Tathāgata granted him permission to go forth. Having gone forth, he practiced with diligent effort and attained the path of Arhatship.
204 (204) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on the bank of the Sūmagadhā Pond in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the brahmin Śarabha, amidst the great assembly, spoke these words:
"I know the teachings proclaimed by the son of the Śākyas; my knowledge and vision surpass those of the son of the Śākyas."
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus entered the city for alms and saw the brahmin Śarabha on the bank of that pond. Hearing what he was saying, they remarked:
"I know all the teachings of the Śākya son; what I know surpasses his."

When the bhikṣus had heard these words, they returned to the monastery, gathered their robes and bowls, washed their hands and feet, and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Today we entered the city to beg for food; having finished our meal, we were returning through it when we passed by the Sumāgadhā Pond. On the bank of that pond was a brahmin named Śarabha, who stood amidst a great assembly and proclaimed these words:”
"I know all the teachings of the Śākya son; what I know surpasses his.
Excellent, World-Honored One! I pray that you will go to the bank of that pond."
At that time, the Tathāgata silently granted his consent and, surrounded by the bhikṣus preceding and following him, proceeded to the Sūmāgadhā Pond.
At that time, Śarabha saw the Buddha approaching from afar; he immediately rose from his seat, prepared a high throne, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Please be seated here."
The Buddha immediately took his seat; having sat down, he addressed him, saying:
"Did you truly say these words:
'I know the Dharma and teachings of the Śākya son; what I know surpasses that'?"
“Did he speak thus?
At that time, the brahmin remained silent.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Why do you remain silent and not answer me?
If you understand it, speak according to your own intent;
if you do not understand it, I shall explain it to you in detail for you, so that you may be fully endowed with it."
If you can now explain this fully, I shall rejoice with you.
Brahmin, you should know that if there were anyone in the world who said,
"The Tathāgata is not an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha," [you would rightly refute them].
"If one speaks in such a manner, I would applaud them, saying 'Excellent! and then ask them:
'On what grounds do you say that the Tathāgata is not an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha?'"

These sentient beings, being undecided regarding the principle, were unable to provide a correct answer; instead, they spoke of other mundane matters, interspersing them with various miscellaneous words, acting with arrogance and self-importance, and giving rise to a mind of malice and harm.
Because you were unable to answer such a question, you remained silent, standing with shame and bowed head,
having lost your ready wit.
Śarabha, you are just like that now.
Furthermore, if there were someone who spoke thus:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is able to skillfully demonstrate that which is subject to transgression," I would likewise commend such a speaker as being well-spoken.
One should ask him:
"By what wisdom do you know such a matter?

He will be unable to answer and will instead speak of other worldly discourses, becoming confused therein; his words exhausted and his reasoning stumped, he will stand in silence with his head bowed in shame, having lost his eloquence—just as you are now, no different at all.
If, moreover, someone were to say:
"The disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama do not possess wholesome dedication of merit and do not fully maintain the precepts," I would also approve of that and ask him:
"By what means do you verify this matter?

He was unable to answer; instead, he spoke of other worldly matters, becoming confused therein. With his words exhausted and his reasoning defeated, he stood in silence with his head bowed in shame, having lost his eloquence—just as you have now.
At that time, Śarabha’s fellow practitioners said to Śarabha:
"Why do you now remain silent and not answer?
In the past, you were always saying in the midst of great assemblies and among many people:"
"What I know and see surpasses all that the Gautama teaches.
You should now question the śramaṇa Gautama; why else would he cause the śramaṇa Gautama to question you in return?
I shall press you to speak, and you shall say these words:
"If what you have said can be fully perfected, I will join you in your joy and celebrate it as most excellent;
if it is not yet complete, I shall analyze and explain it for you so that it may become complete."
When Śarabha had heard these words, he likewise remained silent and said nothing further.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having delivered this lion’s roar on the bank of Lake Sumāgadhā, rose from his seat and returned to the city of Rājagṛha.
Not long after the Buddha had departed, his fellow practitioners rebuked him in various ways, saying:
"Now you are like a hornless ox bellowing in a secluded place; you are just like that."
In a secluded place, you let out a lion’s roar;
yet before the śramaṇa Gautama, you remain silent and say nothing.
You are just like a young girl who wishes to produce a man’s voice but cannot do so, and instead produces only a woman’s voice—you are exactly like that.

Just as a female jackal may wish to let out a lion’s roar but cannot achieve it—though she utters a sound, it remains that of a jackal and can never become the voice of a lion—so too, one who wishes to emulate Gautama by letting out a lion’s roar cannot succeed.
After his fellow practitioners had thus rebuked Śarabha in various ways, they each dispersed in different directions.
205 (Two hundred and five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Cūḍapanthaka who lived on the bank of the Sūmāgadhā Lake. Among that assembly, he made this proclamation:
"If anyone can fully analyze and explain the meaning of the verses I have spoken, I shall become his disciple."

At that time, when the hour for the meal had arrived, the bhikṣus donned their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in succession. Having finished their almsround, they returned to their quarters. On the way, they passed by the bank of the Sumanāmukta Lake and heard those brahmins speaking these words. They immediately returned to the monastery, put away their robes and bowls, washed their hands and feet, and went to where the Buddha was. There they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
On the bank of the Mahāgovinda Lake, there is a brahmin named Cūḍapanthaka who spoke these words:"
"If there is anyone who can fully analyze and elucidate the meaning of the verses I have spoken, I shall become his disciple.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will go to that pond."
At that time, the Tathāgata silently granted his consent and, surrounded by the bhikṣus preceding and following him, proceeded to that pond.
Then, the brahmin Cūḍapanthaka saw the Buddha approaching from afar; he immediately rose from his seat, prepared a high throne, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama!..."
"You may take this seat.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata sat upon that seat and addressed him, saying:
"As you yourself have said:"
"Regarding the verses I have composed, if there were someone capable of fully analyzing and elucidating their meaning, I would become that person's disciple.
Is such a thing possible?
The brahmin replied:
"It is indeed so, Gautama!"
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Recite now for me the verses you have composed; I shall analyze and explain them for you."
At that time, the brahmin Puṇṇaka again spread out a high seat and sat upon it, reciting these verses himself:
"If this bhikṣu is a son of the Śākyas, he ought to live a pure life in accordance with the Dharma;
it is not fitting for him to cause harm to any living beings."
One should distance oneself from all unwholesome dharmas; maintain mental purity and guard the precepts one has received.
Thus disciplined, one follows along with meditative concentration and wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"If you practice in accordance with what has been thus proclaimed externally,
among all virtuous men, you shall be the most excellent."
A bhikṣu dwelling in seclusion, pure and self-disciplined,
does not harm or afflict sentient beings, remaining far removed from all evil.
One who is thus tamed accords with meditative concentration and wisdom.
With a gentle, kind, and supple mind, one commits no evil through body or speech.
One who can thus restrain the three types of action is also said to be in accord with meditative wisdom;
because such a person is a field of merit for the world, they go among the various households with their alms-bowl to beg.
"Examine the mind and cultivate the foundations of mindfulness; remain humble and dwell among the lowly;
eliminate desire and cast off craving; thus one attains fearlessness.
At that time, having heard this verse, the brahmin Cūḍapanthaka immediately thought to himself:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama truly knows my mind; I should now take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Having thought this, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant me permission to leave the household life."

The Buddha immediately granted his permission; he left the household life to pursue the Path, received full ordination, and became a śramaṇa. Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he severed all afflictions and attained arhatship.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
206 (Two hundred and six) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners of the kingdom of Magadha gathered together at the Sūmagadhā Pond and spoke thus among themselves:
"This is the truth of the brahmins; this is the truth of the brahmins."

At that time, while the Tathāgata was in his vihāra, he heard what was being said with his pure divine ear attained through meditative concentration; he immediately arose from samādhi and went to the banks of the Sumāgadhā Pond.
When the brahmins saw the Buddha approaching from afar, they all rose from their seats, prepared a seat for the Buddha,
and said to him, “Please be seated. The Buddha then took his seat and addressed them, saying:
“What discussion were you all engaged in when you gathered together?
The brahmins each addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama, please know this: today we gathered together and spoke as follows:”
"This is the truth of the brahmins; this is the truth of the brahmins.
The Buddha told him: "So it is!"
"So it is! When I formerly sought the Way and first attained Perfect Enlightenment, I had already realized and known this.
To state the essentials: all that exists in the world does not exceed the Three Truths; I shall now analyze them."
What are the three? They are as follows:
first, to refrain from killing all beings; this statement is true and not spoken falsely.
If this matter is true, one should apply oneself with diligent effort and constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; this is the first truth of a Brahmin.
Having known this, I have explained it extensively for others.
Furthermore, O Brahmin!
That all the accumulation of suffering is of the nature of arising and ceasing—such words are true and not false.

If this matter is indeed so, one should apply oneself with diligent effort; in the interim, one should constantly cultivate the mind, perceiving the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and should abide in this manner. This is called the second truth of the brāhmaṇa.
Because I have realized the characteristic of the arising and ceasing of this life, I have attained equal and perfect enlightenment, and I constantly teach such a Dharma to sentient beings.
Furthermore, O Brahmin!
The third truth is that, being free from "self" and "what belongs to self," it is truly without self.
If one is free from these three characteristics of phenomena, one will be able to distance oneself from all evils.
"If this matter is indeed so, you should apply yourselves with diligent effort to seek liberation from all evils; you should abide in this manner.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the many non-Buddhists heard what the Buddha had said and sat in silence.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"This foolish person is constantly obscured by various Māras; within this great assembly, there is not even a single person who can believe these words, conceive the aspiration for learning, or practice the holy life."
At that time, having formed this thought, the Tathāgata rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after the Buddha had left, the deity of the Sumāgadhā Pond spoke these verses:
"Just as one might seek traces by drawing upon water, Or seek a harvest by sowing seeds in salt-waste land,"
Like seeking to perfume foul odors with fragrant incense, Or seeking softness by pouring water upon waves,
Or blowing on an iron pestle to produce a melodious sound, Or seeking a mirage in the midst of midwinter—
So it is with those non-Buddhists: Though they hear the sublime Dharma, they do not believe or accept it.

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the deity of the pond, the brahmins vied with one another to follow after the Buddha, seeking to leave the household life; the Buddha immediately granted them permission.
Having gone forth, he practiced the path with diligence and attained the fruit of arhatship.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
207 (Two hundred and seven). At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was staying at the Gośīrṣa Garden in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
Then there was a brahmin named Cchanda who went to where Ānanda was; after exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and spoke these words:
“For what purpose have you gone forth to study the Path within the Dharma of that śramaṇa Gautama?”
Ānanda replied:
“I have now gone forth to study the Path within the Buddha’s Dharma for the purpose of severing evil and giving rise to goodness; it is for this reason.”
The brahmin spoke again:
"What evils must be severed?
Ānanda replied:
"I now wish to eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion.
The brahmin spoke again:
"Do you also know how to eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion?"
Ānanda replied:
“Only within the Buddha’s Dharma are there teachings that sever such greed, hatred, and delusion, and restrain both body and mind.”
The brahmin spoke again:
"What faults and afflictions do such greed, hatred, and delusion possess?
Do you prohibit them within your Dharma?"
Ānanda replied:
"The defilement of sensual craving can produce agitation and disturbance; in the present life, it increases unwholesome dharmas, and from it arise sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress;
in future lives as well, it is likewise so."
Attached to anger and attached to ignorance, one can destroy one's own mind and also destroy the minds of others; both self and others are afflicted, and in the present life, various evils increase;
in future lives as well, it is likewise, as various evils continue to increase.
Furthermore, if there are those who are stained by and attached to this sensual desire, it can cause sentient beings to become blind and devoid of the eye of wisdom.

With sensual desire as its condition, it causes wisdom to become feeble, diminishes all virtues, prevents one from proceeding toward Nirvana, obstructs the attainment of the three types of supernormal knowledge and the six superknowledges, and leads one away from the path to Bodhi.
As it is with greed and desire, so it is with hatred and delusion.
We have observed that these greed, hatred, and delusion possess such faults and afflictions; for this reason, we prohibit and sever greed, hatred, and delusion.
The brahmin asked again:
"Is there perhaps a path that, when cultivated, developed, and expanded, can sever greed, hatred, and delusion?
Ānanda replied:

"There is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right concentration, right mindfulness, and right intention; these can sever greed, hatred, and delusion, and lead toward Nirvana."
The brahmin spoke again:
"A path such as this is most excellent; by practicing, cultivating, and expanding it, one can sever greed, hatred, and delusion."
"Ānanda, you should know that my current affairs are extremely numerous; I now wish to return.
Ānanda replied, "You should know that this is the time."
Having heard what Ānanda had said, the brahmin departed with joy.
208 (Two Hundred and Eight) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the Tathāgata taught the Dharma to Śāriputra in various ways, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having done so, he remained silent.
At that time, seeing that the Buddha remained silent, Śāriputra rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and returned to his dwelling.
Before he had reached his residence, he encountered a brahmin on the road named Uḍraka, who asked Śāriputra, "From where have you come?"
Śāriputra said, “Brahmin,
you should know that today I went to the presence of the World-Honored One, listened to the Dharma,
and have now returned. Upatiṣya spoke again:
"Are you still not free from the teachings, like an infant who has not yet been weaned from milk?
Śāriputra replied, "I am never satiated in hearing the Dharma now; I am not like an infant."
"Why is this? Because as an infant grows larger, he must wean himself from his mother's milk.
Upatiṣya spoke again:
“I have long since departed from hearing the Dharma and receiving instruction.

Śāriputra said, “In your Dharma, although there is instruction, it possesses no benefit or profit; one walks upon a non-path and is not said to be ‘setting out on the vehicle. It does not lead to Bodhi, but is a ruinous teaching; there is not a single dharma therein that can be relied upon.”
Your teacher is not a Tathāgata, Arhat, or Samyaksaṃbuddha; you should now swiftly depart from that false teacher’s doctrine.

It is like a worn-out ox, whose nature is flighty and restless, who delights in butting and charging, and moreover has little milk; the calf it produces is very small in stature and repeatedly leaves its mother to wander at will and indulge in negligence. Your teacher’s unprincipled teaching is just like this: his nature is flighty and restless, and all his teachings lack any meaningful benefit.
All the disciples, being young and lacking wisdom, having distanced themselves from their teacher, became heedless according to their own whims, each saying:
"I have already departed from the Dharma of instruction."
Within the Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is meaningful instruction.

Possessing meaningful instruction, there is a virtuous vehicle for deliverance that leads toward bodhi; it cannot be destroyed by false views, and there are various wholesome dharmas upon which one may rely.

My World-Honored One is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; his disciples follow him without ever abandoning him, just like well-bred oxen whose nature is not fickle, who do not butt or resist, and who moreover yield much milk. As their calves grow larger in body day by day, they follow their mothers and never depart from them.
The brahmin Udāyin praised Śāriputra:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

You have gained a great benefit; the instructions you have received are supramundane dharmas that lead toward enlightenment. You possess a virtuous vehicle for departure, reaching unto nirvāṇa, which is indestructible and provides a firm reliance.
"Your Teacher, the World-Honored One, is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having spoken these words, they each returned to their respective dwellings.
209 (Two hundred and nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Ujjaya who went to where the Buddha was. Having finished his greetings, he sat to one side and spoke these words:
"Gautama, in the past, various non-Buddhist practitioners gathered together in that great lecture hall and engaged in various debates.
While the śramaṇa Gautama remained in seclusion, cultivating and restraining his mind, I also participated in those discussions with him, using my wisdom and eloquence to say:
'This is consistent; this is inconsistent.'"
"Just as an old ox is further deprived of its eyes, so too are we:
all our teachings are exceedingly base and vulgar, and we are blind, lacking the eye of wisdom."
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great wisdom; dwelling in seclusion and tranquility, he cultivates and restrains his mind. Gautama!
How do you now instruct your disciples?
The Buddha told him:
"In my Buddha-dharma, when boys and girls gather together, enjoying themselves in feasts and banquets, dancing and playing as they please, this is called 'correspondence' (saṃyoga)."

It is like a person over eighty years of age, with white hair and wrinkled face, whose teeth have fallen out; yet he still dances and sings, fashions wooden oxen and horses, plays the lute, the harp, the zither, and the flute, and also makes small chariots and plays the ball-game.
For an old man such as this to perform such an act is called "inappropriate.
Those who see him should consider whether this person is acting with wisdom or with folly.
The brahmin replied, “Such a person is called an infantile fool; he possesses no wisdom.
The Buddha told him:
“In my Buddha-dharma, there is harmony and accord, like the play of children.
O Brahmin, you should know that within the Dharma of the Noble Ones, it is like the play of children.”
Udāyin addressed the Buddha:
“How does a bhikṣu cultivate and accumulate wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha told him:

“The duty of a bhikṣu is to remain far removed from all evil and unwholesome states and to cultivate all wholesome dharmas; for the sake of taming that which is untamed, he should diligently practice and accumulate [these qualities].”
Those who have not attained concentration should diligently cultivate it for the sake of attaining concentration.
Those who are not liberated should diligently cultivate it for the sake of liberation.
That which has not yet been abandoned should be diligently cultivated and accumulated in order to abandon it;
that which has not yet been known should be diligently cultivated and accumulated in order to know it.
Regarding those things not yet cultivated, one should diligently cultivate and accumulate them for the sake of cultivation;
regarding those things not yet attained, one should diligently cultivate and accumulate them for the sake of attainment.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is it that is undisciplined, and for the sake of disciplining it, what should one diligently cultivate and accumulate?”
The Buddha said:
"The eye is untamed, and so on up to the mind which is untamed; in order to tame them, one should diligently cultivate and accumulate [the means].
The brahmin said:
"What is it that is not liberated which one should strive to liberate through diligent cultivation?
The Buddha said:
"The mind is not liberated; for the sake of its liberation, one should strive to cultivate it diligently."
The brahmin asked:
"What is the severing of evil that one should diligently cultivate and accumulate?
The Buddha said:
"Because one must sever desire, ignorance, and craving, one should diligently practice and cultivate [the path].
The brahmin asked:
"What is it that is not known, for the sake of which one should diligently practice and cultivate knowledge?"
The Buddha said:
"Because name-and-form has not yet been understood, one should diligently cultivate and collect [the means] in order to bring about that understanding.
The brahmin said:
“What is it that, being unpracticed, should be diligently cultivated and accumulated for the sake of cultivation?
The Buddha said:
“One who has not yet cultivated concentration and wisdom and has not attained the Eightfold Path should diligently cultivate and accumulate them.”
The brahmin said to the Buddha, “The conduct of a bhikṣu is truly profound; I have many affairs now and wish to return home.
The Buddha told him:
“You should know that this is the time.
The brahmin Uttara then rose from his seat and returned to his dwelling.
210 (210) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the kingdom named Śiṃśapā who went to where the Buddha was. Having finished his greetings, he sat to one side and spoke these words: “Gautama!
"As for what is called 'training' (śikṣā), why is it named 'training'?
The Buddha told him:
"Because one trains, it is called training."
The brahmin asked again:
"By what training is one called a 'learner' (śaikṣa)?
The Buddha said:
“Because one trains from time to time for the sake of higher virtue, it is called ‘training.
Because one trains from time to time for the sake of higher mind, it is called ‘training.’”
"Because one practices and trains from time to time for the sake of superior wisdom, it is called 'training'.
The brahmin spoke again: "Gautama!"

If there is an Arhat who has exhausted all taints, accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, gained mastery over the mind, is free from further afflictions, and has attained liberation through right knowledge—at such a time, what should he still train in?
The Buddha said:

"If there is an Arhat who has exhausted all afflictions, whose mind has attained liberation through right view, then at that time, greed, hatred, and delusion are all completely severed without remainder; this is called 'one beyond training' (aśaikṣa)."

If that Arhat has exhausted greed, hatred, and delusion, and no longer performs evil deeds of body, speech, or mind, having nothing further to seek or attain—for these reasons, he is called "One Beyond Training" (aśaikṣa).
At that time, the brahmin Śiṣuka, having heard what the Buddha had said, departed with joy. 211 (211) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the brahmin Śiṃśapā went to where the Buddha was staying; having finished his greetings, he sat to one side and spoke these words: “Gautama!
If there is a brahmin who speaks thus:
"Whatever karma one performs is entirely the result of past causes previously created; the various karmas performed in the present life can only increase those unwholesome causes of the past."
In the present age, if one does not create karma, one can destroy the bridge of birth and death; the four torrents will be forever severed, and one will no longer transmigrate.
Because karma is exhausted, suffering is also exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, the limit of suffering is reached.
"O Gautama! What do you say to this?
The Buddha told Śyāma:
"As you have said, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak thus:
'Whatever karma one creates is entirely due to the causes and conditions of past fundamental karma, even unto the ultimate limit of the end of suffering.'"
"If this is so, by what causes and conditions do various ailments such as wind and cold, and the increase or decrease of the four great elements, occur in the present life?"
"If it is thus, is it created by itself,
or is it created by another?
Śiṣpa addressed the Buddha:
"Regarding 'the deeds of another,'" the Buddha told Śiṣuka: "What,
then, are one's own deeds?"
They constantly pluck out their hair and beards; some stand with arms raised, never remaining on beds or seats;
others practice squatting as their regular occupation.
Some sit or lie upon thorns, or sit or lie by the rafters of a roof, or sit or lie in ashes and dust, or sit or lie upon ground smeared with cow dung.

Some stand on one leg, turning with the sun; during the months of midsummer, they scorch their bodies with the five heats. Some eat vegetables, some eat millet, some eat śāluka, some eat dregs, some eat oil-cakes, and some eat cow dung.
Some attend to the three sacrificial fires three times a day, while others, during the winter solstice, expose their bodies to the freezing ice.
Such are the immeasurable ascetic practices involving bodily suffering; these are called "that which one has done oneself."
What is called suffering arising from others?
Being used as another's hands or feet, or being struck and pelted with forceful staves, tiles, or stones—such sufferings as these are called suffering obtained from others.
All people in the world experience the increase or decrease of the four great elements, or give rise to such afflictions as wind and cold.

Since these and other such afflictions are matters currently perceived by all, how could those brahmins, if they hold such a view, claim that by this means one can reach the end of suffering? This would be nothing but their own fault.
Such faults as these are known to all people in the world; yet he speaks falsely of them himself, and for five reasons, he causes his own body and mind to undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
What are these five? They are namely:
sensual desire, ill will, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. These five factors can cause sentient beings to experience physical and mental suffering in the present life.
Furthermore, there are five causes and conditions by which, in the present life, one can always attain happiness of body and mind and not undergo suffering or affliction.
What are these five?
That which is called the ability to sever the mind of desire allows one to experience the joy of the Dharma within body and mind in the present life.

Why is this? Because the presence of desire, hatred, and restlessness leads sentient beings to undergo various sufferings and afflictions; if these can be severed, one will experience happiness and be free from anxiety and distress. Therefore, one should sever such desire, hatred, and restlessness.
If one eliminates them, being without fever or affliction, one shall attain liberation without waiting for a specific time and will certainly proceed toward Nirvana, Śiṃśapā!
This is called the Dharma attained in the present life.

Furthermore, there are dharmas attained through direct manifestation, namely: right view, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right intention, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
When this Dharma was being taught, the brahmin Śipha was distanced from dust and defilement, and he attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Having realized the Path, he immediately adjusted his robes, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion and pity, will grant me permission to leave the household life.
The Tathāgata immediately granted him permission to go forth. Having gone forth, he applied himself with diligent effort in a secluded and quiet place, and attained arhatship.
212 (Dvādaśottara-śatam). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the Ambavana grove at the village of Naḷakalāpa.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the village named Nāḷipāli who lived in that hamlet; he was advanced in years, being one hundred and twenty years old.
The people dwelling in that village all claimed that this man was a true arhat; they all showed him reverence and made offerings to him.
However, this brahmin had a close friend whose merit was exhausted and who passed away to be reborn in the heavens.
At that time, this deva thought to himself:
"If I were now to urge Nārāyaṇabala to go to the Buddha's presence, he would certainly not believe or accept it."
"I shall now instruct him; perhaps he will be able to believe me.
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where the old brahmin was staying, his majestic radiance blazing so intensely that it illuminated the entire place where the man resided.
Having arrived there, he spoke to the brahmin, saying:
"How is it that toward one who is truly an enemy, you falsely manifest the appearance of a friend?
And how is it that toward your own good kinsman and friend, you regard him as yourself?"
How is it called "severance"?
How is it "without feverish affliction"?
You should now recite this silently in your mind; you should not speak it aloud.
"If there be anyone capable of understanding such a meaning as this, you should go to them and seek to leave the household life to purely cultivate the holy life.
Having spoken these words, that deva immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
Thereupon, having heard these words, the brahmin Nāṭaputra went to where Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was and silently reflected in his mind on this challenge:
"How can one who is truly an enemy to oneself falsely manifest the appearance of a friend?"
How does one regard one's own virtuous friends as oneself?
What is meant by "severance"?
And what is meant by "freedom from feverish affliction"?
Yet Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was not even able to know what was in his mind, much less answer him.

He then went to Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra and posed the same question within his mind; he did likewise with Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, posing the mental challenge in the same way. Yet that Jñātiputra was not even able to know this thought, much less answer it.
At that time, the brahmin Nālipabala went to all six teachers, but none of them could understand such a difficult question. [He thought:
"If you cannot answer this, why should I now leave the household life to practice the Way within their teachings?"

"It would be better for me to return to lay life and enjoy the pleasures of the five senses; my household wealth is currently very abundant, so it would be more fitting to remain at home, practicing generosity and creating merit.
He then further thought:
"I shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is."
Having had this thought, he immediately went to where the Buddha was. On the way there, he again thought to himself:

"The śramaṇa Gautama left home at a young age, whereas the followers of the six teachers, such as Pūraṇa, are all elderly men of long-standing virtue; if they cannot even know [this], how much less can that śramaṇa Gautama?"
"Since he is young, has not long been a renunciant, and his days of study are still few, how could he possibly understand such a meaning?
While he was thinking this, he turned his carriage on the road and intended to return. Then he reflected further:
"In the past, I once heard such a teaching from an elderly, virtuous, and senior brahmin."
"One who has left the household life should not be treated with contempt, even if they are of tender years. Why is this?
Although they are young in age, they possess great supernormal powers and great wisdom."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to where the Buddha was.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, he paid his respects with reverence and sat to one side.
There, he silently reflected upon these four difficult questions in his mind:
"How is it that one who is truly an enemy to oneself falsely manifests the appearance of a friend?
How is it that one regards one's own virtuous friends as oneself?
And what is meant by 'severance'?"
"What is meant by 'being without feverish affliction'?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that brahmin, spoke these verses:
"Even if one is reviled in private, Or slandered in a hundred thousand ways,"
Praising one’s face-to-face, saying, “This is a good and noble person;
he truly can accomplish all matters,” yet being deceitful and insincere—
the wise should recognize this as an enemy feigning intimacy.
Speaking words of feigned intimacy, yet acting without benefit—
The wise should recognize this as an enemy disguised as a friend.
How can one treat a friend with love and respect as if they were one's own self?
One should not seek out the faults of friends;
friends share the same wishes, and one should always remember them without forgetting.
Such friends as these cannot be thwarted or destroyed by others.
One should always revere and mindfully remember them, holding them dear as one’s own body.
Why is it said that by severing [defilements],
one can attain supreme benefit and reach the state of ultimate peace?
One who is able to cultivate the supreme fruit, a man heading toward the right path—
by virtue of this principle, he abandons [defilements].
How does one attain freedom from fever?
Having attained the taste of tranquility and acquired great wisdom,
one then becomes free from fever and remains far removed from all evils;
entering into the flavor of joy in the Dharma, this is called being "free from fever."
At that time, having heard these verses, the brahmin immediately adjusted his robes and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to leave the household life."
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately granted him permission to go forth. Having gone forth, he practiced the path with diligence and attained arhatship.

214. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Āṭavikā. In the early morning, she put on her robes, took her bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Having finished eating and washed her bowl, she intended to go toward the Vanasaṃpanna Forest.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:

"The śramaṇa Gautama is currently at the Eyegain Grove in Śrāvastī. His disciple, the bhikṣuṇī Āṭavikā, has entered the city to beg for food; having finished eating and washed her bowl, she is now gathering up her sitting mat and intends to go to that grove. I shall create disturbances for her."
At that time, Pāpīyān transformed himself into a young brahmin and, by the side of the road, asked the woman in the wilderness,
"Where do you wish to go?
The bhikṣuṇī replied:
"I now wish to go to a secluded place.
At that time, having heard these words, the Māṇava spoke this verse:
"In all the worlds, there is no one who has attained liberation."
Go to a secluded and quiet place; what do you intend to do there?
You are currently in the prime of your youth; if you do not enjoy the five sensory pleasures now, once old age arrives all at once, do not later give rise to grief and regret.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī thought to herself: "Who is this?
They wish to disturb and trouble me; they are truly deceitful."
"Is this a human being, or is it a non-human?
Having formed this thought, he entered meditative concentration to investigate and knew that it was Pāpīyān who intended to come and disturb him; he then spoke these verses:
"There is liberation in the world; I have now realized it for myself.
Pāpīyān, you are foolish and base; you do not understand such a path.
Desire is like a sharp spear, and the latent thieves pursue one with drawn swords."
As for your statement regarding the enjoyment of the five desires: desire is suffering and is to be feared;
desire can give rise to grief and affliction; desire can give rise to longing remembrance;
desire can produce a hundred sufferings; desire is the root of all suffering.
"Having severed all craving, extinguished the darkness of ignorance,

"One who is dedicated to the practice of pure conduct is cleaner and more excellent than that water.
