"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain Nirvana."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva departed with joy.
247 (Two Hundred Forty-Seven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice as bright as usual, approached the Buddha during the night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, illuminating it with a brilliant brilliance. He withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
"What thing is foremost, the most excellent among all things?
How does it exist everywhere, attaining the highest state?
What single dharma possesses sovereignty over the world?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Among all worldly things, the four aggregates are called the most excellent.
Being skillful in each of those places, one attains supremacy in all."
"The four aggregates are called a single dharma; he exercises mastery over the world.
At that time, the deva again praised him in verse, saying:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain Nirvāṇa."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
Then, having spoken this verse, the deva departed with joy.
248. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, making it brilliantly bright. He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke these verses:
"What is the beginning of a verse?
How is it analyzed?
Upon what does a verse depend?"
“What constitutes the essence of a verse (gāthā)?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“A verse has desire as its beginning; / Syllables constitute the differentiation of the verse.”
"The verse relies upon names, taking literary composition as its essence.
At that time, the deva again praised him in verse:
"In the past, I have already seen the Parinirvāṇa of a Brahmin."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
When this deva had spoken this verse, he departed with joy.
249 (Two Hundred Forty-Nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night. His majestic light shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove, making it brilliantly bright. He withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
"How is a king's chariot known?
How is fire known?
How is a kingdom distinguished?"
"How is a woman known?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"One knows a king’s chariot by its banner; one knows there is fire by its smoke."
"The ruler knows the state; the husband distinguishes the woman.
At that time, this deva praised him with a verse:
"In the past, I have already seen / A Brahmin enter Nirvāṇa."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
Then, having spoken this verse, that deva departed with joy.
The various births in the world; what is the first of the unsurpassed and supreme verses on the non-path?
The tenth section, *Biecche* (Vibhaṅga), translated separately as the twelfth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The Saṃyukta Āgama Translated Separately, Volume Thirteen (in the Danben [Dunhuang manuscript], Volume Seven, from the sixth sheet onwards;
the translator’s name is lost and it is now appended to the Qin Records).
250 (250). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At the Jeta Grove,
there was at that time a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to establish a great assembly. Then,
the World-Honored One, surrounded by the great multitude, went to the residence of that great householder.
At that time, the Venerable Vakkula was on duty guarding the monastery in the course of his service to the Saṅgha.

During that period, many women came to the monastery; among them was one who was upright and possessed of beautiful features. When Vakkula saw this, his mind was corrupted by her beauty, and he conceived thoughts of desire.
He further reflected to himself:
"I have now lost a great benefit through my deluded thoughts, pursuing instead what is not beneficial; a human body is difficult to obtain, and the same is true for the end of life."
If one gives rise to such a thought, it is called unwholesome.
It would be better to sacrifice one's life than to harbor thoughts of desire.
At this moment, I cannot truly be called one who has left the household life.

Why is this? Because upon seeing a young, beautiful woman, one cannot restrain the mind and immediately gives rise to thoughts of desire; I shall now speak of the affliction of revulsion toward such things.
He then spoke in verse:
"I have now abandoned worldly entanglements And abide in the dharma of renunciation;
Yet pursued by ignorance and desire, I am about to lose my original wholesome mind."
Just as a cow eating another's seedlings, If its sweet taste is not restrained, The five desires are likewise; One craves them without shame or remorse.
If they are not checked and controlled, They will surely destroy the seedlings of the wholesome Dharma.
For example, suppose there were a son of the kṣatriya caste who had mastered all the arts and was skilled in archery,
such that he could match a full thousand men; yet even so,
this son of the kṣatriya would prevail over them in the power of combat.
The bhikṣu is endowed with mindfulness, like that son of a kṣatriya;
constantly maintaining the power of wisdom, he cuts off and extinguishes sensual thoughts.
Having eliminated sensual thoughts, he is joyful and eternally in a state of cessation.
I have personally heard before the Buddha that there are two kinds of true friends who lead one toward the path to Nirvana; this is what my heart delights in.
I practice with heedfulness, dwelling in the forest in tranquil seclusion.
I have thoroughly praised the mind; this is called establishing the True Dharma.
Later, one must inevitably face death; when the time comes for Nirvana, you should know that such an evil mind—how could it ever see me?
251 (251) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Vakkali gave rise to arrogance in his heart toward those bhikṣus who were virtuous, humble, compliant, and gentle; he soon recognized this himself and reproached himself:

"I have suffered a supreme loss and gained no benefit at all. A human body is difficult to obtain, and the opportunity for renunciation is rare; yet having obtained both, I failed to exercise vigilance. I treated renunciation lightly and disregarded the precepts I received. With my own intellectual cleverness, I held in contempt those bhikṣus who were humble, compliant, gentle, and virtuous. Now I shall speak of my revulsion for this arrogant mind."
Then he spoke in verse:
"You must completely abandon all pride; you should not be self-exalting.
Do not let pride cause you to retreat, lest regret reach you when it is too late."
All sentient beings are harmed by pride;
because of this harm, they fall into hell.
Therefore, I should not now rely on my talent and eloquence, nor give rise to a mind of arrogance.
One who stays far from arrogance, Is able to abandon all hindrances and obscurations;
With a pure mind and reverent devotion, They attain the three types of supernormal knowledge.
One who is thus humble Is called a bhikṣu possessed of mindfulness.
Kauṇḍinya and Śāriputra, Nāgapāla and Prahāṇa,
Arati and Kāma-saṃyojana, Nairyāṇika and Māna. (252) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Vakkula dwelt alone in a quiet and secluded place; he was skilled in self-cultivation, practiced with diligent perseverance, and never became negligent. Abiding in such a state, he attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā).
At that time, the Venerable Vakkali thought to himself:
"I am now dwelling alone in seclusion and have attained the three types of supernormal knowledge; I wish to praise what I have attained."
He then spoke in verse:
"In the past, like one intoxicated and wandering, I traveled through various cities and towns;
having encountered the Buddha while on my journey, I immediately received great benefit and merit."
Gautama, out of great compassion, Please preach the True Dharma for me.
Having heard the True Dharma, I have immediately attained pure faith.
Reflecting upon those who have gone forth, The Great Teacher of the World—
His guidance and transformation are universal, reaching all—men and women, the young and the old, those in their prime, and the aged and infirm.
The Buddha says he is our kinsman and friend;
he can show us the virtuous path and destination. Sentient beings are blind with ignorance.
I shall guide you and show you its gateway.
What is called the gateway?
It is the Four Noble Truths: suffering arises from causes.
Having gone forth from suffering, seeing the Eightfold Noble Path,
I pull out all sentient beings and lead them safely toward Nirvana.
Cultivating heedfulness in the empty and silent forest wilds, I abide in tranquility.
Having attained the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*), he has completed his work for the Buddha’s teaching. (253) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now wish to expound the Dharma of the four-line verse; listen attentively and listen attentively with a sincere mind, for I shall now speak."
What is meant by the meaning of the four lines?
"Well-spoken is the most supreme, as taught by the Sages and Holy Ones;
kind speech and not harsh speech—this is called the second."
Speaking truth and not falsehood—this is called the third.
Teaching the Dharma and not what is non-Dharma—this is called the fourth.
These are called the exposition of the four lines; such is the meaning of the four-line verse.
At that time, Vakkula was in the assembly and thought to himself:
"The Buddha has now expounded the Dharma in four lines; I now wish to praise one line with a single verse."
At that time, Vakkali rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I, Vakkali, now wish to say something; I only pray that you will grant me leave to speak.”
The Buddha told him,
"Speak as you wish. Thereupon, Vakkula spoke in verse:
Whatever one says that does not distress oneself, nor harms others, is called well-spoken speech.
One should always speak with loving words to gladden others, and never commit any faults or evils.
Whatever is spoken from the mouths of the Buddhas will surely lead to peace and the joy of Nirvana;
it can sever all suffering and is praised as the excellent teaching. True speech is nectar, most unsurpassed;
true speech and appropriate speech bring great benefit. Such a person of noble character is established in truthful discourse.
254 (254). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the world there is a skilled physician capable of treating four types of illness;
he should serve as the royal preceptor. What are these four?
First, he is well able to diagnose the illness."
Second, being able to know from where the illness arises;
third, once the illness has arisen, knowing well how to cure it;
fourth, ensuring that the cured illness does not arise again.
One who is able to do so is called a skilled physician of the world.

The Buddha likewise accomplishes these four kinds of dharmas; as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, he is the unsurpassed skilled physician who also extracts the four kinds of poisonous arrows from sentient beings.
"What are the four? They are:
this is suffering, this is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha to the bhikṣus.

"Birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress—these poisonous arrows are not something that worldly physicians can understand; nor do they know the causes and conditions of the suffering of birth, nor how to sever the suffering of birth, nor the causes and conditions of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress, nor how to eliminate them."

Only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—the unsurpassed, excellent physician—knows the causes and conditions of birth and how to sever suffering; he even knows old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, knowing their causes and conditions and how to eliminate them.
"Therefore, because the Tathāgata is well able to extract the four kinds of poisonous arrows, he is called the Unsurpassed Excellent Physician.
At that time, the Venerable Bakula was seated in that assembly and thought to himself:
"I shall now praise the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata regarding the metaphor of extracting the four poisonous arrows."
He immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, Who has compassion for all classes of living beings;
The most supreme and foremost Honored One, Able to pull out the poisonous arrow."
In the world there are four kinds of physicians who can cure four kinds of ailments:
namely, those who treat physical diseases, and those for infants, eyes, and poisoned arrows.
The Tathāgata’s treatment of eye ailments surpasses that of those worldly physicians.
With the surgical needle of wisdom, he cuts away the cataracts of ignorance.
The Tathāgata treats the ailments of the body far surpassing those of worldly physicians;
for what worldly physicians can treat is merely the four great elements.
The Tathāgata skillfully discerns the six elements and the eighteen elements;
by means of these dharmas, he can treat the grave illness of the body’s three poisons and cure the maladies of ignorance and folly— this is the most supreme and unsurpassed.
Therefore, I now pay homage to the Great Teacher Gautama.
There was a King of Physicians named Kāla, who bestowed many medicinal decoctions upon people;
furthermore, there was another brilliant physician named Bahula.
Jīvaka and Jīvaka’s son, and other such kings of physicians, were all able to cure various ailments.
Those treated by them would certainly recover; yet though they recovered, the illness would break out again.
Nor can one escape death.
That which can be treated and healed is the extraction of the poison to the end of suffering,
ultimately departing from birth and death, so that one shall never again undergo suffering.
Countless billions of nayutas, Asaṃkhyeya sentient beings,
The Buddha has treated so that they end their suffering, Never again to arise from ultimate cessation.
I now address the great assembly, All you worthy ones gathered here:
The ambrosia of the deathless medicine—everyone should take it with a sincere heart.
You all should receive this faith; it is the supreme healer of the eyes, a cure for the body that extracts the poisoned arrow. Among all physicians, none can equal it.
Therefore, with a sincere heart, one should take refuge in the Honored One, Gautama. (255) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the bhikṣu Nyagrodhakappa was dwelling in that foremost forest of wilderness. Within this wilderness, there was yet another grove.
At that time, the bhikṣu fell ill there. The Venerable Bakula attended to the sick bhikṣu Nyagrodhakappa, and because of that illness, Nyagrodhakappa immediately entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, after the Venerable Bakula had made offerings to his preceptor, the nun Gautamī Kāpā, he traveled by stages until he reached the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

Then, at the early hour of dawn, Vakkali dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms. Having finished his meal and washed his bowl, he gathered up his sitting mat and went to where the Buddha was. Arranging his robes and joining his palms toward the Buddha, he spoke in verse, asking:
"I now wish to ask the Buddha, Regarding immeasurable understanding and wisdom;
To sever my doubts in this very life, Within the city of Khaṇḍava."
The bhikṣu has entered nirvāṇa; from birth he possessed merit, guarding and restraining his body, speech, and mind, while also enjoying great renown.
Ni-ku-ta Kapphiṇa—this was the name the Buddha gave him.
The Buddha conferred upon this Brahmin such a name. (256) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the great senior *śrāvakas* each constructed leaf-huts and caves to the left and right of the Buddha and dwelt therein.

At that time, Kauṇḍinya, Bhadrika, Vakkula, Mahānāman, Yaśas, Nanda, Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja, the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākapphiṇa, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Nandaka, the Venerable Kambala, Yaśas, Śarabha, Gavāmpati, Punarvasu, Kubjita, Nikata, and Vīra—these and other such great *śrāvakas* each dwelt within their respective grass huts and caves.

On the fifteenth day of the month, during the poṣadha ceremony, the Tathāgata sat upon a seat spread before the assembly of monks. At that time, the Venerable Vakṣu was also present in the gathering; he rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Please listen to what I have to say."
The Buddha said,
"I now grant you leave to speak as you wish.
Thereupon, Vakkali spoke these verses:
“O great bhikṣus, you must utterly dry up sensual craving,
abandon all accumulations, and be courageous and fearless. Knowing the proper time,
the moderation, and the measure, do not greedily indulge in the five desires.”
Free from all defilements, possessing keen wisdom with a profound mind—
because of such qualities as these, one is called a Great Bhikṣu. (257) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Vakkula went to the hall of Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā and fell ill, becoming critically gravely ill.
At that time, Punika was attending to him while he was ill.
Then, the Venerable Vakkali said to Punika:
"You should go to where the Blessed One is; on my behalf, Vakkali, pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and inquire after his welfare, saying: [insert message here]."
"I hope you have little illness and little affliction, that your daily life is light and easy, and that you are free from all suffering?

At that time, Puṇṇa, having received the Venerable One’s instruction, went to where the Buddha was staying. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
The bhikṣu Vakkula was in the Viśākhā Hall, suffering from a severe illness with a rash. He spoke to me, saying:
"Go to the place of the World-Honored One, mention my name, prostrate at the Buddha's feet, and inquire after the World-Honored One’s health, asking:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and well in your daily life, and free from all suffering?'"
At that time, Pukkusāti again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Vakkali may, due to his severe illness, enter parinirvāṇa at any moment; I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to go there."
The Tathāgata accepted Puṇṇa’s words by remaining silent.
Thereupon, Puṇṇa returned to the Venerable Vakkali and said to him:
"Upādhyāya!..."
After I had offered my greetings, I further addressed the World-Honored One:
"Vajjiputra may have entered parinirvāṇa due to the exhaustion of his illness.
The World-Honored One silently accepted my words.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from his meditative concentration and went directly to the Vaiśākha Lecture Hall where Vakkali was staying.
Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, Vakkali exerted himself to rise; however, the Buddha said to him, "There is no need for you to rise."
At that time, the World-Honored One sat down after arranging a separate seat and addressed Vakkali:
"Is the pain in your body now bearable?
Are you able to eat and drink?"
Then Vakkhila addressed him, saying:

“This pain increases further and shows no sign of abating. My present affliction is like a strong man seizing a weak man by the hair, twisting, pulling, and crushing him; my headache is just like that.”
Furthermore, it is like a strong man who slaughters an ox, piercing its belly with a knife and cutting open its intestines and stomach; my suffering from abdominal pain is just like that.
Again, it is like a thin man who is forcibly seized by a powerful person and roasted over a fire until his body is scorched; my suffering from bodily pain is just like that.
"Today I wish to enter parinirvāṇa; at this final moment, I wish to praise the Buddha.
The Buddha told him:
"Speak as you please."
He then spoke these verses—though originally there were none:

"Like one intoxicated by wine," this four-line praise; "Nāgasena, the extraction of the poisoned arrow"; "Nyagrodha and Kapphiṇa enter parinirvāṇa"; "Praise for the Great Śrāvakas"; "Vakkula’s total extinction. 258 (258). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was traveling through Kosala and returned to Sāvatthī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

At that time, there was a young brahmin named Atimāna (Extremely Arrogant). His lineage, reaching back seven generations, had been of pure descent on both the paternal and maternal sides; they were profoundly learned and widely erudite. Having himself mastered the recitation and study [of the scriptures], he also taught others. Whatever he heard, he could retain it; he had already mastered the essence of the four Vedas:

the Sāṃkhyakārikā-śāstra, the Śikṣā-śāstra, the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra, the Nāṭya-śāstra, and the Vaidalaka-śāstra. He was skilled in understanding the meaning and intent of the Dharma-padas and was thoroughly proficient in all such various treatises.

His appearance was upright and his talents surpassed those of others, making him difficult to equal; furthermore, he was born into a noble clan and lived in wealth and honor. Relying on his own abilities, he gave rise to great arrogance and failed to show respect or obedience toward his parents, as well as toward his preceptors, ācāryas, elders, and relatives, neglecting to pay them due reverence.
At that time, the young brahmin Mānava, hearing that the Buddha had come from Kosala to Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, set out for the Buddha’s dwelling and thought to himself:
“When I arrive there, if the śramaṇa Gautama receives me with hospitality, I shall greet him;
if he does not inquire after me, I shall return in silence.”
At that time, having formed this thought, the Māṇava went to where the Buddha was.

At that moment, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma; although the extremely arrogant Māṇava approached him, the Tathāgata did not deign to look at him even slightly.
At that time, the young brahmin thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama does not take me into his heart at all.
He then desired to seek refuge.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, spoke these verses:
"Having come here for the sake of the Dharma, you wish to return before having attained it.
Why not cause yourself to obtain what accords with the purpose of your heart in coming?"
The Māṇava Atimāna thought to himself,
"The śramaṇa Gautama knows my thoughts.
He immediately conceived faith and desired to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha told the Māṇava:
“I have perceived your mind; there is no need for you to pay homage, for what you have done is already sufficient.
At that time, when the great assembly witnessed this event, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and all spoke thus:

“The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal powers; this extremely arrogant māṇava, who previously showed no respect even toward his own parents, preceptors, and teachers, now, upon seeing Gautama, is able to humble himself and behaves with sincere courtesy and obedience.”
At that time, the haughty Māṇava, seeing that the voices of the great assembly had momentarily ceased, sat to one side, straightened his body, composed his mind, and spoke in verse:
"In what place should one not give rise to arrogance?"
Furthermore, in what place should one give rise to humility?
Who is able to dispel all sufferings?
And who bestows benefit and happiness?
"Which offering is supreme, and which is praised by the wise and virtuous?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"To make offerings to one's parents with a pure, clear full moon,"
Reverently obey your elder brothers and kinsmen, your preceptors and ācāryas,
as well as other seniors; you should not be arrogant toward them,
but should instead practice humility and show them complete respect.
If one sees those who are afflicted by sorrow and distress, one should eliminate their various sufferings and bestow happiness upon them;
all such persons should be universally honored and supported.
If one has severed greed and hatred, and is likewise free from delusion—
The Arhat whose taints are exhausted has attained liberation through right knowledge.
Toward such a superior person, one should remove pride and not exalt oneself;
one ought to take refuge in them and pay homage with palms joined.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the essentials of all dharmas for the sake of Atimāna, up until [the attainment of] no further existence.
The remainder is as explained in the Pāramīya Sūtra.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
259 (Two Hundred Fifty-nine) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was traveling through Kośala and arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Brahmin Uggaṭaśiri was preparing for a great sacrifice. Seven hundred bull-kings were tied to posts, along with cows, calves, rams, and ewes; indeed, such various kinds of livestock, beyond counting, were tethered everywhere within the sacrificial grounds, where various delicacies and diverse foods and drinks had been prepared.
At that time, the brahmins from other countries, having heard of the sacrifice being prepared there, all came and gathered like clouds.
Then, the brahmin Ujjheṭi Śāri, hearing that the Buddha had come from Kosala to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, wished to go to the Buddha’s dwelling and thought to himself:
“I am now preparing a sacrifice; I shall ask Gautama whether the preparations for this assembly are not too few.”

At that time, the brahmin mounted a carriage adorned with feathered ornaments; his garments, both upper and lower, were pure white. Carrying a three-pronged golden fork and holding a golden water-vessel filled with pure water, he was surrounded on all sides by a multitude of *maṇava* students, while various other brahmins from other countries also followed as attendants. Having approached the Buddha’s dwelling and completed his greetings, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha in detail, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
Now, as I have established this great sacrifice, seven hundred bull-kings and various other animals have been bound; even the brāhmaṇas from other lands have all come together like clouds.
Having completed the preparations, he wished to perform a great sacrifice.
He said, "I pray that the Buddha will instruct me so that it may be perfect and excellent, without even the slightest deficiency.
The Buddha said:
“Brahmin! As you serve as the master of sacrifice, seeking merit through great giving, you have also incurred great demerit; to erect these three kinds of blades is called unwholesome.”
One who creates the causes of suffering will also receive the retribution of suffering; even if one obtains the benefits of suffering, the experience of that retribution is likewise suffering.
What are called the three kinds of swords?
They are the swords of mind, speech, and body.
What is meant by the "sword of the mind"?
If, when you perform a sacrifice, your mental karma is unwholesome and you slaughter various animals for a great ritual, this is called "planting the sword of the mind."
What is the sword of the mouth?
When you wish to perform a sacrifice, you say these words:
"Tomorrow I shall kill this many various living beings."
This is called "planting a sword in the mouth.
What is meant by "a sword for the body"?
When you perform sacrifices, if you lead the king of oxen and various other animals with your own hands while receiving the recitation of blessings, this is called "planting a sword in the body."
The Buddha said:

"Furthermore, there are three kinds of fires that are most supreme and most wonderful; you should be cautious regarding them and treat them with reverence, for they are not the fires you serve—the fires of false views."
What are these three?
The first is named the fire of reverence;
the second is named the fire of both suffering and pleasure.
The third is the fire of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
What is called the fire of reverence?
One should make offerings to, honor, revere, and protect one’s parents.

Why is this? Parents seek children by praying to the deities, and only then do they obtain them. The body is formed through the union of the father’s red element and the mother’s white element; they then give birth to and nurture it. For these reasons, it is called the fire of reverence.
Such a fire should be properly honored, providing happiness to all and ensuring they suffer no want.
What is meant by the "fire of shared suffering and pleasure"?

If a son of noble family exerts diligent effort to accumulate wealth, he should provide for his wife and children, as well as his kinsmen, servants, laborers, friends, ministers, and all his relatives; he should supply them with their necessities and grant them benefit and joy. Since such people share both his suffering and his pleasure, this is called the fire of shared suffering and pleasure.
What is called the fire of the field of merit?

If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are able to sever craving and are liberated from craving; are able to sever ill-will and are liberated from ill-will; and are able to sever delusion and are liberated from delusion—such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are called the fire of the field of merit.
Those who ascend to the various heavens and are able to summon pleasant retributions—this is called the fire of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Therefore, sons of noble family, you should with a sincere heart make offerings and show them reverence, so that they may attain happiness.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of fire that must necessarily be extinguished. What are these three fires?
They are the fires of greed, delusion, and hatred. Unlike worldly fire, which sometimes must be ignited and sometimes must be extinguished, these fires are always to be extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The field of merit endowed with reverence— these three fires should be worshipped.
If one makes offerings with a diligent mind, one shall obtain the three kinds of happiness."
What are the three kinds of happiness?
They are the fruits of the three practices: generosity, ethical discipline, and the cultivation of meditative concentration—namely, the happiness of humans, devas, and nirvāṇa.
If a person thoroughly understands the methods for all of these, [they shall attain them].
At the time of performing sacrifices, one who can support their kin and provide for those worthy of offerings— by being able to sustain those who deserve sustenance—
will ultimately and certainly attain a state forever free from calamity and affliction.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Uggaṭaśiri spoke to the young brahmin Udaka:

"You should go to that sacrificial ground and release all those animals previously bound and kept for sacrifice; let them follow wherever they find water and grass for the rest of their lives, and do not restrain them."
The young brahmin Ghoṭamukha replied,
"I am able to do as my preceptor has instructed.
He then went to the sacrificial ground and proclaimed to the people:
"I have received the instructions of Ukkatthasela, by which all animals are to be released and allowed to go wherever they please.

Not long after the young brahmin Udāyin had departed for the sacrificial ground, the Tathāgata immediately taught the essential Dharma to the brahmin Ukkatthasela according to the way of the Buddhas, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him.
At that time, the brahmin immediately received the prohibitive precepts and even attained the vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana*).
The remainder is as described in the *Tuḷādhāra* chapter.
Then, the brahmin Uggaṭasiri adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that tomorrow you will go with the great assembly to the sacrificial ground and accept my offerings.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When the brahmin heard what the Buddha had said and saw that his invitation had been accepted, he departed with joy.
Upon reaching the sacrificial ground, the brahmin prepared various kinds of delicacies throughout the entire night, even arranging seats and providing pure water.
On the following morning, he went to where the Buddha was and said to him,

"The time has come. At that time, the Tathāgata, together with the great assembly, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded to the sacrificial ground, where he spread out a seat before the community of monks and sat down.

At that time, the brahmin, seeing the Buddha and the great assembly seated in silent composure, personally offered pure water and prepared various kinds of delicacies and food; when the meal was finished, he withdrew the bowls.
Then the brahmin spread out a seat before the World-Honored One and sat down, wishing with joy to hear the Dharma.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately offered this blessing:
"Among all great sacrifices, the sacrifice to the fire is supreme."
Among the books of the Brahmins, the Sāvitrī is supreme.
Among all lands, the king of men is supreme.
Among the hundreds of rivers and various streams, the waters of the ocean are supreme.
Among the constellations arrayed in the heavens, the moonlight is supreme;
among all forms of brilliance, the sunlight is supreme.
Within the worlds of the ten directions, the Buddha is the foremost honored one.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached various teachings to the brahmin, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, before rising from his seat and departing.
260 (260). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a young brahmin named Saṃghala who went to where the Buddha was staying. After having exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How does one observe an unwholesome person?
The Buddha said,
"It is like observing the moon."
He asked again:
"How does one observe a truly superior person?
The Buddha replied once more:
“It is also like observing the moon.
At that time, the young brahmin (māṇava) again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In what way does an unvirtuous man observe it as being like the moon?”
The Buddha said:

"An unwholesome man is like the moonlight on the sixteenth day; it gradually diminishes from its fullness, becomes increasingly waning, until finally it is completely exhausted and no longer appears."

If, within the Buddha-dharma, one cannot with faith accept and uphold the prohibitive precepts, recites and chants but little, or practices only meager acts of giving, and subsequently becomes indolent and lacks diligence, gradually losing faith, violating the prohibitive precepts, ceasing to give, associating with evil friends, and failing to go to the monasteries to inquire about and receive the Dharma—because of not hearing the Dharma, one performs unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind; and because of creating such evil, at the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into the evil realms.
"Therefore, you should know that a wicked man is like that moon which gradually wanes until it finally vanishes.
He asked again:
"In what way is a superior, virtuous man also like the moon?"
The Buddha said:
“It is like the new moon, whose radiance blazes forth and gradually increases until, on the fifteenth day, it is full and complete.

Likewise, within the Buddha-dharma, one who possesses faith and practices the prohibitive precepts, cultivates extensive learning, practices giving, eliminates wrong views, and cultivates right view; who attains pure faith in the Buddha-dharma, firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts, skillfully cultivates extensive learning, is able to give without stinginess, and is endowed with right view—such a person, through faith, morality, learning, and generosity, grows progressively. This virtuous man, through the conduct of body, speech, and mind, draws near to spiritual friends, fully cultivates all virtues, and at the dissolution of the body after death, attains rebirth in the heavens.”
"Therefore, you should know that a virtuous man is also like the moon.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as the full moon, Dwells within the void of space,"
The halo of his radiance shines most brilliantly, eclipsing all the stars. Just as a person endowed with faith—
who observes the precepts, possesses learning, and abandons greed and envy—
outshines those who are envious, he is like the moon obscuring the host of stars.
At that time, the brahmin Saṅgārava, having heard what the Buddha had said, departed with leaping joy.
The bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
261 (Two Hundred and Sixty-one) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Jātiśroṇa who went to where the Buddha was. Having exchanged greetings and taken his seat to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard people say:
'The Blessed One has declared:
"Give only to me, do not give to others; give only to my disciples, do not give to the disciples of others. "
"If one can give to me and my disciples, one will obtain a great fruit;
if one gives to others or to other disciples, one will not obtain a fruit.
Is this what you would say in truth?
"Could this not be a slander by worldly people?
The Buddha said, "This is indeed false and a slander against me; such words were never spoken."
If one speaks in this manner, two kinds of refutations arise:
first, the refutation by way of negation; second, the refutation that the recipient suffers diminution.
To speak thus causes great harm and reduction; at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one will fall into the three evil realms.
You should know now that even regarding the water used to wash my alms bowl, I have said:
"If one gives it to insects and ants, one obtains a great reward of merit.
How much more so, then, for giving to me?
He spoke these words in truth:
"One who gives to those who uphold the precepts gains very great merit; one who gives to those who have broken the precepts gains meager merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In all places of giving, I always offer praise;
though one who breaks the precepts gains little merit, one who upholds them reaps great fruit.
Just as black, white, red, and blue cows give birth to calves that each differ,"
A carriage takes its power from its draft animals, regardless of their breed;
human beings are likewise so: whether they be Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Caṇḍālas, or Pukkasas.
One who is able to maintain pure precepts and practices generosity shall obtain great fruit;
it is like carrying away sesame stalks only to discard them and take precious jewels instead.
The infantile and ignorant, lacking wisdom, have never heard the Dharma.
Unable to cultivate the holy life, one who gives obtains but meager fruit.
But if one draws near to the noble and the holy— the Perfectly Awakened One and his disciples—
and can place faith in the Sugata, the faculty of faith will be firmly established.
"Born always in noble and honorable places, one shall finally attain nirvāṇa.
At that time, Jāti, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
262 (Two Hundred and Sixty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
There was an elderly brāhmaṇa who, holding a staff and carrying an alms bowl, was going about begging for food. At that time, the Buddha saw him and said to the brāhmaṇa:
"You are now extremely old; why do you hold a staff and carry an alms bowl while going about begging for food?"
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I have seven sons, each of whom I married off and gave an equal share of my wealth; I now have no portion left.
Because I was driven out by my sons, I am now wandering for alms."
The Buddha said to him, "I shall now speak a verse for you;
are you able to recite this verse in the midst of the great assembly?
He replied:
“I can. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Because a son was born, he rejoiced greatly; for his sake, he gathered wealth and treasures.”
Each has taken a wife and children, and they have driven me away.
These people lack filial piety and compassion;
though their mouths claim to be my parents, they are like the offspring of rākṣasas, who drive me away as I approach death.
It is like a horse stall filled with grain and fodder, where young horses, lacking respect and deference, drive and trample the elders.
This son is just like that; he has no heart of love or reverence.
It is better that you, whom I love, hold this staff for me than that I be cast out to wander for alms.
Now that I grasp this staff, it shall guide my dogs, sheep, and horses;
it shall assist my strength when walking and serve as my companion in the darkness of night.
"One who points to water knows its depth; one who stumbles rises by leaning on a staff.
To remove much learning through the reliance on a staff—that staff is what cherishes me.
Having received this verse, the brahmin recited it until he had mastered it.
At that time, while the seven sons were in the great assembly, the brahmin spoke these words among the multitude:
"You all should now listen to what I have to say."
The great assembly remained silent, and he then recited the aforementioned verse.

The seven sons felt ashamed and remorseful; they rose, embraced their father, and each paid him his respects. They led their father back home and placed him in his original seat. Each of the sons then took out two exquisite pieces of fine cotton cloth (*karpāsa*) and offered them to their father.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"I have now obtained this happiness through the power of Gautama; Gautama is my preceptor (ācārya).
According to the law of the brahmins, it is the duty to make offerings to one's upādhyāya and ācārya."
He selected his finest garments and went to where the Buddha was. After greeting the Buddha, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
That my family now enjoys all manner of benefit and happiness is due to your grace. In the scriptures I have studied, it is said:"
“Ācārya, it should be given as the ācārya’s share.
Upādhyāya, it should be given as the upādhyāya’s share.
“Gautama! [he replied.]
"You are now my preceptor; you should have compassion for me and accept this robe from me.
At that time, out of compassion, the World-Honored One accepted the robe.
The brahmin leaped for joy, rose from his seat, and departed with great gladness.
263 (263) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl, entering the city to beg for food.
There was then an elderly brahmin who, carrying a staff and holding an alms bowl, was walking about begging for food. Seeing the Buddha from afar, he approached him and spoke these words:
"I carry a staff and hold an alms bowl to beg for food from others; you also beg for food. Thus, both I and you are bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One need not beg from others to be called a bhikṣu;
Even while possessing the ways of a householder, One may rightly cultivate the holy life."
"The fruits of merit and the retribution of evil— When both are severed and there is no attachment, All fetters of existence are dried up; This is called the Dharma of a bhikṣu.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
264 (Two Hundred and Sixty-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, to the north of Rājagṛha, there was a brahmin farmer named Drona.
At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and went to that place.
When the brahmin saw the Buddha coming from afar, he immediately approached the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"I am a laborer who eats from the fruits of my own cultivation; I do not beg from others.
Gautama! You too should now cultivate and eat."
The Buddha said, "I,
too, eat what I have cultivated through plowing.
Thereupon, the brahmin Dronaśa spoke this verse:
"You yourself say you know how to plow, yet we have not seen you at the time of plowing.
If you truly know how to plow, explain the method of plowing to me.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"I take faith as my seed, all virtues as my fertile field,
diligence as my well-trained oxen, wisdom as my yoke and pole,
shame and remorse as my plow implements, and mindfulness as the driver who plows."
Body, speech, and mind are well-disciplined; The precepts serve as the yoke-tie.
One plows away the filth of afflictions; Sweet rain falls according to the season.
Weeding with a virtuous mind, One reaps a great harvest of wholesome crops.
Proceeding toward the place of peace, one may achieve eternal security.
Such is my cultivation; thus I have attained the fruit of the Deathless, transcended and departed from the three realms, and shall not return to enter into further existences.
The brāhmaṇa said, "Your plowing is indeed the plowing of the unsurpassed victory.
Upon hearing this verse, the brāhmaṇa conceived faith and understanding; he filled his alms bowl with food and drink and came to offer it to the Buddha, but the Buddha did not accept it.
The remainder is as spoken by the Brahmin Dūrasa, up until "no further existence shall be received.
265 (265) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Brahmā who was traveling through the kingdom of Aṅga. He arrived at Campā and reached the banks of the Gaṅgā Lake. On the following morning, he put on his robes, took his alms bowl, entered the city of Campā, and went from house to house for alms until he reached his own home.
At that time, the Venerable Brahmayu was at the middle gate, casting ghee, rice, and sesame seeds into a mass of fire, hoping to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Venerable Brahmayu stood at the gate, but his mother did not recognize him.

At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa, out of reverent faith in Brahmā, traveled through the air with an immeasurable host of yakṣas. He saw Brahmā’s mother performing a fire sacrifice; she did not see her son, but saw only the ascetic, whom she did not recognize as her own child.
King Vaiśravaṇa then spoke these verses for his mother:
“A woman of the brahmin caste, the Brahmā world is far from here;
To hope for the Brahma realm by sacrificing to fire—this is not the path.”
Not understanding how to proceed toward the Brahma-heaven, why do you labor so diligently at tending the sacrificial fires?
The Brahma among Brahmas stands before your very gate;
he is entirely free from grasping and attachment, and likewise has nothing that he nurtures.
Distant from all evil realms, The fetters and defilements do not adhere.
Far removed from all desires and seeking, Untainted by worldly dharmas;
Like a well-trained dragon-elephant, There is no provocation or irritation.
The bhikṣu of supreme mindfulness, whose mind has attained excellent liberation—
such a true sage (arhat) now comes to receive your offering.
You should kindle the lamp of the mind and swiftly bestow it with a pure heart.

At that time, having heard what Vaiśravaṇa said, her mother immediately attained awakening. Having offered food to the Brahmā and the food to the Brahman, she provided them with illumination as a cause for peace and happiness in future lives.
266. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain brāhmaṇa went to where the Buddha was; having exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The people of the world call you Buddha or Buddhadeva; from where does such a name arise?
The brāhmaṇa spoke this verse in question:
"Buddha is a supreme name; the meaning of 'Buddha' is 'one who brings beings across [to liberation].
Since your parents bestowed this name upon you, I therefore call you Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Now, out of compassion for you, I shall explain this in detail for you;
as to why such a name exists, listen now with careful attention.
The Buddha knows the past, and the future is likewise."
Now he universally and fully knows The characteristic of the decay and destruction of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Clearly penetrating and understanding all dharmas, He practices everything that should be practiced;
He eradicates everything that should be severed. For this reason, he is named Buddha.
Having thoroughly understood and discerned both general and specific characteristics,
and perceiving and knowing all things completely— for this reason he is called a Buddha.
Brahmin, you should know that he has observed thus for immeasurable eons.
All conditioned phenomena are suffering; those who take birth must inevitably perish.
Having distanced themselves from and abandoned the dust and defilements of habitual tendencies, they have extracted the poisonous arrow of affliction.
Having attained the end of birth and death, for this reason they are called Buddhas.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 267 (267) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala and arrived at the village of Sālā.
At that time, the World-Honored One left the path and sat upright with his body straight beneath a tree, binding his mindfulness before him.
Then there was a brahmin of the Agniveśya clan who followed behind the Buddha; seeing the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel within the Buddha’s footprints, he marveled at this unprecedented wonder.

He then reflected to himself: "I have never seen anyone with such footprints; I must investigate whose tracks these are. Having formed this thought, he followed the tracks until he reached the place where the Buddha was.

Beholding the Honored One’s countenance, his expression was one of serene joy; those who saw him felt faith and reverence. All his physical marks were tranquil and composed, and his mind was likewise settled; he had attained the most supreme taming of the mind and the stillness of cessation. His body was of a true golden color, like a pavilion of gold.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
You shall surely attain the state of a deva."
The Buddha said,
“Brahmin! I have not attained heaven.”
The brāhmaṇa said:
"One will become an asura; or will one become a nāga, gandharva, yakṣa, kiṃnara, or mahoraga?"
The Buddha said,
"I have not obtained any of them.
The brāhmaṇa said:
“You have attained humanity,” [the king said].
The Buddha replied,
“I have not attained humanity.”
The brahmin said:
"I asked you whether you had attained the state of a deva, nāga, asura, gandharva, yakṣa, kiṃnara, mahoraga, or human, and in each case you replied that you had not. What, then, have you attained?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I am not a deva, nāga, or asura; I am not a kiṃnara, mahoraga, or gandharva;
Nor am I a yakṣa or a human; My outflows are exhausted, and I have severed all afflictions."
Though I am as well-tamed as a dragon or an elephant, I shall never be controlled by another;
because I am not controlled by another, I have severed doubt, severed craving, attained liberation, and departed from all realms of existence.
Having fully known and severed all rebirth, like a *puṇḍarīka* flower in full bloom,
growing while dwelling within the water, it is ultimately never defiled by that water.

Pure, fragrant, and clean, a delight to all people; unstained by the eight worldly dharmas like a lotus flower, I too am thus born into this world, remaining untainted by and unattached to worldly phenomena.
Having constantly observed throughout immeasurable eons that all conditioned phenomena are objects of suffering,
and that all who are born must eventually pass away; having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, they have severed all habitual tendencies,
extracted the poisoned arrow, and cut off the afflictions, thereby attaining the ultimate end of birth and death.
"For this reason, he is called 'Buddha'.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Vāseṭṭha departed with joy.
Mānatthaddha, Ujjaya, Jāti, Sunakkhatta, Bhikkhu, Ghoṭamukha, and Brahmāyu; Buddha was the tenth, marked by the wheel-sign. 268 (268) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food, arriving at the house of the Brahmin Dhāraṇīśvara of the Agniveśya clan.
At that time, Agnidatta was performing a fire sacrifice before the middle gate. When the Buddha arrived at the gate, Agnidatta saw the Buddha coming from afar and said to him: "Stop!"
Stop! Outcaste! Do not come here!
The Buddha said to him, "Do you recognize the caṇḍāla? Do you know the dharma of the caṇḍālas?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"You do not recognize or know the caṇḍāla or the dharma of the caṇḍāla; do you recognize the caṇḍāla and know the dharma of the caṇḍāla?
The Buddha said to him:
"I recognize the caṇḍāla and I know the dharma of the caṇḍāla."
Then the brahmin rose from his seat, prepared a seat for the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
"Please explain the dharma of the caṇḍālas to me."
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the seat and spoke these verses:
"Those of evil nature who delight in anger and harbor long-standing resentment, Who are harsh and cruel toward others and harbor arrogance,
Who practice inverted views and delusions— Know that these are the *caṇḍālas*."
Possessing anger, envy, and the desire for good and evil, difficult to tame or transform and devoid of shame or remorse—
one who acts in such a way is a caṇḍāla.
With no compassion in their heart, they harm living beings and injure, mutilate, and destroy those of the four modes of birth.
Know that this is a caṇḍāla:
one who robs all the wealth found in villages or in desolate places, and even takes life—
one who acts in such a way is a caṇḍāla.
One who commits various evils without remorse is called a *caṇḍāla*.
One who abandons his own wife and prostitutes, yet commits illicit adultery with the wives of others without restraint—such a person is likewise called a *caṇḍāla*.
One who commits evil acts against their own kin and friends,
engaging in lewdness without distinguishing between the worthy and the unworthy— such a person is also called a caṇḍāla.
To explain the meaning by means of fallacious reasoning is likewise called being a caṇḍāla.
To praise one’s own virtues while disparaging others, and to be greedily attached to pride and base conduct—
this too is called being a caṇḍāla.
Utterly foolish, they slander others without cause; for the sake of minor gain, they give rise to slander—such people are also called *caṇḍālas*.
They cast their own faults upon others and are solely devoted to deceiving and slandering people—such people are also called *caṇḍālas*.
One who possesses abundant wealth and many kinsmen, yet eats fine delicacies himself while giving coarse food to others— such a person is also called a *caṇḍāla*.
One who receives delicious food when visiting another's house, yet gives coarse and inferior food when that other comes to his own—
such a person is also called a *caṇḍāla*.
When parents have grown old and lost their vigor, yet one fails to be filial and instead increases their neglect— such a person is also called a *caṇḍāla*.
When one reviles and uses foul language toward parents, brothers, and sisters, lacking all humility and fraternal respect—
such a person is also called a *caṇḍāla*.
When the time for midday comes near, they do not give; they further revile and become enraged—such people are also called caṇḍālas.
When the poor come begging to their homes, they neither provide food nor drink, nor do they give anything at all.
Such a person is also called a caṇḍāla;
one who reviles the Buddha and his śrāvakas, and further reviles those who have gone forth or those who live at home—such a person is also called a caṇḍāla.
Ultimately not an Arhat yet falsely claiming to be one, he was a predator among gods and humans.
Born into a great family of Brahmins, he was thoroughly proficient in the Vedic scriptures;
yet repeatedly committing various evil deeds, his noble lineage could not prevent his slander and defilement.
Nor can it avert the retribution of hell;
one will be reviled by others in the present life, fall into the evil realms in future lives, and be born among the Caṇḍālas or the Sūta-yanas.
One will surely not hear an ill reputation, but shall instead attain great joy and be born in the Brahma realm;
no lineage can obstruct birth in the Brahma realm, for one who is praised in the present will ultimately be reborn in heaven.
I shall now reveal and explain this for you; such matters should be understood:
birth does not make one a brahmin, nor does birth make one a caṇḍāla.
Through pure deeds one becomes a brahmin, and through evil conduct one becomes a caṇḍāla.
Upon hearing this verse, the brahmin praised it, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
O Great Striver!
It is truly as you have said, O Great Muni!
One is not a brahmin by birth, nor is one a caṇḍāla by birth.
"One who is well able to practice is a true Brahmin; one who performs evil deeds is a Caṇḍāla.

When the Brahmin heard this verse, he rejoiced with faith and understanding. He filled his bowl to the brim with food and drink and brought it to offer to the Buddha, but the Buddha would not accept it.
Why is this? Because it is the food of the Dharma.
The brāhmaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"To whom should this food be given?
The Buddha said, "I do not see any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, or Brahmā who could digest this food; such a person does not exist."
"You should place this food into pure water that is free of insects.
The brahmin then placed the food into the insect-free water, whereupon smoke and flames rose together with a loud, sizzling sound.
At that time, the brahmin conceived a sense of the unprecedented, thinking, "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, even while at his meal, displays such great supernormal powers.
The brahmin returned to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying,
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to leave the household life, so that I may attain the stages of the Path."
The Buddha said, “Welcome, Bhikṣu!

His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately attained full ordination according to the rules for leaving the household life. Thereupon, in a solitary and quiet place, he practiced with diligent cultivation alone.
This is why sons of noble family shave off their hair and beard and don the dharma robes: for the sake of correctly practicing the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*).

When the holy life has been established and what was to be done has been accomplished, these sons of noble family will no longer undergo future existence; they become arhats and attain the bliss of liberation.
And he spoke in verse:
"In the past, I was deluded regarding the true reality; through folly and confusion, I committed perverse deeds.
I did not recognize the path of purity, nor did I know the way of death."
Deluded thoughts give rise to false attachments; With weary toil, one serves the fire.
All for the sake of empty and vain matters, In vain they are diminished with nothing gained.
Now meeting the God among Gods, The darkness receives his gracious light.
Having attained the joy within joys, and possessing the precepts, he has realized the three knowledges; within the Buddha’s teachings, all that was to be done is already finished.
Though originally a brahmin, he is in truth a caṇḍāla.
Today he is truly such: a pure-practicing brahmin, far removed from the mire;
having bathed himself in purity, he has crossed to the further shore of the Vedas.

The eleven sūtras from "Self-conceit" (*ātma-māna*) onwards in Volume Thirteen of the *Separate Translation of the Saṃyukta Āgama* are all absent from the Danzang (Dunhuang canon); furthermore, there are no corresponding texts or variant translations for them within the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*.
However, as its textual characteristics do not differ and it corresponds to the preceding and following sections of the sutra,
those portions absent from the Danzang (Beijing Edition) must have been omitted; therefore,
I have retained them here as they are.
In the Gui-mao year, the Tripitaka Bureau of the Great State of Goryeo, by imperial decree, carved this woodblock edition.
