269 (Two Hundred and Sixty-nine) Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha.

There was a goddess named Kokaṇiśā, who had formerly been the daughter of a courtesan; her radiance was twice that of usual. During that night, she approached the place where the Buddha was, her majestic light shining so brightly that it illuminated this mountain entirely with great brilliance. She prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and spoke these verses:
"One should cultivate goodness in speech and mind, and should not commit any evils.
One should not inflict even the slightest harm upon the world through the body.
Contemplating that desires are empty and without substance, one should cultivate mindfulness and the factors of enlightenment."
"Even if you yourself do not delight in suffering, do not perform actions that cause harm.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the deva, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
It is as you have said:
"One should cultivate goodness in speech and mind; one should not commit any evils."
Do not inflict harm upon the world through even minor evils with your body.
Contemplate that desires are empty and without substance; cultivate mindfulness and the factors of awakening.
If you yourself do not delight in suffering, do not perform actions that cause harm.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the daughter of Puṇḍravardhana rejoiced and prostrated herself; she then vanished from her seat and returned to her celestial palace.
270 (Two hundred seventy) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now wish to expound the Dharma of four lines; you should all receive it well, listen with a sincere and attentive mind, and remember it without forgetting."
What is meant by "expounding the Dharma of the four lines"?
"Speech and mind should cultivate what is wholesome; One should not commit any evil deeds.
Even with the body, one should not inflict harm upon the world, No matter how slight the evil may be."
"Contemplate that desire is empty and without reality; cultivate mindfulness and the factors of awakening.
If you yourself do not delight in suffering, do not perform actions that lead to harm.
At that time, there was a brahmin who, standing not far from Ānanda, heard these verses being recited and immediately reflected upon them:
"The meaning of these verses is profound and far-reaching; they were not composed by a human being, but must have been proclaimed by a non-human being. We should go and ask the Buddha about them."
Having had this thought, the brahmin then went to where the Buddha was; after exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Gautama!
"I heard these verses from Ānanda, and as I reflect upon them, the meaning of these verse lines was not composed by a human being.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"It is indeed so!"
"It is indeed so!
Truly, this was not proclaimed by a human being, nor was it created by a human being.
In the past, while I was at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha, the goddess Gaṇikāśā approached me; having prostrated at my feet, she sat to one side and spoke these verses."
"And these verses were indeed not spoken by a human.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the brāhmaṇa departed with joy.
(271) [Discourse 271] Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a goddess named Kālikaśā, who had formerly been the daughter of Pūraṇa; her bodily radiance was so brilliant as to be like a flash of lightning.

With profound sincerity and ultimate faith, he took refuge in the Triple Gem and approached the Buddha’s dwelling, sitting to one side. By means of this radiance, the entire mountain was universally illuminated, becoming completely and brilliantly clear.
The goddess Kāñcanamālā then spoke these verses:
"I have now praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha with various hymns;
I have now briefly proclaimed them, which is sufficient according to my own inclination."
One should cultivate goodness in speech and mind, and should not commit various evils;
one should not, even for a minor transgression, inflict harm upon the world.
Contemplating that the nature and characteristics of desire are empty, one should cultivate mindfulness and the factors of awakening.
"If you yourself do not delight in suffering, do not perform actions that cause harm.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the goddess, saying: "So it is!"
"So it is! It is just as you have said.
Having heard these words from the Buddha, the goddess Kācanā rejoiced and prostrated herself; she then vanished from that place and returned to her celestial palace.
272 (Dvāsaptatim) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kapiṃjala Monastery on the northern bank of the Monkey River in Vaiśālī.
At that time, the goddesses Pāṃśupradānā and Cūḍā, their radiance and complexion twice as bright as usual, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then these two goddesses emitted a great radiance that illuminated the monkey and Vaiśālī, so that everything became brilliantly bright.
At that time, the goddess Cūḍā spoke this verse:
“The World-Honored One, the Bhagavān, The Peerless, Perfectly Enlightened One.”
Residing in Vaiśālī, dwelling in the Great Forest,
To Kauṇḍinya, Śakra, and the daughter of Trapuṣa—
I prostrate at the feet of the Honored One.
I have heard in the past that the World-Honored One, the Muni, who is skilled in proclaiming the Dharma, is now currently expounding it.
To those who would give rise to criticism and disparagement toward such a profound Dharma as this—
This is what is called folly; one will surely fall into an evil realm thereafter.
Those who can praise the noble Dharma and achieve full possession of mindfulness are called wise;
they will surely be born in a good realm thereafter.
Then the goddess Kācanī said again in verse:
"One should cultivate goodness in speech and mind, And one should not commit various evils.
One should not, even with a minor evil, Inflict harm upon the world."
"Contemplate that the nature and characteristics of desire are empty; cultivate mindfulness and the factors of awakening.
If you yourself do not delight in suffering, do not perform actions that cause harm.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the goddess, saying:
“So it is! So it is! It is just as you have said.”
When the goddesses had heard what the Buddha had spoken, they departed with joy. 273 (273) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva came to the Buddha’s dwelling during the night, his majestic radiance illuminating the entire Jeta Grove. Having prostrated himself, he withdrew to sit at one side and spoke this verse:
"Do not touch that which is untouched; that which is touched will surely be requited.
Because of such consequences, one should not engage in reckless contact."
"If it is not a place for crossing over, one should not harbor the intention to cross.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"One who should be angry does not become angry; pure and free from fetters,"
If one wishes to inflict evil upon another, that evil will surely reach one's own person.
It is like throwing dust against the wind; the dust returns and covers the body itself.
If one seeks to harm another with anger, the other will certainly retaliate in return.
"These two are both called evil; neither is free from affliction.
If one does not retaliate against anger, one can subdue a great enemy.
At that time, the deva again praised him with a verse:
“In the past, I have already seen a brahmin attain nirvāṇa;
having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.
When this deva had spoken this verse, he departed with joy.
274 (Two Hundred Seventy-Four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiant countenance was blazing and whose complexion was extraordinary, approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and spoke this verse:
“The infantile and those of little wisdom, who commit various evil deeds, create enemies for themselves;
later, they shall receive the retribution of great suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“Whatever unwholesome deeds one has committed, having performed them, one burns and suffers;
the fool who creates manifold evils receives retribution through weeping and wailing.
The deity further praised him with a verse:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain *nirvāṇa*;
having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he was able to cross over the world’s craving.
When that deva had spoken this verse, he joyfully prostrated and returned to his celestial palace.
275 (Dvāsaptatipañcama) Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, resplendent with majestic brilliance and of extraordinary countenance, approached the place where the Buddha was. Having prostrated himself, he withdrew to sit at one side and spoke these verses:
"One does not become a śramaṇa merely by words;
it is through this actual pursuit of the Path that one achieves the firm footprint.
If there is a courageous and steadfast person who is able to cultivate meditative concentration deeply,"
Having attained liberation, one destroys the fetters of Māra.
Whether one performs actions or refrains from them, both are spoken of as they truly are;
those who are deceitful and lack sincerity are abandoned by the wise.
"Having truly attained nothing oneself, one boasts in vain out of self-conceit;
speaking with fraud, hypocrisy, and falsehood, such a person is a great thief in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“He does not manifest his own virtues; he does not know the mental conduct of others.
Having known [the truth], he has entered parinirvāṇa; he is able to cross over the world’s craving.
At that time, having heard these verses of the Buddha, this deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I am truly guilty of transgressions now; I only pray that you will accept my sincere repentance.
At that time, the Buddha remained silent.
The deva spoke again in verse:
“I now confess my transgression; you do not accept my confession.
You harbor an evil and unwholesome mind, refusing to relinquish your resentment.
The World-Honored One replied to the deva in verse:
"To speak of one's transgressions while calling it repentance, yet the inner mind does not truly extinguish them—
how can enmity and resentment be removed?
How can goodness be attained?"
The deva spoke again in verse, asking further:
"Who among men is without fault?
Who among men is without error?"
"Who is free from delusion?
Who always possesses mindfulness?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“The Tathāgata, the Bhagavān, has attained liberation through right knowledge;
he is free from all faults and defects, and likewise possesses neither gain nor loss.
Having already abandoned delusion, he is fully endowed with right mindfulness.”
The deva further praised him with a verse, saying:
"I have already seen in the past A brāhmaṇa who has attained nirvāṇa;
Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, He is able to cross over worldly craving."
At that time, having spoken this verse, the deva departed with joy. 276 (276).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, Devadatta’s friend Kokālika went to where the Buddha was and stood to one side.
The Buddha said to Kokālika:
“You have a karmic connection with Śāriputra; do not harbor thoughts of resentment toward him.”
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have purely cultivated the holy life; their minds are supple and gentle. Do not harbor resentment toward them, lest you suffer various afflictions for a long night.

Kokālika replied: "I believe the Buddha’s words and I follow the Buddha; yet Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana truly possess evil desires. They have attained mastery over those evil desires, and they act according to them."
The Buddha again addressed Kokālika:
"Do not now give rise to a mind of resentment toward those two persons.
This was repeated three times.
Although Kokālika heard the Buddha’s words, his evil mind did not change, and he abandoned the Buddha and departed.

Not far from the Buddha, an evil ulcer broke out on his body; at first it was like a mustard seed, but in a mere moment it became as large as a bean, and gradually grew even larger until it was the size of a bilva fruit. His body rotted and溃烂 (festered), pus and blood flowed out, and when his body perished and his life ended, he fell into the Great Lotus Hell.
At that time, there were three devas whose radiance was twice their usual brilliance; during that night, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side.
On the first day, he said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Kokālika passed away during this night."
On the second day, he said:
"He has fallen into the Great Lotus Hell.
On the third day, he immediately spoke this verse:
"When a person is born into this world, an axe is held within their mouth;
by means of their evil speech, they cut themselves down.
Praising what should be censured and censuring what should be praised, such flowery speech issues from the mouth, leading to suffering and calamity hereafter."
Idle chatter that robs others of their wealth is a minor transgression; however, slandering the Buddha and the noble sages is called a great affliction.

One will suffer for a long duration, for a full hundred thousand eons, entering the Nirarbuda hell and the thirty-six [subsidiary hells], entering the Arbuda hell, and even falling into those [other realms].
"Five *āpāyika* [hells]:
those who slander the noble ones and commit evil through speech and mind enter this hell.
At that time, the three devas prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to their celestial palaces.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to hear of the length of the lifespan in that Arbuda hell?
The bhikṣus replied:
“Please speak for us; having heard it, we shall faithfully accept and remember it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Suppose there were twenty khāris of sesame seeds filling a cart to overflowing in Vārāṇasī. If a long-lived person were to take out a single seed every hundred years until all the sesame seeds were completely exhausted, the lifespan obtained in this Arbuda hell would still not have come to an end.”
Twenty *ābuda* hells constitute one *nirarbuda*.
Twenty *nirarbuda* hells constitute one *aṭaṭa*.
Twenty *aṭaṭa* hells constitute one *hahava*.
Twenty *hūhū* hells constitute one Lotus Hell (*padma-naraka*).
Twenty Lotus Hells constitute one Great Lotus Hell (*mahā-padma-naraka*).
Because the bhikṣu Kokālika slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, he fell into this Great Lotus Hell.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“One should not even slander a charred pillar, let alone those who possess consciousness.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
277 (277). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice his usual brilliance and whose majestic countenance shone forth, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove, approached the Buddha, prostrated himself, and withdrew to sit at one side. He then spoke in verse:
"What is it that leads to despising others, and what is it that prevents one from despising others?
By what is one despised by others, and what is considered its primary cause?
I now ask the Tathāgata; O Great Sage, please explain this to me."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"To know well is not to despise; ignorance is called despising.
To delight in the Dharma is called reverence; to be arrogant toward the Dharma is called irreverence."
Not associating with virtuous friends—this is called the foremost form of disrespect.
Delighting in practicing what is unrighteous, one’s own kinsmen and friends give rise to resentment and jealousy.
To take an enemy as a friend—this is the foremost form of disrespect.
Just as there may be a woman who, in her conduct, is not chaste or virtuous,
but delights in illicit sexual unions and performs irrational acts;
so too it is with a man who violates the rules of propriety— their moral failing is likewise the same.
Such as these are called the foremost among the contemptible.
Those who deceive others with scales and measures, who are crafty and dishonest, lacking impartiality,
and who act with negligence while harboring greed for profit— these are called the foremost among the contemptible.
Gambling and mutual deception exhaust one's wealth and property;
such things as these are called the primary categories of contemptible conduct.
Indulging in sleep and fine flavors, going to bed early and rising late—
Those who are indolent in their duties and further delight in anger—
such persons as these are also called the foremost among the contemptible.
[They may wear] earrings and bracelets, hold parasols, and possess fine brocade sandals.
To adorn oneself while in poverty is called the foremost form of self-degradation.
When wealth and possessions are meager, one's attachment and craving only grow more intense;
though born into the Kṣatriya caste, one still hopes and strives to obtain the royal throne.
Such a foolish person is called the foremost among the contemptible.
Though his wealth and resources are vast and his circle of kinsmen and friends is large,
he eats fine delicacies himself and does not share or give them to others.
Having received fine food and drink from others, as well as wealth and profit,
when they come to one's own home, they have no heart to repay the kindness at all;
they do not even give so much as a meal— this is called the foremost form of contempt.
When one's parents have grown old and their decline has set in,
yet they eat only what is sweet and delicious themselves and never know how to provide for them—
such people as these are called the foremost among those who are contemptible.
Parents and brothers, relatives and sisters— beating them, scolding them,
or speaking harsh words to them is called the foremost form of contempt.
When śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas come to one’s home at the time of midday, [one should treat them with respect].
To refuse food that was not solicited nor offered— this is called the foremost of insults.
To revile and insult śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor who beg for alms by refusing them food— this is called the foremost of insults.
Slandering the Buddha and the śrāvakas, whether they be renunciants or householders,
for committing such unrighteous acts, one is called the foremost among the contemptible.
Not being an arhat in truth, yet claiming oneself to be an arhat.
A celestial being, a brahmin, or a śramaṇa who acts as a great thief among them—
if one is such a person, they are called the foremost of the contemptible.
Those of this sort are held in low esteem by others.
Whatever is contemptible in the world, I know and see it all;
one should abandon it from afar, as if fearing a perilous path.
The deva again praised him in verse:
"I have seen in the past a Brahmin who has attained *nirvāṇa*,
who has long since cast aside aversion and fear, and who is able to cross over the world's craving.
Having spoken this verse, that deity departed with joy.
278 (Two Hundred Seventy-Eight). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a deva whose countenance was radiant and whose brilliant complexion was exceedingly luminous, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove. He approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. Then, he spoke these verses:
"Who is it that is called respectful and compliant?
Who is it that is called arrogant and disdainful?
Who is it that acts with infantile folly, like a small child playing with dirt?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“If a man is respectful and compliant, a woman will surely treat him with contempt.
If a man treats her with contempt, a woman will surely be respectful and compliant.”
"The woman’s childish play is like a small child’s toy with dirt.
The deva again praised him in verse, saying:
"In the past, I have already seen a Brahmin attain nirvāṇa."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
When this deva had spoken this verse, he returned to his palace with joy.
279 (279). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, whose bodily radiance was as brilliant as a flash of lightning, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove with a dazzling and intense light, approached the Buddha. Having prostrated at his feet, he withdrew to sit at one side and spoke these verses:
“When vitarka and vicāra arise with intention, they should be restrained;
all should be fully restrained, so that the dust of saṃsāra is not created.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"When vitarka and vicāra arise with intention, one should restrain what ought to be restrained;
yet not everything should be restrained—only evil vitarka and vicāra.
One should restrain evil with evil; having restrained, one is able to maintain that restraint."
"If one can act in this way, one will not be obstructed by birth and death.
The deva further praised him with a verse:
"In the past, I have already seen a brahmin attain nirvāṇa."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, one is able to cross over worldly craving.
When this deva had spoken this verse, he returned to his palace with joy.
280. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain deva, his body radiant with light that illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, approached the place where the Buddha was. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
"How does one obtain renown?
How does one acquire wealth and enterprise?
How does one attain praise?"
"How does one obtain friends?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"By upholding the precepts one gains a good reputation; by practicing generosity one acquires wealth and treasures."
"Truthful speech earns one renown; universal generosity makes one dear to all.
The deva further praised him in verse:
"In the past, I have already seen a brāhmaṇa attain nirvāṇa."
"Having long since abandoned aversion and fear, he is able to cross over worldly craving.
When this deva had spoken this verse, he returned to his palace with joy.
281 (281). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Then a certain deva, his countenance radiant and blazing with a brilliant light that illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and spoke these verses:
"How is it that one is born as a human, seeing with such extreme clarity?
Having gathered various treasures and profits, what is the meaning of their quantity?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"First learn various skills; next, amass all manner of wealth.
Divide the amassed wealth into four parts: one part for food and clothing, two parts for business and labor, and one part to await times of scarcity."
Farming is the first occupation; commerce is the second.
Breeding herds of cattle, as well as lambs and the six domestic animals—furthermore, there are sons and daughters, each of whom seeks a wife or husband.
One should send forth daughters and sisters, as well as the household’s livestock;
through harmony one gains profit and joy, while through discord one suffers affliction.
One should bring all tasks to their completion, never ceasing or abandoning them midway.
The wise person reflects well and deeply understands gain and loss.
Skillfully discerning what should and should not be done, wealth and treasures flow toward them like rivers returning to the great ocean; thus they diligently cultivate their undertakings.
Just as a bee gathers from many flowers, Day after day it grows ever more;
Amassing wealth and undertakings day and night, It increases just like that bee.
Wealth does not wait for one to grow old, Nor does it accompany those who dwell in distant lands.
When an evil person performs base deeds, even if their power surpasses one's own,
one should never give wealth or treasures to such a person.
To grant riches in order to cultivate intimacy leads to anger and strife when the debt is demanded.
Alas for wealth and profit! One loses both wealth and friends through them.
One should accumulate wealth only in accordance with the Dharma; one should not act contrary to the Dharma.
When a man acts according to the Dharma, he becomes dignified and exceedingly radiant.
"Being able to provide for one's own food and clothing, while also bestowing gifts upon others,
and maintaining such conduct with moderation and without excess— one shall, at the end of life, be reborn in heaven.
The deva then praised him further with a verse:
"I have seen in the past, a Brahmin who has attained *nirvāṇa*,
who has long since cast aside aversion and fear, having crossed over worldly craving.
Having spoken this verse, that deva returned to his palace with joy.
282 (Two Hundred and Eighty-Two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, there was a skilled lute player in the kingdom of Kosala named Kūṇa who was traveling along a road.
At that time, six celestial maidens were each riding in palaces, traversing through the air."
The gods and others emerged from their palace and said to this man, "Uncle, you may play the lute for us; we shall sing and dance.
At that time, the lute player beheld his countenance, which was of extraordinary brilliance, and conceived a sense of wonder at such a rare sight.
He asked, "Sisters!
What merit did you perform to be born in this place?"
"First tell me its prior cause, and I shall play for you upon this clear lute.
The goddess replied, "You need only play the lute for me now; within the song, I shall myself recount our past karmic conditions."
At that time, before the six days had passed, Kūṇa played the lute. Then, the foremost heavenly maiden spoke this verse:
"Those who are able to offer their upper robes As gifts to others will be born as noble and superior among humans, And dwell in heaven just as I do now."
My body is like a mass of pure gold, its radiance and color most serene;
among the hundreds of celestial maidens, I am the most honored and supreme.
Because I gave away that which was dear to me, my merit is thus preeminent.
The second goddess spoke again in verse:
"If one bestows the finest flavors, Dishes, and food as offerings,
One will be born as a human, male or female, And among men and women, the most excellent."
If one is born in the heavens, just as I am today,
because of having renounced all that is loved, one experiences happiness at will.
Behold my palace, traveling freely through the air.
My body is like a mass of pure gold, and my radiant countenance is most exquisite.
Among the several hundred celestial maidens, I am the most honored and supreme;
by bestowing food and drink of the finest flavor, I have obtained such a superior retribution.
Then the third goddess spoke again in verse:
“If one practices merit by giving superior and wondrous incense as a gift,
one will attain a position of honor and excellence among humans, and dwell in the heavens like my own body.”
Because you have renounced all that is dear, you experience happiness at will.
Behold my palace; it travels freely through the air, and my body is like a mass of pure gold, its radiant countenance most exquisite.
"Among the hundreds of celestial maidens, I am the most honored and supreme;
because I offered this excellent incense, I have obtained such a reward.
A fourth celestial maiden then spoke in verse:
"When I was in my own home, I served my parents-in-law with filial devotion;
though they reviled me with harsh and abusive words, I was able to endure it all."
Therefore, having now attained this celestial body,
because of my filial piety, I enjoy happiness at will.
Behold my palace, traveling freely through the air.
My body is like a mass of pure gold, and my radiant countenance is most exquisite.
Among the hundreds of celestial maidens, I am the most honored and supreme;
because I was able to practice filial piety, I have obtained such a superior reward.
The fifth goddess spoke again in verse:
"In a previous life, I was a servant belonging to another;
I attended upon my master, Complying with his will and never being angry or perverse."
Exerting oneself with diligence and without indolence, rising early and retiring late,

Therefore, having attained this celestial body, I enjoy happiness at will.
Behold my palace: it travels freely through the air, and my body is like a mass of pure gold, with a countenance of most exquisite brilliance.

He instructed me to be diligent, and I was able to hear his teaching of the Dharma;

I enjoy happiness according to my wish—look at my palace!
Traversing through space with sovereign ease, my body is like the color of pure gold,

283. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain deva, whose radiance was twice that of usual, approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.

At that time, the deva spoke these verses:
"How can that which arises necessarily perish?"
How does one prevent non-arising?
How does one abandon fear?
How does one achieve the joy of the Dharma?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"When anger arises, it must be extinguished; When greed and desire are born, they must be restrained.
Abandoning ignorance brings fearlessness; Realizing cessation is the supreme bliss."
Abandoning ill will and relinquishing desire, emerging from all fetters and latent tendencies, one does not cling to form or name, but contemplates the forest of emptiness of all phenomena.
Desire is the root of birth and death; desire is able to give rise to all suffering.
By severing desire, one attains liberation; so too it is with all sufferings.
