What is the craving for life?
What is the bondage of life?
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"Form cannot know life; Volitional formations do not perceive life.
To be greedily attached to one's own life, And to love life—this constitutes bondage."
Then the Devaputra Indra spoke again in verse:
“As the Buddha has taught, form is not the life-force;
how then can it, together with the mental consciousness, constitute the aggregate of the body?”
The World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“Consciousness depends upon the kalala; the kalala is the very first.
From the kalala the arbuda is born, and from the arbuda the peśī is produced.”
From the flesh-mass, the solid organs arise; from the solid organs, the five viscera arise;
from the viscera, hair and nails arise. From these, the five sense-faculties are produced, distinguished by male and female characteristics.
Thus they undergo transformation without a moment's rest.
"For these reasons and conditions, how could there be such a thing as a life-span?
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that devaputra rejoiced, prostrated himself in worship, and returned to his celestial palace.
299 (Two Hundred and Ninety-nine). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Śakra, whose radiance was twice his usual brilliance. During that night, he came to where the Buddha was; the light from his body shone brilliantly, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove with a great and dazzling light. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and spoke these verses:
"One who has severed all fetters, yet still abandons their various duties,
and teaches others [only for gain], is not called a true śramaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“O Yakṣa, you should know that those oppressed by various kinds of suffering and affliction deserve the compassion of the wise,
who should instruct them by teaching the Dharma.
You must not abandon them so that they fall into the path of suffering.”
"The Arhat harbors compassion and wisdom, rescuing and delivering others without fault.
At that time, the Śakradevendra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, prostrated himself, and returned to his celestial palace.
300. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a son of heaven named Agragṛhapati (The Most Excellent Householder), whose divine radiance shone brilliantly, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and spoke these verses:
"Always study and recite virtuous verses; Draw near to and honor the śramaṇas;
Constantly delight in empty and quiet places; And remain tranquil and composed regarding the sense faculties.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Constantly study and recite virtuous verses; draw near to and honor the śramaṇas;
always delight in empty and secluded places; and bring tranquility to the mind.
When the Devaputra Uttara heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced, prostrated himself, and returned to his celestial palace.
301 (Three Hundred and One). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a deva named Śibi, whose majestic radiance and extraordinary countenance illuminated the entire Jeta Grove with a brilliant light. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and spoke these verses:
"With whom should one dwell?
With whom should one associate?
From whom may one obtain the True Dharma and attain supreme excellence free from affliction?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"One should dwell together with the noble and holy; It is fitting to be in harmony with the virtuous.
By consulting the noble on the True Dharma, One attains excellence and is free from fault."
At that time, the Śibi Devaputra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and prostrated himself, then returned to his celestial palace.
302 (Three hundred and two). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Candrasvāmin, whose majestic radiance illuminated the entire Jeta Grove. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and spoke these verses:
“Practicing dhyāna to its ultimate limit, Observing the fasts of the grass-eating cock and deer, He has accomplished the relinquishing of pleasure And attained the four dhyānas.”
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Though one may practice those meditations, One still remains within the net of birth and death.
But one who can maintain right mindfulness, Dwelling alone with a tranquil mind,"
"Far removed from birth and death, like a swan escaping from a net.
When the Devaputra Candrasvāmin heard what the Buddha had spoken, he rejoiced, prostrated himself, and returned to his celestial palace.
303 (Three Hundred and Three). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a son of heaven named Vinita, whose majestic radiance was brilliant and intensely luminous. He came to the Jeta Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and spoke these verses:
"Those who draw near to the Buddha, None fail to find joy;
may they cause all people To delight in your Dharma teaching,
And enable those who practice and study To attain non-negligence."
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"This Dharma is well-instructed; Knowing the proper time and being heedless of none, One attains mastery over Māra, And Māra finds no opportunity."
At that time, the devaputra Viśuddha, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, prostrated himself, and returned to his celestial palace.
304 (Three hundred four). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Pañcāla, whose radiance was brilliant and exceedingly bright, and whose deportment was dignified and orderly. He approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and spoke in verse:
"Living at home is entangled in manifold affairs; Leaving home is exceedingly vast and open.
The Muni, through single-minded diligence, Emerges from dhyāna with awakened realization."
"Attaining vast enlightenment in an instant, he opened up and manifested great wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Though dwelling amidst the affairs of manifold conditions, one is also able to attain the Dharma."
"One who is able to possess the power of mindfulness, by virtue of being able to concentrate the mind single-pointedly—
only such a person of clear wisdom shall attain and realize Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the devaputra Pañcāla, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, prostrated, and returned to his celestial palace.
305 (Three Hundred and Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a devaputra named Susīma, who, together with a retinue of five hundred, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"If there were anyone in the world who could speak according to reality, they should say:

'The bhikṣu Śāriputra maintains the precepts and is widely learned; he has few desires and knows meditative concentration; he delights in seclusion and quietude, and diligently cultivates samādhi; he possesses great power of mindfulness and achieves wisdom; he has swift, sharp, and penetrating wisdom; he well understands the essential way of deliverance, deeply comprehends the vehicle of liberation, and is perfected in true knowledge.'"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is truly as the Holy Teaching declares; if one were to speak according to the facts, he should say:”
“‘The bhikṣu Śāriputra is foremost in upholding the precepts and in extensive learning, even unto the attainment of true wisdom.

At that time, when the sons of the gods heard the Tathāgata and Ānanda praise Śāriputra, their celestial countenances became increasingly upright and majestic; the radiance of their bodies was twice as extraordinary as usual, illuminating the Jetavana Grove everywhere with a brilliant and great light.
At that time, the devaputra Susīma, his countenance and majestic radiance having become even more intense, joined his palms toward the Buddha and spoke in verse:
“Śāriputra is of great learning, And is universally acclaimed as one of great wisdom;
Upholding the precepts and well-disciplined, He is praised by the World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“Śāriputra is of great learning, And is universally acclaimed as one of great wisdom;
Upholding the precepts and well-disciplined, He is praised by the World-Honored One.”
"Having attained the quiescence of non-arising, you shall destroy Māra and abide in your final body.
When Susīma heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced, prostrated himself in worship, and returned to his celestial palace.
306 (Three Hundred and Six). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Rāśmika, whose radiance was twice as bright as usual. He approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Where can one find that which is without birth, aging, or death; without perishing or emerging;
the ultimate limit of sentient beings? Can such a boundary be known?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the devaputra Crimson Horse, saying:
"That which is without birth, old age, or death, which neither passes away nor is born—no one is able to travel to its limit, nor is there anyone who can go to it and reach its ultimate boundary."
Then the devaputra Rāśmiśva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What the World-Honored One has spoken is most excellent and rare; it is free from birth, old age, and death, and none can reach its limit.”

Why is this? I recall that in the past, I was once a rishi named Crimson Horse (*Raktāśva*). Having severed the fetters of desire, I attained the five mundane superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*); my spiritual power and swiftness surpassed those of the sun and moon, such that with a single leap of my foot, I could cross the great ocean.
I then formed this thought:
"My supernatural power is so swift and fleet; I shall travel until I reach the very limit of sentient beings.

At that time, because my will was solely intent on seeking the limit of sentient beings, my mind was restless and entirely without leisure, except for the moments of washing my hands, eating and drinking, and attending to the calls of nature. Throughout those hundred years, I was ultimately unable to reach the limit of sentient beings, and I passed away.

For this reason, it is known that the Tathāgata has well taught that there is no place where one can go to reach the limit of that which is unborn, undecaying, and undying, neither emerging nor submerging—such a thing is simply impossible.
The Buddha said to the devaputra Crimson Horse: “So it is! So it is!”
If there were no birth, aging, or death, and no arising or ceasing, it would be impossible for there to be a limit to sentient beings.
If one wishes to know this, the limit of sentient beings is itself nirvana; when the limit of suffering is exhausted, that is what is called attaining its limit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Though one possesses such supernormal powers, In the end,
none could ever reach The limit of all sentient beings."
If one does not reach the limit, how can one exhaust the limit of suffering?
Only those of supreme wisdom are called "those who well know the world," for they alone can clearly understand the limit;
having thus established the holy life, they have reached its fulfillment.
"By means of right wisdom, one reaches the limit of sentient beings and crosses over to the other shore.
When the deva Crimson Horse heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced, prostrated himself, and returned to his celestial palace.
307 (Three Hundred and Seven) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there were six devaputras who had originally been followers of the six heretical teachers: the first was named Durdharsa, the second Vaśitā, the third Prabhāsvara, the fourth Nirjita, the fifth Kālotthita, and the sixth Paribhāvaka.
That night, these six devaputras all came to where the Buddha was and sat to one side.
The radiance of these gods was twice as superior as usual, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove with a brilliant and magnificent light.
At that time, Duṣprasaha spoke these verses:
"A bhikṣu who may be subject to reproach and censure, Who self-restrains himself throughout the four watches of the day,
And who, having seen and heard, abides [in mindfulness]— Such a person is free from all evils."
The Devaputra Īśvara spoke again in verse:

“Austere asceticism may be subject to reproach; One should restrain and govern one’s own body, Sever evil speech, anger, and strife, And regard suffering and joy as equal to those of the World-Honored One.”
"Before the Lord of Dharma, one shall not commit any evils.
The Devaputra Khyāpana further spoke in verse:
"Cutting, harming, performing sacrifices, burning with fire, and so forth—"
"There is no retribution for good or evil; this is what Kāśyapa has taught.
The Devaputra Jie-sheng (Decisive-Victory) further spoke in verse:
"The Nirgrantha Jñātiputra always speaks these words:"
"Having practiced austerities through the long night, Having severed the habit of false speech, One is not far from Arhatship;
Such a person is reckoned among the ranks of the World-Honored Ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“From this day forth, whether you are alone or in a great multitude,
I regard you all as loathsome and foul, no different from corpses.
How can you, like jackals, be compared to that Lion King?”
"You who honor the naked ascetics, Who delight in the most wicked falsehoods—
Such as these non-Buddhists, They are far removed from Arhatship.
Then a certain devaputra spoke again in verse:
“Those who practice such asceticism are deeply deserving of censure;
though they dwell in seclusion, their labors are in vain.
I pray that you will protect them and provide them with instruction.”
"He will surely proceed to the realm of form, And be born in the Brahma-world in joy.
Then the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"All forms that exist in the world, Whether here or in other places..."
And those who possess great radiance within the void—
all such as these have entirely fallen into the snare of Māra,
just as a fisherman covers a multitude of fish with a net.
Another deva then spoke a verse:
"Explaining the faults of existence and desire, Along with all delusions, illusions, and evils— He has completely severed them all;
I praise him who has cut the fetters of desire."
One should prostrate before him, Make offerings, and offer praise;
The reason for doing so is that He is indeed the World-Honored One.
Then another devaputra spoke a verse, saying:
"Having spoken of the faults of existence and anger, as well as all the evils of delusion and illusion, he has severed them all;
he praises the severing of the fetters of anger.
One should pay him homage, making offerings and praising him."
"The reason it is thus is that he is the World-Honored One himself.
Then another devaputra spoke in verse:
"He has explained the faults of existence and delusion, Along with all the evils of delusive illusion."
"Having severed them all completely, he praises those who have abandoned delusion.
Then another devaputra spoke in verse:
"He speaks of the fault of pride, along with all the evils of arrogance and illusion."
"Having completely severed all [views], he praises the abandonment of pride.
Then another devaputra spoke in verse:
"He has explained the faults of various views, as well as the evils of the illusions of those views."
"Having completely severed all [defilements], he praises those who have abandoned views.
Then another son of heaven spoke in verse:
"He speaks of the faults of attachment to existence, as well as the evils of the illusions of craving."
"Having severed everything completely, he praises those who have abandoned craving.
Another devaputra then spoke in verse:
"Among all the mountains of Rājagṛha, Vipaśyana is the most supreme."
Among all the mountains upon the great earth, the King of Snow Mountains is supreme;
among all the worlds in the four directions, above, below, and in the intermediate quarters,
the Tathāgata is the most honored among all devas and humans.
At that time, when the sons of the gods had heard what the Buddha taught and each had spoken a verse, they joyfully prostrated and returned to their celestial palaces.

[The following titles are: "Indra Inquires about Longevity," "Severing All Fetters," "The Discourse on the Well-Spoken [Teachings] to the Householder Sūcitta," and "Śibi Inquires about Dwelling Together."
The swift inquiry into the limit; the inquiry of Bāhuka on great joy;
the inquiry of Mahānāma on bashfulness; the first inquiry of Pañcāla-kambala on Suśīma;
and the inquiries of the non-Buddhists regarding various views.
308 (Three Hundred and Eight) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Makha who came to where the Buddha was. His radiance was blazing and his brilliance was magnificent; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side and spoke these verses:
"By harming whom does one sleep in peace?
By harming whom is there no sorrow?
By extinguishing which single dharma is one praised by the Noble Ones?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“He who has overcome anger sleeps in peace; he who has overcome anger finds no sorrow.
Anger is the root of poison; it feigns intimacy to harm others.”
"The extinction of these various phenomena is what the noble ones praise.
At that time, Makha, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, prostrated himself in worship, and returned to his celestial palace.
309 (Three Hundred and Nine) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a son of the gods named Mikhaka who came to where the Buddha was. His majestic radiance was brilliant and his splendor was great, illuminating everything. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
"How does one manifest illumination within the world?
What is this unsurpassed, supreme illumination?
I pray that the Buddha will explain to me such a profound meaning."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"In all the worlds, there are three kinds of illumination.
What are these three illuminations?"
The so-called sun, moon,
and fire can provide illumination everywhere throughout the day and night,
both in the heavens and among humans; yet the Buddha alone is the unsurpassed light.
At that time, the devaputra Mikhaka, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, prostrated, and returned to his celestial palace. 310 (310). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a son of heaven named Dharmasiri who came to where the Buddha was. His majestic radiance shone so brightly that it pervaded the entire Jeta Grove.
He withdrew to sit on one side and spoke in verse:
“The Brahmin now has severed The fetters of desire within the three realms of existence.”
"Having no desire for any state of existence, what indeed remains to be done?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"The Brahmin has nothing to do; he reflects that his task is already finished."
When crossing water, the feet must reach the bottom; only thus can one arrive at the other shore.
If the feet do not reach the bottom, one cannot reach the other shore.
The movement of hands and feet is what is called "having something done."
Using this as a metaphor, I clarify the meaning of non-action;
Dharma, you should know that I have exhausted all outflows,
abide in my final body, and have transcended all faults of craving for existence.
"Having severed everything completely, one transcends and crosses over the ocean of birth and death.
At that time, the devaputra Dharmaka, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, prostrated himself, and returned to his celestial palace.
311 (Three Hundred and Eleven). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Tāla-ketu who came to where the Buddha was. His countenance was radiant and brilliant, its light pervading the entire Jeta Grove. He withdrew to sit to one side and spoke these verses:
“How many phenomena are to be abandoned?
How many phenomena are to be relinquished?
How many phenomena are to be cultivated and increased?”
How many qualities must a bhikṣu fulfill?
How many qualities must he generally cultivate and eliminate to cross over the swift current?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Having removed the five aggregates of grasping born of desire, And having cast off the five hindrances,
One advances in the cultivation of the five faculties And accomplishes the five branches of enlightenment."
"A bhikṣu such as this transcends and crosses over the ocean of birth and death.
At that time, the devaputra Tāla-khaṇḍa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, prostrated, and returned to his celestial palace.
312 (Three Hundred and Twelve) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a son of the gods named Kāmada who came to where the Buddha was. His radiance was brilliant and magnificent, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘that which is difficult to do and difficult to perform’?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“The seeker performs what is difficult to do;
Fully endowed with precepts and concentration, They attain freedom from all worldly affairs, Tranquil and joyful.
At that time, the devaputra Kama again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Truly, as the holy teaching says, silence and stillness are difficult to achieve.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Kātyāyana, you who now desire to attain that which is so difficult to obtain,"
"By practicing meditative concentration day and night, one will surely be able to abide in peaceful silence.
At that time, Kāma addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"The mind is difficult to concentrate."
The World-Honored One replied again in verse:
"By concentration, one gathers the distracted mind; With determination, one dwells where the faculties are difficult to steady.
Destroying the snare of death, One is able to attain noble wisdom."
Kātyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The deep and perilous path is obstructed and difficult; by what means can one cross over it?
The World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Those who are not noble will surely fall into the abyss; once collapsed, there is no way to pass through.
When the sages tread upon the perilous path, they cross over it with ease and security.
At that time, Kāma, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and prostrated himself in worship, then returned to his celestial palace.
313 (313). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Kāmada who came to where the Buddha was. His radiance was brilliant, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to stand to one side and spoke these verses:
“What is the root of greed and hatred?
What is it that constitutes pleasure, displeasure, and fear? Who is it that exists for these things?
When an infant grasps its mother’s breast, from where does the consciousness arise?”
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
"From craving to my own mind, it is like the nyagrodha tree:
its roots and fibers grow from the soil, and only then do they enter the earth."
Each in their respective places, attachment gives rise to desire,
just as the *māluta* creeper entwines and covers the trees of the forest.
If one knows its root, the yakṣa should abandon it.
"Able to cross the ocean of birth and death, having crossed over, they shall not undergo existence again.
At that time, the devaputra Kāma heard what the Buddha had said; filled with joy, he prostrated himself and returned to his celestial palace.
314 (314). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Candana who approached the place where the Buddha was. His countenance was radiant and his brilliance was so intense that it illuminated the entire Jeta Grove. He stood to one side and spoke these verses:
"I now ask Gautama: You who possess the great wisdom of discerning the distinctions between lineages,
who have removed all obscurations, and whose knowledge and vision are entirely clear—
where do you dwell?"
"By practicing what teaching will one have no fear in future lives and obtain the fruit of goodness?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
Abandoning the evils of speech and mind, and not performing unwholesome deeds with the body;
if one dwells at home, practicing generosity like a flowing stream,
frequently receiving the precepts with faith, and restraining the mind while distributing wealth;
"Devas, you should dwell in this place and practice the matters as described above;
if you can act with a diligent mind, there will be no fear whatsoever in future lives.
When the Deva Candana heard what the Buddha had said, he rejoiced, prostrated himself in worship, and returned to his celestial palace.
315. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a devaputra named Candana who came to where the Buddha was. His countenance was radiant and his brilliance was so intense that it illuminated the entire Jeta Grove. He stood to one side and spoke these verses:
"How does one cross the swift current?
Within such a swift current, the waves are exceedingly violent and rapid;
there is no place to grasp or pull, nor is there any ground to stand upon."
"Who is able to dwell within the deep current without being swept away?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"One who is fully complete in all precepts, whose mind is suffused with concentration and wisdom,"
Reflecting within the inner mind, one can cross over that which is difficult to cross.
Having removed the perception of desire, one crosses the stream of the fetters of existence;
having exhausted the craving for existence, one dwells in the depths without sinking.
At that time, the Devaputra Candana, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and prostrated himself, then returned to his celestial palace.
316 (316). Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a son of heaven named Kāśyapa, whose bodily radiance was twice its usual intensity. He came to where the Buddha was, and the light he emitted shone everywhere throughout the Jeta Grove. He withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhikṣu!..."
"I now wish to speak of the benefits for a bhikṣu.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa,
"Speak as you please."
At that time, Kāśyapa spoke these verses:
“The bhikṣu who is able to maintain mindfulness, Whose mind has attained excellent liberation,
Having sought whatever desires there may be, He reaches the stainless state.”
One who can know the world, both its defilement and its purity,
who has abandoned all existence and possesses no accumulations—
such a person is called a bhikṣu, one who possesses the merit of supreme excellence.
When the devaputra Kāśyapa had spoken this verse, he joyfully prostrated himself and returned to his celestial palace. 317 (317).
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a deva named Kāśyapa, whose radiance was twice its usual intensity. During that very night, he approached the place where the Buddha was; his bodily light shone brilliantly, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove. He withdrew to sit at one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Bhikṣu!..."
"I now likewise wish to speak of the merits obtained by a bhikṣu.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
"Speak as you wish.
Kāśyapa then spoke in verse:
"The bhikṣu who is able to maintain mindfulness, Whose mind has attained excellent liberation,"
Wishing to attain nirvāṇa, he has already understood the world;
He understands existence and non-existence, and deeply knows that all phenomena are empty.
Such a person is called a bhikṣu; having transcended existence, he attains nirvāṇa.
When the devaputra Kāśyapa had spoken these verses, he joyfully prostrated and returned to his celestial palace.
Makhā asked about what was harmed; Mikha consulted the Illuminator;
Dhamma recited what ought to be done; and Tārā inquired about her shortcomings.
The extremely difficult-to-attain treasure-trove, the silence that resolves the two doubts,
true wisdom, and crossing the stream— these were spoken by Candana;
as for the stainless existence and non-existence, these two were discussed by the two Kāśyapas.

In this section, the chapter on the yakṣa Indra does not differ from what was previously spoken by the devaputra Indra; because it is redundant, it has been omitted and not transmitted. The subsequent chapter on the yakṣa Śakra does not differ from the previous devaputra Śakra, and thus it too is omitted and not recorded. Herein, at the beginning of the twelfth fascicle of the Eastern Edition (318): Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha, intending to go to the palace of the yakṣa Gopaka.
Then the yakṣa Gopaka went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I only pray that the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus will stay overnight in my palace this night."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Then, the yakṣa Guhacakra, desiring to provide lodging for the Buddha and his assembly, immediately manifested five hundred palaces, fully equipped with couches, mats, and bedding.
Furthermore, he magically manifested five hundred fire-pits, within which the fires blazed intensely yet emitted no smoke at all.
He invited the Buddha to his palace and offered him the upper chamber, while the five hundred bhikṣus took the remaining rooms in succession.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had entered his room and sat down, the yakṣa Guhṇaka stood to one side and spoke these verses:
“Joy is found in right mindfulness; mindfulness of the right is also joy.
When the mind’s intent is never forgotten, one attains peaceful sleep through right mindfulness.”
Through right mindfulness one attains noble happiness;
neither victorious nor defeated, one gives rise everywhere to loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings, remaining free from all enmity and hatred.
"This is indeed the Great Bliss; there is nothing that surpasses it.
Having spoken this verse, the yakṣa Kukkuṭa bowed his head in joyful prostration and departed.
319 (Three Hundred Nineteen). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Pāṇḍava.
At that time, the Venerable Hatthaka was the Buddha’s attendant.
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking in meditation during the night when a light rain fell and flashes of lightning shone brightly.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately manifested a pavilion of lapis lazuli to cover over the Buddha. Having performed this deed, he approached the Buddha’s location, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; yet the Tathāgata continued his walking meditation without yet coming to rest.
At that time, whenever the children of that country cried and would not stop, they would immediately frighten them with the *Bakula* ghost.
However, it is the constant rule for all Buddhas that a teacher must not enter a room until his disciples have entered the chamber first; yet [the Buddha] had fallen asleep beforehand.
At that time, Hastaka made this thought:
"The night has already grown long and the World-Honored One does not sleep; I shall become a *bakkula* spirit to frighten him into sleep."
Having formed this thought, he immediately put it on backward and, holding both ends together, led him to the head of the walking path and said to the Buddha:
"Śramaṇa! Śramaṇa!"
"The Bakkula ghost has come.
At that time, the Buddha said to Nāgita:
"You are truly foolish to attempt to terrify me with the Bakkula ghost. Do you not know that the Tathāgata has long since severed all alarm, fear, bristling of the hair, and every kind of dread?"
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having seen and heard this, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Within the Buddha-dharma, there are also such renunciants as these.”
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas: "Kauśika!
The Gautama clan is exceedingly vast and expansive, possessing great capacity for inclusion; such a person as this shall also before long attain the pure Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one practices the way of a brahmin within one's own dharma,
reaching the further shore, one exhausts all fetters of existence and outflows."
If, within one's own Dharma, one fully practices as a brahmin,
one is said to have reached the further shore, observing the cessation and disappearance of all sensations.
If, within one's own Dharma, one fully practices as a brahmin...
Those who have reached the further shore observe the exhaustion and disappearance of causes.
If one practices the Dharma within oneself as a true Brahmin,
one can cross over to the further shore and observe the cessation of the fetters.
If, within one’s own Dharma, one fully practices as a brahmin and crosses to the further shore,
one contemplates birth, old age, sickness, and death. If,
within one’s own Dharma, one fully practices as a brahmin...
"Those who have crossed to the other shore, / Are able to cross over the piśācas / And reach the further shore of the bālakhilyas.
At that time, Śakra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and prostrated himself, then returned to his celestial palace.
320 (Three Hundred and Twenty). At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha traveled from the Buddha’s presence and arrived at the palace of Hārītī in the kingdom of Magadha.

At that time, during the middle watch of the night, Aniruddha rose early, sat upright with his body straight, and recited the Dhammapada verses as well as the verses of the Mahākaccāyana-bhaddaka, further chanting aloud their meanings and the Sūtras and other texts.
At that time, the beloved youngest son of Hārītī, named Piṅgala, was weeping and shedding tears.
Then Hārītī consoled her son, saying:
"The practitioner is reciting the sūtra; do not weep."
He then spoke in verse:
“Pigala, cease your noise; Listen to the monk reciting the Dhammapada verses.
Having heard these verses, you shall abandon broken precepts, Attain purity, and be able to maintain the prohibitions.”
“Pigala, hush your voice; listen to the monk recite the Dhammapada verses.
Having heard these verses, you shall attain non-killing.
Pigala, hush your voice; listen to the monk recite the Dhammapada verses. Having heard these verses, you shall attain truthful speech.”
"You, Piṅgala, cease your crying; listen to the monk reciting the Dhammapada verses.
Having heard these verses, you shall be released from this ghostly womb; therefore, you should stop your wailing."
321. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the palace of the yakṣiṇī Pūrṇaśikhā in the kingdom of Magadha.
That night, the Buddha stayed in that palace. During the night, his son, the yakṣa Vāsava, and the yakṣī Utpalā wept.
At that time, their mother comforted her son and daughter, wishing to stop their crying, and spoke this verse:
“Vāsava and Utpalā, you two now—”
"You should cease your crying.
The Buddha, the Hero of the World, has taught the essential Dharma; let me hear it. Neither father nor mother can deliver one from suffering and affliction."
Only the World-Honored One, skillfully expounding the Dharma, can cause those who hear it to forever leave all suffering behind.
All sentient beings follow the stream of desire and sink into the sea of birth and death; I wish to listen to the Dharma in order to sever this stream of desire.
"Pūrṇaśa and Udraka, for this reason you all should remain silent.
Then Pūrṇaśa spoke in verse:
"I now follow my mother’s instruction and shall no longer produce a sound;
little sister Utpalā, you too must remain silent now.
I pray that you listen as that śramaṇa speaks the subtle and wondrous Dharma."
The Buddha, supreme among men in Magadha,
has extensively expounded for the sake of all sentient beings the Dharma that severs suffering.
He taught that suffering gives rise to suffering, and he taught the essential path for escaping suffering.
"You have spoken of the Noble Eightfold Path, the secure way leading to Nirvana.
Excellent is it to hear from a śramaṇa the essence of the Dharma you teach.
The mother replied in verse:
“You are one who possesses knowledge and vision; what you have said accords with my own mind.
You have well praised that Guide of the World.
Because of your silence, I have come to see the Four Noble Truths.”
"Uttara, at a later time, you too shall see the Four Truths.
(322) Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and arrived at the palace of the yakṣa Maṇicara.
At that time, the yakṣa Maṇicāra, together with various other yakṣas, was not in his own palace but had gathered at another location.
A woman, carrying fine incense and flowers and bringing along excellent wine, arrived at this yakṣa’s palace.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat within that palace, his faculties tranquil and composed.

Then this woman saw the Tathāgata sitting in the palace, his countenance joyful and serene, his mind profoundly still, and his faculties tranquil and composed; he had attained a well-regulated mind, like a pavilion of gold.
Having seen this, he immediately gave rise to this thought:
"I have now directly beheld the yakṣa Maṇicārin.
Then the woman came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke these verses:
"You are indeed worthy of offerings; please grant me my wish so that you may attain excellence.
All these people of Magadha seek their wishes from you;
you always fulfill their hearts' desires."
"It can bestow blessings and protection.
Now that you have voiced my wish, may I find happiness in the present life and attain rebirth in heaven in a future life.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Be careful not to be negligent, nor give rise to arrogance;
you should always delight in faith and the precepts, and you should bring yourself to transformation and liberation.
If you request the practice of the *maṇi* jewel, what will that accomplish for you?”
"It is not as good as practicing for yourself the karmic conditions for rebirth in heaven.
When that woman heard this verse, she further thought to herself:
"He must certainly not be the yakṣa Maṇi; he is surely the śramaṇa Gautama."
Thereupon, that woman immediately took the fragrant flowers and wine jars, set them aside in one place, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined her palms toward the Buddha, and spoke this verse:
“How can one obtain Joy in the present life and rebirth in heaven hereafter?”
Toward what goal should one proceed to be able to experience happiness?
What kind of karmic actions should one perform?
I now ask you, Gautama: how can one obtain happiness now and, at the end of life, be reborn in heaven?
"Generosity and the taming of the senses can produce happiness;
one who possesses right view and dwells with the virtuous,
who associates with recluses and lives by a right livelihood— what need has such a person to be born there?"
Within the Heaven of the Thirty-three, that is indeed a net of suffering.
You must eliminate desire and attachment; listen with a sincere heart to what I say.
Now, for your sake, I shall expound the Dharma free from dust and defilement.
“You hosts of yakṣas, well done! Listen to the nectar.

Then the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them. In accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas, he spoke on the discourse of giving, the discourse of morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven; he explained that sensual desires are impure and that transcendence from the world is essential.
The Buddha, knowing her mind and that her will was harmonious and compliant, preached for her the Four Noble Truths:

suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. The woman’s intellect was sharp; upon hearing the Dharma, she believed and awakened to it. Like a fresh, clean cotton cloth that easily takes dye, she immediately perceived the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths while seated there. She understood the Dharma, attained the Dharma, fathomed the depths of the Dharma, severed the net of doubt, and crossed to the further shore beyond doubt. No longer following others, she rose and prostrated to the Buddha, joining her palms and saying: "World-Honored One!..."
"I have attained it! I have attained it! For as long as life lasts, I take refuge in the Triple Gem and shall practice non-killing.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the woman was filled with joy; she prostrated herself and departed.
323 (Three Hundred and Twenty-three). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and arrived at the palace of the yakṣa Śarabha, where he stayed for the night.
At that time, the yakṣa Śarabha was gathered with other yakṣas in another location and was not in his palace.
Śarabha’s companion, named Tapana, saw the Buddha staying in Śarabha’s residence; he went to where the yakṣa Śarabha was and said to him, "You have gained great benefit!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is now in your palace, staying there for the night."
The yakṣa Śarabha said,
"How could he have stayed overnight in my palace?
Then the yakṣa spoke to him again:
"Though he is of human form, he is in truth a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Śaraśāṭa spoke again:
"When I return to the palace, I shall know for myself whether he is indeed a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha."

"Is this not so? After the assembly of the Kīṭa Yakṣas had concluded, he returned to his own palace and attempted to touch the Buddha with his body; however, the Buddha’s body moved further away. He then asked the Buddha: "Śramaṇa!"
"Are you now struck with fear?
The Buddha said, "I am not afraid;
it is you who have committed an extremely evil deed."
Śarabha spoke again: "Śramaṇa!
If you can explain my questions now, it would be most excellent and immeasurable."
"If you do not answer me, I shall split your heart so that boiling blood gushes from your face, and I shall further tear out your shoulder and cast it onto the banks of the Vāgī river."
The Buddha said, "I do not see anyone in the world—

whether among gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas— who could cause my mind to become perverted, break my heart so that boiling blood gushes from my mouth, or pull out my arm and hurl it to the other side of the Vaggumudā River."
At that time, Śaraṇa spoke these verses:
“What is the root of sensual desire and ill will?
What are pleasure and displeasure, and what is this fear that makes the hair stand on end?”
Where does that mental consciousness abide?
How is it that an infant, as soon as it is born, knows how to grasp the breast?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Craving arises from the notion of ‘self,’ just like the nyagrodha tree;
wherever sensual craving adheres, it is also like the māluvatī creeper.”
The *nyagrodha* tree is entwined by creepers;
O Yakṣa, you should know this: if one knows its root, one will surely be able to abandon and leave it behind.
He who knows that root can cross the ocean of birth and death.
"Having crossed the swift current of existence, you shall no longer undergo future rebirth.
When the yakṣa Śarabha heard what the Buddha had said, his mind was opened and his understanding clarified; filled with joy and exultation, he immediately took the three refuges.
324. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a certain upāsikā had a son who had undertaken the eight precepts; however, there was a deficiency in his observance of the precepts, and because he had transgressed them, he was possessed by a spirit and went mad.
Then the upāsikā spoke in verse:
"On the fourteenth and fifteenth days, And likewise on the eighth day of the month—
During these months of the Tathāgata’s supernormal power, One should purely observe the eight precepts."
"His practice is without deficiency, and he is not disturbed by ghosts or spirits;
from an Arhat, I have heard such matters as these.
At that time, a yakṣa spoke in verse:
"On the fourteenth and fifteenth days, as well as on the eighth day of the month,
and on the fast days of the month of *śuklapakṣa*, if one maintains the precepts without violation or deficiency,
fully observing the eightfold fast, then spirits and deities will not cause disturbance."
"What you have heard from the Arhat is entirely true.
I shall certainly release you now," said the yakṣa. Thus he spoke.
“Demons vex and toy with those who violate the precepts;
if there is any breach or deficiency, one is tormented by spirits in the present and will reap evil fruits in the future.
Receiving the precepts is like grasping a blade: whether held too tightly or too loosely, both can cause injury.”
The wise Subhūti, having attained the Middle Way, remains unharmed;
But the śramaṇa who does not uphold the Dharma will later suffer the pains of hell.
Like one unskilled in wielding a knife, He is certain to wound his own hand.
"One who grasps well does not cause injury; one who can protect the Dharma of the śramaṇas will surely attain nirvāṇa in the future.
Having finished seizing the child, the yakṣa released him immediately.
Then that upāsikā spoke to her son: "Regarding what the yakṣa has said:
those who are slow in their actions, whose holy life is impure, and who are of wrong livelihood and deceitful—[these will not see the Buddha]."
He will not achieve the great fruit;
he will surely injure his own hand. One who properly maintains the Dharma of a śramaṇa will later certainly draw near to nirvāṇa, just like one who skillfully grasps a sword.
“...lest you injure your own hand.

At that time, after the upāsikā had taught this Dharma to her son in various ways, her son immediately conceived a sense of revulsion. Having become revulsed, he sought to go forth from the household life; he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and became a novice. However, being young, he could not find deep joy in the way of the renunciant life. Because he did not find joy in it, he returned home.
At that time, seeing her son approaching from afar, the laywoman raised her hand and cried out, speaking in verse:
"The house is already burning, with smoke and flames blazing fiercely;
you have skillfully brought out all the goods— why do you come back again, desiring to enter the fire?"
“The house has already been consumed by fire, with smoke and flames blazing fiercely; for what reason have you come back, wishing to be burned and harmed?
At that time, the son spoke again in verse:
“When all people in the world die, they must surely wail and weep.”
"If you do not see [him] now, you too should weep;
for what reason does my mother now cry out like that hungry ghost?
His mother then spoke this verse:
“Since you previously renounced desire and left home to become a śramaṇa,
if you now wish to return to your family, I fear you will be bound by Māra.
For this reason, I weep for you now.”
At that time, the upāsikā rebuked her son in these various ways,
causing him to feel revulsion [for worldly life].
Thereupon, the son went to a forest retreat (āraṇyaka) and applied himself diligently to the practice of the Path, never ceasing day or night, until he attained arhatship.
325 (Three Hundred and Twenty-Five). Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and went to the palace where the yakṣa Āṭavika resided, staying there for the night.
At that time, those yakṣas had gathered in another place for a meeting and were not in their own palace.
There was a yakṣa named Donkey Colt (Khañjaka) who, seeing the Tathāgata staying overnight in the Wilderness Palace, went immediately to where the Wilderness Ghosts were and said to them:
"You have gained great benefit; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is staying overnight in your palace."
The Wild replied,
"How could that man have stayed overnight in my palace?
Then the Mule Colt Yakṣa spoke to him again:
"Although he is human, he is in fact a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Kātyāyana spoke again:
"Are you certain that he is truly a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha?"
"Is this not so? At that time, having finished his assembly in the wilderness and returned to his own palace, he saw the Buddha and spoke these words: "Get out!
“Śramaṇa.
At that time, because of his dwelling place, the Tathāgata emerged in accordance with those words.
He spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"The śramaṇa shall enter.
The Buddha, having severed his conceit (*asmimāna*), entered again in accordance with her words.
A second and a third time, she told the Buddha to come in and go out, and the Buddha complied with her each time.
The fourth one also said,
"Shramana, get out!
The Buddha said:
"You have already made three requests, yet I shall not emerge for you now.
Kātyāyana then said, "I wish to pose difficult questions; if you can explain them, I will allow you to sit."

"If you do not answer me, I shall cause your mind to become deranged and shatter your heart, so that boiling blood shall gush from your face; then, seizing your arm, I will hurl you onto the banks of the Vāgī river."
The Buddha said:
"I do not see anyone in the world—whether among devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—who can speak of me as you have spoken."
"Whatever you wish to ask, ask according to your desire.
Then the Vindhya Ghost spoke in verse:
Among all forms of wealth and treasure, Which is the most excellent?
What virtuous conduct, when practiced, can bring about a pleasant retribution?
Among all delicious flavors, which is the most excellent?
Among all forms of life, which lifespan is the most supreme?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Among all forms of wealth among people, The wealth of faith is foremost and most excellent.
Those who practice the Dharma Are able to attain happiness."
"Truthful speech is the most delicious flavor; wisdom is the supreme life.
Then the Kāntāra Yakṣa spoke again in verse:
"Who crosses the swift current?"
Who crosses the great ocean?
Who is able to abandon suffering?
Who attains purity?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Faith can cross the swift current; Heedfulness crosses the ocean;
Diligence can leave suffering behind; Wisdom can bring about purity."
The wilderness yakṣa spoke again in verse:
"How can one attain faith?
How can one attain wealth?"
"How does one obtain a good reputation?
How does one obtain virtuous friends?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
The Arhat attains faith; by practicing the Dharma, one attains Nirvana.
By performing what ought to be done, one accumulates wealth through diligence.
Truthful speech brings renown afar; generous giving wins friends.
"You may inquire at length with śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas:
'From whom can one obtain true speech?
Apart from me, who possesses the Dharma?'"
"Among the ninety-six kinds of paths, you have observed and questioned them with truth:
whose dharma is non-harming, and who is able to possess self-discipline and composure?
At that time, Āṭavaka spoke again in verse:
"What need is there to further question those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who display great diligence and skillfully analyze and teach the Dharma?
I now call to mind your kindness; it is because you have shown me [the way] that I am here."
May I now behold the Unsurpassed Great Caravan Leader.
From this day forward, wherever I may travel—
be it through cities or villages— I shall always take refuge in the Buddha.
"Manifesting the True Dharma.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the Yakṣa Vana rejoiced and leaped for joy; he took refuge in the Triple Gem, received the prohibitive precepts, and became a disciple of the Buddha.
326. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī in the royal park monastery named Vīrā; "Vīrā" means "heroine" in the language of Qin.

At that time, all the people of that country collectively held the Kummāsapinda festival for seven days and seven nights, gathering in joyous celebration; yet there was no one who invited the bhikṣuṇīs.

At that time, there was a yakṣa who had conceived a heart of faith and reverence for the bhikṣuṇī Vīra. Knowing that none among the people of the various kingdoms had invited her, he recited these verses in the midst of the lanes and alleys:
"The people of Rājagṛha city Are all intoxicated and asleep;
The bhikṣuṇī Vīra Has entered silently into a sublime samādhi."
The practitioner is truly a hero, having accomplished the dharma of a hero.
This bhikṣuṇī has skillfully cultivated her faculties;
forever free from dust and defilement, she has attained the peace of nirvāṇa.
"A person of such great virtue deserves diligent and increased offerings.
Why is it that among you now there is no one at all who extends an invitation?
When the upāsakas of that city heard these verses, each of them took clothing and various delicacies and came to offer them to that bhikṣuṇī.
At that time, the yakṣa saw all these people making offerings one by one, and spoke again in verse:
“The bhikṣuṇī Vīra has severed all fetters;
the upāsaka is possessed of wisdom.”
One who can bestow food upon others, by virtue of that gift of food, attains the increase of great merit.
The bhikṣuṇī Vīrā has severed all fetters and latent tendencies.
The wise upāsaka, who is able to give a piṇḍola robe—
by virtue of giving that robe, he attains great and increasing merit. (327) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī in the royal park monastery named Śuklā.

Then, all the people of the country collectively held a festival for the Puṣya constellation, gathering in joyous celebration for seven days and seven nights; yet, there was no one who invited that bhikṣuṇī.

At that time, there was a yakṣa who conceived a heart of faith and reverence for the bhikṣuṇī Śuklā. Knowing that none among the people of the various kingdoms had invited her, he spoke these verses in the midst of the lanes:
"The people of Rājagṛha Are all intoxicated and asleep;
They do not invite the bhikṣuṇī Who has cultivated her faculties."
Pure and of pure dharma, the bhikṣuṇī is well-concentrated;
forever free from defilement, she has attained nirvāṇa through cessation.
Such a person of great virtue deserves diligent offerings.
"How is it that you all now have no one at all to invite you for alms?
When the people within the city heard these verses, each of them took food and clothing to offer as alms to the bhikṣuṇī.
At that time, seeing that he had obtained food and clothing, the yakṣa spoke again in verse:
"The pure bhikṣuṇī has severed the fetters of craving.
The wise upāsaka was able to give her this food."
Because she gave food to her, she obtained immeasurable merit.
The nun Śuklā severed her stinginess and greed.
The wise upāsaka was able to give her a robe.
"Because of giving those robes to him, one obtains immeasurable merit. (328) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there were two yakṣas:
the first was named Saptaparvata and the second was named Himavat.
These two yakṣas were close friends and made a solemn vow together:
"If a wondrous jewel should appear in your palace, you must tell me;
and if a wondrous jewel should appear in my palace, I shall likewise tell you.
At that time, within the palace of the Yakṣa of the Snowy Mountains, there was a thousand-petaled lotus as large as a chariot wheel, with a stem of deep-blue lapis lazuli and filaments of diamond.
When the yakṣa of the Snowy Mountains witnessed this event, he immediately dispatched a messenger to say to the Seven Peaks:
"In my palace there is such a marvelous object; you should come to behold it."
At that time, having heard these words, the yakṣa Saptaparvata thought to himself:

"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is nearby and not far away; he may be sent to the yakṣas of the Snowy Mountains with this message. I shall certainly go there myself to see the precious flowers."
Having formed this thought, he immediately sent a messenger again, saying:
"In my possession here is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has manifested his form here; what benefit could such precious flowers as you have in your palace possibly provide?"

Since you have been able to leave the household life and abandon all worldly affairs, you should fulfill your original aspiration; do not be overwhelmed by sleep.

The nature of desire is impermanent; it is restless and never still.

This cannot be called "leaving home.

One should be diligent and energetic, never flagging day or night, resolutely seeking nirvana.

With wisdom and consciousness dispelling ignorance, exhausting all outflows and fetters,

since I have attained the essential way out, what further use have I for written words?
"Whatever exists in the world, all things seen and heard—having completely relinquished them all, one does not undergo further existence.
(358) At that time, there was another bhikṣu living in dependence upon a forest in the kingdom of Kośala. His vision became dim, so he requested a physician to examine him.
The physician said to him:
"Bhikṣu! If you can smell the fragrance of a lotus flower, your eyes will regain their clarity."
That bhikṣu believed his words and further asked him,
"Where can I obtain such lotus flowers?
The physician then replied:
"If you wish to obtain the fragrance of lotuses, you should go to the place where the lotus pond is.
At that time, the bhikṣu followed those words, went to the location of the pond, and sat upright to inhale the scent.
At that time, a deva, seeing this, spoke these verses:
"The lotuses born within the pond Exude a most fragrant scent;
Yet you do not see their owner— How can you steal the flowers' fragrance?"
"But you, at this very moment, are truly named a thief.
Great Seer, for what reason have you stolen that incense?
The bhikṣu replied with a verse:
"O Deva, you should know: when a lotus grows from within a pond, I do not harm its roots or stalks, nor do I steal it;
I merely smell its fragrance from afar."
"For what reason is he called the 'thief of fragrance'?
I do not accept this statement.
The celestial deity spoke again in verse:
"In a pond there are fragrant flowers; if one takes them without asking their owner, and the donor has not given them away, people of the world call this theft.
Great Seer, you have stolen these flowers; you have certainly committed the offense of theft."
At that time, a man came and entered this pond, where he used a sickle to cut and sever the roots and leaves of the lotuses, carrying them away on his back in heavy loads.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu spoke again in verse:
"This man has entered the pond, Cutting and uprooting the flowers, roots, and seeds."
"In utter disorder they trampled it, and with heavy burdens they carried it away.
Why did you not stop them? You spoke of their having stolen it!
The deva replied in verse:
“That person who enters the pool constantly commits evil deeds;
like a nursing mother wearing black clothes,
though she has much spittle, she feels no sense of defilement or disgrace.”
You are like a pure white cloth, easily stained by defilement;
therefore, I restrain you, yet I cannot restrain that other person.
An evil person is like a black cloth; they commit evil without being censured.
A fresh white surface with spots, such as those resembling fly-legs,
is seen by all people in the world;
when there is even a slight, subtle fault, the analogy is likewise.
A black spot upon a conch shell is seen by all from afar;
yet one who has severed the fetters of the defilements has all karma purified.
Even a slight evil, as small as a hair or a strand of wool, is seen by others like a mountain peak.
The bhikṣu spoke again in verse:
"The deva now benefits me, for the sake of my deliverance;
wherever he sees me, he repeatedly awakens me."
The deva replied with a verse:
"It was not by means of wealth that you purchased me;
nor did you conquer another kingdom to capture me as a prisoner."
"You yourself shall know your own loss and gain; who can awaken you?
You should now reflect for yourself upon all matters of loss and gain.
(359) At that time, the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa was staying in the Kṛṣṇa Cave in the kingdom of Kośala.
There was a hunter named Liànjiā who, not far from the Venerable One, had set a deer trap.
At that time, the Venerable One, out of compassion for the hunter, preached the Dharma to him, but he did not understand it.
The Venerable Kāśyapa emitted light from the tips of his fingers; although the hunter saw it, he felt no revulsion toward such an evil deed, but thought only to himself:
"Has the deer entered the snare?"
"Is it because he has not entered the snare?
At that time, the deity of the Śiṃśapā Cave spoke in verse:
"The hunter dwells in the deep mountains; Of little wisdom, blind and without eyes."
What you have spoken at this improper time is merely a loss to your own words.
Even if all ten of your fingers were to emit light simultaneously,
you could never cause him to perceive the Four Noble Truths.
Because they utterly lack wisdom, they commit various unrighteous acts;
they take no pleasure [in the Dharma] and indulge in sleep; they feel aversion toward and abandon the perverted notion of purity;
they dwell securely in *śīla* (virtue) and practice the recitation of the *Puṣpakāśyapa*.
360. At that time, the Vajjiputta was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala and stayed in a certain forest.
At that time, all the people of that country were holding a great Kummāsapāka festival for seven days and seven nights.
At that time, having witnessed these things, the son of the Vṛjis felt his mind somewhat falter and withdrew; he then spoke this verse:
"Amidst the forest trees, I am like that discarded log;
I am now like a discarded log, dwelling alone in the empty woods."
"Today the full moon has arrived; who suffers more grievously than I?
At that time, a deva, knowing his thoughts, spoke this verse in response:
"Now you dwell in the empty forest; why do you resemble a discarded log?"
"As those in hell envy the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, so too do the gods long for you.
(361) At that time, there was a bhikṣu in Kośala who dwelt in a certain forest; he practiced the observance of the precepts with complete fulfillment, seeking no further excellence.
Then that deva spoke these verses:
"One should not [rely] on the observance of precepts, On extensive learning, or on meditative concentration,
Nor on dwelling in empty and quiet places, If one has not yet exhausted all outflows and fetters."
"One should not perform such deeds, for they diminish one's wisdom;
by distancing oneself from the ways of ordinary people, one attains the bliss of Bodhi.

(362) At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the kingdom of Kośala named Nāgadatta who resided in that forest. He delighted in the ways of householders; he would enter the village at dawn and return only at dusk.
At that time, a deva thought to himself:
"This young bhikṣu frequents the bustle of the world, going out in the morning and returning in the evening.
I shall now bring him to awakening."
He then spoke in verse:
"Why did you depart so early?
Why have you returned so late?"
Beholding his form and observing his appearance, he seems like one who dwells at home.
Constantly coming and going, his suffering and pleasure are the same as those of the worldly.
O Nāga, you should know this; you ought to reflect upon it yourself.
"Do not be greedily attached to the household life, for it harms pure conduct.
You must now be careful not to do so, lest you be dragged away by that which lacks self-mastery.
(363) At that time, there were also many bhikṣus dwelling in a forest in the kingdom of Kośala.

A great many bhikṣus were restless and could not remain still; they lacked a sense of shame and were frivolous and perverse; their mindfulness was unstable, their minds were agitated, and their faculties were scattered and distracted.
At that time, a deva thought to himself:
"The Dharma of a bhikṣu should not be such as this; it is most unwholesome.
I shall speak a verse of awakening for him."
Then he spoke in verse:
“The disciples of Gautama sustain themselves through right livelihood;
whether begging for food or when dwelling at rest, they constantly contemplate impermanence.”
Whether dwelling, sitting, or reclining there, one should likewise contemplate impermanence.
Having already become difficult to sustain oneself, with a perverse mind wandering and distracted—
just like worldly people who fall asleep after finishing their meal.
Having abandoned one's own home, one associates with and becomes attached to the houses of others.
Like one who is driven by others and forcibly compelled to become a śramaṇa,
lacking reality and faith, one does not even seek to go forth.
"You wear the saṃghāṭī robe as stiffly as an old ox yoked to a plow.
At that time, the bhikṣus replied to him,
"Do you now wish to mock us?"
The deva further replied with a verse:
"I do not consider caste, nor do I mention names;
I now pay homage to the Saṃgha, Who reproaches and censures those who commit transgressions."
"If one can abide in diligence, I now likewise prostrate at their feet.
(364) At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the kingdom of Kośala who dwelt in a forest grove and was a close friend of a certain householder.
At that time, the elder had a daughter-in-law who was young and beautiful. On one occasion, this bhikṣu spoke with her for a short while, and the people all slandered him, claiming it was improper.
At that time, having heard these words, the bhikṣu was distressed in his heart and intended to go into the forest to take his own life.
A deva thought to himself:
"That bhikṣu is truly without fault; if he were to harm himself in this forest, it would be most unreasonable."
"I shall cause him to attain awakening.
Thereupon, that deva immediately transformed himself into the form of the monk’s daughter-in-law and went to where the bhikṣu was.
Upon seeing her, the bhikṣu addressed the transformed woman with this verse:
"Like a marketplace at a crossroads, a place exceedingly vast and wide,
where there are only defiled words among a crowd of three or four people,
one draws near and incurs slander."
"Having understood this matter, you should depart with all haste; do not remain here.
Then the manifested deva spoke again in verse:
"One who has gone forth should endure Words of censure, disparagement, and slander."
Slanderous speech is unreal; one should not give rise to grief or distress.
Empty sounds do not adhere to oneself; they are merely false words.
Reflecting inwardly that there is no fault or transgression, one should not give rise to affliction or suffering.
Hearing slander, one fears; how then can one dwell in the deep forest?
Like that wild deer, who throughout its life does not establish [a fixed course], it is able to endure all sounds—whether good, evil, superior, middling, or inferior.
O person of discernment and noble character, who has accomplished and perfected right conduct, you do not become known as a "thief-like sage" (muni-caura) on account of the words of others.
Now examine yourself: since you are free from all faults, [you are truly a sage].
"The noble sages and the devas likewise know that you are without fault.
Having spoken this verse, the manifested deva immediately vanished from that place and was no longer seen.
At that time, the bhikṣu practiced with diligence day and night; his mind was never lax or weary, and having severed all afflictions, he attained the state of an arhat.
